stories.title: Women take the wheel in Western Canada’s derby scene
stories.summary: At thrilling clashes across rural Alberta and B.C., female drivers go full throttle
stories.author: Kyler Zeleny
stories.content:
Underexposed is a photojournalism series dedicated to shedding light on the unseen lives of Canadians in every province and territory. Learn more and share your thoughts with The Globe.

It’s derby day at Rocky Mountain House, Alta., and Andrée Bourque is about to climb into the car she’s been working on for months just to destroy it.

She grabs her pink Fox dirt-bike helmet, slides into the cab and shouts over the engine’s pitter-patter, “Time to learn how not to drive.”

The atmosphere of a derby is sensory overload: the smell of welding and burnt brakes, the sharp clang of metal colliding, the cheers after a crash and the dust settling on spectators’ cheeks.

At the derbies in rural Western Canada, rounds of carnage are often accompanied by mud bogs, lawn mower races or sausage-eating contests.

Amid the chaos, the event becomes a carnival of car culture and rural pride.

To the uninitiated, the derby can appear as an unnecessary risk and ritualistic destruction – seen as something traditionally masculine and feeding into stereotypes about rural culture.

Cars enter the ring as aggressive machines revamped for controlled crashes only to leave as twisted tin cadavers.

But up close, derby demands mechanical knowledge, strategy, nerve and more money than the spectacle suggests.

North of Edmonton, Valere Leifso and her derby partner work on her truck in a garage devoted to derby builds. “It is gambling, but more expensive,” Ms. Leifso says.

Women are entering male-dominated derby culture in increasingly consequential numbers.

They are competing not only in female-only “powder-puff” races, but also in the main heats – the rounds of competition that make up a derby.

For her first derby, Brooke Evans climbs into a mustard-themed car in Slave Lake, Alta.

She’s nervous, questioning whether a lap belt is really enough, even though it meets the safety requirement. But once the heat starts, the nerves give way to the thrill of the ring.

Record rainfall had left the track muddier than usual, and her run ends when the car got hung up in the muck along the edge and stalled.

But back in the pits, she climbs out with a thousand-watt smile on her face: “I felt like no one could touch me, I was on top of the world.” Ms. Evans is sold.

Tayla Law spent years helping her uncles work on their cars before competing in a car of her own in 2024. On derby day at Rocky Mountain House, she looks almost swallowed by the iron around her.

From the driver’s seat, she can see kids pointing and parents drawing younger girls toward the fence. “Afterwards I’ve had people message me, ‘Hey, my daughter was so excited to see you compete, now she wants to do it.’”

Ms. Bourque enjoys challenging the assumption that derby is for “the boys.”

She built a long-bodied 1984 Cadillac from scratch for this year’s derby.

“It’s pretty cool to be able to say I did the majority of the work,” she says. “And over the years it seems more girls are doing it too.”

At the annual derby in Thorhild, Alta., sisters Hannah and Charlotte Cressman say they discovered derby through their dad. “He has been derbying as long as we can remember,” Charlotte says.

After finishing second in the final heat, Charlotte Cressman runs across the arena to embrace her boyfriend, with her father behind her, at the demolition derby in Thorhild, Alta.

Summers and family vacations revolved around derbies, and when the sisters wanted to drive, their dad returned to the ring. “It is our little bonding time,” Charlotte says.

Men sometimes smirk when they hear she drives or assume her dad does all the work, while women tend to respond with support, she says.

Ms. Leifso echoes the sentiment. Since discovering derby through her partner in 2021, she estimates she has run 40 heats and absorbed or dished out roughly 500 crashes. At registration, people still assume she is there because of a man.

“I want to win more because I’m a female. I’m in there to prove a point every time.”

Like Ms. Leifso, Chelsea Cote came to derby through her now-husband, an experienced builder and driver

Ms. Cote won the first heat she entered in 2018 and has barely slowed since. “Part of the fun is the danger and the adrenaline rush,” she says.

Drivers can absorb double-digit collisions in minutes, resulting in broken bones, slipped discs, punctured lungs and worse.

Chelsea Cote checks a cut on her husband Derek’s back after his heat at the Westlock demolition derby in Alberta. Earlier that day, she had placed first and third at two separate derbies.

A few years ago, just a week before her wedding, Ms. Cote “ate her steering wheel” during a derby and made them stop the heat, worried she might walk down the aisle without her front teeth.

Although she suffered no permanent damage, the hit was a reminder that derby, although a thrill, does come with consequences.

“I have nerves until I get hit or make a hit,” says Ms. Cote. “As soon as that first hit is out of the way, then I’m hyper-focused. I think so clearly.”

That first collision does more than settle the nerves. In a sport still defined by its masculinity, more women are proving they belong in the ring, one hit at a time.

Ms. Cote, driving car No. 701, absorbs a hit at the Glendon demolition derby in Alberta.

Kyler Zeleny PhD, is a Canadian photographer, educator and author of several books. His work has been exhibited internationally in twelve countries and featured in numerous publications, including The Globe and Mail, the Guardian, the Washington Post, Maclean’s, VICE, Canadian Geographic and the Independent. You can find him somewhere on the prairies.

Editing by Ayesha Habib

Digital presentation by Sarah Palmer

stories.title: Knights’ win streak ends in 6-4 loss to Sting
stories.summary: Sarnia outshot London 31-20 and snapped a four-game losing streak to improve to 6-6-1-0 on the season.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The Sarnia Sting rallied from a two-goal deficit to defeat the London Knights 6-4 in Ontario Hockey League action.

Logan Hawery scored twice in the third period, including the game-winning goal on the power play.

Easton Walos recorded four assists, while Alessandro Di Iorio contributed a goal and an assist. Jack Van Volsen, Jonas Gulbrandsen and Simon Katolicky also scored for the Sting.

Sarnia outshot London 31-20 and snapped a four-game losing streak to improve to 6-6-1-0 on the season.

Ryan Brown scored twice and added an assist for the Knights. Marcus Nordmark had a goal and an assist, while Cody Wood scored his first OHL goal.

London goaltender Aleksei Medvedev made 25 saves in the loss as the Knights saw their three-game winning streak come to an end.

Sarnia makes the trip to London on Friday for a rematch at Canada Life Place. Game time is 7 p.m.

stories.title: ‘Destination because of the turf’: Changing baseball landscape in Dorchester, Ont.
stories.summary: A pair of former Major League Baseball players are changing the landscape of baseball in Dorchester, Ont.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A pair of former Major League Baseball players are changing the landscape of baseball in Dorchester, Ont.

Adam Stern and Chris Robinson, who own the Great Lake Canadians (GLC) premier development program are adding a second turf baseball field at the Thames Centre Recreation Complex.

“We’re converting a current baseball field by adding turf in the infield and just adding to what we did at Royal Field to give the ability to play more games,” said Stern who is spearheading the project.

Royal Field is the only all-turf baseball facility in Ontario, aside from Rogers Centre, and the neighbouring diamond is getting a facelift.

This time to save cost, they are only putting artificial surface in the infield because the cause of most rainouts is caused by the flooding of the mound and batter’s box.

“You get a good rainstorm, and the infield is done for the day, maybe two days, depending on how much rain we get,” said Robinson.

“We’ve had several times up on Royal (Field) where we come off the field and you wait till it stops raining and you go right back on and play. On normal days you’d be done on the for the full day on the natural service. So, it’s a huge game changer.”

Stern and his GLC program can get on the turf field as early as February some years and practice into November, whereas grass would not begin until May and end by October at the latest.

“The big thing for us is being able to hold provincial and national type events,” said Stern.

“Having one main field with Royal being turf, adding this one plus the other ones we have around the area, this is huge to accommodate these types of tournaments.”

Stern and his program worked with Thames Centre to build Royal Field with help from the Jays Care Foundation providing some of the turf along with a combination of municipal capital projects and private sponsorships.

This time they are fully funding the project with permission from Thames Centre to renovate the diamond.

“The thousands of kids we put through Thames Centre alone every year for tournaments. This is a destination spot and it’s a destination because of the turf,” said Stern.

He’s seen colleges, universities and even high schools across the United States convert to turf infields. In Alberta, they are pouring money into big complexes, and municipalities are seeing the economic impact.

“It’s the quality of games you can play on here that you’re not worried about 6:00 in the morning, weather, rainstorms coming in,” said Stern.

“Do you have to cancel? Do you lose tournaments? You saw it this year in St. Thomas with them having to cancel their major tournament.”

Stern is thankful that Thames Centre believes in youth sports and has given them free reign to convert the diamond to turf, while adding new dugouts and bleachers. This is privately funded through business, alumni and sponsor donations.

“The more support we have, the better we can make the facility and that’s the reality,” said Robinson, who said they are still looking for funding help.

Robinson also joked that Stern is the driver of the project and when he says they are doing something, he won’t stop until his vision is complete. He understands what needs to be done to make each player’s experience a memorable one.

“You get an energy level when you come out and play on a turf field,” said Stern.

“There’s a different level of it and it’s something that I think should be explored more across the province.”

Adam Stern and Chris Robinson, who own the Great Lake Canadians (GLC) premier development program are adding a second turf baseball field at the Thames Centre Recreation Complex.

“We’re converting a current baseball field by adding turf in the infield and just adding to what we did at Royal Field to give the ability to play more games,” said Stern who is spearheading the project.
Royal Field is the only all-turf baseball facility in Ontario, aside from Rogers Centre, and the neighbouring diamond is getting a facelift.
This time to save cost, they are only putting artificial surface in the infield because the cause of most rainouts is caused by the flooding of the mound and batter’s box.
“You get a good rainstorm, and the infield is done for the day, maybe two days, depending on how much rain we get,” said Robinson.

“We’ve had several times up on Royal (Field) where we come off the field and you wait till it stops raining and you go right back on and play. On normal days you’d be done on the for the full day on the natural service. So, it’s a huge game changer.”
Stern and his GLC program can get on the turf field as early as February some years and practice into November, whereas grass would not begin until May and end by October at the latest.
“The big thing for us is being able to hold provincial and national type events,” said Stern.
“Having one main field with Royal being turf, adding this one plus the other ones we have around the area, this is huge to accommodate these types of tournaments.”

Stern and his program worked with Thames Centre to build Royal Field with help from the Jays Care Foundation providing some of the turf along with a combination of municipal capital projects and private sponsorships.
This time they are fully funding the project with permission from Thames Centre to renovate the diamond.
“The thousands of kids we put through Thames Centre alone every year for tournaments. This is a destination spot and it’s a destination because of the turf,” said Stern.

He’s seen colleges, universities and even high schools across the United States convert to turf infields. In Alberta, they are pouring money into big complexes, and municipalities are seeing the economic impact.
“It’s the quality of games you can play on here that you’re not worried about 6:00 in the morning, weather, rainstorms coming in,” said Stern.
“Do you have to cancel? Do you lose tournaments? You saw it this year in St. Thomas with them having to cancel their major tournament.”

Construction is well underway with the turf to grass transition areas being put in this week. Contractors tell CTV News if the weather cooperates, this field could be complete by the end of November.
“Hopefully others follow suit and see how they can do it,” said Robinson.
“If we can do it in Dorchester, they should be able to do it in some of the bigger centres.”

stories.title: Trump tariffs on steel, aluminum a 'disaster' for the U.S., think tank report says
stories.summary: Donald Trump's tariffs on steel and aluminum have been a "disaster" for the U.S. economy, a new think report has found.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on steel and aluminum have been a “disaster” for the U.S. economy because they’ve fuelled inflation and failed to spur the promised growth in those industries, a new think report has found.

The Montreal Economic Institute report, to be released Thursday, found that steel and aluminum prices in the U.S. market have soared since Trump slapped tariffs on those two critical industrial sectors, while failing to create new jobs.

Not only have the tariffs led to sharply higher steel and aluminum prices, but the two sectors are key inputs in a wide variety of other products, the report found, that have also become more expensive. It’s left consumers and industrial buyers facing higher price tags on autos, aircraft, construction, machinery, and a wide range of other products.

“The United States has imposed on itself a historically large price shock with little protected sector employment or output growth to show for it,” concluded the report, titled Tariffs Deliver a Price Shock, Not an Industrial Revival.

The study, which is in line with economists’ broader analysis of tariffs, found that steel prices in the U.S. have jumped 33.9 per cent since February 2025, while aluminum prices have increased by 58 per cent. By comparison, prices in the Canadian market for those two metals have increased by only one and 26 per cent respectively.

Trump imposed 25 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminum from a wide range of countries, including Canada, in March of last year. A few months later, those tariffs were increased to 50 per cent.

The policy’s desired benefits have been modest at best. During that 19-month period, U.S. steel production has gained 7.6 per cent, with a 0.7 per cent increase in employment. Aluminum production, meanwhile, fell 0.1 per cent, while the number of jobs in that sector increased by just 0.6 per cent.

“Trump’s tariff policy has not helped revitalize the industry as promised,” said Joseph Steinberg, an economics professor at the University of Toronto and the primary author of the study. “I don’t think a single economist will say tariffs on metal is a good idea.”

And consumers and those industries that buy steel and aluminum for their own products have paid the price, according to Steinberg’s study. Without any changes to the inputs, the new steel tariffs alone would mean cost jumps of 6.5 per cent and 13 per cent, for example, in the auto and fabricated metals sectors.

Jamie Tronnes, executive director of the U.S.-based office of the Canadian think tank the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said she’s not surprised by the report’s conclusion and added that the tariff-fuelled price hikes on steel, aluminum and other inputs are also affecting investment decisions in the U.S. In some cases, she said, producers have decided to buy from China and elsewhere, instead of building or expanding their own operation in the U.S. because of the increased costs of construction.

“It makes investors want to stay away.”

Steinberg said the only winners from Trump’s tariff policies have been the U.S. government, which has raked in billions at the country’s international borders, and incumbent U.S. producers in the steel and aluminum industries. “They’re making a lot of money.”

While steel tariffs make little economic sense, he said, the aluminum tariffs make even less.

The Iran war and subsequent shipping problems in the Strait of Hormuz have also contributed to dwindling supplies and rising prices in the aluminum market. Emirates Global Aluminum leans on its country’s abundance of natural gas to power its smelters to produce almost as much aluminum as Canada. But like many other exports from that region, the United Arab Emirates company has had a difficult time in recent months getting its product to markets such as North America.

Trump’s tariffs remain a contentious subject and a key source of friction in U.S. relations with Canada and many other countries. While some previous tranches of his tariffs have already been ruled illegal by American courts, a new lawsuit challenging the 50 per cent tariffs against Canada was launched this week by New Jersey food importer Gellert Global Group. The company imports Canadian cheese, which is on the list of products, along with furniture, clothing, cement, hockey sticks and other dairy products, that were hit by new tariffs in August.

Trump then escalated the conflict last month by announcing an outright ban on nearly $1-billion worth of Canadian exports, including booze, motorcycles and more dairy products.

In each case, Trump used section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, never previously used in a trade dispute or tested in court, to impose the tariffs.

Canada and the U.S. appeared to be close to a new trade deal in late August, but talks fell apart after days of intense negotiating. Negotiators from the two countries remain in contact but there have been no reports of a deal being close.

The U.S. tariffs remain a major sticking point in the talks, while rising consumer prices have been a major issue as Americans are poised to vote in mid-term elections in early November.

Despite the challenges, Canada seems willing to stick by its steel and auto sectors. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced Wednesday a new $9-billion fund, with more than $5-billion of it going to support steel mills in Ontario that have been affected by the Trump tariffs.

stories.title: Sunshine continues as dry stretch holds through weekend
stories.summary: A stretch of sunny skies and dry weather is expected to continue across southern Ontario through the weekend, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A stretch of sunny skies and dry weather is expected to continue across southern Ontario through the weekend, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Thursday will bring a high of 17 C, with northerly winds creating a fresh breeze.

Sunshine is expected Friday and Saturday, with mainly sunny skies Sunday and highs around 18 C.

Temperatures will dip to 16 C Monday before cooler conditions arrive Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing more cloud cover and a slight chance of showers.

Atchison says the dry weather will hold through the weekend before the weather pattern changes next week.

Sunshine is expected Friday and Saturday, with mainly sunny skies Sunday and highs around 18 C.
Temperatures will dip to 16 C Monday before cooler conditions arrive Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing more cloud cover and a slight chance of showers.
Atchison says the dry weather will hold through the weekend before the weather pattern changes next week.

stories.title: Luxury hotel firm faces flak in an Ontario town’s debate over tourism and growth
stories.summary: Kat Florence’s purchases in Elora, Ont., helped put picturesque village on the map – but not without controversy
stories.author: Greg Mercer, Photography by Sammy Kogan
stories.content:
On a warm October evening last year, a few hundred residents of a small Ontario village crowded into the community hall at the local hockey rink. As their mayor strode around the room like a talk-show host, they listed off a litany of complaints about garbage, rising rents, traffic and parking.

Shawn Watters, the landscape architect turned mayor of Centre Wellington Township, had organized the town-hall-style meeting to address concerns about a spike in tourism that some say has overwhelmed the town. The list of grievances was long.

But when a resident named Trevor Wedgewood brought up what he called “the elephant in the room,” a company called Kat Florence, the mayor cut him off. The same thing had happened when a woman tried to raise the issue earlier.

“We’re not going there,” Mr. Watters said, according to a recording of the meeting obtained by The Globe and Mail.

In Elora, a village of about 8,000 around 25 kilometres north of Guelph, the name Kat Florence seems to divide the community almost as deeply as the gorge that runs through it. The luxury hotel company, which has origins in Thailand’s gem trade, has bought up historic properties and become one of the village’s largest landlords in just six years.

Mr. Wedgewood says the mayor’s unwillingness to allow public discussion about the company is proof of the influence Kat Florence has in Elora. The mayor says he was only worried about the risk of a potential lawsuit.

Some who were at the meeting that night told The Globe that Kat Florence has come to wield too much power over the municipality. They allege its promise of donations to the township has given it too much sway within local government, providing a rubber stamp to buy public property and fast-track the zoning and permitting process – something both the company and township flatly deny.

Kat Florence has also been pushing back against its loudest critics in Elora, suing three people for defamation and serving at least a dozen residents with cease-and-desist letters. In May, the company’s lawyer named eight people in a libel notice for comments they posted in a Facebook community forum.

The company’s supporters say legal action was the only way to put a stop to defamatory attacks that have unfairly vilified the couple behind Kat Florence, Kristy Hillis (who sometimes goes by Kristy Florence) and Don Kogen.

“It’s been hard to watch the public narrative surrounding Kristy and Don become really, honestly, very disconnected from the people that I know. They’re good people,” said Teal Parkinson, co-owner of the Ayrshire Hotel, which opened after a private loan from Ms. Hillis and Mr. Kogen.

The couple, in a statement from their lawyer Kim Ferreira, say they’re only trying to preserve and revitalize Elora’s historic downtown “as part of a long-term commitment to the community and its downtown.” Their businesses are focused on creating employment, attracting visitors and contributing to the “community’s economic vitality,” they said.

Since buying its first property here in 2020, Kat Florence has contributed to an economic boom in a former mill town that has reinvented itself into a high-end tourist destination.

But it has also helped fuel concerns over rising real estate values and sparked a debate about who gets to decide how a community grows and changes.

Before it even arrived on the scene, that question was already causing stress in Elora, part of a sprawling rural township mandated by the province to nearly double in size to 60,000 people within 25 years. The tourism issue may be the single biggest topic in the municipal election here on Oct. 26.

For a lot of Canadian tourist towns, the tension over an influx of money and newcomers flooding in since the pandemic is still playing out.

In picturesque Elora, where annual visitors have grown from less than 500,000 to more than 750,000 in the span of a few years, this friction is particularly pronounced.

Elora’s main pedestrian bridge spans the Grand River, which the first settlers used to power timber industries. Visitors can learn about that era from the heritage buildings and archival photos around town.

As Elora’s population and tourist trade grow, some are worried the changes are not sustainable or beneficial to everyone. ‘They’re turning this town into a playground for the nouveau riche,’ local photographer Sophie Hogan says.

Founded by Scottish pioneers in 1832, Elora sprang up around a limestone gorge that cuts deep into the rock of Wellington County.

The settlement relied on the power of the Grand River to run mills that cut lumber from surrounding forests and ground grain from local fields. Blacksmiths, furniture makers, distillers and wagon-wrights followed, and the market town they built remains a charming example of 19th-century Ontario stone architecture.

Elora has long been known to visitors for its river tubing, small-town charm and weddings at the historic Elora Mill. The mill’s owner, Pearle Hospitality, has also invested heavily in the village in recent years, and its condos, hotel, restaurants and other developments have brought a fair share of tourism traffic to the small town.

By the summer of 2020, Kat Florence bought its first property in the village, an 1851 row house in downtown for $2.2-million. Three months later, the company bought an anchor commercial property on Elora’s main intersection for $1.1-million.

At first, people hardly noticed these new owners. It wasn’t until the following July, when the company bought the former Commercial Hotel, a three-storey building originally built in 1848, that residents began to talk about the ambitious restoration plans that would create the posh Kat Florence Hotel. A few months before that hotel opened, the company bought a 19th-century flatiron building that was once the Dalby Hotel, which they later resold.

Mr. Kogen drew attention to these ambitious plans when he announced to the Wellington Advertiser newspaper in 2022 that he and his wife had a “$30-million plan for downtown Elora.” Kat Florence eventually bought at least 19 properties worth $32-million, according to publicly available records.

The company now owns nearly a quarter of all commercial real estate in the four blocks that make up the heart of Elora’s small downtown, including a former municipal laneway turned into an outdoor market, according to an analysis by The Globe.

At Kat Florence’s hotel and private suites, well-heeled guests are pampered with personal chefs, French champagne, massages and access to a chauffeur who tours them around town in Bentleys and Rolls-Royce limos – all included as part of packages that start at $1,300 a night and reach upward to $5,000.

Critics of Kat Florence say it has taken a much more aggressive approach than other tourism operators to doing business here – in its marketing of the village, real-estate acquisitions and legal responses to criticism.

In a 2025 essay in Toronto Life magazine, Ms. Hillis talked about the skepticism she and her husband encountered when they revealed plans to renovate the landmark Commercial Hotel and adjacent movie theatre in Elora. “Backlash soon followed, with accusations that Don and I were ‘buying up the town’ – this despite half the building sitting vacant and the cinema nearing closure. It took time, but eventually, people began to see that I wasn’t trying to erase history but instead to preserve and celebrate it,” she wrote.

The village’s reinvention into a luxury destination owes a lot to Kat Florence’s ability to build an upscale brand around the idea of exclusivity – a skill the company’s founders polished over their years in the global gem trade. Mr. Kogen, a Texas-born, self-styled gemstone trader who starred in the reality TV show Game of Stones as “America’s most extreme gem hunter,” was once called Thailand’s leading Internet impresario by Forbes for his ability to sell precious stones online. Ms. Hillis, a former teacher who grew up on a dairy farm not far from Elora, is the face of both the Kat Florence jewellery and hotel brands.

Both declined interview requests for this story.

Mr. Kogen has told interviewers he was a high-school dropout living in Southeast Asia when he taught himself how to trim and polish rough-cut sapphires.

As a teen, he learned to speak Thai and how to haggle with sellers and buyers, eventually starting a mail-order business. In 1998, he sold his first gemstone over the Internet, according to an interview he gave to Forbes in 2002.

He became skilled in the world of gem trading, a field that attracts big personalities and rewards those who can take raw and unpolished stones and bring out their inner beauty.

In interviews for Game of Stones , originally broadcast on the Discovery Channel in 2014, Mr. Kogen said he was “a driven individual” with a competitive personality that has helped him succeed in the wild fringes of the gem-hunting world. The series features Mr. Kogen and his team racing to remote corners of the world to buy rare stones.

In one scene, Mr. Kogen says his obsession with gems came from his difficult childhood and going through his teenage years without parents. He lost his mother when he was a child and has told colleagues he was living on his own by age 13.

“Sometimes you had to question your purpose in life. You wish, you cry, you hope someone would listen,” he said. “So the gems were my saviour. They kept me from losing my mind.”

Ms. Hillis grew up in Belwood, Ont., and left home at 19 to be a teacher overseas. She met Mr. Kogen at a casting call for Game of Stones in Thailand and appears on the show as his assistant.

Mr. Kogen and Ms. Hillis said in the statement from their lawyer that the Kat Florence group of companies employs more than 100 people and is “committed to revitalizing Elora’s historic downtown while preserving the character and architectural heritage of Elora’s historic buildings.”

Ms. Hillis, through her lawyer, told The Globe that she initially came back to Ontario for personal reasons in 2018, but travel restrictions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic caused the couple to think about moving back permanently. They resettled in Elora in 2024 with their two daughters.

“During this period, Ms. Florence Hillis began taking a closer look at Elora and the increased investment and redevelopment occurring in Elora, including outside of its historic downtown. She saw an opportunity to invest in the downtown community and to contribute to the preservation and revitalization of its historic commercial core,” the company said in the statement provided by Mr. Ferreira.

Elora, a progressive-minded, artsy town, has long been a haven for creative types and retired professionals, the kind of place where newcomers could go to find refuge and a gentler, quieter pace of life. But as more and more buildings fell under Kat Florence’s control, the town began to change in ways that rubbed some people the wrong way.

People complained to the mayor and vented in online Facebook groups and letters to the editor.

“They’re turning this town into a playground for the nouveau riche, without any consideration of the impact on local residents,” said Sophie Hogan, a local photographer who recently received a warning from Kat Florence’s lawyers.

In January, 2025, she wrote a letter to the editor of the Wellington Advertiser, complaining there was “a conflict brewing” in Elora between residents and tourists drawn by Kat Florence.

This summer, her opposition to changes in the town drew the attention of Mr. Ferreira, who warned her not to protest the opening of a new restaurant partly registered to the couple, which was replacing another bar whose lease was recently ended. Ms. Hogan, now running to be a municipal councillor, insists she had made no such plans and the letter didn’t articulate what she did to trigger the legal threat.

In December, 2024, Kat Florence organized a holiday marketing campaign that it said would draw nearly 400 social media influencers to Elora.

The company said it spent $312,000 on Christmas lights, $32,000 on hotel rooms and another $70,000 in “Santa cash,” a promotional currency, according to an e-mail Mr. Kogen sent to downtown merchants.

A focal point was a new pedestrian marketplace on Francis Lane, a property bought from the municipality after a closed-door township council discussion earlier that year.

“Elora at Christmas just hits different,” gushed a post from Caroline Serpe, a Toronto-based Instagrammer. “Our favourite small-town escape outside of Toronto, full of Hallmark-worthy streets, twinkling lights, and the coziest holiday market.”

The campaign attracted thousands of visitors, according to local news reports, but residents complained the town was overrun and unprepared on the opening weekend of the company’s Christmas festival.

Garbage piled up, shops ran out of basic goods and traffic stretched for kilometres, prompting the mayor to call for more police and a shuttle service to ease congested streets.

In an e-mail sent to downtown Elora businesses on Dec. 16, 2024, Mr. Kogen complained the company had spent “millions” on the holiday campaign, and said some people didn’t seem to appreciate that Kat Florence had given the township a $400,000 line of credit to help build public washrooms.

The mayor said that while Kat Florence did provide about $100,000 for Christmas lights and beautification of the village’s green space, the rest of the money Mr. Kogen pledged publicly was never provided. The township later told The Globe it would need to file a Freedom of Information request to confirm how much money the company had given the municipality.

Kat Florence confirms they did not provide the money because, Mr. Ferreira said, plans were shelved after opposition from residents.

Mr. Watters said the company, which made the donation as part of a program to fund community upgrades without raising local taxes, has not received any special treatment.

He said he couldn’t comment on individual companies, but said the township has no control over who buys properties in town and everyone is subject to the same planning processes. Mr. Watters added that as someone who grew up in Markham, Ont., he’s seen a community go through explosive growth before and understands why people are protective of the things that make Elora special.

He also said the municipality is trying to strike a better balance between tourism and the costs associated with it. That includes the creation of a new hotel tax and economic development corporation intended to use tourism revenues to help address some of the challenges caused by visitors, he added.

“Being a popular destination can create pressures, and it is important that tourism is managed in a way that balances the economic benefits of tourism with the needs of residents and the character of the community,” Mr. Watters said in a statement.

Kat Florence’s owners acknowledged that increased visitors have brought some growing pains to Elora.

“Ms. Florence Hillis, Mr. Kogen, and Kat Florence recognize that tourism brings both opportunities and challenges. Their objective has always been to support local businesses and encourage economic activity while working with the Town and the broader community to address the challenges associated with increased visitor activity,” said the statement from their lawyer.

The Christmas market was created to boost tourism for merchants at a time of year when visitors typically drop off, they said. They added that after the Christmas market, the company worked with the municipality to help fund a visitor shuttle and additional garbage removal services.

This spring, Kat Florence evicted a well-known steakhouse owner, Geoffrey Wild, who acknowledged failing to pay employees and hydro bills. Mr. Wild alleged the company owed him mortgage payments for another building he’d sold them, and complained his rent had been increased significantly.

In May, the company did not renew the lease for a separate popular cocktail lounge, the Lobby Bar, and announced plans for a new tapas bar to take its place, prompting calls for boycotts from some residents.

In a case heard in Ontario’s Superior Court, Kat Florence alleged another tenant, an ice-cream shop owner, allowed a squirrel inside their building and refused to open the business year-round. A judge dismissed Kat Florence’s claim to terminate the lease, calling it an “increasingly transparent effort to evict the ice-cream shop for financial gain.” The company’s lawyer said they declined to comment on “individual tenant matters.”

More criticism came after Kat Florence bought the town’s only cinema, which was adjacent to their luxury hotel, and closed it down, citing water damage. The company says it still intends to reopen the movie theatre.

Mike von Massow, a University of Guelph professor who has lived in Elora for 30 years, said the village had tourism long before Kat Florence arrived on the scene. But he said it’s reached a tipping point where residents are avoiding going downtown on most days because of the crowds.

“Tourism has been part of Elora for a long time, but I think what’s happened is we’ve just sort of got tourism on steroids now, and we’re getting to the point where it’s affecting the livability of the community,” he said. “We’ve got this disruption to the village with not very proven economic benefits, and I think that’s where people are getting concerned.”

Kat Florence’s supporters, however, say the company has accelerated an economic boom and restored many underused, and sometimes derelict, properties in the village. They point out there are no more vacant shops in the downtown. Realtors say property values have risen in lockstep with Kat Florence’s investments in the community.

“I can tell you that Kristy’s commitment to Elora, and particularly to preserving and restoring pieces of its history, is absolutely genuine,” said Ms. Parkinson, co-owner of the Ayrshire Hotel.

Ms. Parkinson said some residents don’t see the level of investment Kat Florence has made. She acknowledged the influx of tourists has caused some headaches, but said there’s an upside to having so many visitors.

“Are there hiccups? Of course there are,” she said. “We manage to sustain restaurants and shops and art galleries, events and experiences that I think would be incredibly difficult to support exclusively, you know, through the resident population. So tourism helps us stay alive.”

Lisa MacDonald, a township councillor, said she’s disappointed the opposition to Kat Florence has become what she described as “hateful.” She argues the township is taking steps to get more revenue from tourist traffic, which will allow the village to fund things such as public washrooms.

She defended the mayor’s decision to prevent people from discussing the company at the town hall-style meeting last October, saying it was never supposed to be a venue to complain about specific developers.

On an August day in Elora, visitors queue for ice cream near the now-closed Elora Cinema. Kat Florence says it plans to reopen the theatre, which is next door to its hotel.

The launch of Kat Florence as a global jewellery brand a few years earlier had its own challenges.

There was a short-lived boutique in London, England, which opened in October, 2016, and closed after only a few months. Kat Florence had flown in dozens of customers to celebrate the opening. Mr. Ferreira said his clients “were given the option to leave the location” after the building was sold. That same year, the company reported losses of US$2.9-million in an annual report filed in Cyprus, where Kat Florence Designs was initially based.

Another promotional event at a Berlin hotel that year had to be cancelled because of a court injunction filed by a German company, sparked by a dispute with Kat Florence over its customer list. As part of that conflict, jewellery retailer Elumeo filed a motion to seize the company’s trademark in the European Union.

Kat Florence eventually filed a lawsuit in the United States, in which the company alleged Elumeo had made “slanderous accusations” against Ms. Hillis and Mr. Kogen. In a counterclaim, Elumeo alleged Mr. Kogen had transferred tens of thousands of rare gems stored in a jointly owned Thailand facility to a shell company he controlled in Hong Kong. The German company alleged it was never paid for those gems, which it says later resurfaced for sale in Georgia.

Mr. Ferreira said these “allegations are completely false and were not proven.” The judge ultimately dismissed both Mr. Kogen’s lawsuit and Elumeo’s counterclaim, citing a lack of jurisdiction.

In 2018, an endorsement deal with Sex and the City actress Sarah Jessica Parker dissolved into another legal fight that was eventually settled out of court. Kat Florence sued the actress, claiming she failed to fulfill her promotional duties. In a counterclaim, Ms. Parker alleged Kat Florence had signed a contract for US$7.5-million to use her image to promote its gemstones, but had paid her less than US$1.4-million.

In a legal filing in a New York court, Ms. Parker’s lawyer said that when Kat Florence learned the actress planned to sue, the jewellery company “rushed to the courthouse and filed the present action in the hope of presenting itself, falsely, as the aggrieved party.”

Ms. Parker’s lawyer also claimed during the dispute that Kat Florence Designs moved its assets and operations to a similar-sounding company, Kat Florence Atelier, to protect it from any court judgment. The company denies this.

“The allegations are not true and were not proven,” Mr. Ferreira said in a further statement. “Kat Florence and Sarah Jessica Parker had differences of opinion regarding their business relationship.”

Whether they’re enjoying ice cream at the Elora Mews or scenery along the Grand River, visitors to downtown Elora are seldom far from a Kat Florence-owned property. The company owns nearly a quarter of all available real estate in the four downtown blocks.

By early 2025, Mr. Kogen began pushing back publicly against Kat Florence’s critics in Elora. He told the Wellington Advertiser that he’d been accused online “of bribery, smuggling, money laundering, prostitution and worse.”

He announced he was pausing what he said was nearly $3-million that Kat Florence had planned to give the municipality for the public washroom project, green space upgrades, Christmas lighting and a raceway shuttle.

A few weeks after announcing the funding pause, Mr. Kogen told the online news site Elora Fergus Today that he was pledging $500,000 to help business owners “take on online bullies” by identifying anonymous commenters and pursuing legal action.

His lawyer, Mr. Ferreira, told The Globe “the $500,000 was not used for an online-bullying initiative.” Instead, he said that money was earmarked for the construction of much-needed public washrooms. Kat Florence signed a contract with the municipality to pay for the project, but those plans were ultimately shelved by the company “as opposition to the proposal emerged among some residents,” he said.

In June, 2026, Mr. Ferreira started legal action against online commenters on behalf of his clients.

Kat Florence filed lawsuits against three people: Paloma Von Fielitz, administrator of a local Facebook group; Ben Williams, who was a member of two online forums; and Mr. Wedgewood, who spoke up at the town meeting in October. The company is seeking combined damages of $425,000, plus costs, and an injunction that would prevent all three from commenting publicly about Kat Florence.

The libel claims say the company is painted as “cutthroat” and the online comments are aimed at “discrediting their reputations and holding them up to public scandal, ridicule and contempt,” with a “reckless disregard of the truth.” Mr. Ferreira says his clients are only trying to protect their reputation and their businesses.

“They have exercised what they believe to be their legal rights in response to statements they believe to be defamatory. They do not agree that their actions are intended to silence public speech or legitimate criticism,” he said in an e-mail.

In their statements of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Mr. Kogen and Ms. Hillis complain that online commenters have accused them of predatory business practices and portrayed their company as a “villain” acting “without regard for the rights or interests of others in the community.”

Paul Dollak, the lawyer for Ms. Von Fielitz and Mr. Williams, argued the lawsuits appear to be an attempt to frighten and silence Kat Florence’s critics. He said he intends to defend his clients using anti-SLAPP motions, designed to counter “strategic lawsuits against public participation.”

“My clients made comments, in good faith, because they believed them to be in the public interest,” Mr. Dollak told The Globe.

In the claim against him, Mr. Wedgewood is accused of alleging Kat Florence is involved in “criminal conduct” and forming a “corrupt syndicate” that has “improperly influenced the mayor and municipal decision-making processes in Elora.” Mr. Wedgewood, who said he’s on the brink of homelessness, said he believes he was asking fair questions about what’s happening in his town.

Ms. Hogan, meanwhile, complains the company’s actions and aggressive marketing of the village’s charms have taken pre-existing tension over the tourism issue and put it in a pressure cooker. Elora, she worries, may never be the same.

“They’ve built an invisible dividing line through the town. There’s division here that was never there before,” Ms. Hogan said.

“During this period, Ms. Florence Hillis began taking a closer look at Elora and the increased investment and redevelopment occurring in Elora, including outside of its historic downtown. She saw an opportunity to invest in the downtown community and to contribute to the preservation and revitalization of its historic commercial core,” the company said in the statement provided by Mr. Ferreira.

Elora, a progressive-minded, artsy town, has long been a haven for creative types and retired professionals, the kind of place where newcomers could go to find refuge and a gentler, quieter pace of life. But as more and more buildings fell under Kat Florence’s control, the town began to change in ways that rubbed some people the wrong way.
People complained to the mayor and vented in online Facebook groups and letters to the editor.

“They’re turning this town into a playground for the nouveau riche, without any consideration of the impact on local residents,” said Sophie Hogan, a local photographer who recently received a warning from Kat Florence’s lawyers.
In January, 2025, she wrote a letter to the editor of the Wellington Advertiser, complaining there was “a conflict brewing” in Elora between residents and tourists drawn by Kat Florence.

This summer, her opposition to changes in the town drew the attention of Mr. Ferreira, who warned her not to protest the opening of a new restaurant partly registered to the couple, which was replacing another bar whose lease was recently ended. Ms. Hogan, now running to be a municipal councillor, insists she had made no such plans and the letter didn’t articulate what she did to trigger the legal threat.
In December, 2024, Kat Florence organized a holiday marketing campaign that it said would draw nearly 400 social media influencers to Elora.

The company said it spent $312,000 on Christmas lights, $32,000 on hotel rooms and another $70,000 in “Santa cash,” a promotional currency, according to an e-mail Mr. Kogen sent to downtown merchants.
A focal point was a new pedestrian marketplace on Francis Lane, a property bought from the municipality after a closed-door township council discussion earlier that year.

“Elora at Christmas just hits different,” gushed a post from Caroline Serpe, a Toronto-based Instagrammer. “Our favourite small-town escape outside of Toronto, full of Hallmark-worthy streets, twinkling lights, and the coziest holiday market.”
The campaign attracted thousands of visitors, according to local news reports, but residents complained the town was overrun and unprepared on the opening weekend of the company’s Christmas festival.
Garbage piled up, shops ran out of basic goods and traffic stretched for kilometres, prompting the mayor to call for more police and a shuttle service to ease congested streets.

In an e-mail sent to downtown Elora businesses on Dec. 16, 2024, Mr. Kogen complained the company had spent “millions” on the holiday campaign, and said some people didn’t seem to appreciate that Kat Florence had given the township a $400,000 line of credit to help build public washrooms.

The mayor said that while Kat Florence did provide about $100,000 for Christmas lights and beautification of the village’s green space, the rest of the money Mr. Kogen pledged publicly was never provided. The township later told The Globe it would need to file a Freedom of Information request to confirm how much money the company had given the municipality.
Kat Florence confirms they did not provide the money because, Mr. Ferreira said, plans were shelved after opposition from residents.
Mr. Watters said the company, which made the donation as part of a program to fund community upgrades without raising local taxes, has not received any special treatment.

He said he couldn’t comment on individual companies, but said the township has no control over who buys properties in town and everyone is subject to the same planning processes. Mr. Watters added that as someone who grew up in Markham, Ont., he’s seen a community go through explosive growth before and understands why people are protective of the things that make Elora special.

He also said the municipality is trying to strike a better balance between tourism and the costs associated with it. That includes the creation of a new hotel tax and economic development corporation intended to use tourism revenues to help address some of the challenges caused by visitors, he added.

“Being a popular destination can create pressures, and it is important that tourism is managed in a way that balances the economic benefits of tourism with the needs of residents and the character of the community,” Mr. Watters said in a statement.
Kat Florence’s owners acknowledged that increased visitors have brought some growing pains to Elora.

“Ms. Florence Hillis, Mr. Kogen, and Kat Florence recognize that tourism brings both opportunities and challenges. Their objective has always been to support local businesses and encourage economic activity while working with the Town and the broader community to address the challenges associated with increased visitor activity,” said the statement from their lawyer.

The Christmas market was created to boost tourism for merchants at a time of year when visitors typically drop off, they said. They added that after the Christmas market, the company worked with the municipality to help fund a visitor shuttle and additional garbage removal services.

This spring, Kat Florence evicted a well-known steakhouse owner, Geoffrey Wild, who acknowledged failing to pay employees and hydro bills. Mr. Wild alleged the company owed him mortgage payments for another building he’d sold them, and complained his rent had been increased significantly.

In May, the company did not renew the lease for a separate popular cocktail lounge, the Lobby Bar, and announced plans for a new tapas bar to take its place, prompting calls for boycotts from some residents.

In a case heard in Ontario’s Superior Court, Kat Florence alleged another tenant, an ice-cream shop owner, allowed a squirrel inside their building and refused to open the business year-round. A judge dismissed Kat Florence’s claim to terminate the lease, calling it an “increasingly transparent effort to evict the ice-cream shop for financial gain.” The company’s lawyer said they declined to comment on “individual tenant matters.”

More criticism came after Kat Florence bought the town’s only cinema, which was adjacent to their luxury hotel, and closed it down, citing water damage. The company says it still intends to reopen the movie theatre.

Mike von Massow, a University of Guelph professor who has lived in Elora for 30 years, said the village had tourism long before Kat Florence arrived on the scene. But he said it’s reached a tipping point where residents are avoiding going downtown on most days because of the crowds.

“Tourism has been part of Elora for a long time, but I think what’s happened is we’ve just sort of got tourism on steroids now, and we’re getting to the point where it’s affecting the livability of the community,” he said. “We’ve got this disruption to the village with not very proven economic benefits, and I think that’s where people are getting concerned.”

Kat Florence’s supporters, however, say the company has accelerated an economic boom and restored many underused, and sometimes derelict, properties in the village. They point out there are no more vacant shops in the downtown. Realtors say property values have risen in lockstep with Kat Florence’s investments in the community.
“I can tell you that Kristy’s commitment to Elora, and particularly to preserving and restoring pieces of its history, is absolutely genuine,” said Ms. Parkinson, co-owner of the Ayrshire Hotel.

Ms. Parkinson said some residents don’t see the level of investment Kat Florence has made. She acknowledged the influx of tourists has caused some headaches, but said there’s an upside to having so many visitors.

“Are there hiccups? Of course there are,” she said. “We manage to sustain restaurants and shops and art galleries, events and experiences that I think would be incredibly difficult to support exclusively, you know, through the resident population. So tourism helps us stay alive.”

Lisa MacDonald, a township councillor, said she’s disappointed the opposition to Kat Florence has become what she described as “hateful.” She argues the township is taking steps to get more revenue from tourist traffic, which will allow the village to fund things such as public washrooms.

She defended the mayor’s decision to prevent people from discussing the company at the town hall-style meeting last October, saying it was never supposed to be a venue to complain about specific developers.
On an August day in Elora, visitors queue for ice cream near the now-closed Elora Cinema. Kat Florence says it plans to reopen the theatre, which is next door to its hotel.
The launch of Kat Florence as a global jewellery brand a few years earlier had its own challenges.

There was a short-lived boutique in London, England, which opened in October, 2016, and closed after only a few months. Kat Florence had flown in dozens of customers to celebrate the opening. Mr. Ferreira said his clients “were given the option to leave the location” after the building was sold. That same year, the company reported losses of US$2.9-million in an annual report filed in Cyprus, where Kat Florence Designs was initially based.

Another promotional event at a Berlin hotel that year had to be cancelled because of a court injunction filed by a German company, sparked by a dispute with Kat Florence over its customer list. As part of that conflict, jewellery retailer Elumeo filed a motion to seize the company’s trademark in the European Union.

Kat Florence eventually filed a lawsuit in the United States, in which the company alleged Elumeo had made “slanderous accusations” against Ms. Hillis and Mr. Kogen. In a counterclaim, Elumeo alleged Mr. Kogen had transferred tens of thousands of rare gems stored in a jointly owned Thailand facility to a shell company he controlled in Hong Kong. The German company alleged it was never paid for those gems, which it says later resurfaced for sale in Georgia.
Mr. Ferreira said these “allegations are completely false and were not proven.” The judge ultimately dismissed both Mr. Kogen’s lawsuit and Elumeo’s counterclaim, citing a lack of jurisdiction.

In 2018, an endorsement deal with Sex and the City actress Sarah Jessica Parker dissolved into another legal fight that was eventually settled out of court. Kat Florence sued the actress, claiming she failed to fulfill her promotional duties. In a counterclaim, Ms. Parker alleged Kat Florence had signed a contract for US$7.5-million to use her image to promote its gemstones, but had paid her less than US$1.4-million.

In a legal filing in a New York court, Ms. Parker’s lawyer said that when Kat Florence learned the actress planned to sue, the jewellery company “rushed to the courthouse and filed the present action in the hope of presenting itself, falsely, as the aggrieved party.”

Ms. Parker’s lawyer also claimed during the dispute that Kat Florence Designs moved its assets and operations to a similar-sounding company, Kat Florence Atelier, to protect it from any court judgment. The company denies this.
“The allegations are not true and were not proven,” Mr. Ferreira said in a further statement. “Kat Florence and Sarah Jessica Parker had differences of opinion regarding their business relationship.”

Whether they’re enjoying ice cream at the Elora Mews or scenery along the Grand River, visitors to downtown Elora are seldom far from a Kat Florence-owned property. The company owns nearly a quarter of all available real estate in the four downtown blocks.

By early 2025, Mr. Kogen began pushing back publicly against Kat Florence’s critics in Elora. He told the Wellington Advertiser that he’d been accused online “of bribery, smuggling, money laundering, prostitution and worse.”

He announced he was pausing what he said was nearly $3-million that Kat Florence had planned to give the municipality for the public washroom project, green space upgrades, Christmas lighting and a raceway shuttle.

A few weeks after announcing the funding pause, Mr. Kogen told the online news site Elora Fergus Today that he was pledging $500,000 to help business owners “take on online bullies” by identifying anonymous commenters and pursuing legal action.

His lawyer, Mr. Ferreira, told The Globe “the $500,000 was not used for an online-bullying initiative.” Instead, he said that money was earmarked for the construction of much-needed public washrooms. Kat Florence signed a contract with the municipality to pay for the project, but those plans were ultimately shelved by the company “as opposition to the proposal emerged among some residents,” he said.
In June, 2026, Mr. Ferreira started legal action against online commenters on behalf of his clients.

Kat Florence filed lawsuits against three people: Paloma Von Fielitz, administrator of a local Facebook group; Ben Williams, who was a member of two online forums; and Mr. Wedgewood, who spoke up at the town meeting in October. The company is seeking combined damages of $425,000, plus costs, and an injunction that would prevent all three from commenting publicly about Kat Florence.

The libel claims say the company is painted as “cutthroat” and the online comments are aimed at “discrediting their reputations and holding them up to public scandal, ridicule and contempt,” with a “reckless disregard of the truth.” Mr. Ferreira says his clients are only trying to protect their reputation and their businesses.

“They have exercised what they believe to be their legal rights in response to statements they believe to be defamatory. They do not agree that their actions are intended to silence public speech or legitimate criticism,” he said in an e-mail.

In their statements of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Mr. Kogen and Ms. Hillis complain that online commenters have accused them of predatory business practices and portrayed their company as a “villain” acting “without regard for the rights or interests of others in the community.”

Paul Dollak, the lawyer for Ms. Von Fielitz and Mr. Williams, argued the lawsuits appear to be an attempt to frighten and silence Kat Florence’s critics. He said he intends to defend his clients using anti-SLAPP motions, designed to counter “strategic lawsuits against public participation.”
“My clients made comments, in good faith, because they believed them to be in the public interest,” Mr. Dollak told The Globe.

In the claim against him, Mr. Wedgewood is accused of alleging Kat Florence is involved in “criminal conduct” and forming a “corrupt syndicate” that has “improperly influenced the mayor and municipal decision-making processes in Elora.” Mr. Wedgewood, who said he’s on the brink of homelessness, said he believes he was asking fair questions about what’s happening in his town.

Ms. Hogan, meanwhile, complains the company’s actions and aggressive marketing of the village’s charms have taken pre-existing tension over the tourism issue and put it in a pressure cooker. Elora, she worries, may never be the same.
“They’ve built an invisible dividing line through the town. There’s division here that was never there before,” Ms. Hogan said.
With reports from Stephanie Chambers and Anna Sophie Kühne

stories.title: Power Sustainable acquires B.C.-based Fine Choice Foods
stories.summary: Deal is first step in company’s $10-billion commitment to invest in Canada
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Food- and agriculture-focused private-equity investor Power Sustainable Lios has acquired Richmond, B.C.-based Fine Choice Foods Ltd. from a U.S. fund as part of a push to put capital into Canadian companies that have North American reach.

The deal announced Thursday makes Power Sustainable Lios the majority owner of Fine Choice, which manufactures the Summ! brand of Asian-inspired, refrigerated appetizers such as spring rolls, gyoza dumplings and bao buns. The transaction returns the company to Canadian hands after eight years of U.S. ownership.

Farm Credit Canada and Toronto-based Bonnefield Financial Inc., through its agribusiness fund, are buying minority stakes in Fine Choice, which will keep its existing management team in place. The seller was San Francisco-based private-equity firm Swander Pace Capital, which owned the company since 2018.

Financial terms were not disclosed. But Power Sustainable Lios typically invests in businesses with $150-million to $250-million in annual sales and earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation and amortization (Ebitda) of $15-million to $25-million.

The deal is a first step in a plan that Montreal-based Power Sustainable announced in September to channel at least $10-billion into Canadian companies and infrastructure over the next five years.

Power Sustainable is an asset-management arm of financial-services conglomerate Power Corp. of Canada POW-T , which is led by the Desmarais family. The Lios subsidiary is Power Sustainable’s agri-food investing platform.

The acquisition of Fine Choice is the second deal in a row that Power Sustainable Lios has made where the seller was a U.S. private-equity firm. In January, Power Sustainable Lios bought Ontario-based Crofter’s Organic, which is North America’s largest supplier of organic jams, jellies and spreads.

“We’ve been able to bring ownership back to Canada, and that’s not the mandate, but it’s a moment of pride,” managing partner Jonathan Belair said in an interview.

Fine Choice Foods is the fifth deal made through Power Sustainable Lios’s $285-million first fund, which also owns Food Cycle Science Corp., or FCS, a maker of kitchen appliances for recycling food waste .

The Summ! brand traces its roots to a small, family-run storefront in Vancouver that sold frozen dim sum. The company expanded to become a manufacturer of refrigerated – but not frozen – appetizers sold in national grocery chains in Canada and the U.S., as well as club stores such as Costco.

Swander Pace led Fine Choice through an eight-year program to professionalize the business. Now, Power Sustainable Lios plans to expand its range of products and push into new markets in the United States.

Fine Choice operates in a segment of the food market that is growing in popularity but also hard to replicate, Power Sustainable Lios partner Craig Hanna said.

Ready-made, refrigerated foods are “perceived as fresher, healthier, more convenient,” he said, because they haven’t been frozen and are faster to cook. At the same time, an increasing number of customers in North America are showing an interest in trying new flavours and ethnic foods, he said.

Even as shoppers feel the pinch of higher prices driven by inflation, demand for those foods has held up well. “Consumers are pressed for dollars, but they’re also pressed for time,” he said.

Fine Choice stood out in part because it has an established supply chain, Vancouver-area manufacturing facilities and strong food-safety protocols that allow the company to widely distribute refrigerated, packaged food, he added.

At a tough moment for private equity, with high interest rates and economic uncertainty contributing to a glut of deals, food producers are becoming attractive takeover targets. Canada’s food and beverage manufacturing industry contributes about $35-billion to the country’s gross domestic product, which is more than twice the size of the auto sector.

The sector has a large number of family-owned businesses reaching a stage where they need capital and professional management to continue to expand.

“I’m not sure if everybody realizes how rich the opportunity set is in Canada,” Mr. Hanna said.

Last year, the private-equity arm of Fengate Asset Management acquired Toronto-based healthy-snack maker Sweets From the Earth , taking control of a family-led business but also keeping its founders involved.

stories.title: Scientists report ‘substantial’ declines in loons across Canada
stories.summary: The Atlantic and Prairie provinces saw the biggest reduction in the water birds’ numbers
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
The haunting tremolo of a loon’s call echoing across a northern lake May be the signature sound of the Canadian wilderness, but a sweeping new study suggests the species could be seen and heard less frequently in the future.

“Loons are, unfortunately, not doing as well as we’d like,” said Matthew Fuirst, a research ecologist with the environmental organization Birds Canada, who led the work.

More than 20 researchers in Canada and the United States contributed to the study, published Thursday in the research journal Facets. The landmark three-year effort pulled together decades worth of data on one of North America’s most beloved bird species.

In all but one of the 12 breeding regions that make up the study, loons are exhibiting “substantial long-term declines,” Dr. Fuirst said. “The steepest declines that we saw were in the Atlantic and Prairie provinces of Canada.”

Loons are not currently endangered, with an estimated 254,000 breeding pairs in Canada, accounting for about 94 per cent of the total species population. But regional studies have long hinted that they are under pressure.

The fact that the downward trends are widespread and vary in severity suggest multiple factors are at work, including various human-caused disturbances of loon habitat. But on a continental scale, Dr. Fuirst and his colleagues suggest that climate change May also be playing a role.

For many Canadians, loons are emblematic of both the country’s natural environment and its national identity, symbolized by its presence on the one dollar coin. Their distinctive calls, markings and association with picturesque lakes that also attract cottagers and campers have all helped to make them a quintessential feature in the landscape.

To help illuminate the loons’ status, researchers drew on more than 45,000 breeding records for loons sighted at 3,421 lakes across North America. About half the data in the study came from volunteers who participated in a long-running Birds Canada loon survey.

This, combined with other observations, in some cases reaching back to the 1980s, allowed researchers to compare loon breeding success across time and between regions.

The unifying measurement the researchers used to compare all the data is productivity, defined as the number of chicks per adult loon pair that survive beyond six weeks after hatching.

In the analysis, data were grouped into 12 regions to look at trends in productivity.

The results mostly showed declines, ranging from 0.5 to 2.5 per cent per year, over a time period of two to four decades depending on available data. The exception was northern Maine, where loon productivity has been relatively stable.

A blind area in the study is the northern half of the Common Loon’s breeding range, where there are far fewer people and where data have been difficult to obtain.

Walter Piper, a co-author on the study and a professor of biology at Chapman University in Orange, Calif., said it was not likely that data in the northern part of the loon’s range would show an increase to counterbalance what is being observed in the south or that loons were moving further north in response to environmental change.

He noted that, aside from productivity, the study also indicated there was a decline in chick quality that could signal poorer nourishment.

“We are probably detecting the leading edge of a broad decline in the loon population that is likely to continue in coming decades,” Dr. Piper said. “Loons are long-lived, so it will take a while for this decline to become obvious, but we had better look for causes now.”

One potential cause that has captured researchers’ attention is the possibility that increased precipitation due to climate change is affecting the loons ability to hunt for food and feed their young.

Unlike ducks, which occupy some of the same habitat, loons are built to catch fish in relatively clear water. Even their bones are denser than those of many other species to make it easier for them to stay submerged long.

But more flooding and churning of lake waters as a result of increased precipitation could be lowering visibility and impeding the loons’ hunting success.

James Paruk, a loon expert and biologist at St. Joseph’s College in Standish, Maine who was not involved in the study, said the stability of the loon population measured in that state May offer another clue.

He noted the part of the state that the study encompassed has relatively low human and shoreline development. This might account for some of the variations in the populations trends, he added.

Dr. Paruk also praised the study team for the significant amount of work and co-ordination that was done to conduct such a large scale analysis.

“The data covers such a long time span on such a broad scale that it’s really far reaching in its implications,” he said.

Dr. Fuirst said that he has already embarked on a follow-up study to get at the causes of the declines.

“If we can identify threats before they become detrimental, that’s the best case scenario,” he said.

stories.title: Mark Carney seeks closer Turkey ties. Will Trump object? Should Canada?
stories.summary: Analysts see opportunities in trade, energy and defence, but warn deeper ties could bolster Erdoğan’s legitimacy.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Prime Minister Mark Carney has landed in Turkey for the first-ever dedicated bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Ankara — his latest attempt to diversify Canada’s trading and strategic partnerships amid the trade war with Washington.

Carney will meet with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Thursday, reportedly to discuss furthering the countries’ free-trade talks launched at July’s Nato summit. They will also talk about greater defence and energy cooperation.

Some of the PM’s trips to Europe this year have generated global headlines — from his Davos speech in January to last month’s proposal that Canada could become an associate member of the European Union. Both drew sharp rebukes from the White House. Will his visit to Turkey lead to more criticism?

Anything is possible, analysts say, given U.S. President Donald Trump’s unpredictable nature.

“Carney could sneeze, and Trump would be upset,” said Sinan Ciddi, senior fellow and director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Turkey program. While he acknowledged that a deal presented as a rebuke to Washington could potentially invite a backlash from Trump, Ciddi doesn’t really think presidential outrage over Carney’s visit is likely.

Bessma Momani, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said any criticism from Trump is most likely to target Carney personally, not the talks or any agreement made. “I don’t expect … commentary about the bilateral as much as perhaps to Carney himself,” she said.

But given that Trump and Erdoğan have a good relationship, and both are deferential to one another, the experts doubt Ankara’s outreach to Canada will draw much ire.

“Hosting a leader who has been at odds with the U.S. should not be seen as a message to the United States,” said Bulent Aliriz, senior associate of the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Turkey project.

“(Erdoğan) wants to develop the relationship with Canada, like with many other countries, but never at the expense of … President Trump and the U.S.,” he added.

Ciddi also sees any criticism of Erdoğan as unlikely. “Trump hasn’t called him out on it in other parts of the world. I don’t think that Canada appropriating military capabilities from Turkey is going to upset Trump,” he said.

So what military capabilities might be on the table? Erdoğan and Carney, analysts say, are expected to discuss drone and ammunition manufacturing, and potentially a move to set up Turkish production inside Canada.

“If Carney does make a deal on drones, it would be about manufacturing them (in Canada),” said Momani.

Alper Coşkun, senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, also pointed to Turkey’s advanced defence industrial production, noting that Canadian interest in Turkish weapons could extend to automated weapon systems.

Like many Nato members, Canada is working to replenish its artillery ammunition stocks and expand production. Turkey and Canada could forge a deal on conventional ammunition and drones, Ciddi says. Rather than upsetting Washington, he suggested any such deal could be sold as the Nato burden-sharing Trump has long advocated for.

“If this is spun the right way,” said Ciddi, “there could be … a foreseeable sort of road for Trump actually praising anything that’s reached.”

Because Turkey needs energy, the analysts expect Erdoğan and Carney to have substantive talks about LNG and nuclear power.

Turkey is “always looking for energy and know-how,” said Momani, calling it the “sector to watch” from this week’s talks. She sees nuclear energy as the strongest of the prospects, followed by defence, because Turkey wants energy supplies and technology, while Canada has the expertise.

Coşkun pointed to civilian nuclear cooperation, as well as possible Canadian LNG sales and mining expertise, as strong possible connections. “Potentially, Turkey’s civilian nuclear program is an area where Canada can provide significant help and can present itself as a very useful partner,” he said.

The final area, of course, is bilateral trade between Canada and Turkey.

Given that the volume of trade is currently very low between the two, Ciddi said the “easiest thing that they could conclude is a major expansion of bilateral trade,” noting how Turkey offers advanced manufactured goods.

Anything that Erdoğan does comes at a cost, and I would say that cost is a reputational cost

Furthering discussions about a free trade deal and increasing Canadian investments in Turkey is important to Erdoğan, says Coşkun, given that Turkey faces potential disruptions with the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules, which could favour EU-made products over Turkish goods.

“Canada can’t offset the amount of trade that Turkey has with Europe, which is its biggest trading partner, but at the end of the day, to sort of broaden that agenda would be a welcome sign for Ankara, and something that Erdoğan can use positively, I think,” he said.

Momani sees Canada as the more eager trade partner of the two, given the trade tensions with the U.S., and says a successful visit would need to show “real dollars and cents, and companies doing business with each other.”

“Whether the results will match the rhetoric, which I’m sure will be flowery and positive, we’ll see,” said Aliriz.

Ciddi, meanwhile, is concerned by the political consequences of greater Canadian defence engagement with Turkey. “I would say, look, Canada should go elsewhere,” he said, noting that Erdoğan gains prestige from Carney’s visit.

“We’ve seen Turkish escalation in the Eastern Mediterranean towards Greece, Cyprus, Egypt, potentially a threat to the Israelis in the Middle East. We’ve seen Turkish largesse and growth of military activity inside Syria,” he said, pointing to how the “Europeans don’t say anything.”

“They don’t say anything because Erdoğan has convinced them that Turkey is a vital security partner, by selling them weapons — high-end, medium-end weapons such as drones, such as combat armoured carrier vehicles, munitions, all this sort of stuff.”

Rather than worrying about Trump’s response, he advises Carney to consider what closer Canada-Turkey defence ties could mean for Turkey.

“We’ve seen the consequences of major Western allies engaging with Turkey and enabling Erdoğan’s regime,” he said. “A power such as Canada should not engage with the Erdoğan government. Anything that Erdoğan does comes at a cost, and I would say that cost is a reputational cost.”

Coşkun also suggested that Canadians might have concerns over warmer ties with Turkey.

He warned that warmer relations could draw public scrutiny over Turkey’s democratic backsliding, which “could be a bit of a challenge on the domestic scene.”
