stories.title: Firm behind planned Anthropic data centre in Nova Scotia denies owing fees to N.L.
stories.summary: ST. John's - A company planning a massive data centre in Nova Scotia for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is in the midst of a dispute about land fees for a failed wind-powered hydrogen project in southern Newfoundland.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - A company planning a massive data centre in Nova Scotia for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is in the midst of a dispute about land fees for a troubled wind-powered hydrogen project in southern Newfoundland.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government confirmed Tuesday that it was still trying to collect outstanding fees from EverWind Fuels for Crown lands set aside for the company’s proposed wind-hydrogen operation on Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula.

But an EverWind official said the company doesn’t owe the Newfoundland and Labrador government anything.

“EverWind never signed a Crown land reservation agreement, accepted the province’s proposed reservation fees, or made any contractual commitment to pay the amounts now being claimed,” said a statement emailed Tuesday by Matthew Tinari, EverWind’s chief financial and strategy officer.

The company never agreed to the amount of land the province set aside for its project, nor to the terms of the land payments, Tinari said.

“EverWind categorically disputes the basis for these charges and rejects the assertion that it owes any debt to the Crown,” he said.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government did not respond Wednesday to EverWind’s allegations.

EverWind unveiled its plans last week to build a $10-billion data centre in Point Tupper, a community in Cape Breton just south of Port Hawkesbury. Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has already signed a 20-year lease for the facility, EverWind officials said on Friday.

The company had previously proposed wind-powered hydrogen energy projects in Point Tupper and on the Buin Peninsula, which stretches out from Newfoundland’s southern coast.

In 2023, Newfoundland and Labrador’s former Liberal government set aside nearly 2,700 square kilometres of Crown land for EverWind’s project and began charging the company more than $11.4 million a year — about 3.5 per cent of the land’s market value.

But the company didn’t want all that land, Tinari said. It included watersheds, residential properties and community recreational areas, and more than half was “unsuitable for development,” he said.

EverWind asked the province several times to reduce the reserve, he said. The government obliged in April 2025, saying it would shrink the area to roughly 1,800 square kilometres, according to letters obtained by The Canadian Press earlier this year through an access-to-information request.

They show EverWind officials sending the Newfoundland and Labrador government repeated letters and requests for discussion about the land reserve and its associated fees, though many details are redacted.

“There remains a significant amount of uncertainty in this industry, and high-risk development capital is particularly precious in the early stages of these projects,” wrote Sam Imbeault with EverWind in one such email to government officials in November 2023.

In October 2024, Trent Vichie, the company’s chief executive officer, wrote to then-premier Andrew Furey and other officials with the former Liberal government requesting an “urgent meeting” about “ongoing Crown land reservation discussions.”

There were similar emails from a representative of ABO Energy, a partner in the proposed Toqlukuti’k Wind and Hydrogen Project in eastern Newfoundland. ABO referred a request for comment from The Canadian Press to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, which did not provide any comments.

In the meantime, Tinari said, the province kept charging EverWind for land it didn’t want.

“EverWind made more than $5.6 million in good-faith payments while working constructively with the Province to resolve significant problems with its land reservation and regulatory frameworks,” he said.

In February, shortly after a new Progressive Conservative government was sworn in, the province took the land back from EverWind and two other wind-hydrogen outfits, including Abo’s project, saying they were behind in their reserve fees and their developments had stalled.

Weeks later, World Energy GH2, a company behind a wind-hydrogen operation pitched for Western Newfoundland, filed for creditor protection, saying its project would be worthless if the province took away its Crown lands. Court documents show the company owed Newfoundland and Labrador about $10.5 million in land fees.

A provincial Supreme Court judge granted that protection until next month. In the meantime, World Energy GH2 is selling off its assets and trying to refinance.

At EverWind’s data centre announcement in Cape Breton on Friday, chief executive Trent Vichie would not discuss the value of the facility’s lease. He said the 18,600-square-metre facility is scheduled to come online late next year.

Tony Wakeham, premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, said his province is open to data centres, but he had no regrets withdrawing EverWind’s Crown lands.

“I think what we do is we continue to move forward,” Wakeham told reporters Tuesday. “There’s tremendous opportunities in our province when it comes to hydroelectricity, and we’re looking forward to the opportunities for other developments.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said EverWind’s project in Newfoundland and Labrador had failed.
paragraphs: ST. John’s - A company planning a massive data centre in Nova Scotia for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is in the midst of a dispute about land fees for a troubled wind-powered hydrogen project in southern Newfoundland.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government confirmed Tuesday that it was still trying to collect outstanding fees from EverWind Fuels for Crown lands set aside for the company’s proposed wind-hydrogen operation on Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula.
But an EverWind official said the company doesn’t owe the Newfoundland and Labrador government anything.

“EverWind never signed a Crown land reservation agreement, accepted the province’s proposed reservation fees, or made any contractual commitment to pay the amounts now being claimed,” said a statement emailed Tuesday by Matthew Tinari, EverWind’s chief financial and strategy officer.
The company never agreed to the amount of land the province set aside for its project, nor to the terms of the land payments, Tinari said.
“EverWind categorically disputes the basis for these charges and rejects the assertion that it owes any debt to the Crown,” he said.
The Newfoundland and Labrador government did not respond Wednesday to EverWind’s allegations.

EverWind unveiled its plans last week to build a $10-billion data centre in Point Tupper, a community in Cape Breton just south of Port Hawkesbury. Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has already signed a 20-year lease for the facility, EverWind officials said on Friday.
The company had previously proposed wind-powered hydrogen energy projects in Point Tupper and on the Buin Peninsula, which stretches out from Newfoundland’s southern coast.

In 2023, Newfoundland and Labrador’s former Liberal government set aside nearly 2,700 square kilometres of Crown land for EverWind’s project and began charging the company more than $11.4 million a year — about 3.5 per cent of the land’s market value.
But the company didn’t want all that land, Tinari said. It included watersheds, residential properties and community recreational areas, and more than half was “unsuitable for development,” he said.

EverWind asked the province several times to reduce the reserve, he said. The government obliged in April 2025, saying it would shrink the area to roughly 1,800 square kilometres, according to letters obtained by The Canadian Press earlier this year through an access-to-information request.

They show EverWind officials sending the Newfoundland and Labrador government repeated letters and requests for discussion about the land reserve and its associated fees, though many details are redacted.

“There remains a significant amount of uncertainty in this industry, and high-risk development capital is particularly precious in the early stages of these projects,” wrote Sam Imbeault with EverWind in one such email to government officials in November 2023.

In October 2024, Trent Vichie, the company’s chief executive officer, wrote to then-premier Andrew Furey and other officials with the former Liberal government requesting an “urgent meeting” about “ongoing Crown land reservation discussions.”

There were similar emails from a representative of ABO Energy, a partner in the proposed Toqlukuti’k Wind and Hydrogen Project in eastern Newfoundland. ABO referred a request for comment from The Canadian Press to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, which did not provide any comments.
In the meantime, Tinari said, the province kept charging EverWind for land it didn’t want.

“EverWind made more than $5.6 million in good-faith payments while working constructively with the Province to resolve significant problems with its land reservation and regulatory frameworks,” he said.

In February, shortly after a new Progressive Conservative government was sworn in, the province took the land back from EverWind and two other wind-hydrogen outfits, including Abo’s project, saying they were behind in their reserve fees and their developments had stalled.

Weeks later, World Energy GH2, a company behind a wind-hydrogen operation pitched for Western Newfoundland, filed for creditor protection, saying its project would be worthless if the province took away its Crown lands. Court documents show the company owed Newfoundland and Labrador about $10.5 million in land fees.
A provincial Supreme Court judge granted that protection until next month. In the meantime, World Energy GH2 is selling off its assets and trying to refinance.

At EverWind’s data centre announcement in Cape Breton on Friday, chief executive Trent Vichie would not discuss the value of the facility’s lease. He said the 18,600-square-metre facility is scheduled to come online late next year.
Tony Wakeham, premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, said his province is open to data centres, but he had no regrets withdrawing EverWind’s Crown lands.

“I think what we do is we continue to move forward,” Wakeham told reporters Tuesday. “There’s tremendous opportunities in our province when it comes to hydroelectricity, and we’re looking forward to the opportunities for other developments.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Carney arrives in Turkey for meetings with Turkish president, business leaders
stories.summary: Ankara — Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a three-day trip aimed at deepening political and economic ties with the Nato ally.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
ANKARA — Canada is forming a “strategic partnership” with Turkey aimed in part at securing a free-trade agreement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday after a bilateral meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara.

Carney is making the first official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey.

In a prepared statement delivered alongside Erdogan, Carney said Canadian negotiators will return to Turkey next month to begin negotiations on a free-trade deal.

“Our objectives are clear: more trade between business to build more prosperity between our peoples,” Carney said, noting the partnership comes with a three-year action plan and calling Turkey an “exceptional partner.”

“By lowering costs, cutting barriers and creating greater certainty, we will open new doors for companies and investors in both of our countries.”

The two countries are also signing an air transport agreement which could see the number of flights between Canada and Turkey nearly double, and a new defence partnership which could see Canadian and Turkish companies work more closely together.

“Holding together the relationship is trust, and regular interaction. More frequent meetings between our ministers, including our foreign ministers meeting more consistently as part of this strategic dialogue,” Carney said.

“Trade that opens new markets, defence industries that keep us safe, energy that powers our economies, and people who bring it all together. That’s what today is about.”

In his own remarks, Erdogan said he hopes trade between the two countries will roughly double to $10 billion and said he plans on visiting Canada.

Neither Carney nor Erdogan took questions from reporters Thursday. Carney is expected to speak with Canadian media on Friday in Istanbul.

In a joint statement, the two leaders said they’re also committing to deeper people-to-people ties, something Carney also has sought with the European Union to offer more flexibility to tourists, workers and students.

The statement said Canada and Turkey have shared values, including “human rights, individual liberties, democracy and the rule of law.”

The Erdogan government is under heavy scrutiny internationally right now over reports of official persecution of LGBTQ+ organizers in the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Lower courts' reasoning 'neuters' Emergencies Act, government tells Supreme Court
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government says the courts engaged in "second-guessing with the benefit of 20/20 hindsight" when they ruled it lacked legal justification to use the Emergencies Act four years ago to quell protests.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government’s legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the national capital and at key border points four years ago.

For about three weeks in January and February 2022, downtown Ottawa was filled with protesters, including many in large trucks that blocked streets around Parliament Hill.

While many of the protesters were demonstrating against COVID-19 health restrictions, the protest attracted some with a variety of grievances against then-prime minister Justin Trudeau and his government.

Trucks also jammed key border crossings to the United States, including routes at Windsor, Ont., and Coutts, Alta.

On Feb. 14, 2022, the government invoked the Emergencies Act, which allowed for temporary measures, including regulation and prohibition of public assemblies, the designation of secure places, direction to banks to freeze assets and a ban on support for protest participants.

It was the first time the law had been used since it replaced the War Measures Act in 1988.

In a Feb. 15 letter to premiers, Trudeau said the federal government believed it had reached a point “where there is a national emergency arising from threats to Canada’s security.”

The Public Order Emergency Commission, which carried out a mandatory review after the act was used, concluded in early 2023 that the federal government had met the very high legal standard for using the law.

The Trudeau government’s move was also scrutinized in Federal Court.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and others argued in court that Ottawa lacked sound statutory grounds to deploy the emergency measures.

The government said the steps taken to deal with the turmoil were targeted, proportional and time-limited, and complied with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Richard Mosley, the Federal Court judge who heard the case, concluded the decision to invoke the Emergencies Act did not bear the hallmarks of reasonableness — justification, transparency and intelligibility — and was not supported in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints.

Ultimately, there “was no national emergency justifying the invocation of the Emergencies Act,” Mosley said in his January 2024 ruling.

In January of this year, a three-judge panel of the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously affirmed that ruling.

The Court of Appeal said that as disturbing and disruptive as the blockades and the “Freedom Convoy” protests in Ottawa could be, “they fell well short of a threat to national security.”

The federal government asked the Supreme Court for leave to appeal the decision.

Following its usual practice, the top court gave no reasons Thursday for agreeing to hear the case.

The court also agreed to hear cross-appeals on issues raised by the civil liberties association and the Canadian Constitution Foundation.

Howard Sapers, executive director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, said Thursday that while the extraordinary powers granted to the government through the Emergencies Act are necessary in extreme circumstances, they also threaten the rule of law and the democratic process.

“Courts are responsible for ensuring that the government does not invoke these powers arbitrarily, and Ccla’s mandate is to raise these important issues for judicial scrutiny,” he said in a media release.

In its written submission requesting a Supreme Court hearing, the government said the Federal Court and the Court of Appeal “applied the wrong principles on judicial review.”

The courts should have asked whether — based on the information available at the time — federal officials acted reasonably in concluding a public order emergency existed, the submission said.

“Instead, they asked, with the benefit of hindsight, whether there were reasonable grounds to believe that a public order emergency existed.”

In the end, both courts applied their own view of what was reasonable, the government said.

“This non-deferential approach hamstrings governments’ ability to respond effectively to future crises, neuters the Act” and conflicts with the Supreme Court’s administrative law rulings over the years, the government’s submission said.

“It amounts to second-guessing with the benefit of 20/20 hindsight,” the government added.

“In the end, no one disputes that emergency measures should be a temporary means of last resort. But that does not mean those measures should be available only in the most dire and extreme circumstances.”

In its submission to the Supreme Court, the civil liberties association said the government should be denied leave to appeal because it was attempting to relitigate “the same issues and arguments the Court of Appeal dismissed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

“It amounts to second-guessing with the benefit of 20/20 hindsight,” the government added.

“In the end, no one disputes that emergency measures should be a temporary means of last resort. But that does not mean those measures should be available only in the most dire and extreme circumstances.”

In its submission to the Supreme Court, the civil liberties association said the government should be denied leave to appeal because it was attempting to relitigate “the same issues and arguments the Court of Appeal dismissed.”

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge conspiracy suspect James Bryant pleads not guilty in U.S. court
stories.summary: Seattle — The alleged co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and will go on trial in December.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
James Cody Bryant, centre, is seen in a court sketch drawn during the accused's appearance in U.S. district court in Seattle on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Lois Silver Lois Silver

By Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press

Posted October 22, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated October 22, 2026 12:16 pm.

Seattle — The alleged co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and will go on trial in December.

James Bryant entered the plea in an arraignment appearance in Seattle, after a grand jury last week indicted the 30-year-old Bellingham, Wash., resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, alleges she colluded with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online, helping set up an attempted livestream of the murders.

Bryant, whose trial will begin on Dec. 21, also allegedly advised 18-year-old Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

Van Rootselaar killed eight victims last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before she fatally shot herself as police closed in.

Bryant, who appeared in a tan prison jumpsuit, her hair down to her waist, has been denied bail, and the accusations against her remain unproven.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Our hearts beat together’: Wainwright gathers for prayer vigil
stories.summary: About 150 people gathered at Wainwright's Church of the Nazarene Wednesday night for a vigil as the community continued to grieve and support those affected.
stories.author: Jace Maki, Sarah Ryan
stories.content:
About 150 people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene Wednesday night for a prayer vigil as the community continued to grieve.

The gathering came days after a deadly training exercise at nearby CFB Wainwright . Four Canadian Armed Forces members were killed and dozens of others were injured when soldiers were caught in a fast-moving grass fire on Saturday. The soldiers killed were Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

Wednesday night’s vigil brought the focus back to a community coping with that loss.

Residents filled the church for an evening of prayer, songs and reflection. Ministers representing seven area churches led those gathered in prayer. They asked for blessings for the soldiers who died, those who were injured, their families, first responders and the wider community.

Pastor Ryan Wood said there are no adequate answers for the suffering and loss the community has endured.

Residents bowed their heads during a moment of silence while prayers also recognized those who stepped forward to help.

Bruce Pugh, Wainwright’s mayor, described the gathering as an opportunity for residents to come together and let their “hearts beat together.”

Wood said people in Wainwright have been looking for ways to demonstrate their support. “We just want to let everyone know that’s been affected by this that they’re loved and cared for – and give people an opportunity to express their own sense of grief and mourning as well,” he said.

For many people in Wainwright, the connection to the military is personal, almost every church in the community has a parishioner who is a soldier at the nearby base.

Wainwright resident Elaine Smith said attending the vigil was a way to pay respect to the military and show support. “We’ve taken it just as hard as anybody would, because we’re a small community and we really are close,” she said.

As time passes and residents learn more about the victims, those at the vigil said emotions surrounding the loss continue to surface.

Pugh said feelings that May initially have been pushed aside are now beginning to emerge.

The evening included hugs and other gestures of support as residents continued to mourn together.

stories.title: Commissionaires warn end of contract privilege will erode veteran employment
stories.summary: The organization is challenging in court the federal decision to scrap its preferred bidder status, saying lower-paying private rivals will now set the terms.
stories.author: Ryan Tumilty
stories.content:
Ottawa—With the Carney government making it harder for the Commissionaires to win government contracts, one of the organization’s officials said it will struggle to offer good-paying jobs to veterans as the work goes to American firms that pay lower wages.

Geoff Hamilton, president and CEO of the Commissionaires Great Lakes division, said a recent contract for the Canada Revenue Agency’s security guard services made it clear the government is only thinking about price when it awards security guard contracts.

“I’ve never seen a contract of that size awarded on such a slender price differential to change the vendor where the customer had been happy with the service,” he said in an interview with the Star.

A government spokesperson says Ottawa ‘continues to take action’ to strengthen Canadian supply chains and support Canadian workers, businesses.

The Commissionaires lost the CRA contract in June to Universal Protection Service of Canada, a subsidiary of American firm Allied Universal.

Universal’s bid was less than $100,000 cheaper than the Commissionaires’ proposal for the two-year contract, coming in at about $11.9 million while the Commissionaires bid was just over $12 million.

“We were shocked at how small the margin was in the scoring, and the dollar amount really was driving it as far as we could tell,” said Hamilton.

The loss of the CRA contract combined with a decision earlier this year to end the company’s long-held right of first refusal for many government contracts raised concerns in question period Tuesday. Conservatives said the government was picking an American firm over Canadian veterans.

“We can all agree that employing Canadian veterans and hiring Canadian companies is important. The question to the Liberals is why didn’t they do that in this case,” said Conservative MP Michael Barrett.

Secretary of State for the CRA, MP Wayne Long, said the government supports veterans, but decisions on contracts are made by bureaucrats in a fair and transparent manner.

“We’re always going to stand with veterans who have defended our country, including with respect to employment opportunities. The CRA process is independent and does not involve politicians,” Long said in response to Barrett.

Universal has a Canadian headquarters and employs about 8,000 people in Canada, but Hamilton said it’s just an arm of an American firm, and if the Carney government is as committed to buying Canadian, it should change the rules to require truly Canadian firms.

“Any foreign company can set up an office in Canada and poof, now they’ve been maple washed. It’s a very superficial, I would say completely toothless program.”

The largest private sector employer of veterans in Canada is calling on the Liberal government to reverse a decision to end a federal contracting

Allied Universal has many large American contracts, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The Commissionaires were founded in 1925 with an explicit mandate to hire veterans. They employ security guards for government and some private offices and are the largest employer of veterans in the country.

The end of the right of first refusal that the Commissionaires held for security guard contracts covered about $330 million in annual work for the organization. The firm will now have to enter competitive bids for any contracts against private security firms.

The firm received that privileged contracting position because it is a not-for-profit with a mandate to hire veterans. The right of first refusal began after the Second World War and was based on the goal of the company having a workforce that is at least 60 per cent veterans, a number the company has long struggled to meet.

Hamilton said currently about 27 per cent of its workforce is made up of veterans, which makes it the largest employer of veterans in the country. He said the 60 per cent target was established by the government without any real consultation and the company strives to meet it.

The Commissionaires filed an application for judicial review of the government’s decision to end its right of first refusal. Hamilton said they still haven’t received a clear answer from the government about why it abruptly ended. He said when they were told it was ending, they were assured they would likely still win contracts. And as a not-for-profit, it is well positioned to win contracts against companies that also need to make a profit.

But Hamilton said private firms pay less, and the Commissionaires doesn’t want to keep lowering wages of the veterans they employ.

“It means all of our work that we compete on is gonna have to be price sensitive and that’s gonna be driven by wages, and that is not going to be very supportive for the veteran community, which is what we’re worried about,” he said. “This is going to make it hard for us to meaningfully deliver our mandate.”

Hamilton said for decades the Commissionaires has been a place for veterans to find good, stable employment and the government risks ending that with their recent moves.

“This is a veteran support program of the federal government that we were delivering for them.”

stories.title: Rising diesel prices are causing pain for Canadians and their political leaders
stories.summary: Unlike with gasoline, it’s very hard to reduce dependence on diesel and heating oil. Tax cuts May not make a big dent.
stories.author: Ryan Tumilty
stories.content:
Ottawa—At Feed Nova Scotia , when diesel prices climb, the staff knows they will have more people to feed and less money to feed them.

Executive director Ash Avery says hauling food to partner food banks across the province adds up, and when diesel prices climb, as they have in the last year, they add up quickly.

“For every 10-cents increase per litre, it costs Feed Nova Scotia approximately $900 more a month,” she said in an interview.

That increase has pushed the charity’s monthly fuel bill from $15,000 to $22,000.

The national average price for diesel fuel was $1.52 per litre in January; this month it is $2.61. But that spike is not the only one Avery worries about. Heating oil prices are also up to $2.49 per litre as of Monday, about a dollar more than they were a year ago. A heating oil furnace can consume thousands of litres in a winter, meaning huge price increases for Canadians.

Ash Avery of Feed Nova Scotia says hauling food to partner food banks across the province is getting much pricier due to diesel costs. The increase has pushed the charity’s monthly fuel bill from $15,000 to $22,000.

Diesel is a lifeblood of the Canadian economy, running everything from freight trains to farm equipment to semi-trucks that haul groceries and consumer goods across the country. The increase in prices for diesel gets filtered into the price of everything that is delivered.

Heating oil has been phased out in many parts of the country, but in Atlantic Canada it’s still a common heating source, especially in rural communities. Avery said that leads to very difficult choices for people who still rely on it to keep their homes warm.

“Turning the heat down, only filling your tank halfway, filling it just enough to scrape by, these are definitely all tactics that we hear,” she said.

In Ontario, Natalie Labbée, executive director of the Sudbury food bank , has seen 1,800 new people come to their doors since fuel prices began to spike in January.

She said they’re already looking at hard choices because their resources don’t stretch as far as they did before.

“Right now, we strive to give people five days’ worth of food where they can access the food banks once a month,” she said. “We May have to start scaling back and only offering three or four days of food to make sure that we stretch what we’ve got as far as we can go.”

After more than four years of the war in Ukraine, oil prices were already elevated when Israeli and U.S. forces attacked Iran this year, leading to closures of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil prices around the world. Escalating Ukrainian attacks on refineries in Russia have added to the supply shortage.

Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and the founder of Commodity Context, said there are efforts globally to ease supply, but short of ending the wars in Iran or Ukraine, there are not a lot of good options for addressing the problem.

Canadian gas prices are driven by global market forces, international supply and demand forecasts, and crude oil benchmarks rather than domestic

“In terms of supplies, there isn’t a lot of near-term hope on the horizon, but everyone’s going to be trying,” he said.

He estimates the world is about one million barrels a day short of diesel demand leading to a constant upward push on prices. He said unlike with gasoline, where consumers can often carpool, take transit or find other measures to reduce demand and ultimately reduce prices, diesel demand is constant and so prices keep ramping up.

The heavier fuel runs freight trucks, heavy machinery and agricultural equipment, like combines and tractors, so not filling up is not really an option.

“It really ekes through and touches everything over time,” he said. “Groceries, Amazon deliveries, the EV you would buy to get around high gasoline pump prices would likely be delivered to the dealership on a flatbed fuelled by diesel.

“Virtually all Canadians regardless of what you’re driving or how you live your life, you’re going to feel diesel pain.”

He said Europe is making efforts to release a reserve of oil and diesel that could help, but other initiatives, including U.S. President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to release diesel , are unlikely to make a major dent.

Diesel and heating oil are chemically similar, which means the two are likely to continue rising together.

Ottawa has taken note of the increase in prices. In addition to the Liberals’ move to suspend excise taxes on gas and diesel, earlier this month the prime minister announced a new program offering large rebates on heat pumps with fast approvals so people can make the switch away from oil heating.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser, who is also responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, said the price of oil is unlikely to stabilize, so the best thing the government can do is take people off the roller-coaster.

“If the price of oil is going to be so volatile that it’s causing families affordability challenges, the solution shouldn’t be to have the government eat that increased cost, because that comes from Canadians, too,” he said. “It should be to offer a subsidy that allows Canadians a different solution.”

Food inflation soared in late 2022, which was mirrored by a steep decline in Liberal support that didn’t stop until Justin Trudeau resigned as prime minister and Mark Carney became the new Liberal leader. Fraser said the government is responding with GST rebates, the heat-pump program and other measures, but he knows they May still have more to do.

The report says more than a third of this year’s food bank visits, or nearly 776,000, were made by children.

“To see the many billions of dollars that are directly going to support families with affordability is not a small thing, but we know that there’s still challenges that remain and will seek to do more,” he said.

Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said there will be more programs in the coming budget to help Canadians with these costs, but he thinks voters know there is a limit to what the government can do.

“I do think Canadians understand there’s no magic snap of the fingers” to make the Mideast and Ukraine wars end. “We can respond to it, but we can’t make it go away.”

The Conservatives launched a diesel price relief plan last month, with proposals to further extend the excise tax cut, reduce other taxes and bring more diesel refineries on board.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he wanted to eliminate the gap between Canadian and American prices, but American prices are also more than a dollar over where they were before the attacks against Iran.

“The goals are simple: eliminate the price premium Canadians pay, boost diesel production to a million barrels a day and ensure Canadians everywhere have access to Canadian-made diesel,” Poilievre said in a release.

Mike Millian, president of the Private Motor Truck Council of Canada, said the current excise tax measure is just a four-cent cut, compared to an increase of over $1.20 per litre for many drivers.

He said a truck hauling from Calgary to Winnipeg would have needed about $700 in fuel in January, but today it would require $1,300.

Some carriers are going out of business because of those costs, and Millian said that is only going to increase freight fees, with fewer companies bidding for each load of freight and prices that are ultimately passed onto consumers going up with them.

“The supply starts to dwindle and as the supply starts to dwindle, the rates are going to go up even more,” he said.

Millian said large grocery chains with their own fleets can absorb some of the fuel costs, but not permanently, and consumers should expect to see higher fuel prices show up in prices soon.

Back in Nova Scotia, Avery said some of the government’s programs have been helpful, but people struggling to heat their homes or fill their fridges are going to keep struggling even with the grants and programs in place.

“The thing with poverty is that it’s exhausting. It’s tiring and you are just running around all day trying to survive and don’t necessarily always have the opportunity to go out there and look for the best deal or new grant.”

stories.title: Althia Raj: Danielle Smith’s pledge to Canada rests on what Ottawa delivers
stories.summary: After Albertans rejected separation, the premier is demanding loyalty from her party. Her own record suggests her commitment depends on who is in Ottawa.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
Using her toughest words yet, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith decreed to United Conservative Party members Wednesday: get on the federalist train or get off the platform. No candidate, provincial board or constituency association board member would be permitted to publicly argue for anything other than a stronger Alberta within a united Canada, she said .

But a parsing of Smith’s words since Albertans rejected more sovereignty debates Monday suggests the premier’s public enthusiasm for Canadian unity May be more conditional than she makes it appear.

Tuesday, after 75 per cent of Albertans voted to remain a province in Canada (or 16 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot to pursue separation), Smith gave a video address in which she pledged not to hold another referendum on sovereignty for as long as she remained premier . She promised to vigorously defend provincial rights and assert autonomy — saying, for example, she’ll pursue equalization reform and act on Monday’s successful referenda questions, depending on the final count, possibly the withholding of publicly funded health care and education for asylum seekers or working to abolish the Senate.

Smith said in a televised speech Tuesday she’ll ‘honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum.’

But she suggested those disputes will be settled through political and legal means rather than pushing separation.

“There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us,” she warned, “but I’m also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister.”

She went on to say: “Canada is on the rise again.” The country had changed significantly over the past 18 months, she explained, with the federal Liberals now embracing Alberta’s energy industry. “This is a monumental change,” she said, adding, “Canadians from every region are now supporting Alberta’s vision for a prosperous, energy-rich nation with strong provinces building a Canada we can all be proud of. That’s why I believe Canada can work and thrive.”

But what if Justin Trudeau came back? Or someone of his ilk? What if, post U.S. President Donald Trump’s tenure, the public mood across Canada changes? What if strong environmental policies come back in vogue? Does Canada work then?

Recall, a year ago this month, how Smith told Canadians that a new pipeline to B.C.‘s coast was “a test of whether Canada works as a country.”

Investors, she argued, weren’t willing to fork over billions of dollars to build a new pipeline from Alberta to the west coast because there were too many Trudeau-era policies standing in the way: the oil and gas emissions cap, the Impact Assessment Act (Bill C-69), and the tanker ban.

“If we can’t build with the collaboration of the federal government, and between provinces, if it’s everybody gets to have their products going to market except Alberta, that is not a country. A country is one where we support each other,” she said at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney heard her message: the oil and gas emissions cap was abandoned, the province was allowed to sidestep the Impact Assessment Act and a willingness to scrap the tanker ban was publicly stated (clean electricity regulations were also eliminated, methane regulations delayed, the industrial carbon price weakened and climate targets sidelined). Still, no private investor came. So, Carney announced a new plan to send bitumen to B.C.‘s Lower Mainland and committed some $40 billion of taxpayers’ money to make the pipeline happen.

I believe Smith cares deeply about Albertans who suffered emotionally and financially during the downturn, who lost their jobs or small businesses, and saw family members move away in search of new opportunities. But support for Canada must rest on a deeper foundation than support for a pipeline project, or successful reversal of policies one disagrees with. We should expect political leaders who do not explicitly run on a sovereigntist platform to believe unequivocally in the Canadian project, and not threaten or work to split up the federation when they disagree with Ottawa or don’t get their way.

Smith chose to lower the petition threshold to please Alberta sovereigntists. She promised to hold a referendum if they received the required signatures — despite having no electoral mandate to do so. She decided, despite a judicial ruling that gave her an off-ramp by citing a lack of Indigenous consultations, that she would add a referendum question with a separatist option anyway. It’s no wonder many sovereigntists believed she was in their camp, until it became clear Albertans were not.

Now that the Ucp’s re-election prospects are in jeopardy, Smith has come down firmly on the side of federalists, warning her own party members that not falling in line will mean catastrophe for the province, or, in her words: “radical NDP policies, woke cancel culture, big government, eco-extremism.”

With party unity and her own leadership at risk, Smith is now showing active separatists — anyone who can’t accept the United Conservative Party is not an independence party — the door.

But it May be worth asking how long that May last.

stories.title: Friends of B.C. soldier, 19, killed in CFB Wainwright fire remember his ‘strong passion’ for the military
stories.summary: The childhood friend of Pte. Hayden Lykkemark recalls the shock of learning about the Canadian soldier’s death on Saturday.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
This holiday season, a chair at Caden Orr’s dinner table, saved for his best friend, will be empty.

For more than a decade, Orr and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, were “almost inseparable” until Orr received a text with the news of his friend’s death.

Keeyahn Hakim and Orr, both longtime friends of Lykkemark, one of the four soldiers killed at CFB Wainwright , are in disbelief following the fast-moving grass fire that swept through the Alberta military base, located 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, during training on Saturday.

“We were talking about our plans for the holidays,” 18-year-old Orr told the Star. “I told him (Lykkemark) that he should come to one of my Christmas dinners. I had been looking forward to seeing him, having some good food together, and some gifts.”

Caden Orr, 18, said he and Hayden Lykkemark, 19, right, were “almost inseparable.”

Lykkemark, of Langley, B.C., died alongside Shaun Farrell, 23 , of Prince Albert, Sask., Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, from Edmonton and Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, from North Vancouver. Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday that 33 injured soldiers remain in hospitals, down from 39, adding that the burn victims, their families and health-care workers have been “traumatized.”

Despite repeated pledges from officials to find the cause of the blaze, questions persist around the military response and how the fire could injure dozens and kill four, including Lykkemark, whom friends describe as a passionate young man who had long dreamed of a professional career in the military.

While out for a walk Saturday evening, Orr said Lykkemark’s younger brother told him there had been an explosion at CFB Wainwright and asked him whether he had heard from Hayden.

“So I instantly messaged Hayden, without thinking too much. I’m like, ‘You alive?’ Just as a joke, because I thought he’d be completely fine.”

Orr recalled that he and Lykkemark met when they were around 12 years old at the boys and girls club in Langley. They clicked “instantly” because of their similar humour, and their friendship grew into one that was “almost inseparable” from Grade 11 to 12.

The two used to wake up every day at 4 a.m. and work out together, practice rugby, eat together and Lykkemark would drive them to school, said Orr.

Lykkemark, 19, grew up in Langley, B.C.

“We would do pretty much everything together,” said Orr.

After an hour of multiple unanswered texts and calls, Orr said he searched online for information about the Wainwright military base, where the words “severe,” “explosion” and “mass casualties” filled his phone screen.

Around midnight, Orr went on another walk when he received a second text from Lykkemark’s younger brother.

“Just two words: ‘Hayden’s dead,’” said Orr. After trying to call Lykkemark’s younger brother to ask for more information without success, Orr said he went home and sat in his living room in disbelief.

“I’m kind of just thinking and sitting there for a while, I still don’t believe that he’s, you know, passed, I’m just thinking, what could have happened?” Orr said.

The brother of Shaun Farrell and a friend of Morgan Wong, two of four who died on Saturday,

Lykkemark had always dreamed of joining the military and wrote about his future career in English assignments, said Orr.

“It (the military) was this strong passion that he’s had ever since he was little that stayed (with him) all through high school,” said Orr.

Back in high school at Langley Secondary School (LSS), Hakim recalled when Lykkemark found a wallet full of cash at school and returned it.

“I wish there were more people in the world that were like him,” said Hakim. “That’s one thing I did like about him, just like an awesome guy.”

Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, of Langley, B.C., was part of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The deadly fire at CFB Wainwright has been described by Prime Minister Mark Carney as one of the worst peacetime tragedies on Canadian soil for the country’s military.

On Monday, Carney vowed that the military will conduct a thorough investigation to determine how the tragedy unfolded. He said the cause of the fire is still unknown, but that it was burning during training exercises and jumped nearly a kilometre in less than a minute amid “ferocious winds.”

CFB Wainwright’s “Range Standing Orders,” which the Canadian Armed Forces provided to the Star on Tuesday, say units at the base should plan shooting drills before about 10 a.m. between August and October, when the “fire hazard is normally low enough to permit the firing of most ammunition.” Saturday’s drills were held around 4 p.m.

Mornings are generally safer because of lower temperatures and gentler winds, Mike Flannigan, a fire science expert at Thompson Rivers University, explained to the Star.

This composite of handout images shows Canadian Armed Forces members, left to right, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Sgt. Morgan Wong, who died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

“I’m upset and pissed off at the same time,” said Hakim. “Even with the winds and fire near the base they (the military) still decided to do the training, which baffles me a little bit.”

While Lykkemark was in the military, Orr said he would call him every two weeks to check in, and Lykkemark always said he was having a “great time” even when he had to train while sick or tired. He also loved the Vancouver Canucks.

“He’s my greatest friend. It still doesn’t feel real,” said Orr. “We shared a lot of special moments together, like road trips, we would always be side by side, no one else could fill that same spot.

“I won’t see him at Christmas now.”

With files from Alex Ballingall

stories.title: Are strict screen-time limits the right approach? Here’s what Star readers think
stories.summary: After new research showed more than half of Canadian kids under five exceed screen-time guidelines, readers weighed in on strict rules, quality shows and the “forbidden fruit” effect.
stories.author: Paige Oldfield
stories.content:
After new research showed more than half of Canadian kids under five exceed screen-time guidelines, readers weighed in on strict rules, quality shows and the “forbidden fruit” effect.

Nick Lachance/Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/are-strict-screen-time-limits-the-right-approach-here-s-what-star-readers-think/article_f7f37c33-0557-4ecd-be7c-ac8ecdebd3ab.html)

ByPaige Oldfield Digital producer

After the Star’s health reporter Kerry Gillespie profiled Toronto mom who limits their two-year-old daughter to one hour of screen time a week, readers had plenty to say.

The story came alongside new ParticipAction research finding that more than half of Canadian infants, toddlers and preschoolers spend more time on screens than national guidelines recommend.

Some readers cheered the approach, and many shared their own experiences parenting with or without screen time. Here’s what you had to say:

These comments have been edited for clarity and length.

“A Toronto Public Health nurse advised my toddler to have zero screen time until the age of 4, with the exception of FaceTimes with family as they are both interactive and social. So far so good.” — Dave

“I used to feel like such an outlier and a ‘mean mommy’ for being so militant about it and I feel the judgment. Our son has always come shopping with us and to restaurants and even out to vote in every election since he has been born, without a screen to occupy him. I just simply carry a larger bag with toys and National Geographic kids magazines. He loves those!” — Sarah

“My granddaughters were raised like this. No screens until after 3 years old. The only exception was looking on a phone at videos of themselves taken by me or other family members. After 3, they were allowed to watch a Sunday afternoon movie at home. That’s about it. They are so creative and imaginative!” — Rose-Marie

“When our kids were young and we’d have a get together with our neighbours, we’d usually put a kids’ channel or movie on. All the kids ignored the TV and were running around playing, except one boy. His parents had him on a strict limited screen time regimen. For him the TV had become the forbidden fruit. Any chance he got he was glued to it.” — Ian

“I was raised low-screen and had trouble into early adulthood with houses that had TV or a movie on as ‘background’ because I hadn’t learned to tune it out. I knew TV as a fun way to watch something fully engaging, not as mindless time-filler, and if something was on I wanted to watch! I think screen time should be deliberate and measured. I’m raising my kids without screens as I was.” — Emily

“We did the same in my household. ‘No’ screens before age 3. After age 3, there was minimal screen time. A bit here, a bit there won’t hurt, but you need a simple system to follow or you’ll never keep your rules straight.” — Mark

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

“There is definitely a thing as too much screen time. But there are quality shows kids enjoy that are harmless. My son loved Peppa Pig and I enjoyed watching it with him. There is plenty of garbage too, but this is where you as a parent draw the line.” — Bill W.

“We have rules around screens for our kindergarteners, such as no tablets/video games on school nights and maybe an hour of educational content on YouTube or a short animated show after school. A treat would be a movie on the weekend or during a long drive in the car.” — FO

“As a parent and educator, I say from experience: make the conscious choice to give up the tech and let them explore their world and relationships in slow mode. You’ll reap a better relationship and healthier kid!”

“I have taught pre-device kids and post-device kids. Post device kids are less creative, less literate, less critical versions of themselves.” — NL

Do you strictly limit your child’s screen time, or do think balancing a little TV is harmless? Let us know in the comments section below.

Paige Oldfield is a digital producer for the Star. Reach her via email poldfield@thestar.ca

stories.title: Healing through presence and grace
stories.summary: October 22, 2026
stories.content:
Martha Dyer (L), enjoying an outdoor conversation with Spiritual Care Practitioner, Cathy Regush(R).

October 22, 2026

Hospital stays can often bring uncertainty, fear and grief, but in those moments, sometimes something as simple as having someone there can help with healing and be a source of comfort. Every person that comes through the doors of the hospital brings their own experiences, beliefs and sources of strength, and the Spiritual Care team makes room for all of it.

For Martha Dyer, faith is an important part of her life, and having someone present to support her has made a meaningful difference. Over the past three years, Spiritual Care Practitioner Cathy Regush has become a trusted source of comfort and connection during some of Martha’s most difficult moments at LHSC.

During a previous stay at University Hospital, Martha met with Deb Lines, Recreation Therapist, who recommended meeting Cathy. The first meeting with Cathy led to a years-long relationship of trust and support. “She has become someone that I’ve gotten to know and rely on, and she will always come when I request her and visit with me”, says Martha.

The support became especially meaningful to Martha when she recently experienced two profound losses close together.

While Martha was in hospital, her father was admitted as well. One of her physicians helped arrange for Martha to be in the same room as him during his final days, with Martha commenting that, “being able to be there with him was a gift I can never repay.”

Two weeks after her father died, Martha’s sister also passed away. During that time, Cathy was quietly working in the background to help, asking a simple yet meaningful question.

“Cathy was there with me at my sister’s bedside as she was nearing the end of her life and asked, ‘What can I do for you’. I just said ‘pray’. It gave me a sense of peace.”

For Cathy, being invited into such a personal moment was both a privilege and a responsibility. “When I am invited into these moments, I think of them as sacred ground,” says Cathy. “It is an incredible blessing to be present with someone and to support them in the way they need.”

In the weeks that followed, Cathy continued to offer Martha a place to talk openly about her grief, fears and challenges. She reminded Martha that grief was not something she simply had to “get over,” but something she could move through in her own way and at her own pace.

“She helped me recognize the support I already had around me,” says Martha. “When I felt overwhelmed by everything that needed to be done, she reminded me that things would present themselves as they came and that I would be able to work through them.”

Although faith is important to Martha, Spiritual Care is not limited to those who identify with a particular religion. It is available to people of all spiritual, cultural and religious backgrounds, as well as those who are atheist, agnostic or non-religious. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that Spiritual Care is only about religion or Christianity, but it’s for everyone,” says Martha. “It may be helpful to someone who doesn’t even realize this kind of support is available to them.”

Rather than arriving with a set idea of what a visit should look like, Cathy takes her lead from the person she is supporting. The conversation might explore faith, values or sources of strength, or it may simply provide space to share a story, enjoy a laugh, or feel heard. “I want to learn what they need and how I can best support them,” says Cathy. “Every person and every visit is different. I want people to know they are accepted for who they are. Whether a person is religious, spiritual or neither, the message is the same: You are a human being, and you matter.”

Another common misconception is that Spiritual Care is only available at the end of life. In reality, support is available at any point throughout a person’s hospital journey to help with navigating a lengthy admission or difficult news to experiencing grief, uncertainty or simply needing someone to listen. Spiritual support is also available to families, visitors and staff, and can sometimes help connect people with other services that may better meet their needs.

Cathy emphasizes that there is no expectation for visits to look a certain way as your care team will always find the support that works best for you. “Some visits are light and filled with laughter, while others are deep and profound,” she says. “I am grateful to be able to meet people where they are and offer what they need in that moment. It touches my heart to be able to do this work.”

stories.title: Voting Day is Monday, October 26: What you need to know
stories.summary: London residents can vote in the 2026 Municipal Election on Monday, October 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
stories.content:
London residents can vote in the 2026 Municipal Election on Monday, October 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

On Voting Day, eligible voters must attend their assigned voting location. Voters can find their location on the back of their Voter Notification Card (VNC) or by using the Am I on the List/Where to Vote? online tool at London.CA/elections .

Voters are encouraged to bring their voter notification card if they have received one. You can still vote without a card.

Voters must bring acceptable identification showing their name and address. More than one piece of identification May be needed. A list of accepted documents is available at London.CA/elections .

New ward boundaries are being used for the 2026 Municipal Election, so your ward May have changed. Unlike advance voting, voters must attend their assigned voting location on Voting Day.

The deadline to update voters’ list information online has passed. Eligible voters who are not on the voters’ list can still add their name in person when they go to vote on Monday, October 26.

To vote, you must be a Canadian citizen, be at least 18 years old on Voting Day, and live in London, own or rent property in London, or be the spouse of someone who owns or rents property in London. You must also not be prohibited from voting by law.

Eligible students living in London while attending school can vote here and in their home municipality if they consider their home to be the place they return to when not attending school.

Voters who require accessible voting supports or have questions about voting can contact the Elections Office at 519-661-4535 or elections@London.CA .

For more information about the election, including a list of candidates, visit London.CA/elections .

stories.title: More than 25,000 baby loungers sold at Canadian Tire recalled over fall risk
stories.summary: A total of 25,088 of the affected units were sold in Canada between January 2022 and this past September, Health Canada said.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
More than 25,000 baby nests are being yanked off the shelves across Canada, health officials say.

Simmons Kozy and Nido baby loungers have been recalled over a fall hazard, according to a notice from Health Canada .

Two of the Kozy models (model numbers 59900 and 59902) and four Nido ones (59950, 59955, 59960 and 59965) were removed from store shelves. The Kozy models are grey and taupe in colour, while the recalled Nido models are ivory, taupe, coconut and moonbeam in colour.

Health Canada determined that the baby nests and baby loungers do not meet the regulations for cribs, cradles and bassinets in Canada, creating the potential for fall hazards.

A total of 25,088 of the affected units were sold in Canada between January 2022 and this past September, the health agency said. At least one version of the product is typically available at Canadian Tire .

As of Oct. 19, the company hasn’t received any reports of incident or injury in Canada related to the products.

Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and safely dispose of it in such a way that it cannot be used again, Health Canada said.

The agency reminded parents and caregivers that the safest place for a baby to sleep is on their back on a firm, flat surface intended for sleep.

Simmons baby nets are imported by Jasztex Fibers Inc., a company based in Mississauga that owns Jupiter Industries. Consumers can contact Jupiter Industries by telephone at 1-800-465-5795, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, by email at customerservice@jupiterindustries.com or by visiting the company website.

A different type of baby lounger had a recall totalling in the thousands over a strangulation risk in August of last year. A few weeks later, Health Canada recalled baby nets sold on Amazon.CA while warning of the dangers of baby loungers as a whole due to potential strangulation and entrapment.

Simmons Kozy and Nido baby loungers have been recalled over a fall hazard, according to a notice from Health Canada .

Two of the Kozy models (model numbers 59900 and 59902) and four Nido ones (59950, 59955, 59960 and 59965) were removed from store shelves. The Kozy models are grey and taupe in colour, while the recalled Nido models are ivory, taupe, coconut and moonbeam in colour.
Health Canada determined that the baby nests and baby loungers do not meet the regulations for cribs, cradles and bassinets in Canada, creating the potential for fall hazards.

A total of 25,088 of the affected units were sold in Canada between January 2022 and this past September, the health agency said. At least one version of the product is typically available at Canadian Tire .
As of Oct. 19, the company hasn’t received any reports of incident or injury in Canada related to the products.
Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and safely dispose of it in such a way that it cannot be used again, Health Canada said.
The agency reminded parents and caregivers that the safest place for a baby to sleep is on their back on a firm, flat surface intended for sleep.

Simmons baby nets are imported by Jasztex Fibers Inc., a company based in Mississauga that owns Jupiter Industries. Consumers can contact Jupiter Industries by telephone at 1-800-465-5795, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, by email at customerservice@jupiterindustries.com or by visiting the company website.

A different type of baby lounger had a recall totalling in the thousands over a strangulation risk in August of last year. A few weeks later, Health Canada recalled baby nets sold on Amazon.CA while warning of the dangers of baby loungers as a whole due to potential strangulation and entrapment.

stories.title: Candidates Talk Trash: Stevenson promises to review weekly garbage collection, Morgan challenges costs
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson is pledging a financial and feasibility review that would consider potentially scrapping the current curbside collection schedule in favour of weekly collection of all three-streams of household waste.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson is pledging a financial and feasibility review that would consider potentially scrapping the current curbside collection schedule in favour of weekly collection of all three-streams of household waste.

Since early 2024, organic waste (green bins) and recyclables (blue bins) are collected weekly, but the remaining bagged garbage is collected every second week.

“Residents are raising concerns about odors, hygiene, rats, and the increased appearance of garbage in their neighborhoods and roadsides,” Stevenson said during a campaign announcement in south London.

If elected, she would direct city staff to review the cost of year-round or summertime weekly collection, including an examination of routes, truck capacity, and workforce requirements.

Following public input, the report would be presented to Council for a decision.

“Staff identified encouraging green bin use was a key reason for moving garbage collection to every other week, we should now examine how that choice is working for households and neighborhoods,” Stevenson added.

Incumbent Josh Morgan responded shortly afterwards.

“She doesn’t have to have that costed, I can cost it for her,” Morgan told CTV News. “It’s $1.8 million to $2 million of operating (costs) every year and $3 million of capital (costs). That includes using some of the trucks for multiple purposes.”

Stevenson emphasized any service change would require a “credible funding plan” that’s within her commitment to property tax increases under 1 per cent in 2027 and 2028, and at or below inflation the following two years.

She suggests the review of garbage collection would be a priority, “It is a top concern for Londoners. To know what the timeline would be and what the options are, I think it’s going to be early on the table.”

“What I think Londoners want to hear is her costing out her tax promise,” Morgan countered. “Getting to 1 per cent with this promise is $72 million, and we want to know what you’re going to cut, because there is no magic money to find out there.”

Ten other candidates are running to be mayor of London, John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam, and Mustafa Zeboon.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Skunk in downtown Vancouver that bit people tests positive for rabies
stories.summary: Vancouver - A skunk that bit a number of people in downtown Vancouver has tested positive for rabies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A skunk that bit a number of people in downtown Vancouver has tested positive for rabies.

Vancouver Coastal Health issued a news release notifying the public of the confirmed case on Wednesday.

The health authority said interactions with skunks are rare, but “a small number of people bitten by the skunk have been assessed and received rabies vaccinations and immunoglobulin to prevent rabies.”

Rabies virus is a fatal viral infection that affects the brain and nervous system. It is found in the saliva of infected animals and can be transmitted through a bite or a scratch from an infected animal, Vancouver Coastal Health said.

“Rabies virus is not transmitted through exposure to the spray, urine or feces of infected skunks,” it added.

Though bats are the only known “reservoirs” for rabies in British Columbia, the authority said “occasional spillovers to other animal species in specific geographical areas, including skunks, have occurred in B.C.”

The seriousness of the infection was highlighted in an issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal earlier this year, where infectious disease physicians described the case of an 11-year-old Ontario child who died of rabies in 2024.

Dr. Brian Hummel, the case report’s senior author and a pediatric infectious disease physician at McMaster Children’s Hospital in Hamilton, told The Canadian Press in June that it’s “an extraordinarily rare infection” for humans in Canada, with only 28 cases reported since 1924.

The most recent rabies case before the 11-year-old boy was a man who died after exposure to a bat in B.C. in 2019.

Hummel said once symptoms of rabies start, there is no treatment or cure, but noted the virus has a relatively long incubation period — usually weeks — before symptoms of illness start to show.

Anyone who May have been bitten or scratched by a sick or abnormally behaving skunk in Vancouver’s West End neighbourhood between Sept. 22 and Oct. 17 is being asked to contact Vancouver Coastal Health for assessment.

The release said anyone who lives outside the region should contact their local health authority for assessment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: FSU: Be a Kid Again
stories.summary: The Fanshawe Student Union hosted "Be a Kid Again" on Wednesday in Forwell Hall. This event was made for stude...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
The Fanshawe Student Union hosted “Be a Kid Again” on Wednesday in Forwell Hall. This event was made for students to relax, have a mental health break, and reconnect with themselves during midterm season by the use of nostalgia.

The hall was busy with students stopping in for a quick visit between classes, some came with friends, others came alone.

“It gives people an opportunity to feel nostalgia and take a break from their classes.” said Douglas Peters, vice-president of student life at Fanshawe.

“We’re coming up on midterms, school’s getting a lot more stressful, assignments are stacking up, so this is just a great opportunity to take a break from that for a minute,” Peters said.

During the busy season of midterms, many students focus on approaching deadlines and studying for exams. Time isn’t always made to take a break and focus on mental health, but stepping away, even just shortly from academics to take time for yourself, can make all the difference.

The use of nostalgia gives students a feeling of comfort, safety, and relaxation during these times.

This event had old classics from everyone’s childhoods like cereal, retro video games, board games, bracelet-making, cartoons, Play-Doh, puzzles, and colouring books.

“It’s a bunch of retro stuff that most people would’ve enjoyed from their childhood,” Peters said.

The atmosphere was similar to opening a childhood time capsule. The familiar cartoons and games brought a sense of playfulness to the serious, and busy college atmosphere.

As midterm season continues all students are encouraged to prioritize their well-being alongside academics. It’s important to recognize when support is needed, students should never be afraid to reach out and ask for help, whether it be from friends, family or Fanshawe support services.

stories.title: Publisher cuts ties with Quebec author after saying it found evidence of AI use
stories.summary: Les Éditions du Boréal said in a press release that analysis of some documents' metadata indicated AI was used while writing the book.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
A Quebec publishing house is cutting ties with author Thélyson Orélien after saying it found evidence he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel.

Les Éditions du Boréal said in a press release that analysis of some documents’ metadata indicated AI was used while writing the book.

The publisher said it will not reprint the book or publish more books by Orélien.

Orélien did not respond to The Canadian Press’ request for comment.

The allegations of AI use in his book, “C’était ça ou mourir” (“It was either that or dying”), emerged on social media in September. An account using the name “Balance ton Claude” alleged that, according to the Pangram software, excerpts of Orélien’s novel had been written “almost entirely by artificial intelligence.”

The novel explores a Haitian refugee’s journey to Quebec. The story is based on Orélien’s own experience leaving Haiti after the 2010 earthquake, the author has said.

Initially, the publisher and Orélien said they were working on gathering a detailed record to prove the book had not been written using AI. But a few weeks later, the publisher said the author had decided to end the process.

“While we do not, now or in the future, accept to play the role of investigator in relation to our authors, this extraordinary situation made it clear we could not simply leave matters as they were,” the publisher wrote Wednesday in its press release.

It decided to lead its own investigation and order an external analysis of the different versions of the manuscript, which revealed traces of “AI markers,” said the publisher.

“We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of ‘C’était ça ou mourir,’ and we will likely never have a definitive answer,” it wrote.

The publisher said this case raises a fundamental question on the trust between authors and publishers.

“We chose this book because it moved us deeply, long before its success in bookstores and awards. We understand the disappointment felt by some, and we share it,” it wrote.

The book was set for a new printing this week.

The author has denied using AI to write the book, saying he started working on it in 2017 and finished the first draft in 2019. He said he had used AI for research.

“What I am going through is cruel,” he wrote in an Oct. 13 press release. “By attributing a text, one that is mine … to a machine, they have not only called into question my status as a writer but also my humanity.”

Separately, he admitted plagiarism in some of his early work after media reported resemblances — or, in some cases, near-identical paragraphs — between some of Orélien’s texts and other books or news reports. The author apologized for what he described as unacceptable mistakes of his youth, while maintaining that no sentence in his novel was generated by a machine.

Before the controversy, the novel won the Prix du Roman Fnac and earned nominations for several major French literary awards. Since the allegations emerged, it has been removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt.

Boréal suspended promotional activities surrounding the novel in September, citing concerns for the author’s well-being.

Floriane Claveau, spokesperson for the major Quebec bookstore chain Renaud-Bray, told The Canadian Press Boréal’s decision to cut ties with the author would not make a big difference for the bookstores — until his book runs out.

“If a book is available and there is demand, we simply keep it available. We don’t position ourselves as judges or censors of content,” she said.

She said the book sold out in several Renaud-Bray libraries.

Pierre-Yves Villeneuve, president of the Quebec writers’ union, praised the publisher’s decision.

“We’ve just declared clearly that this type of work doesn’t have its place on our shelves,” he said in an interview.

He denounced how the publisher’s previously ambiguous information on possible AI use in Orélien’s book put the burden on readers to decide whether to buy the book.

While he is happy with the publisher’s decision, he called on Boréal to release more details on the evidence they found indicating AI use. This information could help readers better understand the situation and provide a possible road map for industry professionals in similar situations.

stories.title: Vancouver voters overwhelmingly opposed to open-air drug use
stories.summary: Plebiscite results released Wednesday show 70 per cent of voters want site for 100 involuntary care beds
stories.author: David Carrigg
stories.content:
Canada

Plebiscite results released Wednesday show 70 per cent of voters want site for 100 involuntary care beds

Last updated 12 hours ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/vancouver-plebiscite-voters-overwhelmingly-opposed-to-open-air-drug-use/wcm/dd0dbebf-a214-4ef3-81ea-d52a5ed16135#comments-area)

Scenes from the Downtown Eastside in Vancouver on Sept. 24, 2026.Photo by Rich LAM /National Post

Almost 70 per cent of Vancouver voters want laws banning open-air drug use, according to the results of a plebiscite conducted during last Saturday’s municipal election.

Around the same percentage are also in favour of creating a secure site in Vancouver for at least 100 involuntary care beds.

Voters were asked two questions on the ballot.

Question 1: Are you in favour of the City of Vancouver strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug (Heroin, Meth, Fentanyl, and Crack) use in public spaces?

Question 2: Should the City of Vancouver formally ask the Province of B.C. to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s Hospital, or another similar site, into a secure medical facility that provides acute voluntary and 100-plus involuntary care beds for individuals posing a serious risk to themselves or others due to severe substance use and mental health disorders?

Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format.

A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.

The next issue of NP Posted will soon be in your inbox.

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

Sixty-eight per cent of 200,058 respondents voted yes to question one, while 68 per cent of 199,231 respondents voted yes to question two.

It was noted on the ballot that neither of the plebiscite results would be binding.

The questions were added to the ballot at the request of outgoing Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim and his ABC Vancouver party that was almost completely wiped out in the election.

Following the release of the vote results, Vancouver’s mayor-elect Pete Fry said he was not surprised.

“The issue of course is that the plebiscite is non-binding. In many respects, I feel like it was a cynical sort of get-out-the-vote election ploy,” said Fry, who defeated Sim by more than 30,000 votes.

Fry said he already has a plan to better manage open-air drug use and homelessness, including providing more services.

He said that the provincial government is committed to include forced treatment beds in the new St. Paul’s Hospital currently under construction.

“The province is also constructing a new facility for treatment and detox and secure care at Clark and 1st (streets),” Fry said.

He noted that the results of Saturday’s provincial election could impact decisions around the provision of secure-care beds.

Both the B.C. NDP and B.C. Conservatives have committed to delivering involuntary mental-health and addictions treatment beds. This means the person receiving treatment is not permitted to leave the facility. In July 2026, the B.C. NDP promised 60 new beds in Surrey and 72 in Prince George.

More recently, in October, the B.C. NDP promised to establish involuntary care beds at the Okanagan Correctional Centre.

The B.C. Conservatives have promised to give police more power to use the Mental Health Act to “connect people with mandatory treatment.”
