stories.title: Thousands packed for the Bahamas … but ended up in Canada. Now they’re having a blast
stories.summary: The Oasis of the Seas left New Jersey on Sunday with more than 5,000 passengers, who paid top dollar to go to the Bahamas, only to have stormy weather divert them to Halifax instead.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax – The Oasis of the Seas left New Jersey on Sunday with more than 5,000 passengers who paid top dollar to go to the Bahamas, only to have stormy weather divert them to Halifax instead.

“We were supposed to go to Florida and stay in Port Canaveral for half a day, and then go to the Bahamas, then come back on a seven-day cruise,” said Ron Green, who lives in northern Virginia. “But then the weather got bad and we came here.”

“My husband said to me, this is a joke, right?” said Marie Durning of New Jersey, who added she was given several hours’ notice before boarding the ship, then left scrambling to repack her bags and prepare for a breezier, chillier Nova Scotia.

“I have my winter hat and earmuffs, but I forgot my scarf.”

Cruise line Royal Caribbean International provided cash and travel vouchers to help ease the anguish for some disappointed passengers.

“They did give everybody a little bit of money,” said Green, who found himself back in the Nova Scotia capital again after a recent visit. “We were just here on a cruise ship about three weeks ago.”

When they first heard the news about being redirected to Halifax, the Hicks family from Philadelphia chose to take a deep breath, rather than let the diversion ruin their vacation.

“Due to the fact that we spent a nice penny on this trip, I told everybody to take out their frustrations before they get on the cruise ship, because once we get on the ship, I don’t want to hear about that,” said Dwayne Hicks, a first-time visitor to Nova Scotia. “I think we are halfway to the North Pole, where Santa Claus is from. “

Other tourists were less optimistic, even as the song “Farewell to Nova Scotia” was performed by an accordion player, as travellers disembarked the vessel.

“I’m very disappointed,” said Nicholas Meli, who drove seven hours with his family from Toronto to New Jersey to board the cruise ship. “I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas.”

The thousands of visitors arrived in Halifax for just one day before departing for U.S. waters. While it was not their preferred destination, it offered a chance to explore the Halifax boardwalk, do some shopping and take a boat ride in the harbour.

“It is the way the dice fell for us, but I’m grateful and I’m going to make the best of it,” said Jim Matthews, who lives near Paterson, N.J. “And I have found out that Halifax is a beautiful city.”

Matthews was not the only tourist trying not let the diversion wreck their vacation.

“Angry? Not at all, and I’m glad this happened, because we love coming here,” said Walter MacDonnell of Hamilton, Ont. “I have been here before, and I was really impressed when I came here before.”

Tina Coppola of Connecticut conceded that the temperatures in Halifax was markedly cooler than in the Bahamas, but used the detour as an opportunity to learn about a new place.

“We are making the best of it and making lemons make lemonade,” Coppola said.

The Oasis of the Seas was scheduled to depart Halifax at 6 p.m. Wednesday, followed by three days at sea before returning to New Jersey.

Other tourists were less optimistic, even as the song “Farewell to Nova Scotia” was performed by an accordion player, as travellers disembarked the vessel.
“I’m very disappointed,” said Nicholas Meli, who drove seven hours with his family from Toronto to New Jersey to board the cruise ship. “I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas.”

content_blocks.alt: Oasis of the Seas Halifax Bahamas
content_blocks.caption: The Oasis of the Seas left New Jersey on Sunday with more than 5,000 passengers, who paid top dollar to go to the Bahamas, only to have stormy weather divert them to Halifax instead. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: The thousands of visitors arrived in Halifax for just one day before departing for U.S. waters. While it was not their preferred destination, it offered a chance to explore the Halifax boardwalk, do some shopping and take a boat ride in the harbour.
“It is the way the dice fell for us, but I’m grateful and I’m going to make the best of it,” said Jim Matthews, who lives near Paterson, N.J. “And I have found out that Halifax is a beautiful city.”
Matthews was not the only tourist trying not let the diversion wreck their vacation.
“Angry? Not at all, and I’m glad this happened, because we love coming here,” said Walter MacDonnell of Hamilton, Ont. “I have been here before, and I was really impressed when I came here before.”
Tina Coppola of Connecticut conceded that the temperatures in Halifax was markedly cooler than in the Bahamas, but used the detour as an opportunity to learn about a new place.
“We are making the best of it and making lemons make lemonade,” Coppola said.
The Oasis of the Seas was scheduled to depart Halifax at 6 p.m. Wednesday, followed by three days at sea before returning to New Jersey.

stories.title: National security screening system can be strengthened, senior adviser to Carney says
stories.summary: Ottawa — A senior federal adviser says a government-wide registry of security clearance information would improve efficiency, reduce duplication and help departments identify where relevant personnel security data May already exist.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A senior federal adviser says a government-wide registry of security clearance information would improve efficiency, reduce duplication and help departments identify where relevant personnel security data May already exist.

David Morrison, senior diplomatic and international affairs adviser to the prime minister, told MPs on a House of Commons committee Wednesday such a registry would be one way to strengthen Canada’s national security screening process.

The Commons public safety and national security committee is holding hearings on the screening process following the arrest of a Canadian Nato intern on espionage allegations.

A federal source not authorized to speak publicly about the issue has said that officials in Canada were proceeding on the basis the suspect is Biwei Zhang — also known as Claire Zhang — who was previously employed by Canadian government agencies.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree previously told the Commons committee the woman arrested in Belgium had received a security clearance from Global Affairs Canada.

The clearance was granted even though court records said the federal Public Service Commission found in 2023 that Zhang committed fraud in an appointment process for a position with the Canada Border Services Agency.

The Federal Court dismissed her application for judicial review of the decision the following year. She submitted a letter of apology during the investigation into her actions.

Morrison, a former deputy minister of foreign affairs, pointed out that individual federal departments are accountable for deciding to issue security clearances, informed by centralized expertise.

The Treasury Board Secretariat establishes the policy framework, the Public Safety portfolio — through RCMP and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service — contributes criminality checks and national security assessments, and individual departments collect relevant information, assess risks and make security clearance decisions, he said.

Morrison declined to discuss specific cases, but he said a person screened to work at Nato would likely have a secret-level clearance.

He indicated that open source checks, such as internet searches of a person’s history, are now being done for secret-level security screening — a tightening of the system following the arrest in Belgium.

Morrison told the MPs that open source verification should be used more consistently across government for a wider range of security levels. “Its use would also benefit from common tools, training standards and methodologies across departments,” he said.

Morrison also suggested human resources-related information relevant to an assessment of an individual’s reliability or loyalty should be available to personnel security decision makers without compromising privacy protections or procedural fairness.

Finally, he said a robust personnel security effort should extend throughout a person’s employment in the form of insider risk programs, recurring screening, reporting obligations and security awareness. He said these measures would help identify emerging risks, ensure clearance holders remain reliable and loyal, and confirm that clearances reflect current information.

Security expert Wesley Wark said Csis “shoulders the main burden” of security screening for the federal government, essentially through assessing loyalty to Canada and reliability as it relates to that loyalty. Csis provides advice related to immigration files as well as on security clearance checks.

Wark, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said the current system for security screening in Canada “is simply unsustainable,” noting Csis handles hundreds of thousands of screening requests annually.

“The dual burdens of immigration and security clearance screening on Csis are simply too great and threaten, in my view, to erode the operational effectiveness of Csis as it addresses its core missions,” Wark said.

“An intelligence service should not be a security screening shop.”

He suggested Canada follow the United Kingdom’s lead and set up a separate, centralized organization for security clearances.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sports Notes: Knights new captain, Mustangs to honour Marshall, Cowgirls 1st in field hockey, Falcons compete for Ocaa baseball crown
stories.summary: With a newly named leader, the London Knights are ranked number two in the country heading into a home and home matchup with the Sarnia Sting.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
With a newly named leader, the London Knights are ranked number two in the country heading into a home and home matchup with the Sarnia Sting.

Ryan Brown has been named the 55th captain in franchise history after a vote by his peers.

“I think nothing really changes. I think I bring the same attitude to the rink and be the same guy as I was before I got the ‘C’. I think that’s important that I don’t change and I can’t be a different person.”

“I think it’s very important, the consistency of having the same mannerisms and the same guy and treating people in the right way,” said Mark Hunter, Knights general manager.

London has just one regulation loss through its first nine games and is second place behind Guelph in the Midwest Division.

“We got the points we wanted but I thought we got lucky for a couple of points that we didn’t earn,” said Dylan Hunter, Knights assistant coach.

“It was something that we didn’t like the game and came out with the two (points), which is great, but we’ve got to learn from it. The standings are good, but I think we got some movement here.”

Mustangs to honour marshall as they look for top spot in oua

There are playoff implications on the line when the Western Mustangs take on Sir Wilfrid Laurier Saturday at Alumni Field.

“There’s a lot at stake and that’s kind of why the OUA puts all the games at 1:00 for the last week so there is no scoreboard watching,” said Mustangs head coach Michael Faulds.

“For us to have a chance to finish first (place) we need to take care of business and beat Laurier and then we need some help from McMaster beating Queen’s.”

Faulds has said each week he wants to go 1-0. It’s his way of not looking too far ahead.

He is excited about recognizing the seniors and his former coach prior to the game.

“Coach (Greg) Marshall we’re going to honour him during the game and obviously it’s our last regular season game of the year, so playoff seedings on the line,” said Faulds.

“It’s you know looking like it’s going to be a beautiful fall day 17 degrees and sunny.”

After having a week-one bye, they have avoided the injury bug and would love to get the number one seed and have next week off.

If not, they’ll be home for the first round of the playoffs.

The Medway Cowgirls nearly completed a perfect regular season on the field hockey turf.

They scored 39 times and allowed just one goal all season finishing with a 9-0 record heading into Thursday’s Tvra semifinals.

With first place on the line Tuesday afternoon, the Cowgirls shutout Strathroy 4-0 on the back of a three-goal performance by rookie Nicole Claxton.

The Cowgirls will face Parkside Collegiate in the semifinals with Saunders taking on Strathroy in the other matchup. The winner of the championship game later in the day will get an automatic berth to Ofsaa.

“I think communication is a big thing and just keep putting in the work and putting it in the back of the net,” added Huls.

Falcons to host ocaa baseball final vs lambton college

Playing baseball in late October can be hit or miss when it comes to the weather, but the forecast looks perfect for the Ocaa final this weekend.

The Fanshawe Falcons will host their rival across Highway 402, the third-seeded Lambton Lions in a best of three series at Aldrige Field in London, Ont.

The Falcons are the top seed in the province having finished 17-1 in the regular season and completing a two-game sweep of powerhouse St. Clair College last weekend.

The Falcons will be counting on Ocaa Player of the Year Holden Heipel to lead them on the mound for game one Friday at 3:00 p.m.

Game two is Saturday at noon, with game three if necessary to follow.

stories.title: 19-year-old soldier who died at CFB Wainwright remembered as a great friend
stories.summary: Hayden Lykkemark is from Langley and friends told Global News he showed an interest in joining the military at a young age. He died in the fire at CFB Wainwright.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Grace Ke
stories.content:
One of the Canadian Armed Forces members who died at CFB Wainwright in Alberta is being remembered by his family and friends as a selfless young man.

Hayden Lykkemark is from Langley and friends told Global News he showed an interest in joining the military at a young age.

“I received a text from Hayden’s younger brother. Just two words saying, ‘Hayden’s dead’,” Caden Orr, Lykkemark’s friend said.

Orr said he first met Lykkemark in Grade 9 English class.

He said they shared the same humour and became instant friends.

“He was a great friend,” Orr said.

“I mean, he was my best friend and he was very funny. I feel like that’s why I first connected with him is because we both shared the same humor and we both thought the same way and he was also a very supportive guy to everyone around him all of his friends, his family, especially his family.”

Lykkemark played rugby at Langley Secondary School in Grade 12.

Former Coach Trevor Plater said Lykkemark was a great team player.

“He always looked after his teammates, took care of them,” he said.

“He seemed to know when somebody was having a tough moment and would have a chat with them.”

Lykkemark was one of four soldiers killed in a fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

The victims served in the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton.

Lykkemark joined the military soon after high school.

“It was absolutely tragic,” Plater said.

“He’s such a young kid; so much future in front of him. It really breaks my heart for his family and friends and teammates.”

Lykkemark was just 19 years old when he died.

“I received a text from Hayden’s younger brother. Just two words saying, ‘Hayden’s dead’,” Caden Orr, Lykkemark’s friend said.

He said they shared the same humour and became instant friends.
“He was a great friend,” Orr said.

“He seemed to know when somebody was having a tough moment and would have a chat with them.”

stories.title: Ward 3 candidate pitches village concept to help solve homelessness
stories.summary: Solving London’s homelessness crisis has become one of the most prominent issues in the municipal election. One city council candidate is pitching the concept of an all-encompassing village with shelter, services, and supports.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Solving London’s homelessness crisis has become one of the most prominent issues in the municipal election. One city council candidate is pitching the concept of an all-encompassing village with shelter, services, and supports.

“Let’s get them a community that’s designed around them, specifically for them,” said Ward 3 hopeful Leroy Osbourne.

His idea is for the city to develop a so-called mental health and wellness village.

It’s a community with various housing streams, including micro-shelters and long-term housing with supports. They would tie-in with an onsite Hart-hub a provincial abstinence based housing program.

Osbourne’s village would also house an enterprise centre, thrift store, teaching kitchen and community garden.

“I want a space where folks have dignity and compassion again without having the stigmatization of going through the struggles and day to day. We need buy-in from the city, from Londoners. And I say that this is a better way to make that buy-in happen,” he said.

Sarah Campbell, the executive director of the Ark Aid Mission in London’s Old East Village, says she’s pleased to see homelessness being discussed in the election.

“We’re in a place where I can see where these ideas come from. What we know is this, we need to be innovative as a community. We need to be cohesive as a community in order to get things done. And so, I look forward to seeing what other solutions can come,” she said.

Long time housing activist and researcher Abe Oudshoorn likes the intent of the village idea, but says the model is inefficient.

“It’s very difficult to do the resources to put together affordable housing and supportive housing. You need to find land. You need to find the money to build. And then you need to find the staff, the operations to keep that running. I don’t think we’ll ever see governments doing it. It’s a pretty inefficient way to do it,” said Oudshoorn.

Also running for the ward 3 council seat are Peter Cuddy, Ben Durham, Harkirat Kaur, Riya Philip, and Zak Rahim.

stories.title: Canadian apps and government websites go offline to ward off online danger
stories.summary: Several websites around the world, including Government of Canada sites, went dark as operators raced to patch cracks in a programming language called PHP. Cybersecurity experts call it one of the largest online vulnerability issues they have ever had to fix to protect against malicious actors.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal - Several websites around the world, including Government of Canada sites, went dark as operators raced to patch cracks in a programming language called PHP. Cybersecurity experts call it one of the largest online vulnerability issues they have ever had to fix to protect against malicious actors.

“This is quite significant since 70 per cent of public-facing apps and websites use PHP,” said tech and cybersecurity expert Ritesh Kotak.

Millions of servers could be at risk, and agencies including the Fbi’s cyber division warned that the vulnerabilities increased the risk of a wide range of networks being compromised.

Montreal’s transit authority, the STM, shut down its stm.info website just before noon on Wednesday.

It confirmed to CTV News that this was a precautionary measure in the face of a security risk that affected internet sites globally.

After 2 p.m., website visitors were automatically redirected to a new version of the site, beta.stm.info, which allowed users to access information regarding the state of service on the transit system.

Quebec’s liquor commission, the SAQ, also shut down its site as a preventative measure, though it said no breach was detected in its system.

Evan Solomon, Canada’s minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation, said in an online post that some Government of Canada websites had been temporarily taken offline as a precaution to “protect government systems and Canadians’ information, following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.”

Certains sites web du gouvernement du Canada ont été temporairement mis hors ligne par mesure de précaution afin de protéger les systèmes gouvernementaux et les renseignements des Canadiens, conformément aux directives du Centre canadien pour la cybersécurité. Cette mesure fait… — Evan Solomon (@EvanLSolomon) October 21, 2026

The European Union (EU) Agency for Cybersecurity also identified vulnerabilities and advised organizations to shut down their sites until patches could fix the issue. Finland’s National Land Survey and Helsinki Book Fair sites went dark.

PHP is a programming language that Kotak said is the foundation for a wide range of websites and apps.

“Think of it as the foundation of a building and the vulnerabilities that have been discovered could potentially impact about 70 per cent of things that most of us do online,” he said. “For instance, when we sign in to a website or put things in an online shopping cart, these things require PHP coding.”

Artificial intelligence agents helped uncover two critical vulnerabilities in August. OpenAI said in a blog post that it led a coalition including researchers and security providers to address the vulnerabilities. Programmers at PHP have urged clients worldwide to quickly apply the fix, because just as AI helped uncover the flaws, it can aid attackers.

Hackers could exploit the flaws to steal data, deface pages, or compromise entire systems, and worldwide warnings pushed operators of several websites to go offline as a precaution until they could fully secure their sites.

Experts said individual users should practice good cybersecurity hygiene, which includes checking accounts for any suspicious activity and reporting any issues to organizations like financial institutions.

stories.title: Ottawa expands military space ambitions with launch, satellite funding
stories.summary: Defence Minister says Canada needs independent access to critical space assets as military reliance on satellites grows
stories.author: Irene Galea
stories.content:
Ottawa is investing in rocket-launch capabilities, satellite technology and new specialized military roles as part of its effort to boost Canada’s space and defence sectors and encourage new investment in the industry.

Defence Minister David McGuinty announced the series of commitments at the SpaceBound conference at the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau on Wednesday

The federal government has signed a 10-year, $20-million agreement with Markham, Ont.-based NordSpace Corp. to access its Atlantic Spaceport Complex in Newfoundland and Labrador. This will allow the Canadian Armed Forces to conduct launches and research and development.

Building sovereign launch capabilities means Canada will be able to replace damaged or threatened systems, “on our own terms and on our own timelines,” Mr. McGuinty said.

The deal builds on a similar 10-year agreement with Canso, N.S.-based Maritime Launch Services Inc. Maxq-NE , another company building launch spaceports, that was announced in March.

Mr. McGuinty said Ottawa has earmarked $17.9-million through its Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security program to help Canadian companies develop satellite communications, particularly for remote and Northern regions.

So far, $4.7-million has been awarded to Toronto-based Kepler Communications Inc. for its Kepler Network project, the company’s satellite constellation providing connectivity to the North.

The two-year contract is intended to help Kepler develop and test the laser-based communication links that allow its satellites to exchange data directly, enabling faster and more reliable space-based networks.

“The war in Ukraine has demonstrated modern militaries’ deep dependence on space,” with satellite technology keeping personnel connected, supporting navigation and helping Ukraine monitor Russia’s movements, Mr. McGuinty said.

“The lesson is clear: Canada cannot afford to depend on capabilities that we can’t access, that we can’t protect, or that we can’t replace when we need them most.”

Meanwhile, the Canadian Armed Forces are establishing new roles that will enable the Royal Canadian Air Force to attract, train and retain highly skilled personnel, he said.

CAF has established a new Space Mission Operator occupation, with the first training cohort to begin with 25 members, and public recruitment expected to open late next year, Mr. McGuinty said. The CAF is also working to establish a Space Warfare Officer occupation, he added.

He did not provide further details about what the responsibilities of these occupations would be.

Over the past year, Mr. McGuinty said, Ottawa has signed more than $3-billion in contracts and agreements across its four space priorities: monitoring and surveillance, space domain awareness, secure satellite communications, and sovereign space launch.

These include a $2.3-billion dollar contract with Telesat Corp. Tsat-T to deliver high-speed, secure military connectivity in the Arctic, a $688-million contract with MDA Space Ltd. MDA-T for new radar satellite to help survey the North, and the three-year, $105-million Launch the North program, to help Canadian companies build sovereign rocket launch technology.

While Canadians often see national defence as soldiers, ships, aircraft, trucks and tanks, he said, “increasingly, some of the most important capabilities we rely on are hundreds and hundreds of kilometres above our heads.”

stories.title: Retired teacher testifies he didn’t initiate sexual activity with former student at trial
stories.summary: Murray MacDonald appeared calm when testifying in his own defence at his sexual assault trial taking place at the London Courthouse Wednesday.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Murray MacDonald appeared calm when testifying in his own defence at his sexual assault trial taking place at the London Courthouse Wednesday.

The court has heard that the student was 16 at the time she used fake ID to get into The Bavarian, a one-time bar located at Cherryhill Village Mall.

MacDonald said he ran into her one night in the summer of 1986 saying, “She had a drink when I saw her there, so I assumed she was of age.”

He testified that she told him she was transferring to another high school and moving out of her parent’s home.

MacDonald said at the end of the night, “I gave her a ride home when we left the bar...it was dark.”

When they got to her parent’s apartment building which was nearby he said, “We thought it was going to be the last time we were going to see each other so we gave each other a hug...it lasted 15 seconds.”

Then he said they started kissing and the female complainant was the one who initiated a sexual act, “At that point I was feeling very anxious, embarrassed and ashamed with the possibility of anyone seeing this.”

Then he told the court. “I said, ‘we can’t do this.’”

He said he pushed her away and left, “I never saw her or talked to her again after that night.”

When she testified earlier this week the female pointed the finger at the accused as the one who wanted sexual contact on the night in question and said the alleged incident changed the trajectory of her life.

Asked by his defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi if he ever put his hands down her pants or touched her or any other students inappropriately, MacDonald repeated several times, “No, I did not.”

At the beginning of the trial MacDonald plead not guilty to a single count of sexual assault.

Later, MacDonald was cross-examined by Crown Attorney Jeremy Carnegie and he maintained his version of events.

Carnegie asked the accused, “I’m going to suggest to you, you didn’t believe she was 19 years old?” MacDonald responded, “I certainly did.” He added, “It was not my intention to engage in some sort of sexual activity.”

The Crown again asked, “I’m going to suggest you’ve invented this version of events?” MacDonald responded, “No.”

At the beginning of the day the jury was dismissed when the defence asked to be tried by judge alone.

Justice Kelly Gorman granted the request and now that all of the evidence is in, she is expected to hear closing arguments from the Crown and the defence on Thursday.

stories.title: B.C.’s newest multi-millionaire waited 10 months to claim lottery prize
stories.summary: Richard did not disclose why he waited so long to claim his prize, but he said he and his wife have plans to travel and "move forward slowly."
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Richard Z, only identified by his last initial by the B.C. Lottery Corporation (Bclc), said he was relaxing in his Quesnel home last December when he saw that someone who purchased a ticket in his hometown had won the Lotto 6/49 Gold Ball Jackpot.

He said that’s when he checked his ticket and learned he had won $46 million.

“The ticket was only visually validated,” Richard told Bclc.

“I checked the Bclc website and had an inkling I May have the winning ticket. When it said it was the Gold Ball, that’s when the overwhelming feelings set in; knowing that out of everyone in Canada, I had the ticket that won $46 million.”

He said he first told his wife and they were emotional and overwhelmed by the win.

Richard did not disclose why he waited so long to claim his prize, but he said he and his wife have plans to travel and “move forward slowly.”

“My wife and I want to do some travelling and I want to see the pyramids! We want to experience and enjoy stress-free trips,” Richard said.

The winning ticket was purchased at Billy Barker Casino in Quesnel.

So far in 2026, B.C. lottery players have redeemed more than $135 million in winnings from Lotto 6/49, according to the Bclc.

stories.title: Psac announces nationwide strike votes set for November
stories.summary: Psac says the government has refused to negotiate on key issues such as wages, job security, remote work and protections against artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Canada’s largest federal public service union says 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month after contract talks with the federal government broke down.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada says voting will take place from Nov. 16 to Jan. 22.

The union and Treasury Board have been in contract negotiations for a year and a half, and Psac in May called a government wage offer of less than one per cent per year “insulting.”

Psac says the government has refused to negotiate on key issues such as wages, job security, remote work and protections against artificial intelligence.

“The government has left us no other choice,” said Psac national president Sharon DeSousa. “This is a wake-up call for the government to stop playing games and put a fair offer on the table.”

Workers to take part in strike votes include wildland firefighters, passport and benefit officers, fishery officers, federal teachers, librarians and administrative staff.

If the vote passes, the union would be in a legal strike position for 60 days. But DeSousa says a strike is the last resort option.

“Our goal is to get a good collective agreement, and it doesn’t have to lead to a strike, but we will if required to do so,” she said.

In 2023, 155,000 federal public servants spent almost two weeks on picket lines across the country before winning wage increases amounting to 12.6 per cent over the agreement’s term, which ran from 2021 to 2024.

Since then, federal public servants have faced both job cuts and an increase in their required office presence.

The Liberals’ 2025 budget outlined a plan to slash the public service by 10 per cent by the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year as part of an effort to reduce spending.

The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, says Canada’s parliamentary spending watchdog.

An online tool released by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer last month estimates there were 344,970 federal employees in the second quarter of this year, down 6.5 per cent from two years ago.

At the same time, federal government departments and agencies are set to spend more than $18 million to get their employees to work in the office more often.

Thousands of federal public servants started a new work schedule in July requiring them to be on-site in the office four days a week. Executive public servants returned to the office full-time in May.

In response to an order paper question from NDP MP Heather McPherson, 13 federal organizations said they plan to spend a combined $18,720,150 to reconfigure or acquire office space to accommodate the increased frequency of in-person work.

stories.title: Royal Regina Rifles colours return to Legislative Building after decades
stories.summary: The antecedent regimental colours of the Royal Regina Rifles have returned to Saskatchewan's Legislative Building after almost 50 years.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The regimental colours of a Saskatchewan-based military detachment that fought in both world wars returned to the province’s Legislative Building Wednesday after almost 50 years.

Colours are a British military tradition that Canada kept after Confederation. Historically, the ceremonial flags were used to mark the rallying point for troops while they battled. Many of the Royal Regina Rifles regimental colours, that are now hanging in Saskatchewan’s legislature, were used during First and Second World Wars.

The Rifles have been Regina’s regiment since 1905. In that time, several battalions have operated as Rifles sub-units — including the 28th Northwest Battalion, the 68th Battalion, the 195th Battalion and the 249th Battalion.

“Seeing these colours back in the Legislative Assembly, it just feels so appropriate,” Premier Scott Moe said, speaking to reporters and an audience that included politicians, and active and former members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

“They are an important reminder for each of us that Saskatchewan people have always shown their support and respect for those who serve our country and stand up for our values and principles.”

Formerly, the colours were housed in the provincial assembly in 1919 and remained there until 1977 when they were moved to St. Paul’s Anglican Cathedral in Regina. They remained at the cathedral until 2024, when they were removed for renovations.

As of Wednesday, the province said the consecrated flags returned to being publicly viewable at the Legislative Building.

“I think it is very appropriate that they are returned to this house of democracy,” Moe said.

“We have a democracy in Saskatchewan and in Canada. And the only reason we have that is because of the brave service of our men and women in our Canadian military. That is why we have a democracy in this nation.”

John Watson is the last surviving member of the Royal Regina Rifles who served in the Second World War.

“To see the colours back where they were, it’s a great thing,” the veteran told reporters, adding that he was “very happy” to be at the Legislature.

Kevin Barry, commanding officer of the Royal Regina Rifles, said the colours are a reminder of the humanity of members of Canadian troops. Barry said bringing the historical items back to the Legislature was “truly a humbling thing to finally get to do.”

“These colours were placed here over 110 years ago, and they are now back in the place where they were first placed,” Barry said.

stories.title: $463M Port of Saint John project aims to boost New Brunswick exports
stories.summary: The Saint John Trade Corridor is the first project to receive funding through the federal Trade Diversification Corridors Fund.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Johnny James
stories.content:
Big changes are coming to the Port of Saint John.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt and federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon were in the city Wednesday to announce a $463 million project to strengthen rail, road and marine infrastructure connecting the port to national and international markets.

“Making an investment here in Saint John is an investment that pays off for not just Saint John and New Brunswick, but for the rest of Canada,” said MacKinnon.

The Saint John Trade Corridor is the first project to receive funding through the federal Trade Diversification Corridors Fund.

The federal government is providing $254 million and the province is investing $116.5 million. The remaining $92.5 million will come from partners delivering components of the project.

Those components include dredging the port’s main channel, a new 2,787-square-metre Canada Border Services Agency container examination facility and shoreline stabilization to protect rail capacity at Nbsr Bayshore Rail Terminal.

More than 100 km of existing rail will also be replaced and the Simms Corner intersection will be reconstructed to improve safety and address congestion.

“Dredging is the biggest piece of the project here for us — the widening and deepening of the channel that is going to allow for two-way traffic at high tide and it’s going to increase the tidal window for all users of the port,” said Port of Saint John CEO Craig Bell Estabrooks.

Bell Estabrooks said excitement about the project is being shared by colleagues at other ports in Canada.

“We all need to be razor sharp, building bigger, and focused on infrastructure and I know they have applications that are going to get funded as well, and it’s very exciting for all of us,” he said.

For Premier Susan Holt, the funding and improvements represent a major step toward getting more New Brunswick goods to new markets.

“We have what the world wants and we are going to deliver it to them based on these investments in the port,” she said.

She referenced recent political tensions, tariffs and trade disputes with the United States — saying this was when “things got really serious.”

“Canada has long benefited from our relationship with the U.S. but it was very clear that we needed to look elsewhere for growth for New Brunswick and for our country,” she said.

She added that the announcement will help her government bring more to the table when negotiating with future trade partners, adding she’s already participated in trade missions to Belgium, France, and India.

“They’re wondering how long it takes, what’s the cost of shipment, how many hours they’re spending at sea,” she said.

“And so the fact that we can bring in products that New Brunswickers can add value to, turn them around and get them back out to customers more rapidly reduces the cost and makes us more competitive.”

“Dredging is the biggest piece of the project here for us — the widening and deepening of the channel that is going to allow for two-way traffic at high tide and it’s going to increase the tidal window for all users of the port,” said Port of Saint John CEO Craig Bell Estabrooks.
Bell Estabrooks said excitement about the project is being shared by colleagues at other ports in Canada.
“We all need to be razor sharp, building bigger, and focused on infrastructure and I know they have applications that are going to get funded as well, and it’s very exciting for all of us,” he said.
For Premier Susan Holt, the funding and improvements represent a major step toward getting more New Brunswick goods to new markets.
“We have what the world wants and we are going to deliver it to them based on these investments in the port,” she said.
She referenced recent political tensions, tariffs and trade disputes with the United States — saying this was when “things got really serious.”
“Canada has long benefited from our relationship with the U.S. but it was very clear that we needed to look elsewhere for growth for New Brunswick and for our country,” she said.

She added that the announcement will help her government bring more to the table when negotiating with future trade partners, adding she’s already participated in trade missions to Belgium, France, and India.
“They’re wondering how long it takes, what’s the cost of shipment, how many hours they’re spending at sea,” she said.

“And so the fact that we can bring in products that New Brunswickers can add value to, turn them around and get them back out to customers more rapidly reduces the cost and makes us more competitive.”

stories.title: B.C. billionaire's real estate firms allege 'pattern of misconduct' by CRA in tax row
stories.summary: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a “pattern of misconduct” in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.

Five companies within Hui’s real estate development group are targeted in the audit by the CRA, including Adex Securities, One West Holdings, a B.C. numbered company and two Luxembourg-based shell companies.

The companies filed an application in Federal Court this month, claiming the government has wrongfully moved to collect on tax debts totalling nearly $330 million, most of which is accrued interest.

The application says the group is involved in capital-intensive real estate projects in Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary and the audit, initiated in 2013, focused on transactions that relied on Canada’s tax treaty with Luxembourg.

The companies say in the application that they’ve received tax debt assessments this year, with Adex owing $45 million and interest of more than $65 million, while the two Luxembourg based companies owe together more than $92 million and $127 million in interest.

They want the court to stop the government from collecting on the debts until a related case filed earlier this year is concluded, while objecting to the CRA wanting $115 million security payment from Adex.

Requiring a payment that large and not allowing the company to defer will cause the real estate group to “lose significant capital that is currently being used to fund active development projects.”

The application is one of at least three filed in Federal Court this year related to the dispute, where they claim that being forced to pay will cause “irreparable harm” and that no advance notice from the CRA means that they “could not have reasonably planned for a debt … of this magnitude.”

The companies claim the revenue agency has exhibited a “pattern of misconduct,” alleging its officers acted outside established policies and procedures and “without regard to the impact of their actions on taxpayer businesses.”

Lawyers for the companies were not immediately available for comment, but Justin Kutyan with Kpmg Law in Toronto told The Canadian Press earlier this year that the transactions in the case were similar to a tax structure upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2021.

The court ruled 6-3 in favour of Alta Energy Luxembourg, which had claimed a tax exemption on a capital gain of more than $380 million under Canada’s treaty with Luxembourg, described in the decision as being “well known as an international tax haven.”

The court found in Alta’s favour, ruling that Canadian tax authorities couldn’t use anti-tax avoidance rules to “judicially amend or renegotiate a treaty.”

The dissenting justices in the case, however, said “the federal government did not deliberately set out to create the conditions for unlimited tax avoidance by means of schemes” used by the company.

The dissenters wrote that “the court should not legitimize such blatantly abusive tax avoidance based on the view that Canada should have negotiated different treaty terms.”

The CRA said it did not have a spokesperson available for an interview to comment on tax treaty abuse.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Carney says Canada is holding the Palestinian Authority 'to account' on elections commitment
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he will be holding the Palestinian National Authority to account on its commitment to hold elections.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government will be holding the Palestinian National Authority to account on its commitment to hold legislative elections, after the president postponed the vote until next year.

“We are certainly holding (the Palestinian Authority) to account,” said Carney, during a press conference in Ottawa on Wednesday.

“We’re supporting efforts to have those elections and to have free and fair elections in Palestine, and we’ll continue to do so,” he added.

Last July, Carney announced Canada would officially recognize the state of Palestine , led by the Palestinian Authority. Carney has said Canada remains committed to a two-state solution, which is “critical for peace, stability and security in the Middle East and beyond.”

The recognition was predicated on the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to several reforms, including reforming its governance, holding general elections in 2026 in which Hamas can play no part, and demilitarizing the Palestinian state.

However, Palestinian National Authority President Mahmoud Abbas recently postponed legislative elections that were set to take place next month to September 2027. Reporting by the Associated Press indicates that decision was made following a discussion between Palestinian factions, including the Hamas-allied Islamic Jihad Group.

The Palestine Liberation Organization’s executive committee blamed Israeli military raids, settlement expansion, withheld tax revenues and lack of progress on Gaza reconstruction as the reasons for the postponement.

Israel Foreign Affairs Minister Gideon Sa’ar said Abbas is evading democratic accountability.

“His attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability,” he said, in a post on X on Oct. 10. “Just like the other lies about ‘reforms’ that were never implemented — ending payments to terrorists and their families, and stopping incitement in the Palestinian education system.”

Abbas has been president since 2005 and is now in the 22nd year of a four-year term. Abbas has repeatedly cancelled elections before, including in 2021, citing conflict with Israel over voter participation in East Jerusalem.

Last week, foreign affairs ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia and France, issued a joint statement saying they “deeply regret” Abbas’s decision not to move forward with elections.

“We call on the Palestinian Authority to reconsider the decision to postpone elections and to take the necessary steps to hold legislative and presidential elections, without further delay,” the statement issued on Oct. 13 said.

The ministers also said the “significant challenges and impediments have affected the ability to conduct elections” and called on Israel “to refrain from actions that could impede the conduct of elections, including the practical arrangements necessary for all Palestinians to participate.”

The federal government has pledged nearly $600 million in aid for Palestinian civilians since the Israel-Hamas war started in October 2023. Carney recently announced $100 million in aid at the United Nations General Assembly last month, with $80 million in humanitarian aid, while the rest is intended for development funding in security initiatives.

Carney said difficulty remains in getting Canadian aid to people in Gaza, who are facing a humanitarian crisis.

“We have far more resources dedicated to support than are able to be delivered to Gaza,” he said. “So there are many things that are not working in within Palestine, and there are many who are responsible for that.”

stories.title: Jeremy Hansen tapped by Carney as special adviser to feds on space
stories.summary: In April, as part of the Artemis II mission, Hansen and three other astronauts travelled around the moon and further out into space than any humans before them.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed Jeremy Hansen as a special adviser on space — just as the United States takes note of Canada’s efforts to shift its space partnerships toward Europe.

“I’m just super excited to serve Canada in that role,” Hansen said in a video he posted Tuesday on social media.

“There’s so much opportunity to leverage this position that we’re already in, to do more to provide for our sovereignty, our security, our quality of life on the planet, and at the same time make significant contributions on the global stage.”

The role involves advising Carney and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Hansen said.

In April, as part of the Artemis II mission, Hansen and three other astronauts travelled around the moon and further out into space than any humans before them.

Joly said Hansen proposed helping the government “develop a new space strategy” when he left the Canadian Space Agency.

“We had a conversation of how he could continue to have an impact, to contribute, to serve,” she said at an event Tuesday.

Joly said she’s getting feedback from other Canadian astronauts and people in the aerospace sector on the strategy “in order to accelerate innovation and reinforce our international partnerships.”

The offices of Carney and Joly did not respond when asked for details of Hansen’s role, such as its end date and compensation.

On Wednesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced a $20 million agreement on the use of a space launch complex in southern Newfoundland, which builds on a March agreement involving a complex in Nova Scotia.

“Reliable and independent launch access will enable Canada to place critical satellites into orbit even during global uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, or disruptions in foreign launch markets,” McGuinty’s department wrote in a news release.

“With military, emergency response, and government services increasingly dependent on space-based systems, sovereign launch (capacity) protects national interests and enables continuity of operations.”

Hansen’s appointment comes as Canada looks to expand co-operation with European countries in space — and as Washington warns it could seek partners other than Canada for its space missions.

Joly spoke Tuesday at the SpaceBound 2026 Conference. U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra told that same conference that Canada has decided to “move away” from the American firm SpaceX.

“Canada has said that, ‘We’re going to take a look at the European Space Agency, we’re going do more with them,'” he said.

Hoekstra said it was helpful to know that Canada is not interested in partnering with the firm founded by billionaire Elon Musk, who has close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

“It’s kind of like, wow, Canada is really saying for all the investment, all the innovation, all the excellence that is being driven by Elon, we don’t want to be a part of it? OK. That’s fine,” he said.

Hoekstra said the United States will always have a “bias” toward the private sector.

“Competition breeds excellence,” he said.

“What we fight in the United States all the time is to make sure that we never come in and over-regulate it. We’ve had to fight that, in the digital world … We’ll probably have to fight this in the space realm.”

Hoekstra added that the F-35 jet is “the best fighter in the world.” He did not directly mention Ottawa’s decision to pause a planned purchase of F-35s after Trump launched his trade war and repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty.

“We also recognize that Canada’s going through a re-evaluation of how they want to move forward on defence,” he said.

Hoekstra said Washington is waiting to see whether Canada wants to continue decades of airspace co-operation through Norad. He said Trump’s recent security deal with Greenland — which also followed his repeated threats to annex the island — is meant to shore up U.S. security in the North.

“We’re waiting to see exactly where Canada wants to go on this,” he said. “We’d love to do it with Canada. It would be very, very helpful. But at the same time, and I’ve said this for the past year and a half, we are not standing still.”

stories.title: ‘Investment in the future’: PhD grad advances evidence-based health care
stories.summary: Western PhD grad Edith Otalike developed tool to assess participant data helping strengthen evidence used in health-care decisions.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Working with HIV treatment programs in Nigeria, Edith Otalike often wondered how clinicians decided to stop one treatment and start another.

That curiosity sparked an academic journey that would take her from clinical pharmacy to epidemiology.

Now graduating from Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry with a PhD in epidemiology and biostatistics, Otalike is working to strengthen the quality of evidence used to guide health-care decisions.

Growing up in Kaura Namoda, Nigeria, Otalike stood out academically from an early age. She placed first in a state mathematics competition and earned a scholarship to a government boarding school. At 12, she left home to pursue an education her parents could not otherwise afford.

When she finished school in 2004, her academic results stood out again. Her school principal encouraged her to pursue university, advice that stayed with her.

“When I returned home, I refused to go to college, the normal trajectory for girls in my town, because I wanted to attend university,” she said.

It took three attempts to secure admission to university, but Otalike eventually earned a bachelor’s degree in pharmacy and a master’s degree in pharmacology at Usman Dan Fodio University, Sokoto.

While completing her master’s degree, Otalike worked as a clinical pharmacist, managing the pharmacy unit of an infectious disease centre for about two years.

“I saw patients and counselled them, but I also saw how research findings could change the treatments patients received,” she said. “I wanted to learn how to generate evidence that could improve care for the larger population.”

Her interest in the evidence behind treatment decisions led her to enrol in an online epidemiology course through the University of Washington, which introduced her to the research methods underpinning health-care decisions and inspired her to pursue graduate studies in the field.

In 2022, Otalike moved to Canada to pursue her PhD, leaving her three children in Nigeria with their father. They joined her in Canada one year later.

“Pursuing my PhD was an important step in my education, but it meant living apart from my children. I saw it as an investment in the future of both my family and myself, even though the separation was difficult.” – Edith Otalike, PhD’26

Otalike’s doctoral research focused on developing a critical appraisal tool for assessing the quality and reliability of research that combines individual patient data from multiple studies. This type of research synthesis, known as an individual participant data meta-analysis (IPD-MA), allows researchers to examine detailed patient information across studies to better understand how medical interventions affect different populations.

Improper implementation of the method, however, can undermine the trustworthiness of research findings. Without a consistent way to assess IPD-MAs’ quality, researchers May have difficulty determining how much confidence to place in their findings.

Under the supervision of Joel Gagnier, professor in epidemiology and biostatistics at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, Otalike developed a checklist to evaluate these studies. Created with input from international experts and tested in a real-world workflow, the checklist helps researchers assess whether studies have been appropriately planned, conducted, analyzed and interpreted.

The tool could be used to evaluate IPD-MAs examining health interventions across a range of diseases and conditions, such as the use of cannabidiol to manage chronic pain.

Looking back, Otalike is proud of achieving her academic goals – from a young student determined to attend university to a PhD graduate.

“Leaving home at 12 was a huge adjustment, but I learned to be independent, take more responsibility for myself, and do well in school,” she said. “Looking back, that experience helped prepare me to adapt to unfamiliar environments and led me to where I am today.”

Moving forward, she hopes to apply her expertise in evidence synthesis, informing health-care decisions in both Canada and Nigeria.

“My dream is still in the making,” she said. “I want to independently lead research that helps decision-makers understand which treatments and health interventions offer meaningful benefits and make the best use of available resources. My goal is to contribute to a stronger health system and more equitable access to effective care.”

stories.title: Wainwright residents line highway to salute soldiers after tragic fire
stories.summary: Town of roughly 7,000 wanted to show support for the military, says Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Two buses carrying soldiers from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright were greeted by flag-waving supporters on an Alberta highway Wednesday, days after a deadly military base fire.

Many in the crowd of about 300 also held up signs thanking those troops, who were not among the injured in the fire, for their service.

One sign said, “Wainwright stands with you.”

“Our condolences for your comrades and thank you for your service,” said another.

Troops taking part in training at the base in Wainwright, Alta., southeast of Edmonton, were overwhelmed by a wind-whipped grass fire Saturday. Four were killed and dozens were injured.

The four killed were identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Two buses carrying soldiers from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright were greeted by flag-waving supporters on an Alberta highway, days after a deadly fire. Many in the crowd of about 300 also held up signs thanking those troops, who were not among the injured, for their service. Four were killed in the Saturday blaze.

The Canadian Press

Initially, 39 wounded went to various hospitals.

As of Wednesday, there were 27, with 13 in critical condition, said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

Three are from Ontario, and that province has sent medical staff, including surgeons, and equipment to Alberta to help, she added.

“Some of the burns are 30 per cent to 80 per cent of their entire body,” Smith said. “Sometimes the changing of those dressings can take up to two hours per patient.”

During the highway tribute Wednesday, two military helicopters flew over head as the two Forces buses drove slowly past the crowd.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town of roughly 7,000 people wanted to show support for the military.

“It’s a Highway of Heroes kind of thing in our own little community,” he said.

“After the incident, they continued on with their training and continued to do their jobs. And so I think the least we can do is show a sense of pride in them and appreciation for what they’re doing.”

Among those on the highway were several soldiers from the base, some holding regimental and Canadian flags.

Dolly Brooks and her husband were carrying flags. Her walker was also festooned with a flag and a yellow “Support Our Troops” ribbon.

Dan Brooks spent 33 years in the Forces, and the couple has lived in Wainwright for most of that time. The base is important to both of them.

“I’ve noticed from near and far and all over the world that we’re getting the support that we need and how we come together when we really need to,” said Dolly Brooks.

Her husband said always it’s painful when a soldier dies. “It’s not easy. It’s not the first time I’ve seen a soldier pass on and it’s never nice.

“You always just hope that there’s a learning curve from what happened here, so we can prevent it in the future.”

Rhea Lovely grew up in a military family and her father was driving one of the buses. She said it has hit the community hard.

“Everyone’s been kind of sombre. The whole town’s been really quiet, but we’re just looking to support our troops because they are our town,” she said.

“It doesn’t matter where they were from in Canada. They are still family.”

A huge pile of flowers continues to grow at the cenotaph in Wainwright after four soldiers were killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong. Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically. Six have since been discharged, says the defence minister.

The outpouring of goodwill comes on the same day that churches in the community were preparing to hold a prayer evening vigil for those killed and injured in the fire.

Many in the crowd of about 300 also held up signs thanking those troops, who were not among the injured in the fire, for their service.
One sign said, “Wainwright stands with you.”
“Our condolences for your comrades and thank you for your service,” said another.
Troops taking part in training at the base in Wainwright, Alta., southeast of Edmonton, were overwhelmed by a wind-whipped grass fire Saturday. Four were killed and dozens were injured.

The four killed were identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Many in the crowd of about 300 also held up signs thanking those troops, who were not among the injured, for their service. Four were killed in the Saturday blaze.

Initially, 39 wounded went to various hospitals.
As of Wednesday, there were 27, with 13 in critical condition, said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.
Three are from Ontario, and that province has sent medical staff, including surgeons, and equipment to Alberta to help, she added.
“Some of the burns are 30 per cent to 80 per cent of their entire body,” Smith said. “Sometimes the changing of those dressings can take up to two hours per patient.”
During the highway tribute Wednesday, two military helicopters flew over head as the two Forces buses drove slowly past the crowd.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town of roughly 7,000 people wanted to show support for the military.
“It’s a Highway of Heroes kind of thing in our own little community,” he said.

“After the incident, they continued on with their training and continued to do their jobs. And so I think the least we can do is show a sense of pride in them and appreciation for what they’re doing.”
Among those on the highway were several soldiers from the base, some holding regimental and Canadian flags.
Dolly Brooks and her husband were carrying flags. Her walker was also festooned with a flag and a yellow “Support Our Troops” ribbon.
Dan Brooks spent 33 years in the Forces, and the couple has lived in Wainwright for most of that time. The base is important to both of them.
“I’ve noticed from near and far and all over the world that we’re getting the support that we need and how we come together when we really need to,” said Dolly Brooks.
Her husband said always it’s painful when a soldier dies. “It’s not easy. It’s not the first time I’ve seen a soldier pass on and it’s never nice.
“You always just hope that there’s a learning curve from what happened here, so we can prevent it in the future.”
Rhea Lovely grew up in a military family and her father was driving one of the buses. She said it has hit the community hard.
“Everyone’s been kind of sombre. The whole town’s been really quiet, but we’re just looking to support our troops because they are our town,” she said.
“It doesn’t matter where they were from in Canada. They are still family.”

“These things will live with the person,” Mast said. “I think what we hope to do is to be available for those who are going to be wrestling with this for a few weeks.
“This isn’t something that just goes away.”

stories.title: Deceased male found in St. Thomas park
stories.summary: St. Thomas are investigating after a body was found in Athletic Park Wednesday afternoon.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
St. Thomas are investigating after a body was found in Athletic Park Wednesday afternoon.

The body was located in a body of water inside the park.

St. Thomas police confirmed it was a male, but the identification is unknown.

Officers responded to the area after a citizen discovered the body.

The coroner attended the scene and will continue the investigation along with police.

Police tell CTV News they don’t believe the death to be suspicious, or criminal in nature.

Athletic Park was closed on Wednesday afternoon, police cleared the scene at about 4:30 p.m.

stories.title: Canadian news publishers worried about Meta’s new terms of service
stories.summary: Canadian news companies say they’re worried about changes to Meta’s terms of service and want the company to clarify how they will be affected.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canadian news companies say they’re worried about changes to Meta’s terms of service and want the company to clarify how they will be affected.

Meta’s changes to its terms of service, first reported by Neiman Lab, led some to suggest the terms could allow scraping of websites associated with a business account for AI training purposes.

Meta has now revised those terms and the company says they don’t change how it uses web crawlers, but the anxiety has not abated and European and British publishers are asking governments and regulators to step in.

The Canadian Association of Broadcasters says its members have raised concerns and that, at a minimum, Meta should be transparent about how the new terms will affect Canadian outlets.

Publishers’ association News Media Canada says it is very concerned and seeking clarity.

The fact Meta blocks news content in Canada is creating additional uncertainty over how Canadian outlets could be affected by the new terms.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney won’t rule out giving Alberta a Quebec-style immigration deal
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Tuesday the Liberals have lost control of immigration and provinces should have more control over their intake numbers.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is not ruling out giving Alberta more authority over immigration along the lines of a deal Ottawa signed with Quebec in the early 1990s.

Reporters on Parliament Hill asked the prime minister on Wednesday if Ottawa could reach an agreement on immigration powers with Alberta similar to the one with Quebec.

“We’ll see,” Carney replied in French.

He added that “Quebec is distinct” because of its culture and language and said Ottawa will also talk with the other provinces about immigration levels.

Following the failure of the Meech Lake accord, the federal government signed an agreement with Quebec in 1991 which granted the province the power to set its own economic immigration targets.

Carney’s comments come after just over a million Albertans voted yes on a referendum question calling for more provincial control over immigration policy to reduce the number of newcomers to “sustainable levels.”

About 53 per cent of voters said yes to that question, according to preliminary results available on Wednesday. The officially certified results are due later next week.

At a news conference in Calgary on Wednesday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she told Carney the day before that her government is putting together a “proposal” for the federal government.

“We have been looking for some inspiration from Quebec’s 1991 Canada-Quebec accord,” she said.

In his English remarks, Carney argued his government has “retaken control” of immigration and is listening to the provinces.

“We have been having discussions with the provinces’ first ministers around getting immigration, first and foremost, to the right levels,” Carney said.

“I just want to underscore we will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable. We’re getting them to that level now.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Tuesday the Liberals have lost control of immigration and provinces should have more control over their intake numbers since they must deliver services for newcomers.

“Recently, the prime minister went to The New York Times, a foreign newspaper, to tell them that he wants to increase immigration. That too is a mistake,” Poilievre said in Calgary on Tuesday.

“It shows he is totally out of touch. Immigration is totally out of control.”

Carney told the U.S. newspaper last month that the next question his government faces is when to “resume some controlled increase in the population.”

The federal Conservatives sent out a fundraising email to party supporters this week saying immigration should be “dramatically reduced,” not “ramped back up.”

Immigration Minister Lena Diab did not respond to reporters’ questions when she walked into the weekly Liberal caucus meeting Wednesday. Federal immigration levels are due for an update by next month.

The federal government had set out plans to increase the national target for permanent residents to 500,000 a year. But Ottawa changed course and slashed the targets in its 2024-2025 plan.

The most recent plan sets out targets of 385,000 permanent resident admissions this year, 370,000 next year and the same figure for 2028.

— with files from David Baxter

stories.title: U.S. embassy accuses Canadian politicians of election meddling
stories.summary: Embassy releases list of quotes which it says indicate ‘plans to influence American politics’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed the suggestion of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claims indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

It includes quotes offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

The Canadian Press asked for comment from Joly but she was not made available.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill Wednesday, Carney – flanked by Joly – responded to a question about the U.S. list by pointing out that the United States initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, noting he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities. That’s what we’re going to focus on, and the people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control over Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast released on Oct. 14, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the event.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

stories.title: The PQ's new superminister will be in charge of planning Quebec's next referendum
stories.summary: Catherine Gentilcore will be juggling the crucial jobs of deputy premier and minister for Quebec’s accession to independence, among others.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will have his very own “superminister.”

Catherine Gentilcore, the member of the National Assembly for Terrebonne, will be juggling the crucial jobs of Quebec deputy premier, minister of immigration and integration and minister responsible for Quebec’s access to independence.

On top of that, she will be acting as the government house leader — a crucial job as the Parti Québécois government will have to find dancing partners in a minority situation.

Before entering politics, Gentilcore worked as an administrator in Quebec’s cultural sector. She made her entrance in the provincial legislature after winning a byelection in 2025 and rapidly became one of St-Pierre Plamondon’s most trusted allies.

The PQ is promising to hold a third referendum for Quebec to separate from Canada after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the Oval Office in January 2029.

St-Pierre Plamondon said on Wednesday that Gentilcore will be responsible for preparing for this commitment once the time comes. The PQ has already promised to put aside approximately $130 million to fulfill the promise of this referendum.

“While challenges mount in healthcare, education, and housing, he has chosen to allocate taxpayer money to a minister tasked with laying the groundwork for a referendum,” Milliard wrote.

Gentilcore told reporters that she will be assisted by a team of officials to start the consultation process that will eventually lead to a referendum.

The premier said his minister will be “ensuring that the ensuing debate on Quebec’s independence is grounded in facts, the public interest, and our commitment to securing the best possible future for Quebec among the options before us.”

St-Pierre Plamondon also expressed the desire to have this democratic process unfold in the “best possible conditions.”

“You will therefore serve as the guardian of this space for reflection and as the manager of the critical preparatory stages of this project — leading up to the point when our government consults the people of Quebec regarding their future within Canada.”

The new premier is entrusting her, as minister of immigration and integration, with the complicated task of lowering permanent immigration levels to 35,000 people per year.

Gentilcore is expected to present Quebec’s annual immigration plan next month, as requested by law, once the work of the legislature resumes on November 24.

But most of her work will be carved out for her as she will be busy negotiating with opposition parties to garner support for the government’s bills.

The first piece of legislation from the PQ is expected to freeze the salaries of elected officials and senior executives of Crown corporations until the budget is balanced.

“Quebecers want Parliament to function. You will therefore have a mandate to collaborate with the opposition parties and ensure that progress is made, solely in the interest of the people of Quebec,” St-Pierre Plamondon told Gentilcore.

“You are, I believe, the best person to find common ground, while respecting the principles that guide our political action,” he added.

St-Pierre Plamondon promised a smaller cabinet. He named 22 ministers — six fewer than the CAQ government before him — so many of his picks find themselves juggling multiple portfolios and are expected to deliver targeted results in a short timeframe.

The new premier is himself the minister responsible for combatting homelessness, one of his core priorities. He is promising to reduce homelessness by 50 per cent.

As expected, Quebec’s Lieutenant-Governor was physically absent from the swearing-in ceremony, instead signing the appointment documents from her office.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Quebec lieutenant did not seem to really be bothered by the exclusion of the Crown’s representative.

“Frankly, I don’t think many people in Quebec are concerned about whether the Lieutenant Governor is on-site or in her office,” Joël Lightbound said. “As far as I’m concerned, it’s the least of our priorities.”

National Post calevesque@postmedia.com
