stories.title: U.S. embassy accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections
stories.summary: Ottawa — The U.S. embassy in Canada has released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it says indicate "plans to influence American politics."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed the suggestion of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claims indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

It includes quotes offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

The Canadian Press asked for comment from Joly but she was not made available.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the U.S. list by pointing out that the United States initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, noting he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities. That’s what we’re going to focus on, and the people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control over Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast released on Oct. 14, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the event.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed the suggestion of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claims indicate “plans to influence American politics.”
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

It includes quotes offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.
The Canadian Press asked for comment from Joly but she was not made available.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the U.S. list by pointing out that the United States initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.
Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.
“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, noting he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities. That’s what we’re going to focus on, and the people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms.”
Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control over Congress.
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.
During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast released on Oct. 14, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.
Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.
Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.
Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the event.
In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”
Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”
Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”
Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.
Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: ‘We build it like a jigsaw puzzle’: Canada’s first robotic roof truss manufacturing line opens in Huron County, Ont.
stories.summary: The announcement was made Wednesday by Sarnia-Lambton MP Marilyn Gladu on behalf of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson during a groundbreaking ceremony at the site.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
You’re looking at Canada’s first robotic roof truss manufacturing line, and it is located in Huron County, Ont.

“The robotics go slower than human beings, but they’re consistent,” said the Founder and President of Atlas Engineered Products, Hadi Abassi.

Abassi bought Clinton Truss in 2018, with the idea of revolutionizing how roof trusses were built in Canada. Two years ago, he started construction of this $20 million facility in Vanastra, Ont., to robotically manufacture roof trusses, streamlining the production process from start to finish.

“And not just trusses. We have the same system, and same vision for the component construction, for the walls section and floor sections,” said Abassi.

With 10 factories across Canada, Abassi aims to build homes piece by piece, and deliver them to construction sites across North America, speeding up the on-site home construction process.

“We will take a set of plans. We will break it out. We build it like a jigsaw puzzle. Very simple puzzle. So instead of taking three or four months to build from the foundation up, we can do this with the installation crew in four to five days,” said Abassi.

For the previous founder and former owner of Clinton Truss, Harvey Poirier, seeing his former company on the cutting edge of truss construction is nothing short of astounding.

“We heard them talking about this about two years ago or something like it. It looks pretty good so far,” said Poirier.

Huron East Mayor Bernie MacLellan says he’s happy to see a company started 28 years ago moving into the future and doing so in Huron County.

“People didn’t understand that it was in Vanastra, but they had a great reputation to begin with. And now they’re just taking it to the next level and doing automation that nobody else in Canada has ever done before,” said MacLellan.

Abassi says they’ll have a mix of manual and robotic truss manufacturing for the time being, with an expansion of jobs from the current 40 employees in the near future.

“We’re hoping that we can double that very soon. Right now, we have asked for 20 more people for this facility. You cannot do it without human beings, but it’s a great compliment to the human being. You still need the race car drivers, but you have an amazing car to drive now,” said Abassi.

Helping to enable the expansion in Vanastra, a $4 million grant from Natural Resources Canada’s Forestry Innovation Support Program.

stories.title: Federal government announces billions for tariff-impacted industries in Ontario
stories.summary: Prime Minister Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford have unveiled a nearly $9 billion in supports for the province’s tariff-hit auto and steel sectors.
stories.author: Joshua Freeman
stories.content:
Prime Minister Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford have unveiled a nearly $9 billion in supports for the province’s tariff-hit auto and steel sectors.

The commitments under the “new action plan” include $5 billion to help upgrade Ontario steel mills and $2.5 billion to help the province’s ailing auto industry pivot to electric vehicle production.

There is also $1 billion to help build roads to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region in Northern Ontario.

The prime minister framed the plan as part of ongoing efforts to bolster Canada’s economy in the face of a drawn-out trade war with the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war has dragged on for more than a year and a half, slamming key Canadian sectors, including automotive and steel manufacturing.

“U.S. tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades. They have raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty,” Carney said during a joint news conference with Ford in Ottawa on Wednesday afternoon.

“We can’t control what others do, so we are focusing on what we can control—and building Canada strong at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”

Carney said the investments would help to create 70,000 jobs linked to the Ring of Fire and protect some 220,000 linked to the other industries.

“Protecting what we have is not enough. We must go further. To transform our economy. To secure our future,” the prime minister said.

Premier Ford welcomed the “historic agreement,” which will see Ontario pitching in $2.67 billion.

“As we stand here today, it’s clear that Canada’s relationship with the United States has changed permanently,” Ford said.

“No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were, and we need to plan accordingly.”

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Danielle Smith tells UCP separatists to accept Alberta referendum result or leave the party
stories.summary: Premier stresses need for unity within province’s conservative movement, warns infighting would deliver next election to Alberta NDP
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is urging separatists to accept the results of Monday’s referendum or leave her United Conservative Party in an effort to stave off an internal civil war that she says would sink the party in next year’s provincial election.

Ms. Smith, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday, stressed the need for unity within the province’s conservative movement and warned that infighting would hand the general election scheduled for next October to the Alberta NDP.

But Ms. Smith was not clear about what measures she’s willing to take to smother separatist leanings inside her party. She said she expects MLAs, UCP nominees and members of her party’s board and constituency associations to be committed to “a strong Alberta within a united Canada.”

“As a party, we cannot permit the next year to be one of internal division and endless debates about separation, when Albertans have spoken so clearly against it,” Ms. Smith said in the video.

Until now, Ms. Smith had not shared how she planned to address the large segment of her coalition that supports separation – particularly after the possibility of a future referendum was soundly defeated on Monday night.

Albertans rejected the prospect of separation, with roughly 75 per cent of voters preferring to remain in Canada rather than hold a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith has pledged not to hold another separation referendum as long as she’s Premier, while pointing to her plan to carve out more autonomy from the federal government. She decided in May to put the question to electors after a separatist petition trying to force a binding vote ran into a legal roadblock.

The Premier was explicit in her Wednesday video about the party’s position on separation: “The United Conservative Party is not an independence party.”

“And for those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party.”

She indicated on Wednesday that her party is turning its focus to the next provincial election. Her popularity has suffered in public opinion polls over recent months, underlined by a shocking by-election loss for her party last month in Calgary’s conservative heartland.

Leading up to the referendum, the Alberta NDP under Leader Naheed Nenshi attempted to paint Ms. Smith as a separatist. Ms. Smith said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada, and she campaigned for the remain side last week with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Ms. Smith has been facing frustration from many of those in her party who felled former premier Jason Kenney and subsequently hoisted her to the Premier’s Office in 2022, largely on the back of frustration over COVID-19 restrictions. Many of those people now harbour separatist sentiment.

In the days since the referendum, the same group has set its sights on electing allies to the party board at the Ucp’s annual meeting in November and as party nominees for the next provincial election. Some have vocally agitated to oust Ms. Smith from office while others have quietly supported her leadership.

The separation issue has, at times this year, pitted her against party brass.

In May, UCP President Rob Smith said he believed a majority of party members would vote to leave Canada, and that the party wouldn’t take a position on the referendum.

Last week, Mr. Smith, who holds no relation to the Premier, wrote on social media that there would be no purity test for party members. He did not respond to an interview request on Wednesday.

“No one will be ‘banned’ or disqualified from membership,” Mr. Smith wrote. “Under no circumstances will that happen. No way. Never.”

The video was Ms. Smith’s first public attempt at stifling separatist rumblings in her party. But she refused to clarify whether she would take steps to limit secessionists from running in party board or nomination races.

”I think a lot of people, when they do their own self-reflection, they make their own decisions about what their pathway would be," she told reporters.

“I’m asking people to do some self-reflection, and if they are able to accept the results and the mandate that Albertans gave us through a free and democratic process, then we can have a reset.”

Ms. Smith’s message didn’t sit well with leading separatists.

Keith Wilson, a lawyer and co-chair of Let Alberta Decide, said in an interview that he thought the Premier was implicitly shutting the door on a key segment of the party.

“It felt like what the Premier was saying today is that if you’re a separatist, you’re not welcome in the UCP,” Mr. Wilson said. “I don’t think she said that expressly, but I know that’s how it’s being felt by many members.”

He added: “Rather than trying to correct the split and unify the party, she might have inadvertently driven a bigger wedge into it.”

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said this week that he’s continuing to try getting like-minded members elected to the party board, while his separatist colleague Jeffrey Rath has continued his calls for the party membership to oust Ms. Smith.

Mr. Sylvestre said on Wednesday in an interview that he’s not leaving the party and argued the blame would be on Ms. Smith if the UCP loses the next election.

“We put them there to do a job. They have not done the job,” he said.

Mr. Sylvestre said Ms. Smith has failed on three issues that he believes would give Alberta greater autonomy: withdrawing from the Canada Pension Plan, creating a provincial police force and taking strong action on immigration.

Mr. Wilson, however, encouraged Ms. Smith to ignore Mr. Sylvestre’s agitating, adding that he supports her desire to pursue greater autonomy within Confederation.

The Alberta NDP declined to comment on the Ucp’s internal party politics.

Elections Alberta was still counting ballots on Wednesday evening on the other nine questions Ms. Smith put to voters in Monday’s referendum.

With 96 per cent of polls reporting, most of those proposals on immigration and constitutional issues had received support ranging between 50 per cent and 55 per cent. Two constitutional proposals on judicial appointments and federal funding had dropped below 50 per cent and one proposing proof-of-citizenship at provincial election polls had earned 60-per-cent support.

Ms. Smith said the results provide her a mandate to work with Ottawa to give Alberta more say over immigration.

But she hedged on whether she would move forward with the other proposals, such as limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services and charging them premiums for using Alberta’s education and health care systems.

“I would say that the results that I saw suggest we proceed with caution,” she said.
paragraphs: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is urging separatists to accept the results of Monday’s referendum or leave her United Conservative Party in an effort to stave off an internal civil war that she says would sink the party in next year’s provincial election.

Ms. Smith, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday, stressed the need for unity within the province’s conservative movement and warned that infighting would hand the general election scheduled for next October to the Alberta NDP.

But Ms. Smith was not clear about what measures she’s willing to take to smother separatist leanings inside her party. She said she expects MLAs, UCP nominees and members of her party’s board and constituency associations to be committed to “a strong Alberta within a united Canada.”
“As a party, we cannot permit the next year to be one of internal division and endless debates about separation, when Albertans have spoken so clearly against it,” Ms. Smith said in the video.

Until now, Ms. Smith had not shared how she planned to address the large segment of her coalition that supports separation – particularly after the possibility of a future referendum was soundly defeated on Monday night.
Albertans rejected the prospect of separation, with roughly 75 per cent of voters preferring to remain in Canada rather than hold a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith has pledged not to hold another separation referendum as long as she’s Premier, while pointing to her plan to carve out more autonomy from the federal government. She decided in May to put the question to electors after a separatist petition trying to force a binding vote ran into a legal roadblock.
The Premier was explicit in her Wednesday video about the party’s position on separation: “The United Conservative Party is not an independence party.”

“And for those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party.”

She indicated on Wednesday that her party is turning its focus to the next provincial election. Her popularity has suffered in public opinion polls over recent months, underlined by a shocking by-election loss for her party last month in Calgary’s conservative heartland.

Leading up to the referendum, the Alberta NDP under Leader Naheed Nenshi attempted to paint Ms. Smith as a separatist. Ms. Smith said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada, and she campaigned for the remain side last week with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Ms. Smith has been facing frustration from many of those in her party who felled former premier Jason Kenney and subsequently hoisted her to the Premier’s Office in 2022, largely on the back of frustration over COVID-19 restrictions. Many of those people now harbour separatist sentiment.

In the days since the referendum, the same group has set its sights on electing allies to the party board at the Ucp’s annual meeting in November and as party nominees for the next provincial election. Some have vocally agitated to oust Ms. Smith from office while others have quietly supported her leadership.
The separation issue has, at times this year, pitted her against party brass.
In May, UCP President Rob Smith said he believed a majority of party members would vote to leave Canada, and that the party wouldn’t take a position on the referendum.
Last week, Mr. Smith, who holds no relation to the Premier, wrote on social media that there would be no purity test for party members. He did not respond to an interview request on Wednesday.
“No one will be ‘banned’ or disqualified from membership,” Mr. Smith wrote. “Under no circumstances will that happen. No way. Never.”

The video was Ms. Smith’s first public attempt at stifling separatist rumblings in her party. But she refused to clarify whether she would take steps to limit secessionists from running in party board or nomination races.
”I think a lot of people, when they do their own self-reflection, they make their own decisions about what their pathway would be," she told reporters.
“I’m asking people to do some self-reflection, and if they are able to accept the results and the mandate that Albertans gave us through a free and democratic process, then we can have a reset.”
Ms. Smith’s message didn’t sit well with leading separatists.
Keith Wilson, a lawyer and co-chair of Let Alberta Decide, said in an interview that he thought the Premier was implicitly shutting the door on a key segment of the party.

“It felt like what the Premier was saying today is that if you’re a separatist, you’re not welcome in the UCP,” Mr. Wilson said. “I don’t think she said that expressly, but I know that’s how it’s being felt by many members.”
He added: “Rather than trying to correct the split and unify the party, she might have inadvertently driven a bigger wedge into it.”

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said this week that he’s continuing to try getting like-minded members elected to the party board, while his separatist colleague Jeffrey Rath has continued his calls for the party membership to oust Ms. Smith.
Mr. Sylvestre said on Wednesday in an interview that he’s not leaving the party and argued the blame would be on Ms. Smith if the UCP loses the next election.
“We put them there to do a job. They have not done the job,” he said.

Mr. Sylvestre said Ms. Smith has failed on three issues that he believes would give Alberta greater autonomy: withdrawing from the Canada Pension Plan, creating a provincial police force and taking strong action on immigration.
Mr. Wilson, however, encouraged Ms. Smith to ignore Mr. Sylvestre’s agitating, adding that he supports her desire to pursue greater autonomy within Confederation.
The Alberta NDP declined to comment on the Ucp’s internal party politics.
Elections Alberta was still counting ballots on Wednesday evening on the other nine questions Ms. Smith put to voters in Monday’s referendum.

With 96 per cent of polls reporting, most of those proposals on immigration and constitutional issues had received support ranging between 50 per cent and 55 per cent. Two constitutional proposals on judicial appointments and federal funding had dropped below 50 per cent and one proposing proof-of-citizenship at provincial election polls had earned 60-per-cent support.
Ms. Smith said the results provide her a mandate to work with Ottawa to give Alberta more say over immigration.

But she hedged on whether she would move forward with the other proposals, such as limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services and charging them premiums for using Alberta’s education and health care systems.
“I would say that the results that I saw suggest we proceed with caution,” she said.

stories.title: Highway 26 closed in Meaford following crash
stories.summary: Highway 26 is closed in Meaford after a crash at the intersection of Highway 26 and Grey Road 15.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Highway 26 is closed in Meaford after a crash at the intersection of Highway 26 and Grey Road 15.

Police have confirmed that emergency services are on scene and those involved are being assessed for injuries.

Drivers are told Highway 26 is closed in both directions from 28th Avenue East to 8th Concession North. Grey Road 15 is also closed from Highway 26 to Concession Road A.

You are asked to avoid the area and use different routes while crews work on scene. Updates to come as OPP makes them available.

stories.title: Toddler critically injured as car hits five children, daycare worker in Oshawa
stories.summary: Two-year-old girl suffers life-threatening injuries, is rushed to Toronto-area trauma centre by air ambulance
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Durham regional police say a two-year-old girl was critically injured when a car struck a group of young children and a daycare worker in Oshawa.

Acting Sgt. Nicholas Gluckstein says the daycare worker was on her daily walk with five children through a residential neighbourhood this morning when they were all struck by a car while crossing the street.

He says the two-year-old girl suffered life-threatening injuries and was taken to a local hospital before being rushed by air ambulance to a Toronto-area trauma centre.

The officer says police are “hoping for the best” but the girl’s injuries are “very serious.”

The four other children who were hit, ranging in age from three years to just seven months, were hospitalized with minor injuries, Gluckstein said, while the adult daycare worker suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Gluckstein says the driver of the car was heading south and making a left turn through an intersection controlled by two stop signs when they struck the six pedestrians.

“The person driving southbound, there are no stop signs for them to potentially stop and take a look around there. But five children and an adult female crossing the road is a pretty large sight to see,” the officer told reporters at the scene, noting investigators are looking into what speed the car was travelling and whether distracted driving played a role in the crash.

Gluckstein said there’s no indication the driver, who remained at the scene and is co-operating with police, was impaired.

He said the driver was hospitalized with minor injuries after the crash.

Gluckstein said investigators are exploring possible charges as they continue to speak with witnesses and look to pull surveillance camera footage from residents in the area.

He urged drivers to slow down, obey the rules of the road and be aware of their surroundings.

stories.title: Feds pull multiple government websites after critical vulnerability uncovered by AI
stories.summary: Multiple Government of Canada web pages were pulled offline for "urgent maintenance."
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Multiple Government of Canada websites were pulled offline for “urgent maintenance” after two major cybersecurity flaws were discovered in a programming language that underpins the majority of web pages around the world.

On Wednesday, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomo n confirmed that the government had pulled an undisclosed number of its websites temporarily to patch the vulnerabilities revealed earlier in the day. The “critical” flaws were discovered in PHP, a popular programming language that supports a “substantial” proportion of websites across the world.

“Some Government of Canada websites have been temporarily taken offline as a precaution to protect government systems and Canadians’ information, following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security,” Solomon said.

He encouraged all Canadian website owners who also use impacted PHP websites to install fixes immediately.

On Wednesday, PHP issued an advisory as well as patches to two major cyber vulnerabilities that were sitting in its software code for years and were recently discovered by artificial intelligence.

Php’s advisory left network defenders scrambling to either take their systems offline or develop a fix of their own until PHP released its own patches a few hours later. But the effects — and potential intrusions — caused by the major vulnerabilities likely won’t be discovered by impacted organizations for days or weeks.

Canada’s warning to quickly patch the two flaws discovered by PHP echoes stark advisories issued by European, American and Asian government agencies, underscoring how the critical the newly-discovered vulnerabilities truly are.

The website for the department of Industry, Science and Economic Development (Ised) appeared to be one affected by the vulnerability. On Wednesday, the department’s homepage displayed an error and told users that the “service is temporarily offline while we carry out urgent maintenance.”

Queries to Ised and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cccs) were redirected to the Treasury Board Secretariat, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Cccs joined international partners such as the United States National Security Agency in calling on all owners of websites using certain versions of PHP to patch their websites immediately or risk an intrusion by cyber threat actors.

The U.S. agency’s warning was extremely direct: patch your system immediately or take your website offline for the time being.

In its advisory, the Cccs also noted it had seen reports of evidence that the vulnerabilities could be exploited by criminal actors, but that there is “no active exploitation being identified at this time,” though “that can change quickly.”

Experts said that the vulnerabilities would have been extremely difficult for hackers to discover previously, but AI has since exponentially reduced the speed at which such issues are discovered.

Ramy Rahman, a senior engineer at U.S.-based cybersecurity firm ArmorCode, said in a release that AI now gives network defenders far less time to guard themselves when a new vulnerability is discovered.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Multiple Government of Canada websites were pulled offline for “urgent maintenance” after two major cybersecurity flaws were discovered in a programming language that underpins the majority of web pages around the world.

On Wednesday, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomo n confirmed that the government had pulled an undisclosed number of its websites temporarily to patch the vulnerabilities revealed earlier in the day. “Some Government of Canada websites have been temporarily taken offline as a precaution to protect government systems and Canadians’ information, following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security,” Solomon said.
He encouraged all Canadian website owners who also use impacted PHP websites to install fixes immediately.

Php’s advisory left network defenders scrambling to either take their systems offline or develop a fix of their own until PHP released its own patches a few hours later. But the effects — and potential intrusions — caused by the major vulnerabilities likely won’t be discovered by impacted organizations for days or weeks.

stories.title: Anti-racism group calls for investigation into OPP recruit evaluations
stories.summary: An anti-racism organization is calling for an investigation into how Ontario’s provincial police force assesses new recruits, as three Black recruits allege they faced racial discrimination during their year of probation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An anti-racism organization is calling for an investigation into how Ontario’s provincial police force assesses new recruits, as three Black recruits allege they faced racial discrimination during their year of probation.

The Black Class Action Secretariat says it wants the province’s inspector general of policing to examine Ontario Provincial Police probationary evaluation and coaching practices as well as probationary outcome data across the force to look for racial disparities.

The group’s director of advocacy says that while the OPP has an internal office that aims to ensure its policies and practices are inclusive, “the question is whether that commitment reaches the coach officer’s notebook, the probation file, and the release decisions.”

In a news conference today at the provincial legislature, Alain Babineau said there are people within police ranks quietly deciding “who belongs in uniform and who does not.”

The call for an investigation comes as the non-profit says three Black recruits stationed in different regions faced a “strikingly similar pattern of discrimination.” The OPP says it’s looking into those concerns.

The secretariat says the recruits, who are sharing the allegations under pseudonyms under fear of reprisals, were mocked and penalized for their accents and communication styles and disciplined for behaviours common among white officers.

Two of the recruits were dismissed before the end of their probation period, while the other remains on medical leave, the group said.

A spokesperson for the OPP said the force acknowledges the concerns raised by the Black Class Action Secretariat on behalf of the three recruits.

“We take these matters seriously and are reviewing the various concerns brought forth,” Staff Sgt. Joe Brisebois said in an email.

The force can’t comment on specifics when it comes to employment-related matters, he said.

“What we can say is that the OPP is dedicated to ensuring open, accessible, equitable and respectful workplaces, and is committed to reflecting the diverse communities it serves,” as well as ensuring a workplace that fosters a safe and inclusive environment, he said.

“We do not condone or tolerate discrimination or harassment of any kind.”

The Inspectorate of Policing, an independent oversight office that opened in 2024, acknowledged The Canadian Press’s request for comment Wednesday but did not immediately provide one.

One of the recruits, who used the pseudonym Paul, said Wednesday he has two master’s degrees and excelled at the police college, but found himself ridiculed and judged for the way he spoke after joining a detachment in the province’s southeast.

“I caught my coach officer and my colleagues ridiculing me. A dispatcher joked on the record about my accent affecting a radio call,” he said, phoning into the news conference.

“When I tried to discuss it, it was used against me,” he said.

Paul said he was one of three Black officers in his detachment and was released from his position after 10 months. The experience changed his career, he said, adding he is “still trying to heal from the mistreatment and discrimination.”

Another of the recruits going by the pseudonym Peter said he “immediately felt isolated” after reporting for duty at a detachment in central Ontario.

“My sergeant would make fun of how I pronounced some words, asking me to repeat things in front of my colleagues so everyone could laugh,” he said in a call played at the news conference.

“I wasn’t coached at all, it just felt like I was being watched to be documented.”

Peter said he was reprimanded for using his phone’s GPS to navigate the city when it was a “common practice” among his white colleagues.

The stress eventually caught up with him, and he went on medical leave in the spring, questioning whether to continue on this career path, he said.

Organizers also shared a statement on behalf of the third recruit, who went by the name John. John said he spent a decade in the human service field before becoming an officer, and was stationed at a detachment in southwestern Ontario — the only Black recruit in his platoon.

“I felt there was no trust or confidence in me from Day One,” the statement said. “It felt like not only did they expect me to fail, they wanted me to fail.”

He also faced reprimand for using his phone GPS when others were doing the same without issue, and at one point had his driving privileges taken away without explanation, he said.

John said he was let go two weeks before the end of his probation, ON grounds that he was not a good fit.

“What it really meant was that I didn’t belong, that they didn’t see me as one of them, that they didn’t want me there,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: New beds added to Saskatoon hospital, full expansion deadline pushed back
stories.summary: The remaining 49 beds are facing delays due to construction at both Market Mall and Saskatoon City Hospital, says Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatchewan is celebrating the addition of more than a dozen new hospital beds at Saskatoon’s City Hospital, but the provincial government is delaying the date when all of its promised beds will be available.

The province’s health ministry says 20 acute-care beds have been added, bringing the total number of new general medicine care beds at City Hospital to 60.

Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill says the remaining 49 promised acute-care beds at the hospital will not be made available by the end of this year as planned due to “construction challenges” at both the hospital and at Market Mall, a shopping centre where some outpatient and continuing care services will relocate to make way for the remaining beds.

“I think it has also given us the opportunity to ensure that when beds and services do come online, they’re staffed and they are ready to go for patients on day one,” Cockrill told reporters at a press conference on the bed expansion Tuesday.

The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) says the construction company tasked with renovating Market Mall has wrapped up the work, with the department receiving keys to the spaces this week.

“Now we’re preparing the space to be able to move over the coming weeks through November,” said Derek Miller, Sha’s chief operating officer.

Miller adds that the geriatric evaluation management unit on Saskatoon City Hospital’s seventh floor, along with the surgical pre-assessment clinic on the fourth floor, will be moved to Market Mall over the next month, making space for the new beds and a pre-assessment clinic.

The initiative is part of a $15 million investment by the Government of Saskatchewan in March 2025 to add 109 acute-care beds at Saskatoon City Hospital to address capacity pressures in the province, with the first 40 beds available at the hospital last November.

The province says it has also completed the expansion of acute-care units at Saskatoon’s two other hospitals, as laid out in its health care plan announced earlier this year. This includes 36 additional inpatient beds at Royal University Hospital (RUH) and 24 acute inpatient beds at St. Paul’s Hospital.

The province says it has hired all required positions for the new beds added to Saskatoon City Hospital and is still looking to fill 39 positions between RUH and St. Paul’s Hospital.

Cockrill said several times Tuesday that the province is moving “expeditiously” to add new beds to address capacity pressures. But the Opposition NDP is pushing back, pointing to a string of incidents in recent months where patients and loved ones recounted receiving treatment in hallways or after hours-long delays.

“The minister thinks that beds treat people and keeps forgetting that staff treat people,” said Keith Jorgenson, associate health critic for the NDP, adding that staffing retention is a major issue within the province’s health-care system.

Jorgenson also pointed to the ongoing negotiations between Saskatchewan and the Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe) Local 5430, representing more than 14,000 health-care workers in the province. The local voted 99 per cent in favour of job action September.

Edmonton resident Neal Ferniuk stood with the NDP Tuesday calling for change after he said his 94-year-old mother with dementia received care in the hallway of RUH for three days after falling and breaking her collarbone in late September.

“It was a year ago that my mom went through this similar thing. It sounds like nothing’s changed. So why is that?” Ferniuk said.

The SHA expects that adding new beds over the coming months will lead to improvements in patients receiving more timely access to services, said Miller, adding that the health authority monitors “very closely” the number of patients who wait for services and how long they are waiting.

The health authority was unable to provide Global News with specific wait-time numbers at Saskatoon City Hospital before and after adding the 60 new acute-care beds over the past 12 months.

Miller adds that the geriatric evaluation management unit on Saskatoon City Hospital’s seventh floor, along with the surgical pre-assessment clinic on the fourth floor, will be moved to Market Mall over the next month, making space for the new beds and a pre-assessment clinic.

The initiative is part of a $15 million investment by the Government of Saskatchewan in March 2025 to add 109 acute-care beds at Saskatoon City Hospital to address capacity pressures in the province, with the first 40 beds available at the hospital last November.

The province says it has also completed the expansion of acute-care units at Saskatoon’s two other hospitals, as laid out in its health care plan announced earlier this year. This includes 36 additional inpatient beds at Royal University Hospital (RUH) and 24 acute inpatient beds at St. Paul’s Hospital.

This includes 36 additional inpatient beds at Royal University Hospital (RUH) and 24 acute inpatient beds at St. Paul’s Hospital.

content_blocks.text: The province says it has hired all required positions for the new beds added to Saskatoon City Hospital and is still looking to fill 39 positions between RUH and St. Paul’s Hospital.
Opposition questions expansion efficacy

Cockrill said several times Tuesday that the province is moving “expeditiously” to add new beds to address capacity pressures. But the Opposition NDP is pushing back, pointing to a string of incidents in recent months where patients and loved ones recounted receiving treatment in hallways or after hours-long delays.

“The minister thinks that beds treat people and keeps forgetting that staff treat people,” said Keith Jorgenson, associate health critic for the NDP, adding that staffing retention is a major issue within the province’s health-care system.

Jorgenson also pointed to the ongoing negotiations between Saskatchewan and the Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe) Local 5430, representing more than 14,000 health-care workers in the province. The local voted 99 per cent in favour of job action September.

content_blocks.text: Edmonton resident Neal Ferniuk stood with the NDP Tuesday calling for change after he said his 94-year-old mother with dementia received care in the hallway of RUH for three days after falling and breaking her collarbone in late September.
“It was a year ago that my mom went through this similar thing. It sounds like nothing’s changed. So why is that?” Ferniuk said.

The SHA expects that adding new beds over the coming months will lead to improvements in patients receiving more timely access to services, said Miller, adding that the health authority monitors “very closely” the number of patients who wait for services and how long they are waiting.

stories.title: Bombers need victory to punch their playoff ticket
stories.summary: Vernon Adams Jr. and the Calgary Stampeders will be B.C. Lions fans this weekend.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
TORONTO – Vernon Adams Jr. and the Calgary Stampeders will be B.C. Lions fans this weekend.

Calgary (9-9) finishes its regular season on a bye week after downing B.C. 32-13 on Saturday. But the Lions will play a key role in determining the Stampeders’ playoff fate.

Calgary is currently third in the West Division. Although the Stampeders are tied with the Saskatchewan Roughriders (9-8) in points, they get the higher spot based on claiming the season series.

But right behind both teams are the Winnipeg Blue Bombers (8-9).

Saskatchewan and Winnipeg each have one regular-season game left to play.

Winnipeg faces B.C. (10-7) in Vancouver on Friday night, needing a win to clinch a post-season berth and end Calgary’s season. But a Lions’ victory would put the Stampeders into the playoffs.

Saskatchewan has already cemented a playoff spot but can finish either third or fourth in the West. The Riders host the Edmonton Elks (13-4) on Saturday.

If the Bombers and Riders both win, Saskatchewan finishes third and faces B.C. in the West semifinal Oct. 31. Winnipeg would take fourth and visit the Toronto Argonauts (9-8) in the East semifinal.

A Winnipeg win and Saskatchewan loss would leave the Bombers third. The Riders would end up fourth.

Should Winnipeg lose and Saskatchewan win, the Riders will finish third, and Calgary would get fourth.

And finally, if Winnipeg and Saskatchewan both lose, Calgary would finish third ahead of the fourth-place Roughriders.

Edmonton and B.C. have cemented the top two spots in the West. Likewise, the Montreal Alouettes (13-4) and Toronto had clinched first and second, respectively, in the East.

Winnipeg will certainly have more to play for Friday night and face a Lions squad that will be missing several regulars. That includes starter Nathan Rourke, as backup quarterback Kaidon Salter will be under centre versus the Bombers.

Winnipeg should remember Salter well. He led B.C. past the Bombers 35-19 on July 30 in his first CFL start.

Salter completed seven-of-15 passes for 96 yards and a touchdown but rushed for 160 yards. Salter also caught a pass for a two-point conversion.

Running back Zander Horvath had 191 yards rushing on 17 carries and three touchdowns in that game. Horvath enters the regular-season finale having scored 18 rushing TDs and 21 overall, leaving him within striking distance of two CFL single-season marks.

Mike Pringle holds the league record for most rushing TDs in a season (19) while Milt Stegall’s 23 touchdowns in 2002 remains the CFL single-season standard.

Pick: Winnipeg.

Montreal Alouettes vs. Toronto Argonauts (Friday night)

At Toronto, both teams will likely rest key regulars in a contest that has no impact on the East Division standings. Quarterback Chad Kelly (lower body) won’t play for the Argos after being injured in last week’s loss to Ottawa. Veteran Nick Arbuckle should start, but Tucker Horn and Luis Perez could also see action. Montreal rested many of its top players in last week’s loss to Saskatchewan and is expected to do the same for this contest.

Pick: Toronto.

Ottawa Redblacks vs. Hamilton Tiger-Cats (Saturday afternoon)

At Hamilton, rookie Bryson Barnes makes a second straight start after leading Ottawa (1-16) to its first win of the year, a 40-39 decision over Toronto. Barnes threw for 339 yards and two TDs — both to Ayden Eberhardt — in his first CFL start. The Ticats (5-12) come off the bye week and downed the Redblacks 34-16 at TD Place on Oct. 2 with veteran McLeod Bethel-Thompson under centre. At least the home team has film on Barnes to evaluate in its preparation. Harrison Frost threw for 342 yards and two TDs versus Ottawa three weeks ago but didn’t practise either Tuesday or Wednesday with an elbow ailment.

Pick: Ottawa.

Edmonton Elks vs. Saskatchewan Roughriders (Saturday afternoon)

At Regina, Taylor Powell is expected to start for Edmonton, which will host the West Division final Nov. 7. With that in mind, incumbent QB Cody Fajardo likely won’t be the only veteran who’ll not see the field. Veteran Trevor Harris is expected to see time for the Riders given they’ll be in action next week to open the CFL playoffs. Harris completed 27-of-39 passes for 253 yards with a TD and an interception last week versus Montreal and was also his team’s rushing leader with 36 yards.

Pick: Saskatchewan.

Last week: 2-2.

Overall: 52-25.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon sworn in as Quebec premier, adds independence minister to cabinet
stories.summary: Catherine Gentilcore will be responsible for the sovereignty debate, as well as the PQ’s plan to cut immigration
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was sworn in on Wednesday as Quebec’s 34th premier at the head of a minority Parti Québécois government that includes a minister responsible for charting a path toward the province’s independence.

The new Premier has promised to hold a third referendum on secession, though he has said it will not take place before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029. With just 60 out of 127 seats in the National Assembly, his government May not outlast Mr. Trump’s term in office.

Still, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon highlighted his commitment to sovereignty as he unveiled his 23-member cabinet in Quebec City on Wednesday, ushering in a new government and the possibility of a more fractious relationship with Ottawa.

“The people of Quebec have made their decision,” he said. “They chose to entrust a sovereigntist party with the mandate to form government.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon led his party to victory during Quebec’s Oct. 5 election, but has ended up four seats shy of the 64 he needed for a majority. With most Quebeckers opposed to the idea of a referendum, he won just 28 per cent of the vote, the lowest share of any government in Quebec’s history.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s first cabinet appointment was a minister responsible for Quebec independence. He has chosen Catherine Gentilcore, who was first elected to the National Assembly in a 2025 by-election, for the role. She was also named deputy premier and House leader.

The new minister will be responsible for ensuring the debate on Quebec’s independence “is based on facts, the public interest, and our desire to see Quebec have the best possible future,” the Premier said.

Ms. Gentilcore has also been named Immigration Minister and is tasked with making substantial cuts to the province’s immigration levels.

During the ceremony, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon pointed to areas of friction with the federal government, which he accused of an “abuse of power.”

He said Ottawa’s recent decision to impose dollar-for-dollar countertariffs on the United States “and to exclude Quebec from trade negotiations showed a lack of consideration for Quebec and our interests.”

Louis Aucoin, a communications strategist and former Bloc Québécois staffer, said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon is sending a signal to Ottawa by making the same minister responsible for both independence and immigration, a file that has long been a source of tension between the two levels of government.

He also pointed to the nomination of former prosecutor Marie-Claude Sarrazin to multiple portfolios, including justice, secularism and Canadian intergovernmental affairs – a notable combination of files as the Supreme Court of Canada prepares a highly anticipated decision on Quebec’s controversial secularism law, Bill 21.

“If I were in the federal government, I would hear the message that working with this government is going to be difficult,” Mr. Aucoin said.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has indicated sovereignty is not one of his early priorities, and that he will focus on more urgent issues first, such as tackling the cost of living and cutting government waste. He named himself minister responsible for the fight against homelessness.

The PQ cabinet is smaller than the 29-member Coalition Avenir Québec cabinet that preceded it – the smallest in nearly two decades, the Premier said. He has pledged to reduce government spending and improve efficiency.

Though his caucus includes many political newcomers, several high-profile portfolios went to more experienced legislators. The new Finance Minister is Nicolas Marceau, who occupied the same role under the previous PQ government, elected in 2012.

Marie-Karlynn Laflamme, who won a by-election earlier this year, is Quebec’s new Health Minister, and has been tasked with abolishing Santé Québec, a Crown corporation created by the previous government to operate Quebec’s health care network.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon named newly elected MNA and former party president Dieudonné Ella Oyono as his Minister of International Relations, describing him as one of the most “pro-independence activists” he had met in his time with the PQ.

Earlier this week, the PQ announced that Pascal Paradis, a former MNA who lost his Quebec City seat on Oct. 5, would become the province’s “chief negotiator,” focused on the trade dispute with the U.S. The party said Mr. Paradis, the former executive director of Lawyers Without Borders Canada, would work closely with the province’s International Relations Minister “to restore Quebec’s strong voice and real influence on the international stage.”

This is the province’s first Parti Québécois government since former premier Pauline Marois’s minority government was defeated in 2014. On Wednesday, Ms. Marois told reporters in Quebec City that it wasn’t easy to run a government without a majority of seats in the National Assembly.

“What I found hardest were the roadblocks,” she said.

The PQ won 59 seats on Oct. 5, but a judicial recount on Wednesday found the party had won a 60th riding previously claimed by the Liberals.

Quebec’s Lieutenant-Governor was absent from the ceremony following a request from Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who has promised to abolish the monarchy in Quebec, raising the threat of a constitutional battle.

stories.title: Security camera in Air Canada cargo warehouse could have caught insider in Toronto airport gold heist but wasn't working
stories.summary: But court heard the security camera wasn't working the day a crate carrying more than $22.5 million in almost pure gold and cash was stolen.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
A crucial surveillance camera inside an Air Canada cargo warehouse was not working the day a crate carrying more than $22.5 million in almost pure gold and cash was stolen, a security slip hiding the identity of an airline insider who helped pull off the gold heist, court heard.

Parmpal Sidhu, a 56-year-old former Air Canada cargo warehouse employee, is accused of using his inside access to print off an official Air Canada air waybill that was used by a truck driver to collect the high-value crate stolen in the Toronto airport gold heist in 2023.

Sidhu has pleaded not guilty to theft and conspiracy and his ongoing trial in Ontario Superior Court in Brampton, Ont., featured internal Air Canada security video showing the crate being moved around the airline’s large cargo facility at Pearson airport, loaded onto a truck, and driven off.

Nowhere on the video footage, however, was anyone seen printing or collecting the waybill that was the key to releasing the crate to a gold heist gang instead of to Brink’s security guards, who arrived later to pick it up for a Toronto bank but learned it was nowhere to be found.

The court has heard that Sidhu’s employee ID number was used to access an Air Canada printer within the building to print it, but has also heard that airline cargo employees had woeful computer hygiene and routinely swapped and shared login credentials.

A Peel Regional Police detective, testifying on the witness stand for a second day Wednesday, revealed why the identity of who took the air waybill off the printer and got it into hands of the driver is in any doubt.

Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, asked Det. Sarah Angevine about the police evidence in the case against Sidhu.

“There was no fingerprint of Mr. Sidhu on the air waybill,” Wagman asked.

“Correct,” replied Angevine.

“Do they have cameras at Air Canada cargo?”

“Was that looked at? Was that searched, the surveillance cameras?”

“I do recall that cameras in the area of where that printer was, that printed the waybill, was inoperable on that date,” she said. “Whoever picked it up from the printer was not captured on video.”

Court was not told how long that camera had been inoperable, how it failed, or who might know the status of internal security video monitoring.

Angevine was asked by Wagman about phone contact between Sidhu and another accused in the gold heist who was also an Air Canada employee at the time and was Sidhu’s manager, a man named Simran Preet Panesar.

Court heard earlier there was frequent contact between the phones registered to the two men, both texting and talking. Sidhu had more contact with Panesar leading up to the heist than he did with his wife, court heard.

Wagman suggested it wasn’t strange or odd for an employee and a boss to text and talk more with each other than with a spouse.

“Based on my experience and my relationship,” Angevine said, “I would say it’s a little odd, but maybe not for everybody.” She agreed, though, that it is not strange for a boss and employee to socialize outside work.

Sidhu was working a double shift on the day of the heist, from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

He was on a dinner break at the time the gold was stolen, court heard.

The airplane carrying the gold shipment from Zurich, Switzerland, arrived shortly before 4 p.m., after a nine-hour flight on April 17, 2023. The driver arrived to pick it up around 6:30 p.m., had it loaded onto the truck and left the cargo facility at 7:30 p.m.

Angevine said the phones of the two were in contact multiple times throughout the day, starting early in the morning at 5:35 and continued periodically until 9:44 p.m.

Wagman asked about Sidhu being arrested in January 2024 and charged with mischief after allegedly damaging the front door of someone not accused in the gold heist. Wagman asked the detective if the wiretaps heard in court on Tuesday, appearing to show Sidhu angrily trying to get money and complaining of needing a lawyer, could have related to the mischief charge rather than the gold heist.

“Sure. It could be anything,” she said.

Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic said there were no more witnesses being called in the government’s case. Wagman said he doesn’t expect to call any witnesses.

Judge Gordon Cudjoe said court would reconvene on Wednesday afternoon to hear his rulings on some evidentiary matters.

The Crown and defence will submit written arguments and closing submissions later this week before Cudjoe will deliver a verdict.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Kamloops - The union representing some 1,200 workers at a Teck Resources Ltd. copper mine in the British Columbia Interior has served a 72-hour strike notice.

United Steelworkers Local 7619 says the notice follows unsuccessful negotiations to reach a fair collective agreement with the operator of the Highland Valley Copper site near Logan Lake, B.C.

Feds investing $1 billion for road to Ring of Fire in Ontario: Carney

stories.title: Feds investing $1 billion for road to Ring of Fire in Ontario: Carney
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is putting down $1 billion to help build the road to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region in northern Ontario.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal government will put down $1 billion to help build a controversial road to the Ring of Fire region in northern Ontario, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday.

The region is said to be rich in nickel, chromite, copper and gold and Carney said its development will secure Canada’s critical mineral supply chain.

“Canada is matching Ontario’s $1-billion investment to build road infrastructure to reach the Ring of Fire,” Carney said as he and Premier Doug Ford announced in Ottawa an $8.7-billion joint plan to help Ontario’s tariff-affected industries, including steel and automotive sectors.

The Ring of Fire sits partially in the James Bay lowlands, part of North America’s largest wetland, and is home to a number of remote, fly-in First Nations. Its mineral development has been a major focus for Ford since he took office in 2018.

“We can secure a sovereign supply chain and bolster Canada’s position as a critical minerals leader,” Carney said. “Now, to build those mines, we need roads.”

Earlier this year, Ford announced construction had begun on two of the roads that will eventually connect the provincial highway system to the mining area some 500 kilometres north of Thunder Bay, Ont.

Ford had long called for the federal government to match the province’s $1-billion investment in the road project. Ontario’s previous Liberal government had also asked Ottawa to match that money.

“Last December, I joined the prime minister here in Ottawa to sign an agreement that would eliminate federal duplication for the roads to the Ring of Fire,” Ford said Wednesday.

“Thanks to that agreement, we got shovels in the ground on the roads to the Ring of Fire this summer and are well on our way to unlocking, as the prime minister mentioned, 70,000 jobs and $22 billion in economic activity that will be powered by the Ring of Fire’s critical minerals.”

The province has signed partnerships with three First Nations who want the road, while many others are decidedly against it.

Webequie First Nation and Marten Falls First Nation, both remote fly-in communities, want a road to connect to the provincial highway system as well as the economic opportunities in mining the Ring of Fire. They both say it will lift their communities out of poverty.

Aroland First Nation sits further south and its road will be upgraded to handle greater traffic.

Australian mining giant Wyloo and Juno Corp, a Canadian junior mining company, own the vast majority of stakes claimed in the Ring of Fire. Wyloo has proposed to build several mines up north if the road gets built, including a large underground nickel mine.

However, many other First Nations in northern Ontario are against the proposed road and mines. They say they haven’t been consulted and the development will change their way of life.

Neskantaga First Nation and Attawapiskat First Nation have built a settlement where the proposed road will cross the Attawapiskat River. The Canadian Press visited the region last year, including the settlement, where community members plan to block the road whenever construction crews arrive, years from now.

Sol Mamakwa, the provincial New Democrat who represents the riding of Kiiwetinoong, where the Ring of Fire sits, said he was dismayed by the latest news.

He said First Nations are livid at several pieces of provincial and federal legislation, some that have become law, which propose to speed up approvals of large projects, including mines.

“I’ve talked to enough people on the ground that live on these lands for a long time, they’ll be there to protect them and I stand with the rights holders,” Mamakwa said. “Without the proper, free, prior informed consent ... I think that’s going to become an issue.”

Carney said speeding up mine approvals will be imperative, framing it as a way to counter U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods.

But the prime minister said Canada and Ontario are creating “a working group to engage with local Indigenous communities so together we’ll identify opportunities for economic development, conservation and Indigenous protected areas.”

Mamakwa said those words are meaningless.

“It’s just two white men in Ottawa deciding what’s going to happen with our lands,” he said.

“That project will not happen.”

With files from Sarah Ritchie in Ottawa

“Last December, I joined the prime minister here in Ottawa to sign an agreement that would eliminate federal duplication for the roads to the Ring of Fire,” Ford said Wednesday.

“Thanks to that agreement, we got shovels in the ground on the roads to the Ring of Fire this summer and are well on our way to unlocking, as the prime minister mentioned, 70,000 jobs and $22 billion in economic activity that will be powered by the Ring of Fire’s critical minerals.”
The province has signed partnerships with three First Nations who want the road, while many others are decidedly against it.

Webequie First Nation and Marten Falls First Nation, both remote fly-in communities, want a road to connect to the provincial highway system as well as the economic opportunities in mining the Ring of Fire. They both say it will lift their communities out of poverty.
Aroland First Nation sits further south and its road will be upgraded to handle greater traffic.

Australian mining giant Wyloo and Juno Corp, a Canadian junior mining company, own the vast majority of stakes claimed in the Ring of Fire. Wyloo has proposed to build several mines up north if the road gets built, including a large underground nickel mine.
However, many other First Nations in northern Ontario are against the proposed road and mines. They say they haven’t been consulted and the development will change their way of life.

Neskantaga First Nation and Attawapiskat First Nation have built a settlement where the proposed road will cross the Attawapiskat River. The Canadian Press visited the region last year, including the settlement, where community members plan to block the road whenever construction crews arrive, years from now.
Sol Mamakwa, the provincial New Democrat who represents the riding of Kiiwetinoong, where the Ring of Fire sits, said he was dismayed by the latest news.
He said First Nations are livid at several pieces of provincial and federal legislation, some that have become law, which propose to speed up approvals of large projects, including mines.

“I’ve talked to enough people on the ground that live on these lands for a long time, they’ll be there to protect them and I stand with the rights holders,” Mamakwa said. “Without the proper, free, prior informed consent ... I think that’s going to become an issue.”
Carney said speeding up mine approvals will be imperative, framing it as a way to counter U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods.

But the prime minister said Canada and Ontario are creating “a working group to engage with local Indigenous communities so together we’ll identify opportunities for economic development, conservation and Indigenous protected areas.”
Mamakwa said those words are meaningless.
“It’s just two white men in Ottawa deciding what’s going to happen with our lands,” he said.
“That project will not happen.”
With files from Sarah Ritchie in Ottawa

By Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press

OTTAWA - Some government websites have been taken down temporarily as a precaution against a security risk, says Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon.

In a social media post, Solomon says the websites went dark to protect government systems and Canadians’ information following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

He says this is being done in response to a vulnerability identified in PHP, a widely used programming language.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Solomon says this is a global issue and governments and organizations around the world are also taking protective measures.

The FBI’s cyber division says the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, says it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Some Canadian government websites taken offline due to vulnerability: Solomon
stories.summary: Some Government of Canada websites have been taken offline due to a vulnerability identified in the software, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon says.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Some Government of Canada websites have been taken offline due to a vulnerability identified in the software, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon says.

In a social media post, Solomon said this response is temporary and is only a precaution to protect government systems and Canadians’ information.

The guidance came from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

“We take this situation extremely seriously. Thank you to the cyber security teams working to protect the services Canadians rely on. Affected websites will be restored once patches are applied,” said Solomon.

He added this is a global issue and other governments and organizations are also taking protective measures.

Among the websites that appear to be offline are Statistics Canada and Measurement Canada, which is a regulatory agency of Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.

The Fbi’s cyber division says the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, says it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

With files from the Canadian Press

stories.title: Life-threatening injuries reported after Middlesex County collision
stories.summary: In a post on social media, OPP said at least one person appeared to have sustained life-threatening injuries and was expected to be transported for treatment.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A serious two-vehicle collision has closed a rural intersection in Middlesex County, according to Ontario Provincial Police.

Middlesex OPP, along with Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Ornge air ambulance and local fire crews, responded to the crash at the intersection of Nairn Road and Centre Road on Wednesday.

In a post on social media, OPP said at least one person appeared to have sustained life-threatening injuries and was expected to be transported for treatment.

No further information on the extent of injuries or the number of people involved was immediately available.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and seek alternate routes.

stories.title: Man dead in ‘chaotic’ Richmond Hill fire that resulted in homes, vehicles ablaze
stories.summary: It was a “chaotic scene” with three cars fully engulfed in flames between the two houses that were also ablaze, fire crews told reporters Wednesday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man is dead after a fire ripped through two homes and several vehicles in Richmond Hill Wednesday morning.

It was a “chaotic scene” with three cars fully engulfed in flames between the two houses that were also ablaze, fire crews told reporters Wednesday.

The fire began on Crosby Avenue between Newkirk Road and Bayview Avenue around 3 a.m., York Regional Police said. A man was found unresponsive and was transported to hospital where he was later pronounced dead, police said.

The chaos of the environment made it challenging for fire crews to tackle the blaze, said Richmond Hill Fire Chief Tom Raeburn at a morning news conference.

Crews were still putting out hot spots on one of the homes when a man was pulled from the basement window, said Raeburn. Several other residents were able to escape on their own.

It was challenging to access the entrances to the houses, as some of the vehicles on fire were blocking the path, he said. The cause of the fire is unknown, and it is too early to determine if the incident is suspicious, said Raeburn.

David West, the mayor of Richmond Hill said Wednesday that “this is a heartbreaking morning for our community.”

“The hearts of the community of Richmond Hill are with the family and everyone affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement published to social media.

The Office of the Fire Marshal has been called and is working alongside investigators to determine the origin of the blaze.
