stories.title: Poll suggests PQ referendum pledge cost party majority as Alberta vote fuels sovereignty debate
stories.summary: A post-election poll suggests the Parti Québécois could have won a majority government if it had not pledged to hold a sovereignty referendum in its first mandate.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
A new poll suggests the Parti Québécois’ pledge to hold a sovereignty referendum in its first mandate cost the party a majority government as Quebec politicians draw competing lessons from a referendum in Alberta.

The Léger survey for Le Journal de Montréal, conducted after the Oct. 5 election, found the PQ would have received 35 per cent of the vote if it had not promised to hold a referendum.

That is seven percentage points higher than the 28 per cent of the vote the party received in the election and, according to the poll, would have been enough to secure a majority government.

Instead, the PQ will enter the next legislature with a minority government.

“I think seeing this new poll just confirms what many people thought,” said Daniel Béland, political sociologist and director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.

The same poll found just 20 per cent of respondents favour the PQ organizing a referendum during its first mandate.

“This idea of a third referendum is just not popular. It’s actually very unpopular, and even after this victory of the PQ, there is no change here,” Béland said.

The poll comes as Quebec politicians debate what lessons should be drawn from Monday night’s referendum results in Alberta, where about three-quarters of voters opted for the province to remain in Canada, rejecting a proposal for a future referendum on separation.

Albertans also voted for their province to negotiate changes to the Constitution to secure more powers from the federal government.

Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Tuesday the results show cracks in the Canadian federation and suggested provinces could work together to gain more powers from Ottawa.

The PQ leader wrote on social media that Albertans had proven “there is nothing to fear from expressing one’s views through a referendum.”

“The message they are sending to Ottawa could not be clearer: Canada, as it stands, is not working, and the status quo is no longer acceptable,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

“Like Quebecers, they see the Canadian federation as a straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies, in order to meet their own needs.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said Quebec, under the Coalition Avenir Québec government, had already tried and failed to get more autonomy from Ottawa. He said his predecessors’ approach “only led to rejections and setbacks for Quebec” and accused the federal government of becoming increasingly interventionist.

The PQ leader has promised Quebecers a third referendum on independence after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he sees common cause with Alberta and promised to collaborate with other provinces “that come to the same conclusion as Quebec and Albertans: change is needed.”

But Quebec’s opposition parties said the Alberta results should instead prompt St-Pierre Plamondon to abandon his referendum pledge.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said Quebecers should align themselves with Alberta to secure a balance of power in the federation, but said he does not support secession.

He urged St-Pierre Plamondon to drop his promise to hold a referendum on independence.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard made the same request, saying the Canadian federation remains the best option for Quebec.

“The results reflect a desire to unite and work to build Canada rather than divide it,” Milliard said. “Canada is the envy of the world.”

The new Quebec poll is also providing ammunition to the Liberals as they prepare to serve as the official Opposition.

Milliard received a warm welcome Tuesday as his party held its first official meeting as a sworn-in caucus.

“We’re going to have a strong official Opposition,” he said.

Liberal MNA Michel Leblanc said Quebecers will see in the coming months and years how central a referendum is to the PQ’s agenda and how it could affect Quebec’s relationship with the rest of Canada.

“Quebecers don’t want a referendum. The PQ wants one, and it will cost them,” Leblanc said.

A minority government typically lasts 18 to 24 months, and the Liberals are already looking ahead to the next election.

“We’ll make sure to be ready for the next rendez-vous électoral,” Milliard said.

Béland said the polling should also give the PQ pause over its commitment to a referendum deadline.

“This poll and other polls should give them pause about emphasizing the referendum with a hard deadline,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon is set to officially become premier Wednesday when he and his cabinet are formally sworn into office.

stories.title: Victims of Wainwright fire remembered as young people dedicated to service
stories.summary: Devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base in Alberta claimed lives of four soldiers, injured 39 others
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Colin Freeze, Jana G. Pruden
stories.content:
Just days ago, Sergeant Morgan Wong was a volunteer medical responder with St. John Ambulance in Edmonton, excited about a recent promotion within the military, and eager to deploy on his second tour in Europe.

“He had so much potential,” his friend Rhyneice Cook said. “You know, kind of one of those people that you’re like, that guy’s going to change the world. And then, to lose him – it’s a great loss for humanity in general.”

Sgt. Wong, 26, was one of four soldiers killed in a devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday afternoon.

The others were Private Shaun Farrell and Pte. Aidan Goulding, both 23, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19.

Thirty-nine other soldiers in their battalion were injured. As of Monday, 33 remained in hospital, many with serious burns covering much of their bodies. Nineteen of them remained in critical condition.

All of the victims were members of the Canadian Armed Forces serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

In social-media posts, crowdfunding campaigns and media interviews, relatives and friends have described the victims as young people dedicated to serving their country and communities, and who, in some cases, were burned while trying to help other victims.

A huge pile of flowers continues to grow at the cenotaph in Wainwright after four soldiers were killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong. Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically. Six have since been discharged, says the defence minister.

The Canadian Press

The military has released few details about how exactly the soldiers were injured, saying only that a grass fire burning in the area spread suddenly in gusting winds and overtook the battalion during training.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House of Commons on Monday that 50 investigators are on the ground in Wainwright conducting three separate probes, including a military board of inquiry , which will consider how to prevent similar events in the future.

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, told The Globe and Mail Monday that the inquiry could take a year, but promised the results would be made public.

The youngest of the victims who were killed on Saturday, Pte. Lykkemark, was remembered by his high-school rugby coach, Trevor Plater, as an athlete who stood out for his speed, fearlessness and self-confidence. But the coach said the teenager’s most exceptional attribute was how he cared.

“He took care of people,” Mr. Plater said in an interview. “There were moments where I, as a coach, was thinking about checking in on somebody or was worried about somebody, but a lot of the time he was already there, having a chat with them and supporting them.”

Nadine Dunford, who helped raise the teen in Langley, B.C., said he dreamed of being a police officer and joined the military after high school as a step toward that goal. She told CTV Vancouver she talked to Pte. Lykkemark last week and that he said he was looking forward to the exercises in Wainwright.

“It’s just not fair. It was a training exercise,” she said, breaking down. “I understand that accidents happen – but why?”

The Prime Minister spoke individually about each of the four victims in Parliament on Monday. He said Sgt. Wong’s family remembered him as “someone who was always there for those who needed him.” He described Pte. Goulding as a young man who “met every hardship with a joke,” adding, “When others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked.”

In a statement, Pte. Goulding’s family said he was an exceptional athlete who quit his career as a mechanic to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto Csis,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said.

They described him as “the guy that kept people’s spirits up,” with a contagious laugh and cheeky smile.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Mr. Carney said Pte. Lykkemark and Pte. Farrell were best friends who were “seldom seen apart.” Pte. Lykkemark was “known for his gift for lightening a hard day, for his quick wit,” and Pte. Farrell was “a generous and deeply loyal friend.”

He said Pte. Farrell was known in his battalion as the “grandmaster of chess” and planned to spend his career in the Armed Forces.

A statement posted online by family friend Heloise Vermeulen describes Pte. Farrell as “a young man of exceptional character” who was “absolutely devoted to serving his country.”

City officials in Prince Albert, Sask., posted a statement saying the 23-year-old will be remembered as a hometown hero.

On Tuesday, a memorial continued to grow at the front gates of CFB Wainwright, with pictures of the four men surrounded by flowers laid in the prairie grass, and another in support of the injured.

Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically. Six have since been discharged, says the defence minister.
The Canadian Press

The military has released few details about how exactly the soldiers were injured, saying only that a grass fire burning in the area spread suddenly in gusting winds and overtook the battalion during training.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House of Commons on Monday that 50 investigators are on the ground in Wainwright conducting three separate probes, including a military board of inquiry , which will consider how to prevent similar events in the future.
General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, told The Globe and Mail Monday that the inquiry could take a year, but promised the results would be made public.

The youngest of the victims who were killed on Saturday, Pte. Lykkemark, was remembered by his high-school rugby coach, Trevor Plater, as an athlete who stood out for his speed, fearlessness and self-confidence. But the coach said the teenager’s most exceptional attribute was how he cared.

“He took care of people,” Mr. Plater said in an interview. “There were moments where I, as a coach, was thinking about checking in on somebody or was worried about somebody, but a lot of the time he was already there, having a chat with them and supporting them.”

Nadine Dunford, who helped raise the teen in Langley, B.C., said he dreamed of being a police officer and joined the military after high school as a step toward that goal. She told CTV Vancouver she talked to Pte. Lykkemark last week and that he said he was looking forward to the exercises in Wainwright.
“It’s just not fair. It was a training exercise,” she said, breaking down. “I understand that accidents happen – but why?”

The Prime Minister spoke individually about each of the four victims in Parliament on Monday. He said Sgt. Wong’s family remembered him as “someone who was always there for those who needed him.” He described Pte. Goulding as a young man who “met every hardship with a joke,” adding, “When others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked.”
In a statement, Pte. Goulding’s family said he was an exceptional athlete who quit his career as a mechanic to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto Csis,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said.
They described him as “the guy that kept people’s spirits up,” with a contagious laugh and cheeky smile.
“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Mr. Carney said Pte. Lykkemark and Pte. Farrell were best friends who were “seldom seen apart.” Pte. Lykkemark was “known for his gift for lightening a hard day, for his quick wit,” and Pte. Farrell was “a generous and deeply loyal friend.”
He said Pte. Farrell was known in his battalion as the “grandmaster of chess” and planned to spend his career in the Armed Forces.
A statement posted online by family friend Heloise Vermeulen describes Pte. Farrell as “a young man of exceptional character” who was “absolutely devoted to serving his country.”
City officials in Prince Albert, Sask., posted a statement saying the 23-year-old will be remembered as a hometown hero.
On Tuesday, a memorial continued to grow at the front gates of CFB Wainwright, with pictures of the four men surrounded by flowers laid in the prairie grass, and another in support of the injured.

stories.title: The Alberta referendum by the numbers
stories.summary: While final results are still pending, preliminary tallies already reveal how voters have responded to the questions posed by the government
stories.author: Tom Cardoso, Chen Wang, Yang Sun
stories.content:
Five months after Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced her government would call a vote on whether the province should pursue secession from Canada, Albertans at last know the results of its historic referendum.

The separation question, as well as nine other ballot questions on issues such as immigration, social services and judicial appointments, led to intense rhetoric and fierce campaigning. In the end, roughly a quarter of ballots cast supported a new, separate vote that could begin the legal process allowing the Prairie province to secede from Canadian federation.

While final results are still pending – Elections Alberta has said a full count is expected to take several days – preliminary tallies already reveal how voters have responded to the questions posed by the government.

Here’s a look at Alberta’s referendum by the numbers.

Preliminary results show that roughly 62 per cent of the province’s 3.1 million eligible voters cast a ballot on Question 10, which asked whether the province should hold a separate vote that could commence the legal process to separate. Turnout on that question was similar to the 2023 general election, when around 60 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot.

Many voters chose to vote in advance or through a mail-in ballot. Roughly 43 per cent of eligible voters – 1.4-million people – cast a ballot this way during the referendum, according to Elections Alberta. This is far in excess of the 28 per cent of eligible voters who did so in 2023.

But an analysis also found that this turnout wasn’t uniform across the province.

While Elections Alberta has not yet published a breakdown of eligible voters in 2026 for each of the province’s 87 electoral divisions, it has done so for 2025. The Globe tallied up votes on the separation question for each district and compared that to the 2025 eligible-voter figures.

That analysis shows that turnout in divisions won by the United Conservative Party in 2023 was five percentage points higher than in areas that went to the New Democrats.

Preliminary results show that only two of Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions voted in favour of a separation referendum – and, in both cases, it was a slim majority.

Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, represented by United Conservative Party Finance Minister Jason Nixon, saw the strongest support for a separation question, with 51 per cent voting in favour of a referendum. The only other division to vote in favour of a separation question was Central Peace-Notley, represented by Forestry and Parks Minister Todd Loewen, also with 51-per-cent support.

In fact, the next 42 divisions with the most support for a separation referendum were all won by the United Conservative Party in 2023, the data show. On average, areas won by the UCP in 2023 voted for separation 33 per cent of the time, while divisions won by the Alberta New Democratic Party voted for separation roughly 15 per cent of the time.

The NDP district with the strongest support for separation was Banff-Kananaskis, a district located in the Rocky Mountains in southwest Alberta, at 20 per cent. The NDP division most staunchly in support of remaining in Canada was Edmonton-Strathcona, where 10 per cent of valid votes supported a separation referendum.

At a glance, a map of the votes for and against separation falls along familiar Albertan lines: The big-city NDP strongholds of Calgary and Edmonton were strongly in favour of remaining in Canada, while rural areas, which have traditionally gone to the UCP, were more likely to vote to separate.

The Globe analyzed Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions and divided them into four buckets: districts representing Edmonton, those representing Calgary, those representing other major cities and those representing the rest of the province, much of which is rural.

Edmonton and Calgary saw the strongest support for federalism, at roughly 86 and 83 per cent, respectively. Other cities hewed more closely to the provincial average, with 73 per cent of districts voting to remain.

The rest of the province, meanwhile, was more supportive of a separation referendum. Those districts, which represent lesser-populated areas like Camrose, Peace River and Lacombe, saw 60 per cent support for remaining in Canada – a 26-point difference compared to Edmonton.

Indigenous leaders in Alberta have been vocal opponents of Alberta’s separation movement, arguing that a break from Canada would infringe on their negotiated treaty rights.

While Elections Alberta’s data does not identify which votes came from Indigenous people, an analysis of polling stations located within Indigenous communities shows that voters in those areas overwhelmingly want Alberta to continue being a part of the Canadian federation.

The Globe identified 50 voting locations that sit primarily on First Nations land or Métis settlements and were reporting votes as of publication time. Of the 13,602 ballots cast at those locations, 95 per cent were in favour of Alberta remaining in Canada.

Some locations were even more vigorously opposed to separation. At a polling station located on the Tsuut’ina Nation southwest of Calgary, 98 per cent of 342 ballots cast were in favour of Alberta remaining a part of Canada. A polling location on Siksika Nation land that received 512 ballots was 99 per cent in favour of staying in Canada, and a voting location in the Tallcree First Nation, which had counted 102 votes as of publication time, did not see a single ballot cast in favour of separation.

Votes are still being counted on the nine other questions put to people in Alberta. Elections Alberta said it was giving priority to tallying votes on Question 10, which concerns separation.

Preliminary results for most of the other nine other measures – including questions about Senate and judicial appointments, immigration and self-determination – are still close.

Question 5, which asks whether the government should implement stricter voter ID requirements, has the strongest support so far at 64 per cent. Seven other questions have support between 49 and 58 per cent.

As of publication time, only Question 8 – which asks whether voters support amending the Canadian Constitution to “allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education, and social services” – has a majority “no” vote, at 51 per cent. Elections Alberta has said it expects its count to take two days.

stories.title: Danielle Smith makes plea to separatists in televised speech, vows no more secession referendums
stories.summary: The Alberta premier called on disillusioned Albertans to "believe and hope in Canada again" after an emphatic vote to stay in the country.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
In a province-wide address on Tuesday evening, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith vowed not to hold another referendum on the secession issue, while also urging separatist voters to “believe and hope in Canada again” following Monday’s referendum results.

In her first public remarks since referendum polls closed, the premier again sought to elevate the various deals and major projects her government has signed with Prime Minister Mark Carney in an effort to mend Alberta’s fractured relationship with Ottawa. Her comments came one day after Albertans voted with a decisive three-to-one margin to reject a proposal to hold a second legally-binding vote on whether to leave Confederation.

“And I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said. “It is time to move forward together as a strong and free Alberta within a united Canada.”

As of 7:00 p.m. MT on Tuesday, more than 1.95 million votes had been counted on the referendum’s 10th question, which asked whether Alberta should stay in Canada (Option 1) or hold a second vote on the matter (Option 2). Seventy-five per cent voted to stay in Canada while 25 per cent opted for the second option, with 90 per cent of voting stations reporting results.

Smith, who could now face an internal political reckoning from the very base of pro-independence supporters who helped get her elected, also made a plea to the one out of every four Albertans who supported Option 2.

“You love this province, and you want your family and neighbours to have every opportunity to succeed,” she said. “Many of you view Ottawa as having threatened your freedoms and blocked your path to prosperity. I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt — most especially during the Justin Trudeau Liberal-NDP coalition years.”

The premier based her optimism on a claim that the country has “changed significantly” in the last 1.5 years, evident in Ottawa’s newfound support for expanding oil and gas exports and its recent decision to desginate Alberta’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline as being in the national interest. In recent months, Smith and Carney have announced various major projects like oil project, a proposed passenger rail line between Edmonton and Calgary, and a recent $8-billion commitment toward four military bases in the provinces.

“So tonight I want to invite every Albertan who May still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again,” Smith said.

“We are reversing course away from a lost decade and towards a bright future with Alberta’s prosperity at its centre.”

The premier called for patience among Alberta’s most disillusioned voters, who have for decades raised concerns over Ottawa’s mistreatment of the province. Many Albertans have long accused the federal government of choking off personal freedoms, overstepping its jurisdictional boundaries and enacting restrictive environmental policies that stifled oil and gas sector growth, and Smith suggested that frustrations over those matters won’t dissapear overnight.

“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved,” she said. “There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us. But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister (Trudeau).”

The premier also commented on the results from the referendum’s other nine questions, for which Albertans seemed mostly poised to support. Five of the 10 referendum questions focused on immigration rates, and proposed giving Alberta more control over immigration and limiting access to some public services for non-permanent residents, among other things. Voters seemed likely to support each of those five questions as of 7:00 p.m. MT, as well as supporting other constitutional questions proposing to, for example, work with provinces to abolish the federal Senate.

“Although results are still coming in, it appears that Albertans have directed the provincial government to take greater control over immigration so we can moderate the extraordinary population growth our province has experienced and prioritize jobs and opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” Smith said. “They have given us direction to ensure temporary residents pay a portion of the cost of public services used by themselves and their families. They have spoken in favour of requiring proof of Canadian citizenship in order to vote.”

She said her UCP government would “continue to boldly assert our province’s autonomy” through provincial rights guaranteed to the provinces under the constitution.

“We will use every legal and political tool at our disposal to protect and advance the interests of Albertans,” she said. “And when Ottawa interferes with those rights, we will be unrelenting in our response.”

stories.title: Alberta First Nations criticize lack of ballots and delays for members to vote in referendum
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says extra ballots were delivered as voter turn out was higher than expected
stories.author: Patrick White, Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Elections Alberta ran short of ballots in several First Nations during the provincial referendum on Monday, prompting criticism of how the agency administered the vote.

Residents voted on 10 questions, including whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or trigger a subsequent secession vote and others related to immigration and constitutional issues in the referendum, which the province had been planning for months.

The question of separation was of particular interest to First Nations , who have spoken out against it for months and launched legal challenges arguing that it went against treaty rights.

In some communities the ballot shortage led to long waits at polling locations, according to a statement from Siksika Nation, a southern Alberta First Nation with nearly 8,000 members.

“It is unacceptable that First Nations communities continue to encounter barriers to participating fully in Alberta’s democratic processes,” Siksika Chief Samuel Crowfoot said in a statement. “Our people have fought too long for their democratic rights to be treated as an afterthought. The right to vote must be supported by meaningful and equitable access to the ballot box.”

Elections Alberta spokeswoman Michelle Gurney said in an e-mailed statement that the agency delivered extra ballots to five First Nations – three of which received multiple shipments.

Samson Cree Nation, Louis Bull Tribe and Ermineskin Cree Nation received three separate ballot deliveries, she said.

Whitefish First Nation and a voting location serving Siksika Nation and Blood Tribe needed at least one extra delivery.

The agency predicted the number of ballots needed at each of the province’s 1,400 polling stations based on past voter registry data. It sent 1.5 times as many ballots as it deemed necessary, Ms. Gurney said.

“This means we have seen higher turnout at these locations than we have in the past,” she said. “This is a good news story, showing higher voter engagement in these locations.”

But some First Nations leaders saw the miscalculation as a failure to appreciate Indigenous engagement in an issue that so squarely encroaches on treaty rights.

“This shouldn’t have come as a surprise because it was the First Nations people who were most vocal and most against the referendum from the beginning,” said Jay Telegdi, senior manager of intergovernmental affairs for Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation.

First Nations in Alberta have challenged the legality of provincial separation in court, arguing that it would violate treaties with the Crown and breach the government’s duty to consult Indigenous peoples on matters affecting their rights.

Two Alberta judges ruled that First Nations must be considered in the decision to call a referendum on provincial independence. In a December decision, Court of King’s Bench Justice Colin Feasby ruled that “First Nations, as founding partners in the creation of Alberta, cannot be ignored or bypassed as Alberta contemplates its future whether that is as part of Canada or not.”

Last week, a number of First Nations raised concerns that their members were not given the opportunity to vote in advanced polls , which were meant to be available from Oct. 13 through to Oct. 17, because of staff shortages.

Results from voting locations in First Nations across the province were overwhelmingly opposed to separation.

At the Tallcree First Nation band office, a total of 102 voters cast ballots with not a single one favouring independence. And at one location on the Alexis Nakota Sioux Nation, just seven of 363 voters selected separation.

Elections Alberta did not make an overall turnout figure for First Nations available.

In the lead up to the referendum, many First Nations held information sessions and rallies to encourage voting. Some issued social media posts imploring members to vote in favour of remaining in Canada.

“First Nations and Albertan voters turned out in huge numbers and stood up for our shared past, present and future in Canada and rejected a divisive proposal that would bring needless upheaval, conflict and uncertainty for everyone,” Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said in a press release. “The results of this vote speak volumes: We are stronger together.”

With a report from Matthew Scace

stories.title: Two Globe reporters shortlisted for the Lane Anderson Award for Canadian science writing
stories.summary: Greg Mercer, Eric Andrew-Gee are up for annual prize recognizing jury-selected books
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Two Globe and Mail journalists, Greg Mercer and Eric Andrew-Gee , are nominated for the Lane Anderson Award for Canadian science writing.

The annual prize recognizes jury-selected books in two categories, adult and young reader. The winners in both are awarded $10,000.

The shortlisted books in the adult category are Andrew-Gee’s The Mind Mappers: Friendship, Betrayal and the Obsessive Quest to Chart the Brain , published by Penguin Random House Canada; Mercer’s The Lobster Trap: The Global Fight for a Seafood on the Brink , published by McClelland & Stewart; and Sarah Boon’s Meltdown: The Making and Breaking of a Field Scientist , published by University of Alberta Press.

The contenders for the young reader prize are The Buzz on Wild Bees: The Little-Known Pollinators that Keep Our Planet Humming, written by Globe contributor Kira Vermond and illustrated by June Steube for Owlkids Books; The Gland Factory: A Tour of Your Body’s Goops, Juices, and Hormones , written by Rachel Poliquin and illustrated by Clayton Hanmer for Greystone Kids; and The Story and Science of Hope , written by Andrea Curtis and illustrated by Ana Suárez for Groundwood Books.

The award was created in 2010 by the Fitzhenry Family Foundation, a private charitable group founded by Robert Fitzhenry, one of the founding partners of Canadian publishing and distribution company Fitzhenry & Whiteside. The prize’s name originates from the maiden names of his mother, Margaret Lane Fitzhenry, and his wife, Hilda Anderson Fitzhenry.

Recent winners in the adult category include Jennifer Grenz’s Medicine Wheel for the Planet , John Vaillant’s Fire Weather , and Ontario’s Old-Growth Forests by Michael Henry and Peter Quinby.

Prize-takers in the young readers division include A Planet Is a Poem by Amanda West Lewis and Oliver Averill; Polar by L. E. Carmichael and Byron Eggenschwiler; and It Takes Guts by Jennifer Gardy and Belle Wuthrich.

The 2026 award winners will be announced in January at an event in Toronto.

stories.title: Danielle Smith calls for unity after separatism rejected in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: A day after Alberta voters rejected the idea of further pursuing separating from Canada, the Premier Danielle Smith delivered a message on where the province goes from here.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
One day after Alberta voters rejected the idea of pursuing separation from Canada, Premier Danielle Smith said the turnout was a historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for the country and province.

“Yesterday, Albertans made their choice. Today, we begin the next chapter,” the premier said in a speech that was broadcast Tuesday night during airtime paid for by the Alberta government.

“Let us move forward not as a people divided by how we voted yesterday, but as neighbours, friends, Albertans and Canadians. Let us treat one another with respect and compassion. Let us stand proudly for this province.”

The outcome of the referendum ‘s separatism question mirrors more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026 consistently showed about 70 per cent of Albertans wanted the province to remain in Canada .

Albertans roundly rejected leaving Canada by roughly 75 per cent, with 1.9 million ballots counted for the separation question as of late Tuesday afternoon, representing about 61.9 per cent of voters so far.

“At the end of it all, the people of Alberta cast their votes in an open and democratic referendum. And the resulting vote from Albertans has given our government a clear mandate.

“Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians."

Alberta will continue to assert its autonomy and stand up for the issues important to residents, Smith said, but disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions rather than pursuing the option of separation.

Smith indicated the question of independence has been put to bed.

“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said. “It is time to move forward together.”

It was a debate Smith said was many years in the making, as Albertans have struggled to address many long-standing and legitimate grievances with Ottawa .

“I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you've felt."

Nearly half a million ballots were cast in favour of continuing down the road towards leaving Canada. In some ridings such as Central Peace-Notley and Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, the leave votes narrowly outnumbered the ones cast to stay.

Smith addressed those voters directly on Tuesday night.

“I recognize you as loyal Albertans. You love this province, and you want your family and neighbours to have every opportunity to succeed. Many of you view Ottawa as having threatened your freedoms and blocked your path to prosperity,” she said.

“You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians."

Smith’s message was one of unity and moving forward.

“Tonight, I want to invite every Albertan who May still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again.”

But, it doesn’t appear Smith will get her wish that all Albertans will simply accept the results of the referendum and move on.

Instead, going forward, Smith and the governing United Conservative Party will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take further control of the party.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the central figures in the separatist movement who had a hand in former premier Jason Kenney’s ouster, told Global News he will be pushing for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith as well.

Smith, in her speech, made the case that Canada has changed significantly over the past 18 months and credited all Albertans for helping make happen.

“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved. There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us,” she said.

“But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister.”

“In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven’t seen in a generation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven't seen in a generation."

Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Smith said there is a renewed understanding that Canada cannot achieve prosperity by preventing its strongest industries from succeeding.

She said pipelines that were once declared impossible are now being built as national priorities, in reference to the Pacific Link project that received national interest designation on Oct. 1 , with the goal of construction of the line to the B.C. Lower Mainland beginning next September.

“Canada is once again producing more energy, exporting more resources, building more major projects and attracting more investment,” she said. “I believe it’s working better every day, and it can work even better in the future if we keep fighting together for it.”

Smith’s speech was pre-recorded, so she did not answer questions from journalists. Smith is slated to do that on Wednesday at an 11:30 a.m. media availability in Calgary.

While the question of leaving Canada appears to have been put to bed, the results for the other nine referendum questions have revealed Albertans are divided.

Ballots were still being counted by hand as of Tuesday afternoon, but an Elections Alberta website sharing minute-by-minute updates showed the yes option was leading on eight of the nine questions, including all five on immigration.

The leads were tight, ranging from 51 to 63 per cent provincewide .

The questions asked whether Alberta should have more say over who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary workers who seek access to health care and education.

The remaining four questions asked for Albertans’ blessing for Smith to lobby her provincial counterparts for support on amending the Constitution to take more power from Ottawa and abolish the Senate.

The yes side was leading on all of the immigration questions with roughly 54 to 58 per cent of the votes as of Tuesday afternoon.

One exception was Smith’s question five proposal to require proof of citizenship to vote provincially, which was leading with about two-thirds of the vote.

Broken down geographically, voters in Edmonton said no to all nine questions while in Calgary, voters said no to eight of the questions except question five.

The only question in which the no vote was leading provincewide on Tuesday afternoon — albeit by a tight 51 per cent for “no” to 49 per cent for “yes” — was question eight.

It asked if Alberans would support its government working with other provinces to opt out of federal programs like health care, education, social services without losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.

Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative Party press secretary turned government relations consultant, told The Canadian Press the results present a clear mandate for the premier.

“Governments get elected on less than 50 per cent in this country, and then they move forward with implementing a mandate,” said Aitchison, a managing director with Enterprise Canada.

“Regardless of the size of the mandate, it is a clear mandate, and with voter turnout, I think it’s something that (Smith) can definitely point to when she’s trying to negotiate (with Ottawa),” he said.

Smith has said immigration is beneficial to Alberta, but that it must be balanced with the high cost of social services. Her government has yet to give specifics about how the proposals would work or how they would be implemented.

Avnish Nanda, a lawyer who had campaigned against the immigration proposals, said Tuesday he was shocked by the results so far, as he was expecting the questions to pass with much larger margins.

“We thought we would be blown out,” Nanda said in an interview.

Nanda said he didn’t think the results represent the will of Albertans. He pointed to polls that suggest some voters were confused by the wording of the questions and would vote differently depending on how the question was framed.

“These are hard questions (and) a (government) propaganda campaign that has misled Albertans to vote for things that are contrary to, I think, what they actually want and what’s in their best interest.”

On Tuesday, Carney said he favours pursuing pragmatic “common solutions” with the provinces on issues under federal jurisdiction.

When speaking to reporters as he welcomed the rejection of separation , Carney said pursuing constitutional changes can be a difficult, drawn-out process.

Conservative Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday the Liberals allowed immigration to run “totally out of control” and he supports provinces being able to set their own levels.

The prime minister said disputes in areas like immigration can be resolved without constitutional amendments, adding his government has moved to bring immigration back under control.

With files from Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

“Let us move forward not as a people divided by how we voted yesterday, but as neighbours, friends, Albertans and Canadians. Let us treat one another with respect and compassion. Let us stand proudly for this province.”

The outcome of the referendum ‘s separatism question mirrors more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026 consistently showed about 70 per cent of Albertans wanted the province to remain in Canada .
content_blocks.html: The outcome of the referendum‘s separatism question mirrors more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026 consistently showed about 70 per cent of Albertans wanted the province to remain in Canada.

content_blocks.text: Albertans roundly rejected leaving Canada by roughly 75 per cent, with 1.9 million ballots counted for the separation question as of late Tuesday afternoon, representing about 61.9 per cent of voters so far.
“At the end of it all, the people of Alberta cast their votes in an open and democratic referendum. And the resulting vote from Albertans has given our government a clear mandate.

“Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians."
content_blocks.html: “Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians."

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta referendum results show decisive support for staying in Canada'

content_blocks.text: Alberta will continue to assert its autonomy and stand up for the issues important to residents, Smith said, but disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions rather than pursuing the option of separation.
Smith indicated the question of independence has been put to bed.

“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said. “It is time to move forward together.”
It was a debate Smith said was many years in the making, as Albertans have struggled to address many long-standing and legitimate grievances with Ottawa .
content_blocks.html: It was a debate Smith said was many years in the making, as Albertans have struggled to address many long-standing and legitimate grievances with Ottawa.

content_blocks.text: “I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you've felt."
content_blocks.html: “I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you've felt."

content_blocks.text: Nearly half a million ballots were cast in favour of continuing down the road towards leaving Canada. In some ridings such as Central Peace-Notley and Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, the leave votes narrowly outnumbered the ones cast to stay.
Smith addressed those voters directly on Tuesday night.

“I recognize you as loyal Albertans. You love this province, and you want your family and neighbours to have every opportunity to succeed. Many of you view Ottawa as having threatened your freedoms and blocked your path to prosperity,” she said.

“You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians."
content_blocks.html: “You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians."

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta referendum reveals urban-rural split in separatism vote'

content_blocks.text: Smith’s message was one of unity and moving forward.
“Tonight, I want to invite every Albertan who May still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again.”
But, it doesn’t appear Smith will get her wish that all Albertans will simply accept the results of the referendum and move on.

Instead, going forward, Smith and the governing United Conservative Party will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take further control of the party.
content_blocks.html: Instead, going forward, Smith and the governing United Conservative Party will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take further control of the party.

content_blocks.text: Jeffrey Rath, one of the central figures in the separatist movement who had a hand in former premier Jason Kenney’s ouster, told Global News he will be pushing for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith as well.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta referendum: Separatist leader Jeff Rath says province will never be independent as long as ‘avowed federalist’ Danielle Smith is UCP leader'

content_blocks.text: Smith, in her speech, made the case that Canada has changed significantly over the past 18 months and credited all Albertans for helping make happen.
“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved. There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us,” she said.

“But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister.”

“In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven’t seen in a generation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven't seen in a generation."
content_blocks.html: “In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven’t seen in a generation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven't seen in a generation."

content_blocks.text: Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Smith said there is a renewed understanding that Canada cannot achieve prosperity by preventing its strongest industries from succeeding.

She said pipelines that were once declared impossible are now being built as national priorities, in reference to the Pacific Link project that received national interest designation on Oct. 1 , with the goal of construction of the line to the B.C. Lower Mainland beginning next September.
content_blocks.html: She said pipelines that were once declared impossible are now being built as national priorities, in reference to the Pacific Link project that received national interest designation on Oct. 1, with the goal of construction of the line to the B.C. Lower Mainland beginning next September.

content_blocks.text: “Canada is once again producing more energy, exporting more resources, building more major projects and attracting more investment,” she said. “I believe it’s working better every day, and it can work even better in the future if we keep fighting together for it.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta separatists skeptical over Pacific Link pipeline designation'

content_blocks.text: Smith’s speech was pre-recorded, so she did not answer questions from journalists. Smith is slated to do that on Wednesday at an 11:30 a.m. media availability in Calgary.
What about the other referendum questions?
While the question of leaving Canada appears to have been put to bed, the results for the other nine referendum questions have revealed Albertans are divided.

Ballots were still being counted by hand as of Tuesday afternoon, but an Elections Alberta website sharing minute-by-minute updates showed the yes option was leading on eight of the nine questions, including all five on immigration.
content_blocks.html: Ballots were still being counted by hand as of Tuesday afternoon, but an Elections Alberta website sharing minute-by-minute updates showed the yes option was leading on eight of the nine questions, including all five on immigration.

content_blocks.text: The leads were tight, ranging from 51 to 63 per cent provincewide .
content_blocks.html: The leads were tight, ranging from 51 to 63 per cent provincewide.

content_blocks.text: The questions asked whether Alberta should have more say over who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary workers who seek access to health care and education.
content_blocks.html: The questions asked whether Alberta should have more say over who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary workers who seek access to health care and education.

content_blocks.text: The remaining four questions asked for Albertans’ blessing for Smith to lobby her provincial counterparts for support on amending the Constitution to take more power from Ottawa and abolish the Senate.
The yes side was leading on all of the immigration questions with roughly 54 to 58 per cent of the votes as of Tuesday afternoon.
One exception was Smith’s question five proposal to require proof of citizenship to vote provincially, which was leading with about two-thirds of the vote.
Broken down geographically, voters in Edmonton said no to all nine questions while in Calgary, voters said no to eight of the questions except question five.
The only question in which the no vote was leading provincewide on Tuesday afternoon — albeit by a tight 51 per cent for “no” to 49 per cent for “yes” — was question eight.

It asked if Alberans would support its government working with other provinces to opt out of federal programs like health care, education, social services without losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta separation: The province’s road to a historic referendum'

content_blocks.text: Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative Party press secretary turned government relations consultant, told The Canadian Press the results present a clear mandate for the premier.
“Governments get elected on less than 50 per cent in this country, and then they move forward with implementing a mandate,” said Aitchison, a managing director with Enterprise Canada.

“Regardless of the size of the mandate, it is a clear mandate, and with voter turnout, I think it’s something that (Smith) can definitely point to when she’s trying to negotiate (with Ottawa),” he said.

Smith has said immigration is beneficial to Alberta, but that it must be balanced with the high cost of social services. Her government has yet to give specifics about how the proposals would work or how they would be implemented.
content_blocks.html: Smith has said immigration is beneficial to Alberta, but that it must be balanced with the high cost of social services. Her government has yet to give specifics about how the proposals would work or how they would be implemented.

content_blocks.text: Avnish Nanda, a lawyer who had campaigned against the immigration proposals, said Tuesday he was shocked by the results so far, as he was expecting the questions to pass with much larger margins.
“We thought we would be blown out,” Nanda said in an interview.

Nanda said he didn’t think the results represent the will of Albertans. He pointed to polls that suggest some voters were confused by the wording of the questions and would vote differently depending on how the question was framed.

“These are hard questions (and) a (government) propaganda campaign that has misled Albertans to vote for things that are contrary to, I think, what they actually want and what’s in their best interest.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta referendum: Where does the separatist movement go from here?'

content_blocks.text: On Tuesday, Carney said he favours pursuing pragmatic “common solutions” with the provinces on issues under federal jurisdiction.
When speaking to reporters as he welcomed the rejection of separation , Carney said pursuing constitutional changes can be a difficult, drawn-out process.
content_blocks.html: When speaking to reporters as he welcomed the rejection of separation, Carney said pursuing constitutional changes can be a difficult, drawn-out process.

content_blocks.text: Conservative Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday the Liberals allowed immigration to run “totally out of control” and he supports provinces being able to set their own levels.
The prime minister said disputes in areas like immigration can be resolved without constitutional amendments, adding his government has moved to bring immigration back under control.

stories.title: Premiers welcome separatist loss in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Provincial leaders largely steer clear of commenting on other ballot questions about immigration, judges, Senate
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Provincial leaders outside Alberta welcomed the province’s rejection of separatism in Monday’s referendum, but mostly steered clear of the other questions on the ballot, including those that asked Albertans whether they endorse restricting immigration and changing the Constitution.

According to unofficial results posted by Elections Alberta on Tuesday evening, about 75 per cent of voters rejected the separation question, which asked them about holding a future, second vote on leaving Canada.

But for eight of the ballot’s other nine questions, which included proposals for Alberta to take control of immigration, appoint its own higher-court judges and abolish the federal Senate, results showed majorities voting Yes, as Premier Danielle Smith had urged.

Several of these questions raise the spectre of potentially tangled constitutional negotiations, something Canadian politicians have shied away from for decades after the wrenching national debates of the 1980s and 1990s. But some of these ballot items also echo complaints that other premiers have regularly made to Ottawa in recent years.

In a statement posted to X on Tuesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford praised the result on separation. He also reiterated his vow to build a new pipeline to bring Alberta’s oil to refineries in Ontario, in order to avoid routes that now bring the resource through the United States.

“I’m thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love,” Mr. Ford said. “Now it’s up to the rest of Canada to deliver on our commitment to Alberta by building new pipelines, unlocking our natural resources and unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.”

In Saskatchewan, which also has its own small separatist movement, Premier Scott Moe applauded Alberta’s vote to remain in Canada. But he also said the West’s grievances within Confederation need to be addressed.

“There is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa,” Mr. Moe said on X. “But Canada is worth that effort. Saskatchewan will continue to work with Alberta to make our provinces stronger within a united Canada.”

In Quebec, where separatist Parti Québécois just returned to power, premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the results on the other nine questions show Albertans agree with Quebeckers that Confederation, and an “increasingly interventionist” federal government, are not working.

“As in Quebec, they recognize that the Canadian federation is a straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies, in order to meet their own needs,” he said in a statement on X.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who will be sworn in as premier on Wednesday, has promised to hold a third referendum on independence in Quebec, though not before 2029.

B.C. Premier David Eby, who, as his province’s NDP Leader was campaigning for re-election in Kelowna on Tuesday, thanked Albertans who voted to stay in Canada.

“It feels like a no-brainer to me, but I am glad to see that was confirmed by the people of Alberta,” Mr. Eby said. “We’re stronger together as a country.”

Speaking to reporters in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew congratulated Albertans for voting to “remain a part of the No. 1 country on Earth.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston also welcomed the referendum results. “Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this,” he said on X.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, who leads a province that many have left to work in Alberta, said he was delighted with the vote. When asked about the quarter of Albertans who chose the separatist option, Mr. Wakeham told reporters at the techNL Summit in St. John’s that many people are frustrated with governments.

“Nothing is perfect, and so we have to find ways to keep moving forward and improve the lives of people, whether they are in our own province or in another province,” he said.

Among the other referendum questions that received majority support from Albertans was one about the province seeking more power over immigration to cut it to “more sustainable levels.” Voters also endorsed proposals that would create an “Alberta-approved immigration status,” and restrict access to health care and other services for those with non-permanent status.

Ontario and other provinces have also long advocated for more control over immigration policy, pointing to Quebec’s degree of autonomy in the area – even as Ottawa has recently slashed immigration levels.

Albertans also voted Yes to a question on changing the Constitution to appoint higher-court judges provincially, rather than federally. In a March open letter, Mr. Moe, Ms. Smith, Mr. Ford and then-Quebec-premier François Legault asked Ottawa to ensure all candidates for higher-court judicial appointments are both recommended and approved by the provincial government concerned. Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser flatly rejected the idea at the time.

With reports from Jameson Berkow, Maura Forrest and Ian Bailey

stories.title: Accused Toronto airport gold heist gang turned on each other in nasty fight for loot
stories.summary: As a police net tightened, suspects fled Canada, tried to dodge surveillance, hired lawyers, and viciously turned against one another.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
While suspects in the Toronto airport gold heist were under intense, around-the-clock police surveillance, one of them franticly made increasingly angry and desperate phone calls chasing down money, feeling cheated and abandoned by his friends, court heard.

“It’s already falling apart,” a caller identified in court as Parmpal Sidhu said over the phone nine months after more than $22.5 million in gold bars and cash was stolen after arriving at Pearson airport on a flight from Switzerland.

As a police net tightened around them, suspects fled Canada, tried to dodge surveillance, hired expensive lawyers and viciously turned against one another, police wiretaps show.

“Everybody’s on their own. Everybody’s worried about themselves,” he said in a call. “Everyone got money and I’m stuck here,” he said in another.

Sidhu was an Air Canada employee in the Pearson airport cargo warehouse from where the crate was stolen on April 17, 2023. He was arrested April 5, 2024, one of the first of nine men to be charged and the first to plead not guilty and face trial in the spectacular case. Only about a kilogram of the gold has been recovered.

His trial on Tuesday in Ontario Superior Court in Brampton, Ont., heard a handful of the thousands of wiretap recordings Peel Regional Police made in their probe.

“I am not paying 10 grand for this lawyer. I am going to make a f–king deal. I’m in my car. My other phone is here. It’s probably tapped. I got a tracker on my phone. I am fed up of the lies,” he said in a call.

“You guys literally threw me in the ditch. That’s what you did.

“I’ve been trying to get you guys to do the right thing. Nobody’s listening to me, and now I’m the one who’s getting all the f–king heat.”

The phone calls, by a voice identified by a Peel police officer as Sidhu’s, reveal a man facing a financial apocalypse. His credit cards were maxed; his American Express card had been declined; he took money out of his line of credit, “freaking out” his wife. He spoke of borrowing from his mother.

“I am not joking,” he said in one call, “I am telling you, I am in a hole, and I am going to have to look out for myself.”

Peel police Det. Sarah Angevine testified that people suspected of pulling off the largest gold heist in Canadian history were under police scrutiny, including physical surveillance, phone wiretaps and microphone probes planted in their homes and cars.

The wiretap recordings, most of which are partially obscured by background music and noise, show an apparent escalation of paranoia, anger, financial problems and efforts to be paid money.

Angevine said the people on the wiretaps often used code names or nicknames for people that police believed to be some of the others accused in the heist.

There are references to someone called by the Punjabi word for “Black,” believed to be code for Durante King-Mclean, the accused driver in the gold heist who is Black and the only person not of South Asian descent accused in the heist.

Someone named “Grove” is a reference to Archit Grover, Angevine said, who is accused of supplying the truck used to move the stolen gold from the airport warehouse.

There are also references to someone referred to as “Dubai.” Court heard earlier that Ansalan Chaudhary, who admitted he was one of the masterminds of the heist, had flown to Dubai after the heist.

“This is what Dubai doesn’t f–king understand: I’ll make sure if I lose my cut then f–king Grove will lose his too,” Sidhu is heard saying in one of the wiretaps, court heard. “You think Grove’s just gonna walk away unscathed? No f–king chance.”

He also complained of people leaving Canada after the heist — “who’ve just taken off and left,” he said. Grover, Chaudhary and the man who court heard was the second mastermind behind the heist, Simran Preet Panesar, a former Air Canada manager, are all known to have travelled abroad.

Sidhu complained in another call, “I didn’t know he was going to f–king vanish,” court heard. “His promises are absolutely, utterly worthless.”

He implored the person on the other end of one call to intercede on his behalf: “Make it clear. You need to explain the situation,” he said. He said the guy “didn’t believe me that I got charged.”

“You know how f–king angry it makes me, because I never cheated anybody.”

He also made apparent threats amid his anger.

“I’m going to f–king tear him apart now,” he said.

In a call on Jan. 14, 2024, he said he had been warned he “can’t go after them” or he risks being “arrested,” but that money was coming, however, it is “not going to be what you’re expecting.”’

By the sound of the calls, the payout never came.

In one call, he is heard musing with someone about sending a frightening message with what sounds like a drive-by shooting.

“Can somebody just go there and like spray them — not hurt anybody — but spray like the cars, the house, or something like that, or whatever. Something to worry?”

Court also heard that an analysis of Sidhu’s phone records showed he talked and texted with Panesar, his Air Canada manager and fellow accused in the heist, more than he did with his wife before the theft.

Court heard that three months before the Toronto airport gold heist, a bank draft for $30,000 was deposited into Sidhu’s bank account.

Const. Michael Asanin, a Peel police fraud investigator, testified that he examined 1,121 pages of bank records for Sidhu, spanning several bank accounts and pointed out a large bank draft deposit of $30,000 on Jan. 5, 2023, which was three months before the gold heist.

Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, asked Asanin if he knew whether the gold heist plot was underway at the time of the deposit. He said he didn’t know.

Wagman asked him if the money could have an innocent source.

“I have nothing to say that this particular draft was or was not fraudulent,” Asanin said.

The trial continues.

stories.title: ‘You just feel so helpless’: Family of soldier badly burned in CFB Wainwright fire holds onto hope
stories.summary: The family of a 24-year-old Canadian soldier seriously injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright is holding on to hope as he faces a long and uncertain recovery.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Edson, Alta. - The family of a 24-year-old Canadian soldier seriously injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright is holding on to hope as he faces a long and uncertain recovery.

Cpl. Sean Hiatt, who grew up near Edson, Alta., suffered second-degree burns to approximately half his body in Saturday’s fire, which killed four soldiers and injured 39 others . He is being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton, which has a specialized burn treatment unit.

“We have each other,” said Teresa Hiatt, his older sister. “And we know that Sean would want us to be strong too.”

Despite the heartbreak, Teresa and Sara Dizon, Sean’s girlfriend of four years, shared smiles as they sat together inside Teresa’s coffee shop in Edson.

The business is temporarily closed as Teresa focuses on supporting her brother. Both women are determined to remain positive, saying that’s what Sean would want.

“Sean is very easy to love,” Sara said, describing him as outgoing and bubbly.

But behind those smiles are memories of a terrifying weekend that neither woman will soon forget.

Teresa was out for dinner Saturday when she came across a social media post about an incident at CFB Wainwright. Knowing her brother was there for military training, she immediately contacted Sara to find out when she had last heard from him.

“I kept telling my husband, like, I can’t do this, I can’t do this, I can’t do this,” Teresa recalled.

Her husband began calling hospitals, eventually learning that Sean had been taken to hospital in Wainwright.

Sara, meanwhile, repeatedly tried calling her boyfriend, but received no answer.

When Sean’s mother called her in tears, Sara feared the worst.

“She was like, ‘he is alive.’ And I’m like, ‘thank God.’ That’s everything that we had to know at that time,” she recalled.

‘The nation is in mourning’: Canada’s leaders react to Wainwright tragedy

The following morning, Teresa and Sara travelled to Edmonton, where Sean had been transferred for specialized care. Nothing could have prepared them for what they saw.

Sean was sedated, with a breathing tube down his throat and bandages covering his face. His ears and nose had also been burned.

“We both broke,” Teresa said.

“You just wanted to take him into your arms and just, like, hold him and tell him it was OK,” she said. “You just feel so helpless.”

Sara said seeing the man she loves in such a condition was devastating.

“I never saw him like that. It was very hard,” she said. “And I can’t stop imagining what he’d been through.”

The tragedy unfolded Saturday afternoon as soldiers conducted live-fire training at the military base in Alberta. Military officials say a nearby grass fire, initially considered under control, was driven by a sudden shift in powerful winds, rapidly overtaking soldiers in the training area.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

For Sean’s family, the immediate concern is getting him through the critical early stages of recovery.

What happened at Wainwright? Canada’s top general tells CTV News the inquiry findings will be made public.

Teresa said doctors are focused on stabilizing his condition while assessing the extent of his injuries, including possible damage from smoke inhalation. He May require surgeries and skin grafts.

Doctors have warned the family that recovery will be a marathon, not a sprint.

For now, even the smallest movements offer hope.

“When we said goodbye to him last night, he actually wiggled his thumb,” Teresa recalled. “We were just so happy to see that.”

For the family, it was a small but meaningful moment as they wait for signs of recovery.

Sean comes from a family of 11 siblings, with relatives living in different communities and provinces. His parents are staying in Edmonton, while other family members are trying to balance work, children and travel to be at his bedside.

Teresa said the support from the military community has been overwhelming, with veterans, restaurants and others providing food and assistance to families at the hospital.

“The military family is very close. We’re getting a glimpse of that, and now I know why he loved it,” she said.

The tragedy has also left the family grieving for the soldiers who died. Teresa said one of those killed was someone Sean knew from his military unit, adding another emotional challenge he May face during his recovery.

For Sara, the message to her boyfriend is simple: his loved ones will be waiting and fighting alongside him for as long as it takes.

“We’re just here for him,” she said. “We’re not giving up this easy. And we know that he’s not giving up too.”

“He’s very tough. He doesn’t go down that easy.”

Edson, Alta. - The family of a 24-year-old Canadian soldier seriously injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright is holding on to hope as he faces a long and uncertain recovery.

Cpl. Sean Hiatt, who grew up near Edson, Alta., suffered second-degree burns to approximately half his body in Saturday’s fire, which killed four soldiers and injured 39 others . He is being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton, which has a specialized burn treatment unit.
“We have each other,” said Teresa Hiatt, his older sister. “And we know that Sean would want us to be strong too.”
Despite the heartbreak, Teresa and Sara Dizon, Sean’s girlfriend of four years, shared smiles as they sat together inside Teresa’s coffee shop in Edson.
The business is temporarily closed as Teresa focuses on supporting her brother. Both women are determined to remain positive, saying that’s what Sean would want.
“Sean is very easy to love,” Sara said, describing him as outgoing and bubbly.
But behind those smiles are memories of a terrifying weekend that neither woman will soon forget.

content_blocks.alt: CFB Wainwright soldier badly burned
content_blocks.caption: Cpl. Sean Hiatt suffered second-degree burns to approximately half his body in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright. (Teresa Hiatt)

content_blocks.text: Teresa was out for dinner Saturday when she came across a social media post about an incident at CFB Wainwright. Knowing her brother was there for military training, she immediately contacted Sara to find out when she had last heard from him.
“I kept telling my husband, like, I can’t do this, I can’t do this, I can’t do this,” Teresa recalled.
Her husband began calling hospitals, eventually learning that Sean had been taken to hospital in Wainwright.
Sara, meanwhile, repeatedly tried calling her boyfriend, but received no answer.
When Sean’s mother called her in tears, Sara feared the worst.
“She was like, ‘he is alive.’ And I’m like, ‘thank God.’ That’s everything that we had to know at that time,” she recalled.
‘The nation is in mourning’: Canada’s leaders react to Wainwright tragedy
The following morning, Teresa and Sara travelled to Edmonton, where Sean had been transferred for specialized care. Nothing could have prepared them for what they saw.
Sean was sedated, with a breathing tube down his throat and bandages covering his face. His ears and nose had also been burned.
“We both broke,” Teresa said.
“You just wanted to take him into your arms and just, like, hold him and tell him it was OK,” she said. “You just feel so helpless.”
Sara said seeing the man she loves in such a condition was devastating.
“I never saw him like that. It was very hard,” she said. “And I can’t stop imagining what he’d been through.”

The tragedy unfolded Saturday afternoon as soldiers conducted live-fire training at the military base in Alberta. Military officials say a nearby grass fire, initially considered under control, was driven by a sudden shift in powerful winds, rapidly overtaking soldiers in the training area.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
For Sean’s family, the immediate concern is getting him through the critical early stages of recovery.
What happened at Wainwright? Canada’s top general tells CTV News the inquiry findings will be made public.
Teresa said doctors are focused on stabilizing his condition while assessing the extent of his injuries, including possible damage from smoke inhalation. He May require surgeries and skin grafts.
Doctors have warned the family that recovery will be a marathon, not a sprint.
For now, even the smallest movements offer hope.
“When we said goodbye to him last night, he actually wiggled his thumb,” Teresa recalled. “We were just so happy to see that.”
For the family, it was a small but meaningful moment as they wait for signs of recovery.

content_blocks.alt: CFB Wainwright soldier badly burned
content_blocks.caption: Cpl. Sean Hiatt suffered second-degree burns to approximately half his body in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright. (Teresa Hiatt)

content_blocks.text: Sean comes from a family of 11 siblings, with relatives living in different communities and provinces. His parents are staying in Edmonton, while other family members are trying to balance work, children and travel to be at his bedside.
Teresa said the support from the military community has been overwhelming, with veterans, restaurants and others providing food and assistance to families at the hospital.
“The military family is very close. We’re getting a glimpse of that, and now I know why he loved it,” she said.

The tragedy has also left the family grieving for the soldiers who died. Teresa said one of those killed was someone Sean knew from his military unit, adding another emotional challenge he May face during his recovery.
For Sara, the message to her boyfriend is simple: his loved ones will be waiting and fighting alongside him for as long as it takes.
“We’re just here for him,” she said. “We’re not giving up this easy. And we know that he’s not giving up too.”
“He’s very tough. He doesn’t go down that easy.”
