stories.title: London cyclists call for safer streets at Crticial Mass ride
stories.summary: London cyclists called for safer roads as part of a 'Critical Mass' ride Saturday, following a slew of crashes...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
Photo credits – Riley Seferiades

London cyclists called for safer roads as part of a ‘Critical Mass’ ride Saturday, following a slew of crashes.

The protest aimed to bring awareness to things that make Londoners feel unfomfortable biking on the streets, like missing bike lanes, intimidating drivers and road safety concerns.

Organizers wanted the ride to spark change and help make cyclistes feel more supported.

Laura Galvis Daza, who helped organize the event, is a year-round cycling commuter, as well as a London region community ambassador for The Biking Lawyer LLP and volunteers with London Cycle Link.

“I would say people are upset, people are scared. There has been some discussion online where people are like, ‘hey, you know what, this is kind of the last straw for me. I’m going to stop road cycling for a while. It’s getting a little iffy out there and dicey,'” she said.

Recent crashes include:

October 6: a cyclist was taken to hospitail after colliding with a police cruiser . September 30: a 34-year-old- cyclist died after crashing with a vehicle on Richmond Street in Thames Centre. Sepetember 16: a cyclist collided with a vehichle at Dundas and Maitland street leaving the cyclist with life threatening injuries.

Andrew McCleneghan , owner of London Bicycle Cafe, said safer infrastructure and harsher enforcment of traffic rules are essential right now.

London cyclists called for safer roads as part of a ‘Critical Mass’ ride Saturday, following a slew of crashes.
The protest aimed to bring awareness to things that make Londoners feel unfomfortable biking on the streets, like missing bike lanes, intimidating drivers and road safety concerns.
Organizers wanted the ride to spark change and help make cyclistes feel more supported.
Laura Galvis Daza, who helped organize the event, is a year-round cycling commuter, as well as a London region community ambassador for The Biking Lawyer LLP and volunteers with London Cycle Link.

“I would say people are upset, people are scared. There has been some discussion online where people are like, ‘hey, you know what, this is kind of the last straw for me. I’m going to stop road cycling for a while. It’s getting a little iffy out there and dicey,'” she said.

stories.title: Watch for deer on roads: police
stories.summary: Provincial police are reminding drivers to watch out for deer at this time of year, noting that hitting one co...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Provincial police are reminding drivers to watch out for deer at this time of year, noting that hitting one could cause serious injuries.

“Heading into October and November between dawn and dusk you can possibly encounter a deer on any part of roadways and maybe on our highways.” said Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) officer Edward Sanchuk.

(Credit: Ruth Fremson/The New York Times)

The longtime officer said he once hit a deer, and the crash caused $5,000 in damages to his vehicle.

Sanchuk said drivers should never swerve away from deer, because swerving cuold lead to a head-on collision with another car.

“The last thing we want to do is to tell a loved one that you have been killed or seriously injured in a crash,” he said.

Making sure your car is working is half the work as you must also be aware of your surroundings.

“Before leaving make sure your headlights are bright and working, keep your eyes peeled, and scan fields, ditches, and any other areas deer can hide,” said Sanchuk. “If you see a deer crossing sign it’s not a suggestion it’s a warning.”

Deers tend to be out during the day as they start to rut caused by the change of weather.

“This is deer-breeding season as the daylight gets shorter which causes the bucks to start chasing the female deer’s during the day. This causes them to lose much of there caution and not pay attention crossing roads.” said James Belfry the land management supervisor at Upper Thames Conservation Authority.

(Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

High deer populated areas include waterways with vegetated areas, open fields, and forested areas as they look for high energy food like nuts and acorns to help them over the winter.

Deer whistles are designed to warn deer and other animals away from road areas. Sanchuk has heard they both do and don’t work to keep animals away and doesn’t promote using them.

Deer whistles can be electrical powered or use the wind driving up to 50 km/h using driven audio sound waves. In one study by the westside journal in 2026 it found deer whistles tend to not make a difference compared to not having one.

(Credit: Google images)

If you end up hitting a deer you are legally required to contact local police or OPP and report the incident if the damage is more then two thousand dollars.

stories.title: 33 military members injured in fire remain in hospital
stories.summary: Ottawa — Defence Minister David McGuinty says 33 members of the Canadian Armed Forces remain in hospital after a deadly fire swept through a training ground at the military base in Wainwright, Alta., ON Saturday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Teresa Hiatt wasn’t worried about her younger brother while he was training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta before deployment to Latvia.

All that changed Saturday when news broke that a fast-moving grass fire at the military base had killed four soldiers and injured dozens of others.

Sean Haitt, a 24-year-old corporal in the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, is one of 19 in critical condition.

He’s sedated in an Edmonton hospital with burns to his face, arms and legs.

“You don’t expect it to happen when they’re training, right?” his sister said in a phone interview Tuesday from Edson, Alta.

“You have your fears if they’re deployed or in the line of combat. But when he left for his 20 days (in Wainwright), ‘Oh, he’ll be back.

“What we’ve been told, he’s going to need skin grafting. There’s going to be surgeries. There’s going to be therapy that he’s going to need to go through to regain the use of his limbs.”

She said they also don’t yet know the extend of the damage to his lungs.

“And there’s also the mental piece of it, right?”

The military has said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area at Wainwright, 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, as a grass fire burned about a kilometre away.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, said sudden, strong winds rapidly increased the fire’s intensity and flames were “right on top” of the soldiers within 30 seconds to a minute.

The four killed have been identified as: Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

As of Monday, 39 wounded were in hospital.

On Tuesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty said 33 were still being treated in various hospitals.

He said he wouldn’t comment on their medical conditions out of respect for their privacy.

McGuinty visited the Wainwright base Monday and visited some at the local hospital. He described the situation as “delicate and evolving” for those injured.

“We will provide all the support that we possibly can to make sure they get the help that they need,” McGuinty said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said 50 investigators on the ground are examining what happened.

McGuinty said there are three investigations going on.

This includes the RCMP working with military police on the formal investigation, the fire marshal’s work and a Forces board of inquiry, which examines matters of unusual significance or complexity resulting in the death or serious injury of military personnel.

McGuinty said it’s difficult to determine whether training protocol around wind should be changed until they have all the facts.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who was in Wainwright for two days, said he heard astonishing stories of bravery.

“The courage of soldiers who literally ran into walls of fire to pull their brothers and sisters out of danger,” he said.

“The story of the soldiers who were burned head to toe in the hospital, some with their vision lost, actually joking around with the nurses to try and make the nurses feel more comfortable.”

Teresa Hiatt said her first inkling something was wrong was around suppertime Saturday. She saw Facebook posts about the fire at the base.

She texted her brother’s girlfriend, who hadn’t heard from him since early that afternoon.

The family began calling hospitals and learned that he was in the Wainwright hospital. He was transferred to the University of Alberta hospital in Edmonton.

“He’s strong — that’s what the doctor said. He’s strong,” Hiatt said.

“He’s 24, he’s strong, that’s what he’s got going for him.”

She spent two days at her brother’s beside, and their parents are now with him.

His injuries could be life-altering, she said, and there’s questions about whether he’ll be able to return to the military as a reservist or to his job as a railway track maintenance supervisor with Canadian National.

She has organized a GoFundMe campaign to raise funds to help her brother.

“He’s always wanted to be a hero. Since he was a little boy, he’s loved anything to do with that — superheroes and the brotherhood that the military has. He loves it,” she said.

“He’s a strong man and he just loves pushing his body to the extremes. He loves all of that.

“And he wanted to serve his country.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray and Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

Ian Bickis, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Nursing association says London hospital cuts will hurt patients
stories.summary: A health care association was "flabbergasted" to learn that St. Joseph's Health Care London was laying off 85 ...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
A health care association was “flabbergasted” to learn that St. Joseph’s Health Care London was laying off 85 registered nurses, a spokesperson said Monday.

In an announcement last week, the hospital said cuts included 60 full time and 25 part time positions for registered nurses (RNs) and many frontline workers would be reassigned due to a $4.7 million deficit.

The decision, amid a demand for mental health support in London, could mean St. Joseph’s will also no longer be a part of the city’s Community Outreach and Support Team (Coast), said John Lowe, region five vice president of the Ontario Nurses Association (ONA). Coast is a service that includes RNs working with the London Police Service to provide on-scene community outreach to those in need.

“We are flabbergasted! No other province is laying off registered nurses, and we don’t understand why the government thinks it’s a safe thing to do,” said Lowe. “This will not bring good outcomes for the patients that rely on these services.”

Peggy Sattler, the provincial NDP for London-West, agreed.

“It is going to have an impact on patient care no matter how you try to justify it, the provincial government needs to be held accountable for this,” said the MPP.

The hospital said job changes are part of restructing and did not confirm specific layoff details.

“We’re creating 82 new full-time and 24 part-time direct care roles, including Rpn’s, personal support workers (Psw’s), occupational therapy/physiotherapy assistants, social service workers and therapeutic recreation assistants and removing 83 full-time and 31 part-time registered nurse roles,” said the hospital in its news release Thursday.

As the full scale of the layoffs has yet to be released, hospital staff wait in hopes of a change of course.

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Leaders react to Alberta referendum results to remain in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada on Monday in a historic referendum vote.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada on Monday in a historic referendum vote.

In early returns, about three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution.

Here’s what some Canadian leaders are saying.

“Thank you, Alberta! I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.

“Thank you to all Albertans who took time to vote on these critically important referendum questions.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“It’s a great day for Canada … I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose, high ambition.

“I’d like to thank all of the volunteers who supported the election, of course those who campaigned on all sides, the electoral volunteers who were still counting some of the votes, above all, Albertans for turning out in numbers, participating in the democratic process.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney

“Alberta voters have overwhelmingly chosen a stronger, more prosperous future for their province by remaining in Canada.

“I’m thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love. Now it’s up to the rest of Canada to deliver on our commitment to Alberta by building new pipelines, unlocking our natural resources and unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.

“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians, this result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford

“Alberta’s residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of a stronger Alberta within a united Canada. Canada’s promise is worth fighting for. We must now focus on concrete results in the lives of Canadians: affordable grocery baskets and housing, safe streets, strong borders, and reduced immigration. Your story is an epic of the most brilliant exploits.

“Well over one million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days: a moment of hope.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre

“So proud of Albertans for proving yet again that we are true Canadian patriots with the resounding vote for national unity!

“We are a province of dreamers, builders, and doers. We are optimists with an entrepreneurial culture. That’s why Alberta has never been fertile soil for the separatists’ inward-looking divisiveness, anger, and recrimination. Now let’s get on with the hard work of building an ever stronger Alberta in the true North, strong and free!”

Former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney

“We know things are tough in Alberta, from health care to the cost of living, to the embattled education system and so much more … But as so many Albertans have shown us, we don’t fix our problems by turning on each other.”

NDP Leader Avi Lewis

“Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this. Many Nova Scotians have strong ties to Alberta, either having worked there or with friends and family going to their province to help build up their industry.

“Here in Nova Scotia, we’ll keep doing our part to develop our own natural resources, create opportunities and contribute to a stronger Canada.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Leaders react after Albertans vote to remain in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa - Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada on Monday in a historic referendum vote.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada in Monday’s historic referendum vote.

In early returns, about three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution.

Here’s what some Canadian leaders are saying.

“Thank you, Alberta! I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.

“Thank you to all Albertans who took time to vote on these critically important referendum questions.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“It’s a great day for Canada … I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose, high ambition.

“I’d like to thank all of the volunteers who supported the election, of course those who campaigned on all sides, the electoral volunteers who were still counting some of the votes, above all, Albertans for turning out in numbers, participating in the democratic process.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney

“Albertans have decisively voted for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.

“The promise of Canada is worth fighting for.

“Now our focus must be on results in people’s lives: affordable food and homes, safe streets, strong borders, and less immigration.

“And may God keep our land glorious and free.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre

“The First Nations of Alberta have made their votes. Our people stood strong and reminded everyone that treaties matter. We are proud of our nations, our leadership, and everyone who stood up for all treaty people.”

Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi

“Thank you! We saved Canada. Now, we save Alberta.”

Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi

“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians, this result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division.

“Well over one million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days: a moment of hope.

“We know things are tough in Alberta, from health care to the cost of living, to the embattled education system and so much more … But as so many Albertans have shown us, we don’t fix our problems by turning on each other.”

“Businesses, workers and communities in Alberta understand that connections to the rest of Canada are a source of strength. At a historic time of unstable market access for them, they know there’s no advantage in cutting reliable customers and neighbours off.

“These results amplify the fact that Albertans remain overwhelmingly united that we’re better off with Canada, especially when we partner and help set a win-win economic agenda with the rest of the federation. That’s who Alberta is and will always be.”

Jason Kenney, former Alberta premier and co-chair of Stronger Together

“Small businesses in particular have been battered by years of economic barriers. This period of added uncertainty has not been welcome for them, or those thinking of starting a business. Business knows that communities depend on them, and they conversely depend on others across Canada to help stock their shelves, build new things or innovate their service.

“Going it alone isn’t a recipe for a better, stronger economy. I know many Alberta businesses and possible investors are counting on this question being settled once and for all. As we move forward, let’s commit to delivering that finality for them.”

Rachel Notley, former Alberta premier and co-chair of Stronger Together

“I’m glad to see Albertans vote overwhelmingly in favour of remaining in Canada.

“There is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa. But Canada is worth that effort.

“Saskatchewan will continue to work with Alberta to make our provinces stronger within a united Canada.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe

“Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this. Many Nova Scotians have strong ties to Alberta, either having worked there or with friends and family going to their province to help build up their industry.

“Here in Nova Scotia, we’ll keep doing our part to develop our own natural resources, create opportunities and contribute to a stronger Canada.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston

“Newfoundland and Labrador welcomes the decision of Albertans to remain within a strong and united Canada. While Canadians may hold differing views on these issues, the result affirms the value of working together to address challenges and advance shared interests. Canada’s strength comes from the ability of provinces and territories to work together in pursuit of common goals.

“A strong federation depends on constructive dialogue, respect for provincial jurisdiction and a commitment to collaboration. These principles are essential to building a more prosperous, competitive and resilient country.”

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham

“A strong Canada means that we need to make sure every part of our federation knows their essential value and that they feel valued and understood by the whole country. Alberta is central to economic security and opportunity in Canada and we must now turn our attention squarely to the needed work to collaboratively build a stronger, resilient, united economy from coast to coast to coast.

“Political disagreements between governments are inevitable, but our democracy is strong enough to resolve our differences. We can embrace unity without unanimity. Let’s move forward, stronger together.”

Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce

“The Business Council of Alberta is delighted with the decision by Albertans to remain a province of Canada.

“It is now time to move forward and get Alberta focused on generating prosperity and opportunity through economic expansion, job creation, innovation and education. Enough time has been lost to this referendum. There’s much work to do. Let’s get going.”

Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta

“Alberta’s economic success has been built on more than a century of trade relationships, shared infrastructure and strong connections with partners across Canada. At a time of growing global competition and trade uncertainty, Albertans have delivered a clear mandate: we want to be at the table, helping shape Canada’s prosperity and ensuring our province’s contributions and potential are fully recognized.

“Now is the time to build on that mandate by strengthening relationships across the country, removing internal trade barriers, expanding market access and ensuring businesses have access to the skilled workers they need. Alberta’s energy resources, entrepreneurial spirit and capacity to deliver major projects position us to play a leading role in advancing Canada’s nation-building agenda and getting things built.

“We recognize that the concerns that contributed to this debate have not disappeared, but we now have an opportunity to address them constructively, with a shared focus on delivering results.”

Deborah Yedlin, president and CEO of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce

“We’re stronger together as a country.

“I thank the people of Alberta for standing strong for Canada, and we’ll strong with Alberta. We won’t agree on everything, but we will work together to make this country strong.”

British Columbia Premier David Eby

“We can now move on to the meat and potatoes of what the vast majority of us are interested in, rather than being beholden to a very small niche within the UCP Party membership.”

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas

“We’re incredibly pleased by the result, but I don’t want anyone to think that we’re going back to business as usual in Ottawa.

“I think people realize that Alberta has these legitimate grievances and even a lot of people that voted to stay in Canada recognize that Alberta has these grievances, and we want to see action in Ottawa to address those.”

Conservative MP Dane Lloyd

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.
paragraphs: OTTAWA - Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada in Monday’s historic referendum vote.
In early returns, about three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.
The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution.
Here’s what some Canadian leaders are saying.

“Thank you, Alberta! I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.
“Thank you to all Albertans who took time to vote on these critically important referendum questions.”
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“It’s a great day for Canada … I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose, high ambition.

“I’d like to thank all of the volunteers who supported the election, of course those who campaigned on all sides, the electoral volunteers who were still counting some of the votes, above all, Albertans for turning out in numbers, participating in the democratic process.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney
“Albertans have decisively voted for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.
“The promise of Canada is worth fighting for.
“Now our focus must be on results in people’s lives: affordable food and homes, safe streets, strong borders, and less immigration.
“And may God keep our land glorious and free.”
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre

“The First Nations of Alberta have made their votes. Our people stood strong and reminded everyone that treaties matter. We are proud of our nations, our leadership, and everyone who stood up for all treaty people.”
Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi
“Thank you! We saved Canada. Now, we save Alberta.”
Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi
“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians, this result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division.

stories.title: Canada urges travellers to avoid demonstrations as France grapples with rioting
stories.summary: Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.

On Monday, Global Affairs Canada updated its travel advice for France amid nationwide demonstrations , which began in September with students protesting school conditions. Those protests have since swelled into a broader movement targeting issues like the rising cost of living.

With some demonstrations leading to vandalism, looting, arson and violent clashes with police, French authorities have responded with tear gas, water cannons and localized curfews.

Global Affairs Canada is now urging travellers to France to avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place and to follow local curfew orders, which are currently in place in parts of Paris such as the Place de la République square and around the Les Halles food market.

We have updated our travel advice for #France due to ongoing demonstrations and local curfews. More details here: https://t.co/tA5PyGcwyR pic.twitter.com/edVUKzDJ3z — Travel.gc.CA (@TravelGoC) October 19, 2026

Other restrictions on gatherings, such as curfews for minors, are also in effect in cities like Lyon, Marseille, Nice and Lille.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu credited the “targeted curfews” with helping maintain calm overnight into Tuesday, and warned that local authorities are considering whether to impose similar measures for a further night.

“Check with local authorities to determine whether you are in an area subject to a curfew,” Global Affairs Canada advises. “Even peaceful demonstrations can turn violent at any time.”

Canada is also advising travellers to France to monitor local media for the latest information and follow the instructions of local authorities.

“Be prepared to adjust your travel plans in the event of disruptions,” Global Affairs Canada says. “Expect heightened security measures and an increased police presence.”

Canada has long advised travellers to France to “exercise a high degree of caution” due to the potential threat of terrorism.

More than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands.

With files from CNN

stories.title: Alberta referendum vote to remain is ‘great result for Canada,’ Carney says
stories.summary: Albertans have opted to remain part of Canada — decisively voting to reject the idea of holding a formal referendum on separatism.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Albertans voting decisively not to pursue separation was a “great result for Canada,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday.

Carney said he was “thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity.”

“They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose,” Carney said.

He spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the phone on Tuesday morning, Carney said.

The “first focus” of the call was the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and the supports that both governments can provide for the victims and families affected by the fire.

“Then we turn to the referendum and moving forward in the spirit of cooperative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities of the federal government, the provinces,” Carney said.

The nation’s focus must now be on questions of affordability, safety and immigration, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Tuesday.

“Albertans have decisively voted for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada. The promise of Canada is worth fighting for,” Poilievre, MP for the Alberta riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, said in a statement.

Elections Alberta began releasing the results of the province’s referendum on the topic late Monday night, with around 76 per cent of Albertans voting to remain part of Canada.

The separatism question asked voters if Alberta should remain in Canada or if the provincial government should begin the legal process of holding a future binding referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

–With files from Global’s Karen Bartko

stories.title: Carney says Alberta’s choice of unity is ‘a great result’ for Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says it was "a great result for Canada" when Albertans chose unity in a referendum on Monday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Edmonton — Danielle Smith says Albertans have spoken in Monday’s referendum and that as long as she is premier, separation is a dead issue.

Smith, in a TV address to the province, says there will be no more referendums on separation as long as she is in charge.

And she says separation will not be used as a tool to fight Ottawa, but instead any challenges will be waged through political avenues and the courts.

The mandate is clear, Smith said in a 14-minute speech.

“Alberta will remain a province of Canada.

“Albertans will continue to be Canadians.”

Her comments come after three-quarters of votes cast in Alberta’s referendum called for the province to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding vote on leaving Confederation.

Smith called the vote to put to rest what she viewed as a widespread, divisive debate. She said Tuesday that debate is over, and so is the subject of separation in Alberta.

“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue.

“Make no mistake,” she added. “Our government will continue to boldly assert our province’s autonomy by exercising the provincial rights guaranteed to us under Canada’s Constitution.

“But those disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions of our nation rather than pursuing the option of separation.”

She said she recognizes and respects those Canadians she says suffered under the policies of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, but stressed it’s a new day under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

She noted the two levels of government are co-operating to build Alberta and Canada through projects like a new pipeline to the B.C. coast.

“Albertans have turned the tide of this nation and reset the relationship with our federal government in a positive direction,” she said.

She said it was time for Albertans to put aside differences, now that the vote is done.

“Let us move forward not as a people divided by how we voted yesterday but as neighbours, friends, Albertans and Canadians.

“Let us treat one another with respect and compassion.”

Smith said she voted yes to stay in Canada, and public opinion polls before she called the referendum, after she called it, and on referendum night consistently indicated a strong majority of Albertans were also happy in the Confederation fold.

To that end, critics say there was never a broad-based movement to quit Confederation and accused Smith of rolling the dice on national unity simply to placate restive separatists who wield outsized influence in her United Conservative party.

Earlier Tuesday, Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said Smith must now find a way to win back the trust of Albertans distressed over the vote, who are scheduled to go to the polls in a general election less than a year from now, ON Oct. 18, 2027.

Across Canada Tuesday, other provincial and national leaders weighed in on the referendum. They stressed it was heartening to see Albertans place their faith in the federation.

“It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Prime Minister Carney told reporters in Ottawa. “They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other.”

In Calgary, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the vote was welcome but was also a message to Carney.

“After 11 years of Liberal government, there’s a quarter of Albertans, a third of Quebecers, that voted for a separation option in the last month,” Poilievre said.

“It’s time to deliver real results in people’s real lives.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa and Dayne Patterson in Calgary.

Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada’s PBO slashes economic forecasts, warns debt will rise
stories.summary: Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down at the end of August followed by a new round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Parliamentary Budget Office has trimmed its outlook for economic growth for this year and next amid new U.S. tariffs and Canadian countermeasures.

In a revised outlook on Tuesday, the federal budget watchdog said it now projects real gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

The forecast is down from estimated growth of 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively, issued in June.

“Canada faces a more challenging economic and fiscal outlook than we projected in June,” Annette Ryan, parliamentary budget officer, said in a news release.

“Additional trade measures and ongoing uncertainty are weighing on growth in real output – what we produce as a country.”

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down at the end of August followed by a new round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.

1:37 Canada’s GDP rises 3.3% in 2nd quarter, but US trade war could halt that momentum

The PBO said it also now projects a budgetary deficit of $63.3 billion for the 2026-27 fiscal year, which will peak at $70.2 billion in 2027-28.

Relative to its June outlook, the deficits are $3 billion higher per year on average over 2026‑27 to 2030‑31, as new spending measures more than offset stronger revenues, the watchdog said.

“The PBO continues to maintain that debt-to-GDP ratio is an important benchmark for measuring fiscal health,” Ryan said. “It will rise steadily over the five-year horizon.”

She added: “Over the longer term, Canada’s economic and fiscal outlook will depend heavily on whether recent capital budget investments can translate into stronger productivity, economic capacity and prosperity.”

Meanwhile, the PBO assumes the Bank of Canada will start raising its policy rate in early 2027 “to keep inflation expectations anchored,” reaching 2.75 per cent by midyear.

On inflation, the watchdog expects higher energy prices will keep the annual inflation rate elevated in 2026, averaging 2.8 per cent, before easing to 2.4 per cent in 2027.

stories.title: Air Canada adds fee for phone bookings. Here’s how much
stories.summary: Travellers who book an Air Canada flight via its call centre should brace for an extra charge of $30 per passenger, as the airline encourages customers to opt for its “digital tools” instead.
stories.author: Ethan Morneau
stories.content:
A Canadian airline is putting a price on phone calls.

Travellers booking an Air Canada flight via its call centre should brace for an extra charge of $30 per passenger, as the airline encourages customers to opt for its “digital tools” instead.

The new fee — which took effect on Oct. 15 — does not apply to customers who purchase tickets through its website or app.

But for those who do call to reserve, the fee is non-refundable, even after cancelling a ticket or booking, according to Air Canada. For a booking with two passengers, the fee would equal $60.

“The booking fee will appear as its own charge … not included in the airfare or carrier-imposed charges associated with your ticket,” the airline says on its webpage announcing the fee .

Air Canada is highlighting its “easy self-serve options,” encouraging customers to use its website or app to book flights.

“Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support,” it says.

Some flyers exempt

Call agents remain available over the phone for bookings — and some customers can forego the additional fee, which already applied to Aeroplan flight reward bookings made by phone.

“Customers who require specialized care and support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt…” Air Canada says.

“There is also no change to the support available to you, and no booking fee will apply if your trip is affected by a delay, cancellation or other travel disruption,” the airline adds on its website.

“The booking fee will continue to apply for Aeroplan flight reward bookings made through our Contact Centre.”

Customers can still call Air Canada for help with existing reservations, travel disruptions and other questions without paying the new fee.

Other Canadian airlines, including WestJet and Flair , already charge a service fee for bookings made over the phone.

stories.title: Grifols reopening two Canada locations after two-month pause
stories.summary: Health Canada says Winnipeg site where woman donated before death remains closed
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Grifols, Canada’s only major commercial collector of blood plasma, says it will gradually begin reopening its centres starting Tuesday.

The Barcelona-headquartered company announced in August it was pausing collections at its 17 Canadian centres following a series of critical Health Canada inspections and public outcry over the deaths of two donors.

Grifols said it is reopening two locations – in Edmonton’s Windermere neighbourhood and in Winnipeg on Innovation Drive – for a limited number of appointments.

The company said it has used the two-month pause to improve employee training and supervision, and strengthen operating procedures. Grifols says it is reopening in co-ordination with Health Canada.

Health Canada said staff have visited centres to verify that the company has taken corrective actions in response to the regulator’s concerns.

“Grifols is expected to demonstrate ongoing compliance as operations resume,” spokesperson Karine LeBlanc said in a statement.

Health Canada said the licence for Grifols’ location on Taylor Avenue in Winnipeg remained suspended . The regulator had taken the unprecedented move of suspending that licence after finding issues with assessing donor suitability and not thoroughly investigating some errors.

Taylor Avenue was also the site of a donation last year by a 22-year-old university student named Rodiyat Alabede, who began having heart problems during the donation and was pronounced dead at a hospital shortly afterwards.

A Health Canada report later said Grifols staff should have terminated Ms. Alabede’s donation early because of alerts that sounded on the donation machine.

Plasma is a golden-coloured fluid found in blood that is used to produce some types of medicine.

Grifols operates in Canada in partnership with Canadian Blood Services, which spends more than $1-billion a year on plasma-derived drugs and related pharmaceutical products.

Canadian Blood Services said in an unsigned statement that it believed Grifols was taking “prudent and effective steps” to improve operations. The charity said its partnership with the company is still needed to achieve its goal of greater domestic production of plasma-derived drugs.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY (October 21, 2026)– Today we recognize the dedication, skill, and compassion of those working hard to educate, care for and help shape the next generation of County residents.

This year, the theme for Early Childhood Educator & Child Care Worker Appreciation Day is Care Counts. This highlights the importance of care in early learning and child care and the pride that ECEs and child care workers take in their work.

Middlesex County extends its sincere thanks to all Early Childhood Educators and child care workers for the positive impact they make in the lives of children and families. Your care, guidance and expertise, builds strong foundations for lifelong success.

Today and every day, we count on that care that you provide.

"We are proud to recognize the incredible work of child care workers and early childhood educators across Middlesex County and the important role they have in supporting our families. Thank you to every educator and child care professional for the compassion and commitment you show everyday,” says Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke.

Learn more aboutChildren's Services in Middlesex County.

stories.title: Five takeaways from Alberta’s separation referendum
stories.summary: Separatists now look at other options, including rallying UCP members to oust Premier Danielle Smith at next month’s annual party gathering
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Albertans have voted against separating from Canada in a historic referendum, according to preliminary results released in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

The results, however, will likely do little to silence separatist sentiment across the province and could further escalate questions about whether Alberta Premier Danielle Smith can maintain control of her party – and the province.

The political fallout will now take centre stage as Alberta’s United Conservative Party, Opposition New Democratic Party, federalists and separatists decide how to leverage this pivotal moment in the province’s history.

Here are five key takeaways following Monday’s vote.

Elections Alberta tallied the results of the separation question first. At 3:01 p.m. MT (5:01 p.m. ET) on Tuesday, with 88 per cent of voting locations reporting, the agency said almost 1.45 million Albertans supported staying in Canada, or 75 per cent, while more than 477,000 elected to launch the legal process to hold a second referendum on secession, or 25 per cent.

Early results indicate voters in Calgary and Edmonton threw their weight behind Confederation at a rate outpacing their rural counterparts. The more the spread widens, the more difficult it will be for the Premier to keep the peace within the United Conservative Party.

There were roughly 3.15 million eligible voters in Alberta, and residents came out in droves. Nearly 1.36 million Albertans cast an advance vote or special ballot before referendum day, exceeding the turnout for the 2023 provincial election. Just over 43 per cent of eligible electors voted in advance, compared with 27.5 per cent in 2023.

The ballots are being hand counted because the province no longer allows electronic tabulators. Polls closed later than planned Monday after delays in opening at multiple voting locations.

The outcome of Monday’s vote didn’t matter: Separatists have been clear that their work is far from over.

Mitch Sylvestre, leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the province’s most prominent separatist organizations, said his first option in trying to advance his agenda was the referendum. Now, he’s looking at other options.

“You have to get involved in government. That’s the different way,” he said, though he added he believes an independence party would have slim chances of winning a general election.

Mr. Sylvestre said he would meet with “independence leaders” for breakfast on Tuesday to decide next steps.

His partner at the Alberta Prosperity Project, Jeff Rath, was more defiant in defeat, taking aim at the Premier.

“The next phase for us moving forward is an institutional phase where we move forward to take control back of our party, which is the United Conservative Party of Alberta,” Mr. Rath said.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who co-founded the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said Monday night that the results show many people want change. “At least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better.”

Federalists will be pleased that Albertans have voted to stay in Canada but the outcome is unlikely to position Ms. Smith as an ally to the movement.

The Premier has a contentious relationship with the pro-Canada crowd, who have accused her of pandering to separatists and voiced dissatisfaction with her muddled messaging on Alberta’s place within Canada.

While Ms. Smith has said repeatedly that she wants Alberta to be part of a “united Canada,” she has been relentless in her push to squeeze Ottawa for additional powers for the province. It has also not gone unnoticed by many federalists that there is significant overlap between the people who pushed her into power and the separatists.

Former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, the head organizer of Forever Canadian, the largest federalist group, said he isn’t confident that Ms. Smith won’t hold another referendum in the future.

Ms. Smith is now left with the difficult task of maintaining control of her party while broadly appealing to Albertans. Already, some separatists are rallying UCP members to oust her at next month’s annual party gathering.

The Alberta NDP, which has positioned itself as staunchly pro-Canada, has capitalized on widespread opposition to the referendum, gaining political momentum in recent months after a long period of stagnation.

A sign that the separatism debate was weighing down the Ucp’s popularity came in September when NDP candidate Kyle Campbell won a by-election in the reliable conservative riding of Calgary-Shaw.

Ms. Smith blamed the stunning upset on a vote split between two conservative parties and low voter turnout. But political strategists argued the referendum turned the by-election into a protest vote against separation.

Recent polling also suggests that the divide between the UCP and NDP has narrowed, with the two parties locked in a virtual tie.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said the referendum has hit a nerve with voters. His job now, he said, is to make sure Albertans hold on to that feeling until the next provincial election.

“My challenge is really to help Albertans remember what happened, remember how frustrated they were today but also remember that they deserve better,” Mr. Nenshi said on Monday night.

Still, it’s a full year before a scheduled provincial election, giving the UCP significant runway to calm any lingering tensions from the referendum.

Ms. Smith’s relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney has warmed over the past year, particularly over his approach to energy and pipelines. On Friday, the pair stood side by side in Red Deer to rally support for Alberta to remain in Canada.

But the complicated – and often tense – relationship between the province and Ottawa is a tale as old as Alberta.

The two leaders still have areas of disagreement, including on the other nine questions included in the referendum. While Ms. Smith urged voters to say yes to proposals on topics including immigration, health care and constitutional reform that would wrest power away from Ottawa, Mr. Carney wanted voters to reject them.

Votes on the other nine questions were still being tallied early Tuesday. The full count is expected to take two days to complete.

Ms. Smith has said that the new mandate from the other ballot questions would be used as leverage to increase provincial autonomy, shaping the federal-provincial relationship in the days and months to come.

With files from Matthew Scace and Temur Durrani in Edmonton and Emma Graney and Carrie Tait in Calgary

stories.title: How the son of the original ‘Iceman’ furthered his father’s legacy
stories.summary: Growth required a fresh perspective and a willingness to cede some control of The Iceman. Unexpected exposure from Drake hasn’t hurt either
stories.author: Nickie Shobeiry
stories.content:
Right after university graduation in 2011, Jake Silva put on his “investor glasses” for a Toronto ice-distribution business even though he didn’t have a financial stake in the company.

He had the fresh eyes of a younger generation that could bring new ideas and perspective to The Iceman, which his father John Silva had started 24 years earlier.

Jake saw a reputable company with steady demand, but also an operation that lacked structure and that had unrealized potential. Payroll would take days, clients still used paper invoices and filing cabinets were filled with physical records.

Jake decided to apply his degree in commerce and finance from Concordia University to the family business – involvement that would eventually fulfill expansion aspirations that John had always held but had never acted on.

However, transforming the regional ice distributor into a manufacturer with a production facility in Ontario and one in Alberta was a years-long process that required the founder to give up some power.

“I’m very hands-on,” John, 64, acknowledges. “I try to control stuff, and you can’t be like that” to grow.

The business moved away from having most decisions revolve around John, which had created bottlenecks. He is now much better at allowing departments to run their own teams, says Jake, who joined The Iceman full-time in 2012 and has been president since 2020. “I don’t think we would have grown as much as we have without him [ceding] some control.”

The founder of a business entering a new chapter must allow incoming leaders to “exercise real authority,” says Jill Renton, executive director of Kpmg Canada’s family office. Succession is ideally a gradual transfer where the next generation proves their capability over time, she adds.

Transitioning The Iceman’s leadership is an example of such progression. Jake, now 37, grew up delivering bags of ice by golf cart each summer to bars, restaurants and events such as pride parades as well as running and car races. Once he joined permanently, he held a wide variety of roles throughout the enterprise.

When John’s business partner at the time wanted out in 2017, Jake, who was handling all accounting and finance matters, bought a stake. Until then, The Iceman was primarily a distributor, relying on an ice manufacturer that was also its competitor for product. “The dynamic was problematic,” Jake says, “because they could really control which kind of customers we could go after and which ones we couldn’t.”

He devised a business plan for The Iceman to build its own ice plant. His father was excited, Jake recalls, saying it’s something that John had always wanted to do, “but maybe he wasn’t able to put together all the pieces” when it came to financing and bank loans.

Jake secured the necessary funding and the company opened its first ice plant in 2018 in Vaughan, north of Toronto. The facility makes about 50 metric tonnes of ice daily but they’ve had to turn away clients in the last two years because of a lack of capacity. A second Toronto-area plant set to open early next year is expected to triple output.

Today, The Iceman supplies restaurants, events and businesses including Costco with cocktail cubes, packaged ice and dry ice, as well as heat-relief water bottles and freezers for construction sites. It also sells, rents and services ice machines. In 2024, it acquired an Edmonton company that produces and distributes ice across Alberta. The Iceman has grown to 80 employees in the summertime from around 30 when Jake first joined.

He also helped move the company toward software-based payroll, accounting, invoicing and dispatch systems. “If we had the old way of doing things, growing would have just been so painful,” Jake says.

John, who now manages The Iceman’s sales and customer relationships, appreciates his son’s leadership: “I see Jake’s done what he’s done and I’m very happy and lucky that he’s taken over.”

While Jake says he sometimes still seeks his father’s advice, “I’m already driving the bus, and he’s happy to have the role he’s in now.”

Ms. Renton notes that it’s important for a successor to understand the founder’s “unique qualities” that allowed the business to flourish in the first place. New leaders must treat their predecessors as “an important point of continuity,” she says.

John entered the industry in the mid-1970s when an ice plant in downtown Toronto closed and his parents’ nearby variety store became a local ice collection point. When restaurants asked if they could send taxis to the shop to retrieve bags of ice, John began delivering them himself in a pickup truck. He later bought a truck that doubled as both a delivery vehicle and storage for six pallets of ice and then expanded into dry ice and ice-machine rentals and repairs.

“I always learned how to hustle,” John says. However, in the early days, “I didn’t have the whole business plan together.”

The company’s profile got an unexpected boost this spring through a collaboration with the musical artist Drake, tied to the rollout of his 2026 album Iceman . After connecting through a mutual friend, the Canadian rapper and singer filmed video footage at The Iceman’s plant.

The attention sent millions of people to The Iceman’s website every day. “People pay a lot of money for a viral moment like that, so the fact that we were able to get it very coincidentally – it was great,” Jake says.

The Drake partnership sparked demand for The Iceman merchandise – previously only available to employees – such as jackets, hoodies and hats. Within two weeks of Drake’s single release, the company added an online store, selling more than 1,200 orders since, Jake says.

“It’s kind of cool to think that there’s people all over the world wearing Iceman T-shirts.”

stories.title: Police asking for public’s help finding missing George Nash, 80
stories.summary: London police have asked residents of a southeast London neighbourhood to search their yards, sheds, garages a...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
London police have asked residents of a southeast London neighbourhood to search their yards, sheds, garages and cars for an 80-year-old man, who was last reported seen a week ago.

Police say them and George Nash has been missing since Oct. 14, when he was seen near Wellington Road and Weston Street. He is vulnerable and his family is concerned for his well being, police said.

There have been no updates since Saturday, when police announced they would be searching the Chelsea Green neighbourhood.

“The investigation is ongoing and the most recent media release that was shared asking members of the public to search their properties and outbuildings,” is still the message police are sending, said Sergeant Sandasha Bough in a comment today

There will be a bigger police presence in the Chelsea Green neighbourhood as they officers continue to search for him, police said in an October 17 update.

George Nash, 80 Photo Credits: London Police Service

Nash is desribed as white, around 5’2 and 120lbs, with balding white hair and blue eyes.

He was last seen in a light blue shirt, a dark blue striped jacket, casual pants and a beige baseball hat.

Police are asking that if anyone has any information to call them at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Woman dies after single-vehicle crash in London
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to the 600-block of Upper Queen Street at about 1:20 a.m. for reports of a serious crash.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A woman has died following a single-vehicle collision in London early Tuesday morning, according to police.

Emergency crews were called to the 600-block of Upper Queen Street at about 1:20 a.m. for reports of a serious crash.

Police said a female passenger was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. She later died from those injuries.

The male driver was arrested at the scene and remains in police custody.

Police continue to investigate the collision and have not released the identities of those involved or details about what led to the crash.

Upper Queen Street remains closed between Chiddington Avenue and Ferndale Avenue while investigators examine the scene. Motorists are being advised to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

stories.title: One person extricated following London crash
stories.summary: Fire crews responded to the scene and extricated one person from a vehicle involved in the collision.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A section of Upper Queen Street has been closed in London following a motor vehicle collision that required a rescue by fire crews.

London police said Upper Queen Street is closed between Chiddington Avenue and Ferndale Avenue as officers investigate the crash. Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

Fire crews responded to the scene and extricated one person from a vehicle involved in the collision.

Police have not released information about the extent of any injuries or how the crash happened.

The road is expected to remain closed for an undetermined amount of time.

stories.title: Albertans mixed on other referendum questions after rejecting separation
stories.summary: Albertans decisively rejected moving toward separation in Monday’s referendum, while several of the remaining questions produced narrower margins.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Albertans decisively rejected moving toward separation in Monday’s referendum , while several of the remaining questions produced narrower margins.

Elections Alberta reported results from 75 per cent of voting locations as of 5 a.m. MT Tuesday. The figures remain unofficial and May change as counting continues. Official results are expected on Oct. 29.

The referendum posed 10 questions, including one asking if the province should hold a formal referendum on separation. Around 76 per cent of respondents said no .

The margins on several of the nine other questions were considerably narrower. Five involved immigration and services for non-permanent residents, while four concerned potential constitutional changes.

The immigration questions asked if Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work, and whether it’s time to put more limitations — or even fees — on some who seek access to health care and education.

The constitutional questions asked whether the province should pursue constitutional negotiations with other governments on gaining control from Ottawa and abolishing the Senate.

Unofficial results showed nearly 59 per cent in favour for the first question, which sought support for increased provincial control for the purpose of decreasing immigration.

A similar result was reported for the second question on access limits for programs like health care, education and social services. About 57 per cent supported limiting those programs to citizens, permanent residents and those with approved immigration status.

Roughly 63 per cent supported requiring proof of citizenship to vote, which was asked in question five.

Question six, which asked if Albertans want the government to try and amend the constitution to allow provinces to select justices for provincial courts, had 50.7 per cent support.

About 52 per cent opposed the proposal in question eight, which asked if Alberta should opt out of federal programs like health care, education, social services without losing federal funding.

Nearly 51 per cent supported question nine, which asked if the government should try to amend the constitution to give provincial laws priority over federal laws when they conflict.

Global News continues to track the live results to each question, which can be viewed here .

After decisive defeat, Alberta separatists turn their attention to Smith and the UCP

stories.title: Home seller rejects weak spring offer, waits for a better one
stories.summary: Four-bedroom house has 2,510 square feet of living space and finished basement with direct access to heated garage and driveway
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
64 Thompson Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $3,548,000 (August, 2026)

Previous asking price: $3,698,000 (April, 2026)

Selling price: $3.5-million (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $12,867 (2026)

Days on the market: 13

Property days on market: 128

Listing agent: Luisa Piccirilli, Re/Max West Realty Inc.

This four-bedroom house has 2,510 square feet of living space and a finished basement with direct access to a heated garage and driveway. There’s also a rear exit to a hot tub and cabana on the 35- by 120-foot lot. Though buyers this spring were intrigued by the home’s design and convenient location a block from Bloor Street West, there was only one offer, and that was far below the asking price.

“There are excellent schools in the area that certainly attract a lot of young families,” said agent Luisa Piccirilli.

“It was a very spacious house, but a lot of feedback was [that buyers] wanted it a little bigger. Otherwise, the upgrades more than made up for that.”

In August, the home was relisted with the asking price cut by $150,000. Within two weeks, one buyer negotiated a deal at $3.5-million, with another potential buyer waiting in the wings.

“All of a sudden, we had so many more eyes on the listing,” Ms. Piccirilli said.

“I like to work with one offer at a time, but we could have had a choice of other offers. We had someone potentially waiting if something went south with this offer.”

This two-storey house has an office and open-concept living and dining areas with 10-foot ceilings.

The kitchen has an island, a pantry and sliding doors to the patio. There is a barbecue station, a cabana with a wet bar and a powder room.

There are five bathrooms, and a sauna in the basement. Also downstairs is a recreation area with a wet bar and heated flooring.

“The cabana was great because it was multifunctional,” said Ms. Piccirilli.

“It could have been a yoga studio, definitely an office or even a cigar lounge.”

stories.title: A family looks for just enough space in Niagara Falls
stories.summary: What can this downsizing family get for $550,000?
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Dhana Dias immigrated from her native Brazil to Toronto in 2016. Three years later, in 2019, she met fellow Brazilian Ronald Augusto, a 41-year-old data analyst, through Toronto’s Brazilian community. In 2021, the two became roommates, sharing an apartment near Wellesley Station before their friendship evolved into romance. Ms. Dias, 39, became pregnant, and just before their son, Max, was born, the couple moved to a larger two-bedroom condo in Humber Bay Shores, which they rented for $2,600 a month.

As Max got older, the family felt cramped in their condo (they also had two cats). After visiting friends who lived in Welland, Ont., just west of Niagara Falls, they fell in love with the area. “It was so quiet and seemed so safe,” Ms. Dias explains. They moved into a new three-bedroom townhouse rental in Welland at the end of 2022, paying $2,200 a month. But the couple struggled with loud neighbours. Their second son, Alex, was born in 2023, and they moved to a four-bedroom detached home in the Brown area of Niagara Falls in 2024, paying $2,700 per month.

At the same time, Ms. Dias was undergoing a career change and became a real estate agent. Her work brought her in and out of homes for sale and opened the couple’s eyes to what might be possible for their family. “Seeing people with a similar background and making the same money as we were … affording a house. We thought, maybe we can do it,” Mr. Augusto explains. They figured they could buy a smaller house and spend roughly the same amount on a mortgage as they did on rent. “We realized we didn’t need all this space,” Ms. Dias explains.

Home Run: With a $1.5-million budget for a new home, what did this expecting Toronto couple buy?

Because Ms. Dias was now self-employed, they had to wait until she had two years of tax returns as proof of income to qualify for a mortgage. By early April, 2026, they filed their 2025 taxes, were pre-approved for a mortgage and hit the ground running.

The couple wanted at least three bedrooms, plus an additional bedroom or a finished basement for guests and a kids’ playroom. A garage was a must to park their car in the winter, as was a good backyard for the kids to play in. But the most important element was location: they wanted to be close to Forestview, where their kids’ daycare was located. “It’s a very family-friendly neighbourhood,” Ms. Dias says. “People tend to take care of their homes and yards with a bit more care.”

With their preapproval in place and additional help from savings back in Brazil, they set themselves a budget of $550,000. Here were their top three options:

Small three-bedroom townhouse in Forestview

Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias were eager to see this home because it was within walking distance to their sons’ daycare, a public school, and a great playground. It was a newer home, around ten years old and move-in ready. It had three bedrooms and three bathrooms, but the basement wasn’t finished, leaving no space for guests or a kids’ playroom. And while the family was up for downsizing, at 1,125 square feet, they worried the house would be too small for them. The layout had less natural light, so the home felt darker. But it did have a single-car garage and a nice fenced-in backyard for their kids to play in. The listing price of $520,000 was also under their budget.

Older four-bedroom detached home in Dorchester

Despite the fact that it was 15 minutes east of their target neighbourhood, Ms. Dias had viewed this home with a client and thought it might work for her family, so she returned with Mr. Augusto. The home felt spacious at 1,512 square feet, and it had four bedrooms and two bathrooms. It was an older house that had been recently renovated, but the basement was unfinished. In addition, one of the bathrooms in the basement needed some renovation work that the couple wasn’t keen to take on. There wasn’t any carpet in the home, which they saw as a bonus, since it’s easier to keep clean with kids and pets. It had a detached garage and a sizable backyard with a shed. But the neighbourhood was noisier and closer to the tourist district, which meant more traffic. It was listed just under their top budget, at $549,999.

Spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

The couple wasn’t initially going to see this home in Fernwood Estates, just west of Forestview, because it was over their budget, priced at $579,900. But Ms. Dias figured the sellers might be willing to negotiate. They loved that the neighbourhood was in an enclave with one entrance and exit, which felt safe and private. The neighbours’ homes were very well-kept with tidy front yards, which they liked. The 1,501-square-foot house had a one-and-a-half-car garage, three bedrooms and a finished basement. The backyard was spacious and fenced in, which would be great for the kids to play in. However, there was only one full bathroom – the second bath was just a powder room – and there was carpet on the top level, which they felt wasn’t ideal with two cats and two kids under five.

Their home: The spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias worried that the detached home in Dorchester wasn’t the best neighbourhood for their kids, and an older home would require too much maintenance. They actually submitted an offer on the small three-bedroom townhouse in Forestview for $500,000, but an administrative oversight resulted in another buyer with the same bid getting the property. The couple was glad it turned out that way since, in retrospect, they believe that home would have been too small for their family. They liked that the Fernwood Estates townhouse was bigger and brighter. “It was love at first sight, for sure,” Mr. Augusto explains.

The couple offered $545,000 for the spacious three-bedroom townhouse. Since Ms. Dias was a realtor, she was able to waive her 2 per cent commission, which she thinks helped sweeten the deal. The purchase was finalized at the end of April, 2026, only a few weeks after they first started looking for a home, and the family moved in by June.

Right now, their two sons are sharing a bedroom (“They love it,” says Mr. Augusto. “They wanted to sleep together.”) while the couple is in the primary bedroom and the third bedroom is their shared office. The kids have enjoyed turning the basement into their playroom, running around in the backyard and biking to a nearby playground.

Downsizing from 2,500 square feet to 1,500 square feet as a family of four might seem like a less-favourable transition. But Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias believe it was the right move for them. “We didn’t even have enough furniture for the whole house,” Ms. Dias says about their former rental home. “It was a lot to clean and a lot of work for us.”

While they initially thought the fourth bedroom in their old home would be great for overnight guests, they realized that having a larger house just for occasional visitors wasn’t worth the space or expense. The couple plans to add a sofa bed to the finished basement to host guests in the future.

As their sons grow older and need separate bedrooms, Ms. Dias and Mr. Augusto will think about upgrading in about five years. Meanwhile, they’re enjoying life in their new home. “Every day, I wake up and say, ‘I love this house,’” Ms. Augusto says.

There wasn’t any carpet in the home, which they saw as a bonus, since it’s easier to keep clean with kids and pets. It had a detached garage and a sizable backyard with a shed. But the neighbourhood was noisier and closer to the tourist district, which meant more traffic. It was listed just under their top budget, at $549,999.
Spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

The couple wasn’t initially going to see this home in Fernwood Estates, just west of Forestview, because it was over their budget, priced at $579,900. But Ms. Dias figured the sellers might be willing to negotiate. They loved that the neighbourhood was in an enclave with one entrance and exit, which felt safe and private. The neighbours’ homes were very well-kept with tidy front yards, which they liked. The 1,501-square-foot house had a one-and-a-half-car garage, three bedrooms and a finished basement. The backyard was spacious and fenced in, which would be great for the kids to play in. However, there was only one full bathroom – the second bath was just a powder room – and there was carpet on the top level, which they felt wasn’t ideal with two cats and two kids under five.
Their home: The spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias worried that the detached home in Dorchester wasn’t the best neighbourhood for their kids, and an older home would require too much maintenance. They actually submitted an offer on the small three-bedroom townhouse in Forestview for $500,000, but an administrative oversight resulted in another buyer with the same bid getting the property. The couple was glad it turned out that way since, in retrospect, they believe that home would have been too small for their family. They liked that the Fernwood Estates townhouse was bigger and brighter. “It was love at first sight, for sure,” Mr. Augusto explains.

The couple offered $545,000 for the spacious three-bedroom townhouse. Since Ms. Dias was a realtor, she was able to waive her 2 per cent commission, which she thinks helped sweeten the deal. The purchase was finalized at the end of April, 2026, only a few weeks after they first started looking for a home, and the family moved in by June.

Right now, their two sons are sharing a bedroom (“They love it,” says Mr. Augusto. “They wanted to sleep together.”) while the couple is in the primary bedroom and the third bedroom is their shared office. The kids have enjoyed turning the basement into their playroom, running around in the backyard and biking to a nearby playground.

Downsizing from 2,500 square feet to 1,500 square feet as a family of four might seem like a less-favourable transition. But Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias believe it was the right move for them. “We didn’t even have enough furniture for the whole house,” Ms. Dias says about their former rental home. “It was a lot to clean and a lot of work for us.”

While they initially thought the fourth bedroom in their old home would be great for overnight guests, they realized that having a larger house just for occasional visitors wasn’t worth the space or expense. The couple plans to add a sofa bed to the finished basement to host guests in the future.

As their sons grow older and need separate bedrooms, Ms. Dias and Mr. Augusto will think about upgrading in about five years. Meanwhile, they’re enjoying life in their new home. “Every day, I wake up and say, ‘I love this house,’” Ms. Augusto says.

stories.title: Porter flights prompt London Transit Commission to explore better bus service to YXU
stories.summary: Recent announcements by Porter Airlines about new flights coming to London International Airport (YXU) has prompted the London Transit Commission (LTC) to investigate improving bus service for travellers.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Recent announcements by Porter Airlines about new flights coming to London International Airport (YXU) has prompted the London Transit Commission (LTC) to investigate improving bus service for travellers.

On Monday, a motion by London Transit Commissioner Coun. Sam Trosow called for a review before the next LTC meeting, “The airport is currently served by Route 36 which runs from Fanshawe College, and the purpose of this motion is request a staff report about the potential for direct service from downtown London to the airport.”

“It’s generally felt in this city that the connections to the airport are very poor,” Trosow told CTV News after the meeting. “People are forced to take very expensive connections, or use a motor vehicle, so this would be a great opportunity for us to up our service.”

Trosow’s motion received no support from colleagues on the commission, but it was followed by a related motion from Mayor Josh Morgan.

Morgan’s motion directed the LTC to engage with the airport and city hall about potential passenger volumes and possible destinations within the city for those arriving or departing from the airport.

It also didn’t exclude a direct link to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stop at Fanshawe College.

Trosow broadened the scope of the motion with an amendment that added consultation with Tourism London and the RBC Place Convention Centre.

“I want Tourism London and the Convention Centre to be part of this discussion because they’re going to have a lot of information about how many people might be affected,” Trosow explained. “We might want to use the front of the Convention Centre or some other downtown depot as a starting place for this. Let’s make it easy for people when they get off the plane in London to see that there are alternative routes to get into downtown.”

In August, Porter announced it would begin offering winter flights from London to sun destinations in Florida, Mexico and Jamaica.

Earlier this month the airline announced it will begin domestic flights to Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver in Spring 2027.

stories.title: Sunshine and autumn colours on display across southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: A stretch of sunny and mild fall weather is expected across southwestern Ontario this week, with temperatures remaining above seasonal norms and plenty of opportunities to enjoy the region’s autumn colours.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A stretch of sunny and mild fall weather is expected across southwestern Ontario this week, with temperatures remaining above seasonal norms and plenty of opportunities to enjoy the region’s autumn colours.

CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison said the region can expect mainly sunny skies Tuesday with a high of 17 C and light winds.

“It’s going to be beautiful, gorgeous, mainly sunny,” Atchison said.

The pleasant conditions are expected to continue through the remainder of the work week. Atchison said full sunshine is forecast Wednesday through Friday, with daytime highs ranging from 17 C to 18 C.

While overnight temperatures will be cool, Atchison said a gradual warming trend is expected heading into the weekend.

A mix of sun and cloud is forecast for Saturday and Sunday, with daytime highs expected to range between 16 C and 19 C.

Atchison said the weather will provide an ideal backdrop for residents hoping to take in the area’s fall colours.

“We have some gorgeous fall colours. Make sure you get outside and enjoy,” she said.
