stories.title: Stevenson resurrects BRT debate about north and west routes, Morgan refutes claim
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson would tap the brakes on work underway at city hall that lays the groundwork to potentially expand London’s Bus Rapid Transit system with routes in the north and west parts of the city.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson would tap the brakes on work underway at city hall that lays the groundwork to potentially expand London’s Bus Rapid Transit system with routes in the north and west parts of the city.

“BRT 2.0 is already moving through the planning process,” Stevenson warned at the beginning of her campaign announcement.

She held up documents from a Request for Pre-Qualification procurement process seeking a consultant to do preliminary design, determine property requirements, update cost estimates, and implementation planning.

The anticipated study schedule runs from Fall 2026 to Fall 2027.

“I’m calling for a pause on further commitments to the north and west BRT expansion until Londoners have the costs, the traffic impacts and a real opportunity to weigh the alternatives,” Stevenson announced while standing in the middle of a transit stop along the yet-to-be-completed East London Link route.

Specifically she called for the following steps before Council decides on a path forward:

Full cost disclosure covering existing commitments, proposed expansion, confirmed funding, and exposure to overruns.

A coordinated construction plan addressing traffic, business access, emergency routes, and overlapping roadwork.

Costed alternatives and public input including frequency, express service, and better connections to jobs and growing neighbourhoods

“Josh Morgan is all about bike lanes and BRT, with the goal of getting people out of their cars, and yet the BRT business case only predicted a 5% increase in ridership,” Stevenson emphasized.

However, incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan emphasized that a public decision to extend the BRT system would come after the consultants’ reports are finished.

Morgan pointed to the 25-year Mobility Master Plan (MMP) approved by council this term.

“At best this is a misunderstand of the process, and at worst it’s just an irresponsible way to try to plan transit in the city,” Morgan said about Stevenson’s announcement. “This is part of the Master Mobility Plan, an integrated plan that is not just for rapid transit, or conventional transit, but how we move cars and how we build active transportation across the city.”

“I know it was approved in the Master Mobility Plan, but I don’t know that Londoners are really on board with this,” explained Stevenson. “When I got elected, people were shocked that we were moving forward with the BRT. They thought that they’d voted no to it at election time.”

The 2018 municipal election was dominated by debate about BRT, and whether London should accept provincial and federal funding for the mega-project.

stories.title: NDP Leader Eby vows not to use Wainwright tragedy for political gain
stories.summary: Eby’s promise follows criticism from the BC Conservatives
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Tensions rose on the campaign trail in British Columbia on Monday as B.C. NDP Leader David Eby scrambled to explain comments he made earlier in the day about the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, which followed suggestions that some BC Conservatives harbour separatist sentiments.

BC Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson called the remarks unacceptable.

Later in the day speaking in Hope, B.C., Mr. Eby said he didn’t use the tragedy for political gain and will steer clear of the topic through to voting day.

“Let me say unreservedly I would never, ever use the sacrifice of these young men, the grief of their families for political advantage to attack another party,” Mr. Eby said.

Earlier, he referenced the loss of the four soldiers lives in the fire as being “our true heroes” who had put their lives on the line to defend Canada.

“What we can do for them is stand up for a united Canada, to stand up for our country,” he said.

During the same appearance, he drew a contrast with three Conservative candidates – Bryan Tepper, Heather Maahs and David Williams – who the NDP said are present in openly separatist Facebooks groups, including the BC Prosperity Project advocacy group, which is associated with an Alberta group advancing sovereignty.

“They are enabling and legitimizing a fringe political project in British Columba to try and separate us from Canada, and that is how you end up with a referendum on separation,” Mr. Eby said.

But hours later, Mr. Eby acknowledged that Mr. Doerkson had criticized Mr. Eby for using the horrific events in Alberta for political purposes.

And that’s when Mr. Eby sought to clarify his commentary.

Mr. Doerkson said that his party “unequivocally” stands for a strong and united Canada.

“That is who I am, that is who our team is, and no desperate attack from David Eby will change it,” Mr. Doerkson said in a statement,

“Invoking soldiers we lost this weekend in an attempt to save his own job is beyond the pale. Their sacrifice belongs to their families and to our country, never to a premier’s re-election campaign. This is a pathetic, desperate distraction from his record.”

The BC Conservatives did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment regarding Mr. Eby’s allegations. E-mailed requests for comment from the three candidates were not returned.

The back and forth played out as Albertans went to the polls to decide whether the province should pursue separation through a future binding referendum.

Also, in the House of Commons, MPs held a moment of silence and adjourned the House of Commons for the day in honour of the victims of the fire.

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke of the four soldiers killed. “These were sons, brothers, partners, and friends. Young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause. We will honour them always.”

B.C.’s advanced polls are open through Wednesday and the general provincial election is Saturday.

stories.title: In just minutes, tiny Wainwright hospital became scene of horrors and heroism
stories.summary: The small town’s 20-bed hospital transformed into something resembling a war-zone trauma centre
stories.author: Jana G. Pruden, Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Brandon Simmons heard the Code Orange announced in the hallways on Saturday afternoon.

“Code orange, attention everyone. Code orange, all units.”

Mr. Simmons, who became quadriplegic after a truck accident and lives in the long-term care area of the Wainwright Health Centre, then watched as the hospital roared into action. Nurses began preparing medical supplies and lining up stretchers and gurneys and machines around the entrance, then down the hallways of the small community hospital.

When a friend told Mr. Simmons there had been an explosion at the military base, he wheeled outside and tucked himself into a corner near the emergency doors, out of the way of people coming and going, and sheltered from a wind so strong it was bending trees near the hospital almost in half.

Mr. Simmons was recording video as the first vehicles arrived with injured soldiers from the base. It didn’t take long for him to see the scope of the tragedy that had occurred, and get a sense of what was coming.

“I knew that hell was about to break loose,” he says.

Mayor Bruce Pugh calls the Health Centre “our little Wainwright hospital,” a small facility in a small town, where the people working May personally know the patients they’re working on. Even if the hospital had been completely empty, and it wasn’t, there are only 20 acute care and surgical beds. The disaster for which doctors and nurses were bracing on Sunday afternoon would bring double – or even triple – that number of injured.

The Department of National Defence has said that around 4 p.m. a grass fire that had been burning for hours on the base rapidly changed direction toward personnel that were taking part in live-fire exercises.

The first vehicle to pull up to the hospital was a white SUV, which parked in the emergency bay at 4:11 p.m. Mr. Simmons’s video shows four men in army greens emerging, and moving quickly but carefully into the hospital. Two had their pants hanging in tatters below the knee.

A large military truck pulled up next.

Military personnel unloaded one person and carried them into the hospital on a stretcher. Someone was screaming. Another victim, limping into the hospital himself on burned legs. Another, wrapped in a foil blanket. Another, unmoving on a gurney. Someone was moaning. The wind blew pillows and sheets onto the gravel.

And then ambulances, one after the other, after the other.

At some point, Mr. Simmons turned the camera away.

“I didn’t want to even have it on film,” Mr. Simmons said. “I didn’t even want to see it with my own eyes.”

Dr. John Damian Paton-Gay was on-call for the Stars air ambulance service on Saturday night, when he got a call that help was needed in Wainwright.

The wind was so strong it wasn’t clear whether they’d even be able to fly, but a shift in the weather allowed them to get off the ground in Edmonton with a helicopter full of supplies.

They landed at the Wainwright hospital 45 minutes later to an almost unbelievable scene.

By the time Dr. Paton-Gay arrived, the injured from CFB Wainwright had already filled up the tiny emergency department and were overflowing into the rest of the small facility.

He saw injured people in every corner and upstairs. About 30 patients crammed into a small space, with staff moving quickly around them. A scene, he says, “that would make a medical TV show look fairly tame.”

Burns are measured both in severity and surface area. The injuries Dr. Paton-Gay saw on Saturday evening had no specific patterns, but a consistently high total body surface area burned. This type of injury meant the conditions of the patients were deteriorating rapidly.

“All of the personnel there knew that that was the case,” he said. “They knew they had to move through the first wave of injured very quickly and prepare for the next ones who were going to get sicker. That was very palpable. The sense of urgency was very clear.”

Even as a specialist working in critical care and trauma for almost a decade, the scene was unlike anything he’d ever seen. It was more like a “mass casualty that would happen in a war or a natural disaster,” he said.

Nurses and doctors sped to the hospital. Throughout the evening, help kept coming. Medical supplies were brought from other communities by truck, medical equipment flown in by helicopter, and additional hands arrived from the sky, as paratroopers landed in the next - door football field.

The injured were stabilized and then sent by ambulance or air to other hospitals around Alberta and Saskatchewan.

As of Monday, there were four soldiers dead and 39 others injured, 19 of those in critical condition.

Mr. Pugh acknowledges the health centre itself was “built for a different time and place,” and that the medical needs of the area have long outgrown the building. Local officials in the town of 7,000 have been working to get a new hospital built for nearly 20 years. It’s the place where Mr. Pugh was born, where all his children were born, and where his parents died. A place where friends and family work.

“But how could you prepare for an event like the one that happened on Saturday?” he added.

Mr. Pugh says he was told that none of the injured died at the hospital in Wainwright and that all of the victims were transported alive to bigger hospital facilities to continue the care. He toured the facility privately, away from the cameras and media, ON Monday to thank those who came to the soldiers’ aid, with federal dignitaries who made the visit.

He said he is praying none of them have to go through something like that again and is hoping that they can look back at what they did with pride.

“I hope, in a sense, some of them will be able to look back and say, “You know what? We did it.”

Long before the paratroopers landed and the last ambulance sped away, Mr. Simmons stopped recording and went back to his room, inside the long-term care area of the hospital. He has posted some of his videos online, but not that one.

“You can hear the guy in the back crying and screaming. Those are our strongest people,” he said. “Those are the sounds that will never get out of my head. No matter if I delete that stuff.”

With a file by Stephanie Chambers and Matthew Scace

stories.title: Two charged, 127 kg of cocaine seized at Ambassador Bridge: Cbsa
stories.summary: Canada Border Services Agency says two men were charged after the seizure of 127 kilograms of suspected cocaine at Ambassador Bridge border crossing in Windsor, Ont., last month.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
Canada Border Services Agency says two men were charged after the seizure of 127 kilograms of suspected cocaine at Ambassador Bridge border crossing in Windsor, Ont., last month.

The CBSA alleges the drug was seized from a commercial truck arriving from the United States after it was referred for a secondary examination on Sept. 11.

The federal agency says officers discovered the cocaine in the truck’s trailer with the help of a detector dog.

Officials say CBSA officers arrested a 61-year-old and a 41-year-old, both from Mississauga, and transferred them to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

They say both suspects were charged with the importation and possession cocaine for the purpose of trafficking by the Mounties.

The CBSA says its southern Ontario region has seized 1.67 metric tonnes of cocaine so far this year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Retired teacher faces historical sexual assault trial
stories.summary: A London courtroom heard on Monday that Murray MacDonald, 68, was a biology teacher and swimming coach at Central Second School in London between 1985 and June 1986.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A London courtroom heard on Monday that Murray MacDonald, 68, was a biology teacher and swimming coach at Central Second School in London between 1985 and June 1986.

When testifying she told the court that when she was in grade 11 she went to The Bavarian, a one-time bar in Cherryhill Mall on Oxford Street West.

She said she got in using fake ID and that once there she ran into MacDonald. “I remember him buying drinks...more than one drink,” she said. “I had no interest in this person, we had no relationship.”

She said near the end of the night, MacDonald offered to drive her home and when they got to her apartment building she said, “He drove me to the far left end of the parking lot and it was pretty dark.”

While fighting back tears on the stand she said, “All of a sudden he was all over me, hands up my shirt and hands down my pants...I remember feeling frozen.”

She then said she was forced to perform a sexual act. “It just seemed it was over very quickly...I got out of the car as fast as possible... I went to the bathroom and made myself throw up.”

The woman who was on a fast track to complete high school said the alleged incident changed her life. “I just remember being terrified...I knew I couldn’t tell my parents, I couldn’t tell the school...I’m going to be blamed and marked,” she added. “My life just fell apart. I never swam again, I never did anything again.”

The woman said she transferred to other high schools before attending university but that the night would always haunt her. “It didn’t go away so I had to address it finally...I didn’t want to be a victim.”

Then years later while living in another city she looked MacDonald up on the College of Teachers registry and in 2024 she contacted police.

“I just wanted him to turn in his licence and I want him to apologize to me because I lost about a decade of my life.”

Seated next to his defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi, MacDonald has plead not guilty to sexual assault.

The court has heard that the female complainant is expected to be the only witness to be called by the Crown.

The trial resumes on Tuesday.

stories.title: Amira Elghawaby launches portal to turn Muslim research into policy briefs
stories.summary: Online hub from ex-envoy offers community groups, journalists and politicians short, usable summaries of studies on Canadian Muslims
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
When the Carney government pulled the plug on her role as the Special Representative on Combating Islamophobia in February, Amira Elghawaby walked away, feeling the weight of unfinished business.

In Ottawa, the former cabinet adviser had raised awareness within government and through public campaigns about the scourge of Muslim hate. She commissioned research and wrote a seminal guide on Islamophobia.

But despite the research from her and others, in the form of numerous reports and policy recommendations made to the federal government, little seemed to change.

Meanwhile, she has seen and spoken publicly about disturbing reports of hate. In recent months, shots were fired at a Winnipeg mosque, a fake severed, bloodied hand was thrown into a Montreal mosque and an imam was attacked in Victoria, B.C., and left with a fractured jaw.

Elghawaby has launched a global research and policy portal — said to be the first of its kind dedicated to research on Muslim communities — that will publish available studies on Muslims and make them accessible for community members and elected officials by using the recommendations in the studies to create policy briefs.

Elghawaby spoke to the Star just before her office released a new guide on understanding and addressing Islamophobia in Canada.

The resource will help community members and policymakers find information in digestible bits they can use to help keep the issues in the spotlight.

“We keep saying the same things, and official studies come out to say them, but nobody remembers,” Elghawaby said. “And nobody is keeping anybody accountable for that.”

The Muslim Communities Research Observatory (Mcro) portal, called macro for short, goes live Friday. It will be a global hub, a one-stop shop for advocacy groups who May “not even be aware of what research is out there” and for academics who “struggle with knowledge mobilization.”

“This is about raising the ability to ask for policy changes that are fully rooted in the evidence,” she said.

The site will be an important platform to disseminate a new five-year survey of Muslims in Canada by the University of Toronto’s Institute of Islamic Studies on social issues, faith and belonging that will also be announced Tuesday.

The last research on Muslim identities was the landmark Environics Survey in 2016, in which a question was, “Do Muslims want to embrace Canadian values or Muslim values?” said lead author Anver Emon. In this survey, researchers did away with that binary and found a majority of Muslims and non-Muslims saying Muslims in Canada want to adopt both Canadian and Muslim values.

It also found that while first-generation Muslim immigrants would overwhelmingly choose to immigrate to Canada again, nearly half (47.5 per cent) of second- and later-generation Canadian Muslims would choose to live in another country over concerns of affordability and inequality. The study reflects the perceptions of 903 Muslim households and 1,072 non-Muslim households across Canada, making it the largest sample of Canadian Muslims surveyed to date, Emon said.

Mcro is an ideal partner for the dissemination of research, said Emon, because, “as academics, we’re not the best at putting our ideas in 30-second sound bites, let’s be honest, right?”

Elghawaby’s experience with government, knowledge of policy and background as a journalist makes her “ideally suited” to translate that knowledge, he said.

While sites such as Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative exist, Elghawaby said Mcro, which has a team of three people, will function as more than a library — it will break down the data into accessible policy fact sheets.

She hopes this will help members of the public meeting politicians, journalists looking for context in a hurry, and politicians seeking information to inform policy on Muslim lives.”

For example, a constituent at a mosque wants to ask a visiting mayoral candidate a question but doesn’t know what to ask. Mcro’s tool kit could offer a brief on the issue of parking near mosques on Friday. Having access to policy priorities would allow people to feel confident when they’re engaging with politicians “so that it becomes less a photo-op and more of a conversation,” Elghawaby said.

Mcro is a project of the Muslim Fund, a grassroots charity organization.

Elghawaby said the initiative comes based on some of her learnings in government.

“The relationship between our communities and the federal government has weakened,” she said.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and the revenue minister had promised the Muslim community that they were going to address the issue of disproportionate scrutiny of Muslim charities, she said. She commissioned research for which academics, including Emon, spent nine months finding a policy solution before producing a report.

When she met Prime Minister Mark Carney in the summer of 2025, she reminded him of the promise made and said he told her it would be addressed by summer of 2026.

“But nothing has been done,” she said. The Prime Minister’s Office referred the Star’s query to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

A CRA spokesperson said charities are selected for audit based on potential non-compliance with tax rules and not on faith, denomination, or religious affiliation. The agency has implemented recommendations made by other reviews of its auditing processes and is committed to ensuring “its compliance activities are conducted in a fair, evidence-based, and unbiased manner,” Sylvie Branch said.

“Sometimes,” Elghawaby said, explaining the rationale that pushed her toward founding Mcro, “if you’re waiting for the government, even if you’ve got the promise from the highest person in government, the prime minister, himself or herself, it will not trickle down into the bureaucracy. You have to come with the solution essentially written up, with a bow on top.”

stories.title: Six charts that show how B.C.’s fiscal outlook has gotten worse
stories.summary: Provincial election on Oct. 24 pits the NDP and Conservatives’ economic visions against a complex and grim reality
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
Regardless of which party comes out on top in British Columbia ’s impending election, the next government faces the grinding task of putting the province’s troubled fiscal house back in order.

Over the last four years, under Premier David Eby’s New Democratic Party, the B.C. government has swung from a small surplus to a deep and prolonged deficit outlook. As of the latest quarterly fiscal update, released in September, the province’s deficit was expected to hit $13.8-billion this fiscal year, or 2.9 per cent of GDP – the largest budget shortfall since at least 1991.

Yet, despite a backdrop of rising deficits, a mounting debt load and tumbling credit ratings, neither of the main parties in the Oct. 24th race – the NDP and Lorne Doerkson’s Conservative Party of B.C. – has provided a clear path back to fiscal stability in the near or even medium term.

At the same time, the headwinds facing the B.C. economy, from slower immigration numbers to the effect of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, is adding to anxiety about the province’s finances within the private sector.

That nervousness among businesses in B.C. “likely points to continued slow growth in the province and, regardless of the election outcome, a weaker fiscal impulse – or reduced government contribution to growth,” Ali Jaffery, chief economist at Kpmg Canada, wrote in a recent note. “Bond markets will have little tolerance for high deficit spending in a province with weak private demand growth.”

Here are six charts showing how B.C.’s fiscal situation has deteriorated and why the province is at a critical juncture with its finances.

No path back to balance from either party. Both the NDP and Conservative parties have now released costed platforms and neither goes very far in bringing B.C.’s budget back to balance.

The Ndp’s plan shows the deficit falling from roughly $13.8-billion this fiscal year (after adjusting for the government’s pause to its planned expansion of provincial sales taxes on professional services) to $11.97-billion in fiscal 2028-29.

To achieve even that modest reduction, the party’s plan relies on a tax increase on high-income earners and up to $730-million a year of new revenue from “targeted economic growth” tied to major projects. However, planned new spending would absorb most of the new revenue.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives said their plan will bring B.C.’s annual deficit down to $10.8-billion by 2029-30, though that would still be more than twice the province’s 2023-24 shortfall. To reach its target, the party said it would reduce the province’s contingency reserve fund, enact a hiring freeze, review spending at most ministries and cut outside consultants. The plan bakes in $2.6-billion of extra revenue from faster growth over three years, but tax cuts of about $3.4-billion a year would offset most of those measures.

B.C.’s debt picture has eroded faster than other large provinces. Four years of growing deficits have piled up and caused the province’s debt load to balloon. Taxpayer-supported debt is set to more than triple to $187-billion in 2028-29, as compared to when Mr. Eby took office in the 2022-23 fiscal year. That pace of debt growth far outstrips other large provinces. B.C.’s net debt relative to gross domestic product, which measures total liabilities less financial assets as a share of the economy, has soared to a projected 27.4 per cent for this fiscal year from 17.2 per cent three years ago.

Nearly 10 cents of every dollar that B.C. collects will soon go to debt payments. As recently as fiscal 2022-23, the province had the lowest debt charges relative to its revenues, but an explosion of debt has rapidly redrawn that picture. Interest costs are now rising far faster than in Ontario, Quebec and Alberta.

That means an ever-larger share of B.C.’s revenues is being eaten up by making payments on its debt, with 9.5 per cent of what the province takes in annually projected to go to interest charges by 2028-29, according to RBC Economics. As an increasing share of revenue goes to interest, that will leave less to cover for services, and threatens to push B.C.’s deficit even higher unless taxes rise or spending is cut.

The province has faced a barrage of credit-rating downgrades. None of this has gone unnoticed by bond markets and credit rating agencies. “Under Premier Eby’s administration, B.C. has been downgraded eight times in total by the main credit rating agencies,” Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, wrote in a recent note.

Fitch, one of the most recent rating agencies to downgrade B.C. debt in April, said the rating cut “reflects our expectation that meaningful erosion of debt metrics is likely given projected operating deficits and capital spending. With only modest offsetting actions so far and no plan to return to balance in the near term, further erosion is possible.”

Against that backdrop, he also noted that investors now demand a premium to hold B.C.’s 10-year bonds that is nearly as large as Quebec’s, the widest among Canada’s four largest provinces. And increasingly, those higher interest payments are heading south. Between April 1 to June 30, B.C. borrowed $14.9-billion in long-term debt from domestic and foreign markets with the latter, largely U.S. investors, accounting for 82 per cent of that lending.

The province’s public-sector hiring spree never slowed down. B.C. has added public-sector workers far faster than it has created private-sector jobs. Since the start of 2023, the province added four times as many workers in public administration, health care and education than in private jobs, according to numbers reported by Statistics Canada. But while all provinces and the federal government ramped up public-sector hiring during the pandemic, B.C. never reversed that trend in the way some other governments have recently.

While the NDP costed plan makes no mention of what public hiring would look like under a new Eby government, the Conservative plan set out a hiring freeze; a review of ministries outside of health, education and a few others; and a target of returning administrative and management staffing to where it would have been relative to population growth since 2016-17, though it did not provide a proposed headcount.

Top earners in B.C. face a steep tax hike under Mr. Eby’s plan. A key part of the Ndp’s re-election platform proposes new measures to tax the province’s top earners, including a new top bracket for incomes above $1-million, taxed at a rate of 24.5 per cent. Income in the $265,545 to $1-million range would increase by two percentage points to 22.5 per cent, starting next year.

Once added to the federal government’s top marginal rate of 33 per cent, the province’s combined top rate would be one of the highest among countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The NDP said the higher taxes on top earners would generate roughly $1-billion a year in additional revenue by fiscal 2028-29. However, the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, a left-leaning think tank, estimated the additional revenue from the tax moves would be closer to $750-million.

content_blocks.text: Against that backdrop, he also noted that investors now demand a premium to hold B.C.’s 10-year bonds that is nearly as large as Quebec’s, the widest among Canada’s four largest provinces. And increasingly, those higher interest payments are heading south. Between April 1 to June 30, B.C. borrowed $14.9-billion in long-term debt from domestic and foreign markets with the latter, largely U.S. investors, accounting for 82 per cent of that lending.

Since the start of 2023, the province added four times as many workers in public administration, health care and education than in private jobs, according to numbers reported by Statistics Canada. But while all provinces and the federal government ramped up public-sector hiring during the pandemic, B.C. never reversed that trend in the way some other governments have recently.

stories.title: Coven Fest 2026
stories.summary: London's first Coven Fest took place on Oct. 17 on Dundas block. The fest was a pop-up market with over 30 ven...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
London’s first Coven Fest took place on Oct. 17 on Dundas block. The fest was a pop-up market with over 30 vendors, featuring tattoos and piercings, tarot card readings, and photo opportunities.

This event was made to connect people, share experience, and grow the alternative and occult community in London. Attendees came from London and surrounding to show their support.

“I came to see the good energy that’s around, see the nice Halloween spirit, the costumes, the vendors, and to show my support.” said Darnell Gomez an attendee who just moved to London.

Vendors and business owners came from all over Ontario to join Coven Fest.

Photo by: Samantha Luis (Coven Fest pumpkin photo stand)

“It’s a nice opportunity just to welcome everybody. Everyone’s in good spirits and it’s nice to see everyone out supporting the community.” said Steve Ianni, the owner of Raven and Rune in Dutton.

“When we travel, we travel with a very small portion so we’ll always bring our incense and smudging. We do mystery bags, blind date with a bag or blind date with a book.” said Jennifer Haralampopoulos, owner of Sacred Spells in Tillsonburg.

Lots of items were on display across vendors including broomsticks, hats, candles, tarot cards, and books with a large majority being handmade.

“Next year I want it bigger and better. I want double the vendors, to expand, to bring Hex House to a household name, and I want the community in London to know there’s always a place.” said Katey Sawyers, host of Coven Fest and owner of Hex House.

Sawyers also said that she was quite happy with the turnout this year.

stories.title: Mounties investigate after man flashes knife at youth in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.
stories.summary: Mounties in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., say a man is in custody after flashing a knife at youth over the weekend.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Tumbler Ridge — Mounties in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., say a man is in custody after flashing a knife at youth over the weekend.

They say the incident happened late Saturday evening in the small town, which gained international attention earlier this year after a mass shooter killed eight victims, including six children, before turning the weapon on herself.

Police say officers responded to the knife report at the 100-block of Kinuseo Avenue and apprehended the man under the Mental Health Act.

They say he was brought to a hospital by officers but was released Monday and brought back to Tumbler Ridge, where he will remain in custody until he attends court.

Cpl. Jennifer Cooper says the Mounties want to assure the public that they are taking the situation very seriously and there is no further risk to the public, though the investigation is ongoing.

She says the detachment appreciates all the information received from the public and commends the youth involved for quickly reporting it to police.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Election results are tied between mayoral candidates in Lytton, B.C.
stories.summary: Lytton - The municipal election in Lytton, B.C., has resulted in a tie between two mayoral candidates with differing views on the community's recovery from a devastating wildfire that destroyed much of the village five years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Lytton - The municipal election in Lytton, B.C., has resulted in a tie between two mayoral candidates with differing views on the community’s recovery from a devastating wildfire that destroyed much of the village five years ago.

The results posted to the village’s website on Monday show Denise O’Connor, the incumbent, and challenger Jennifer Thoss each received 45 votes.

stories.title: Alberta voting locations extend hours after late openings, delaying referendum results
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says that for various reasons some locations opened late, so it cannot release unofficial results until 10 p.m. when the last polling station closes.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Several voting locations in Alberta will remain open later Monday after delays prevented them from opening on time, affecting when unofficial referendum results will be released.

Elections Alberta officials said unofficial results will only begin to be released once all voting locations across the province are confirmed closed. Because of delays earlier in the day, the last voting location is not expected to close before 10 p.m.

Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure authorized extended hours at affected locations to ensure voters receive the full advertised hours of service.

Officials said the late openings were caused by various issues that have since been resolved. The release did not provide further details about those issues in the material provided.

Regular voting hours at all other locations are from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Officials are also asking Albertans to be patient and respectful toward election workers.

content_blocks.text: Several voting locations in Alberta will remain open later Monday after delays prevented them from opening on time, affecting when unofficial referendum results will be released.

Elections Alberta officials said unofficial results will only begin to be released once all voting locations across the province are confirmed closed. Because of delays earlier in the day, the last voting location is not expected to close before 10 p.m.
Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure authorized extended hours at affected locations to ensure voters receive the full advertised hours of service.

stories.title: Witness at Toronto gold heist trial says snitching is never 'a positive thing' but his sudden memory loss isn't out of fear
stories.summary: The Crown asked Arsalan Chaudhary if his reticence to answer questions was more about fear of snitching consequences than mental health.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The star witness at the Toronto airport gold heist trial — who admitted to being a mastermind of one of the biggest gold heists in history — said several times that he didn’t have an opinion on snitching, but it turned out he really did.

After days of court testimony marked by low-energy, little memory, and complaints of “feeling triggered” by questions, Arsalan Chaudhary was asked if his reticence was more about prison culture than mental health.

“It’s hard giving evidence against someone when you yourself are in custody,” Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic asked him.

“I have no opinion,” Chaudhary replied.

“It’s challenging to snitch against someone, particularly when you’re in custody,” she asked again.

“I have no comment, ma’am.”

Vlacic reminded him that when he was previously testifying as a prelude to his own guilty plea — during which he gave detailed testimony — he asked in court if there were “any newspapers here,” and was told there weren’t. “You were concerned about the media attention,” Vlacic said, before noting that reporters were in court in Brampton, Ont., this time.

He agreed he was snitching but on Simran Preet Panesar, one of the co-accused in the heist who is considered a fugitive and living in India, but not against the accused currently on trial, Parmpal Sidhu. Vlacic suggested it was easier to snitch against someone who isn’t in the country.

Chaudhary became more animated, his voice clearer and louder, his replies much longer.

“When you’re in jail and when you snitch on somebody, it doesn’t matter where they are. If snitching is a snitch, it doesn’t make a difference,” he said. “People in jail, they don’t look at one snitch compared to another snitch any differently. So it doesn’t matter if I’m snitching on somebody who’s out of the country or someone who’s in the country. It doesn’t make a big difference in jail.”

“I guess you do have some opinion on it, then, right?” Vlacic said. She asked him if snitching was a positive thing in prison.

“I don’t think so, ma’am. It’s never been a positive thing anywhere.”

“I’m feeling triggered,” Chaudhary said when asked for details about the gold heist. “It just takes me to a place where it makes me very uncomfortable,” he said. “I’m just getting triggered by everything, and kind of nerve shaking, bringing me back memories.”

Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., has pleaded guilty to theft for the 2023 heist, when a crate containing more than $22.5 million worth of almost pure gold and cash was stolen from the Air Canada cargo warehouse at Pearson airport soon after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland. He is serving a four-year sentence.

He was a reluctant witness, ordered by a judge to be brought from his cell and into court to take the stand at Sidhu’s trial.

He admitted that he was one of two masterminds who planned and orchestrated the astonishing gold heist. The other, he said, was the inside man at Air Canada, Panesar, who was a manager in the cargo facility and came up with the plan.

Chaudhary started testifying last week and easily recalled details of his harrowing attempt to flee to his native Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by Pakistani police who tortured him into giving up all his loot. When he was asked by Vlacic about the others who helped him pull off the heist, his memory evaporated.

After two days of him telling court he couldn’t remember, and that post-traumatic stress from his kidnapping and poor treatment in prison diminished his memory and state of mind, Judge Gordon Cudjoe of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton ordered last Wednesday that Chaudhary be returned to his federal prison where he could take his medication and catch up on sleep before returning to the stand.

His testimony Monday reconvened with little apparent change of heart or state of mind.

“I don’t remember, ma’am,” was a frequent response.

After being shown his previous sworn testimony, the transcript of his guilty plea hearing, an agreed statement of fact he and his lawyer agreed to in court, and copies of text messages extracted from a phone police seized from his apartment, he still couldn’t recall much of it.

He asked the judge to let him speak to his lawyer. He said reading the transcript “will hurt me mentally.”

She asked him about text messages about melting gold after the heist that were extracted from a phone police seized in his condo. He repeatedly said he didn’t recognize the messages, didn’t know what they meant, and couldn’t say who sent them. He didn’t recognize the phone or remember his phone number.

He said he didn’t recognize who was in photos he was shown, including himself, and didn’t recognize what the Crown suggested was his Range Rover.

He testified with a scowl on his face and occasionally rubbing his head with both hands.

Eventually, Vlacic asked Cudjoe for permission to treat Chaudhary as an adversarial witness so she could more directly challenge his answers, which was granted.

Chaudhary said he communicated with Sidhu but had only vague recollection of what was said. Mainly it was about him passing messages to Panesar, Chaudhary said. He previously said he spoke with Sidhu three times on the day of the heist, but on Monday he wasn’t so sure.

Chaudhary said he and Panesar agreed to split the gold, with Panesar getting 70 per cent and Chaudhary getting 30 per cent. He previously said he needed to take care of others he had used in the plot and Panesar was going to do the same, but in court he didn’t know whether Panesar did that or who he might have shared it with.

In previous testimony he agreed he exchanged text messages with Sidhu including receiving a message asking: “you manage to melt down all that gold yet lol.”

“Theres too much heat right now,” was the reply. “We’re gonna have to wait now. Melt gold is a process lol,”

“I heard they call you 2 chains of tdot,” Sidhu allegedly texted, using a slang term for Toronto.

“I wish I had it. Love to be called 2 chains lol.”

He said in court Monday he doesn’t remember the exchange, but he recalls hearing about the “2 chains” joke.

“I’ve read this in the newspaper many times,” he testified. “That 2 chain line, everybody talked about it in jail.”

He also said the prosecutors overestimated his intelligence.

“I haven’t finished my high school. I’m trying to do that thing right now, actually, so I don’t know how smart you think I am,” he said when he claimed he didn’t know what the word “delegated” meant.

He said he was born in Pakistan and moved to the United States when he was very young and then came to Canada when he was around 12 and became a citizen. He grew up speaking English, he said, but still didn’t know the word the prosecutor used.

Vlacic eventually got him to agree that the things he agreed to at his own court hearing for his guilty plea were “probably, mostly” said because he believed them to be true at the time. “I’m not saying it’s not true.”

Under cross-examination by Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, Chaudhary said he doesn’t know how much Sidhu would have known about the heist plans, and that for Chaudhary he was primarily a conduit to reach Panesar.

Chaudhary agreed that he never saw Sidhu at his condo or at his second condo he used as a stash house, and he had no financial dealings with Sidhu.

The trial continues.

stories.title: Politics Insider: The final push for unity – or separation
stories.summary: Albertans vote today on whether to remain in Canada or begin the process of pursuing separation
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. I’m Laura Stone, filling in for Ian Bailey this week. Let’s look at what happened today.

Albertans vote today on whether to remain in Canada or begin the process of pursuing separation, the culmination of a campaign that has divided the province and transfixed the country.

Premier Danielle Smith announced in May that she would use a previously planned referendum on a range of other issues to also ask Albertans to weigh their future in this country.

As Matthew Scace reports, the separatist and federalist camps made their final pitches in duelling rallies at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton over the weekend, part of a last-minute push that also saw Prime Minister Mark Carney make several stops in the province late last week urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

The referendum has inflamed debate about national unity at a time when the country’s sovereignty is also being challenged by the trade policy and rhetoric of the Trump administration in the United States. And today’s vote takes place just two weeks after Quebec’s provincial election brought a separatist government to power there.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Canada’s top soldier has pledged to make public the official board of inquiry probe into a grass fire that left four soldiers dead and 39 wounded during a live-fire training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday.

Committee hearings have started on the Liberal government’s latest bill aimed at fast-tracking major projects, with MPs working on a tight timeline that critics say is inappropriate given the legislation’s complexity.

Cleveland-Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves criticized Prime Minister Mark Carney for “snatching defeat from the jaws of victory” in trade, as the U.S. steelmaker remains locked in conflict with Ottawa over hundreds of job losses in Canada.

With 10 days remaining in a campaign where Toronto’s notoriously clogged roads have been a central issue, the City has released figures that could shift the tone of the mayoral debate.

On our radar

“To their friends, to their families, to their colleagues, to the people of Wainwright, please know that you have the entire nation at your side, because in Canada, we take care of one another.” - Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking during a tribute to the soldiers who died this weekend after a fire ripped through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s training grounds in Alberta on Saturday.

In 2024, the Royal Canadian Geographical Society discovered the wreck of famed explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton’s last ship, Quest, at a depth of 390 metres, off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador. In what year did the famed polar explorer die suddenly during an Antarctic voyage?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

Alberta’s separation referendum is coming: What happens in the days and weeks and months after?

What does the post-referendum Alberta agenda look like? What cards does Premier Danielle Smith play next? What does the federal government do? Where do Albertans and Canadians go from there? — Shannon Proudfoot

But timid tax reform is not just bad policy. It’s bad politics. — Andrew Coyne

The future of this country is being diminished because of how much it costs to build big things, and how often they go terribly off the rails. — Matti Siemiatycki

The answer to today’s question: Sir Shackleton died on his voyage in 1922. Read how the wrecks connected to Sir Shackleton and Captain Robert Falcon Scott have been replicated using 3-D imagery in minute detail, in Marie Woolf’s feature story .

stories.title: Poilievre defends Alberta referendum, says ‘the goal should not be to beat one side or the other’
stories.summary: Federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre defended holding a referendum that puts a path to Alberta separation on the ballot.
stories.author: Bill Kaufmann
stories.content:
Wainwright — As some of the last voters cast their ballots on a referendum offering a path to Alberta independence, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre asked people to vote for Canada.

Some critics, including the opposition Alberta NDP, say the referendum is a waste of money — possibly costing more than $130 million — and places a dangerous strain on the country’s unity in the face of threats from the U.S.

But Poilievre said he hopes the vote’s aftermath will see a greater sense of unity and that he understands grievances separatists have with Ottawa.

“I hope there’s a strong result for Canada tonight, and then tomorrow we can begin the work of healing the divisions,” he said.

“I think the goal should not be to beat one side or the other.”

Poilievre defended the UCP government’s decision to include referendum questions on giving the province more power over immigration. Other questions centre around charging some newcomers fees for health care and constraining education eligibility.

He said the immigration questions are based on important issues of sustainability.

“There’s no question we have to get immigration under control, we need to cut back on the deluxe benefits that are given to people here illegally,” said the opposition leader, who’s MP for Battle River—Crowfoot, which includes Wainwright.

He rejected accusations by critics that the UCP government is scapegoating immigrants for their own failure to keep pace with population growth.

“I don’t think that’s an accurate characterization either of what the critics are saying or what the situation is,” said Poilievre.

“Nobody’s blaming individual people, they’re blaming Liberal immigration policies.”

The federal government has made moves to reduce immigration and Alberta’s intake of them has recently dramatically plummeted, but Poilievre said those levels are still too high.

When asked if separatist forces should give up their fight to break Alberta away from Canada if they lose Monday’s vote, he urged the pro-independence side to give Canada a chance.

“I don’t like the term ‘give up,’ I’d rather them join and be part of making the Canadian family everything they hoped for,” said Poilievre, who was in Wainwright to lend the community support after last weekend’s grass fire that killed four soldiers at the nearby training base.

“We don’t need to look at beating people in this referendum.”

Some separatist leaders say they’ll continue to fight for an independent Alberta regardless of the referendum’s outcome.

Successive public opinion polls have shown the pro-Canada side to be the significant majority in Alberta.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct an inaccurate paraphrasing of Poilievre’s comments and the headline on this story was edited to reflect the change.

stories.title: Repair bills piling up for aging Sarnia Police Headquarters
stories.summary: After a failed bid to fund a new facility, the Sarnia Police Service Board (Spsb) now says it needs $3.5 million for urgent repairs to the existing station.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The repair bills continue to pile high for the aging Sarnia Police Headquarters.

After a failed bid to fund a new facility, the Sarnia Police Service Board (Spsb) now says it needs $3.5 million for urgent repairs to the existing station.

“There hasn’t been any money spent inside the police services building. Not just the last three years, it’s been a lot of years. But there’s been no major investment into that building,” said Spsb chairperson, Kelly Ash.

Broken concrete, rusted rebar, orange cones, yellow tape, and a long metal barricade greet visitors to the Christina Street headquarters.

In August, the Ontario Ministry of Labour ordered the stairs to be closed.

People are now directed to enter the building via the ramp next to the stairs.

Ash says that out of the $3.5 million dollar projected costs, the stairs alone will cost $1 million. That’s because they form part of the actual structure of the building. The problem was explained at a recent Spsb meeting by Deputy Chief Mike Van Sickle.

“In the best possible terms, if you were to scrape away our stairs, you’re going to look into the basement of the police service. So, it’s not something that can simply just be removed. What leads to that is water intrusion,” he told the board.

Other immediate needs include replacing a fuel tank, Hvac upgrades, parking lot security improvements, expanding the sally port for police transport vehicles, improving emergency alert system, electrical upgrades for an emergency generator.

“They put no money away for repairing the building on the belief they were going to get a $120 million police station,” exclaimed Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley.

The must-do repair list follow’s Bradley’s veto last year of the board’s bid to build a new police headquarters.

“They think we’re the bank of Sarnia. And there’s been a 44 per cent increase in the last four years in the police budget. Forty-four per cent. They’ve also drained our reserves that are there for the rainy days. We don’t have the money there right now. We will have to find a way to deal with this. It is a labour, occupational health issue. That part I get. But it’s really sad how they’ve approached this,” he said.

Bradley says the next city council will be tasked with dealing with the $3.5 million dollar repair bill. Senior governments will also be approached for funding.

stories.title: Canada’s 2-year measles outbreak officially over: Phac
stories.summary: The measles outbreak started in October 2024 and has continued for about two years, with more than 6,400 cases reported during that time.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Canada’s measles outbreak that lost the country its global elimination status is officially over after two years.

The Public Health Agency of Canada (Phac) said Monday the multi-jurisdictional outbreak is over because more than two months have passed since the last case linked to the outbreak was reported.

It began in October 2024 in New Brunswick and saw more than 6,400 cases reported across 10 provinces and territories.

In total, 6,417 cases were linked to the outbreak, including 1,032 reported this year. Ontario saw the highest number of total cases with 2,390 reported, followed by 2,299 in Alberta and 1,033 in Manitoba. Other cases were seen in all provinces and territories except Yukon, Nunavut and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Most of the people who became ill had not been vaccinated against measles, Phac said.

The agency said in November 2025 that the Pan American Health Organization (Paho) had notified Phac about losing its elimination status.

At the time, Phac said a Paho commission had reviewed recent epidemiological and laboratory data, “confirming sustained transmission of the same measles virus strain in Canada for a period of more than one year.”

Global elimination status can be regained. Canada will need to keep the strain stamped out for at least 12 months, but also show it’s beefed up its surveillance systems and ability to quickly stop outbreaks if measles cases arise, according to Paho.

Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Joss Reimer commended the work of public health authorities, health-care providers, community organizations and families across the country for their work to end the outbreak.

But her comments came with a cautionary note while urging Canadians to ensure routine vaccinations, like measles, are up to date to prevent future outbreaks.

“While this milestone is encouraging, measles continues to circulate globally, and we can expect to see further travel-related cases here at home,” she said in a news release.

Phac’s announcement the national outbreak had ended comes only a few days after Manitoba declared on Oct. 16 its 20-month outbreak was over , following weeks without a confirmed case. The last confirmed instance of measles was reported in August, the provincial government said in a news release.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel said in a news release Monday that cases are still being seen around the world.

“So while the outbreak is over, our work to increase vaccination rates and protect the health of Canadians continue,” she said.

Measles is still being seen in Canada, but recent cases have not been linked to the two-year outbreak. According to the federal government, three new confirmed cases were reported between Oct. 4 and Oct. 10.

stories.title: B.C. victim of Wainwright fire was everybody's best friend, says rugby coach
stories.summary: The former rugby coach for Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, one of four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, says all of the teenager's team and his schoolmates thought of him as their best friend.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The former rugby coach for Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, one of four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, says all of the teenager’s team and his schoolmates thought of him as their best friend.

Trevor Plater, who coached Lykkemark in his senior year at Langley Secondary School in Langley, B.C., says Lykkemark was “always looking out for everybody.”

stories.title: BC Ferries vessel collides with humpback whale in Howe Sound near Metro Vancouver
stories.summary: Vancouver - A humpback whale has been struck by a BC Ferries vessel in waters near Metro Vancouver.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fisheries and Oceans Canada says in an email that they were alerted to the collision on Sunday, when the Queen of Surrey reportedly struck the whale near Keats and Grace islands in Howe Sound.

The 139-metre-long Queen of Surrey provides regular service between Vancouver-Horseshoe Bay terminal and the Sunshine Coast.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10

The DFO says witnesses reported two humpback whales near the ferry at the time of the collision, and one was struck after it surfaced in front of the vessel.

The federal agency says the whale was seen behind the vessel after the collision, and investigators are working to identify it and assess its condition.

BC Ferries has also confirmed the collision and is co-operating with the DFO, adding that initial reports showed crew had “very little time to react.”

“We recognize how upsetting this is, particularly for those who witnessed the collision, including our crews,” BC Ferries spokeswoman Lilian Kim says in a statement. “They work on these waters every day and care deeply about protecting the marine life around them.”

Kim says BC Ferries crew receive special training on whale awareness, and vessels operate under specific protocols to reduce collision risks.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada would not comment on whether the whale has been found, only stating that the agency is “currently reviewing the situation.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta referendum sparks Chinese community push to vote
stories.summary: With Albertans voting on the province's referendum, Chinese community leaders are mobilizing to help voters understand its 10 complex questions.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
With Albertans voting on the province’s referendum on Monday, Chinese community leaders are mobilizing to help voters understand its 10 complex questions.

Many voters are struggling to understand the ballot, but community leaders say the desire to vote has never been stronger.

“Even English-speaking Canadians, people born and raised here, many don’t fully understand these 10 questions, because altogether they’re over 400 words, and they’re not asked in a direct way,” said Teresa Woo-Paw, chair of the Acct Foundation.

The 10 questions cover a wide range of issues. Beyond the question on Alberta’s separation, the other nine address a range of topics from immigration to the constitutional division of powers.

“This referendum, I believe, is the largest and most complex vote in Canadian history,” Steven Tsang, a member of Asian Canadian for United Canada, said.

Former Alberta MLA Woo-Paw says that since July, community leaders have built a cross-ethnic coalition to address the information gap.

Woo-Paw and Tsang say they believe most Chinese voters support Alberta remaining in Canada.

“We believe that among ethnic communities, over 90 per cent support Alberta remaining in Canada,” Woo-Paw said.

Geopolitical commentator Sam Choi says the referendum carries particular significance for first-generation immigrants.

“The government doesn’t know who you voted for, but it knows whether you voted. Technology is so advanced now, they type in your surname and they know how many Chinese voted or didn’t vote,” Woo-Paw said. “If we don’t vote, we’re not important; when they make decisions on how to allocate resources.”

Choi says participation offers an opportunity for Chinese Canadians to better understand Canada’s political system.

“For Chinese to come out and vote is a very good opportunity,” Choi said. “A channel for the community to understand our federal system, the division of powers with the provinces, and how to further improve going forward.”

Results for the 10 questions on the referendum will be released in batches. Meanwhile, the results of the stay-or-leave question is expected early Tuesday morning.

stories.title: Marginalized patients have increased risk of early death from newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, study finds
stories.summary: A Western University-led study found higher risks of early death for marginalized people with de novo metastatic breast cancer
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
People who are marginalized or lack access to a primary care provider are at greater risk of early death from newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, according to research in Cmaj (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

The Ontario study found nearly one-quarter of people with stage four metastasized breast cancer that has already spread to other sites in the body when it is found – also known as de novo breast cancer – died within six months of diagnosis.

The study was led by researchers at Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, including Dr. Priya Thomas, a plastic surgery resident and Dr. Phillip Blanchette, professor of oncology and medical oncologist at London Health Sciences Centre, along with their collaborators.

“The relationship between early death from breast cancer and a person’s sociodemographic factors hasn’t been previously examined in Canada,” Thomas said. “It’s important to investigate the role of factors like income and housing because patients with existing barriers can be especially vulnerable to disparities in health equity, including access to care.”

One in nine women will receive a diagnosis of breast cancer within their lifetime and 3,000 patients are diagnosed annually in Ontario. The type of breast cancer the team studied, de novo metastatic breast cancer, makes up three to six per cent of all breast cancer diagnoses.

Survival rates are steadily increasing for metastatic breast cancer, with numerous new treatments available, but there are long wait times for specialty care and disparities in accessing it.

The research team looked at Ices data from 4,004 patients with de novo metastatic breast cancer who were treated in Ontario between 2010 and 2019. They used the Ontario Marginalization Index tool to understand if other factors influence the risk of death, including housing stability, income, age and employment status.

An increased risk of early death (within six of their metastatic breast cancer diagnosis) was associated with age, concurrent health illnesses and marginalization and observed in 23 per cent of the study population.

For people who were treated for breast cancer, rural residence was also associated with early death, possibly because of challenges travelling for tests or treatment, which is commonly coordinated in larger urban centres.

People linked to a family physician had 26 per cent lower odds of early death. Of those, 60 per cent had received a mammogram within two years of diagnosis, compared to 42 per cent of people without a primary care provider.

The study underscores the critical role of primary care in Canada.

“Access to a primary care provider is a growing challenge in Canada, with one in four Canadians lacking regular access to primary care,” said Thomas. “Without the ability to be seen by a family doctor, people with advanced breast cancer May face delays in getting diagnosed and starting treatment.”

That’s essential to help Canadians – and a strained health-care system, the researchers said.

“Our study highlights the need for better primary care access. It is pivotal in preventing and diagnosing cancer, as well as managing symptoms and treatment side effects, mental health concerns and palliative care,” Blanchette said.

“The demand for cancer care is rising exponentially, and specialist oncologists are unlikely to be able to meet these care needs alone.”

stories.title: U.S. won’t drop digital issues in trade talks: former negotiator
stories.summary: While digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the United States, Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests, Canada’s former chief trade negotiator said Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.

“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues.”

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.

Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues, he said.

Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.

“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Eric Miller, president of the consulting group Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, spoke on a separate panel at the conference and gave the example of Netflix, which gets more than half of its revenue outside the U.S.

“If you begin to have policies which are unfavourable to large U.S. tech companies, it doesn’t take too many markets like Canada and the European Union co-ordinating to see how this would have very detrimental effects to them,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

Canada will host an Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where the two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms, also known as discoverability. The Crtc is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

It’s not clear exactly which element of the Online Streaming Act is the source of the conflict. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in late August the United States had withdrawn its position on discoverability.

But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the United States is streaming companies having to make financial contributions toward Canadian content — a proposal the Liberal government has backed away from.

Meredith Lilly, a professor at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs, took part in the panel with Miller. She said Canada and the United States are likely to come to an agreement.

“I think that there is a landing zone that both sides will be able to agree on, and I anticipate that that will be keeping mandatory payments off … and Canada is going to be able to keep the discoverability piece of that,” she said.

The conference also heard that the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.

Lilly said that means the United States could retaliate on things like cars or canola. “And so there is some potential that is going to pit parts of Canada against the cultural sector,” she said.

She said while the United States might have tolerated the cultural exemption when Canada was using it to subsidize arts and culture, that might not be the case if it extends to demanding financial contributions from American companies for Canadian content.

“If we start trying to use it to extract capital from large American firms to subsidize the creation of Canadian content and they can’t even use those subsidized funds, they are going to play hardball with us and it could be the end of the cultural exemption,” Lilly said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bombers can secure CFL playoff spot with victory
stories.summary: The Winnipeg Blue Bombers enter the final week of the CFL regular season controlling their playoff fate.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Toronto – The Winnipeg Blue Bombers enter the final week of the CFL regular season controlling their playoff fate.

Winnipeg (8-9) faces the B.C. Lions (10-7) on Friday night needing a win to make the playoffs. Watching intently, though, will be the Calgary Stampeders (9-9), who end the season on a bye week.

The Saskatchewan Roughriders (9-8) have already cemented a playoff spot but can finish either third or fourth in the West. The Riders meet the Edmonton Elks (13-4) on Saturday.

If the Bombers and Riders both win, Saskatchewan finishes third and faces B.C. in the West semifinal Oct. 31. Winnipeg would take fourth and visit the Toronto Argonauts (9-8) in the East semifinal.

A Winnipeg win and Saskatchewan loss would leave the Bombers third and visiting B.C. in the West semifinal. The Riders would end up fourth and cross over to take on Toronto.

Should Winnipeg lose and Saskatchewan win, the Riders will finish third. Calgary would get fourth and head to Toronto.

And finally, if Winnipeg and Saskatchewan both lose, Calgary would finish third ahead of the fourth-place Roughriders.

Edmonton and B.C. have cemented the top two spots in the West. Likewise, the Montreal Alouettes (13-4) and Toronto had clinched first and second, respectively, in the East.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.
