Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is “open” to amending the Canadian constitution to deal with major questions of structural change but only where there is strong “consensus” in the country.

In little-noticed comments during a podcast interview with host Ryan Jespersen, the prime minister addressed how he intends to respond to Alberta’s concerns, and why he advocated for voters to reject a future binding independence referendum, along with urging them to say “no to the nine” other questions and vote against Premier Danielle Smith’s other proposals for change.

Monday’s referendum vote asks 10 critical questions about Alberta’s place in Canada, including nine demands for more power over immigration, judicial appointments and withdrawal from federal programs with compensation guarantees. A demand to abolish the unelected Senate — long on Alberta’s wish list — would require constitutional change.

In the interview recorded Friday after he appeared alongside Smith in Red Deer, Carney insisted the federal Liberal government under him is already working with provinces on immigration reform and on changing the rules around investment in this country.
He went on to say, “The constitution is not unamendable, to be clear.”
“But it requires building a real consensus around what’s necessary to change and why it (should) change and which elements you are going to change,” said Carney.

In last week’s whirlwind trip between Calgary and Edmonton, Carney repeatedly outlined his belief that Canada “is working” and on the podcast repeated his view is that it is important to make “positive” change by working with provinces.

“Through cooperative federalism, through making the country work, we’re building that track record in Alberta,” and he added, making progress with other provinces, citing Quebec, Newfoundland and Labrador, Ontario, the territories, Nova Scotia and others in the Atlantic region. “You build that, and then you say, ‘OK, where do we need to change?’”
“I get the point about an unelected Senate,” Carney said, but he pushed back against calls to make that a priority.

The prime minister argued that where Alberta representation counts is in the elected House of Commons. He said the number of seats in that chamber is periodically updated to reflect changes in population, and Alberta has gained seats as a result. “The primacy of the House of Commons in developing legislation and governing the country is reinforced by that democratic legitimacy.”

“Am I open to constitutional reform?” Carney continued. “Yes, I’m open to it,” he said. “But I’m not open to — or I’m open to it with laying the groundwork for consensus. And part of the way you, in my judgment, the way you lay groundwork for that is you build trust, you build on success, you move forward … And that in my view is the most effective way to do that.”

Carney said his job as prime minister is to “work with the facts on the ground, the governments we have in provinces, the governments that exist around the world and working with all stakeholders, including First Nations.” At another point, he noted the difficulty of renegotiating the Crown’s relationship with the First Nations who signed Treaties 6, 7 and 8 on territory that covers Alberta.
‘It’s hard to think of a worse time to have a referendum, or a better time for the province,’
The prime minister made clear that he views Alberta’s concerns as “issues,” not grievances.
Carney reminded listeners the constitution’s amending formula was developed by former Alberta premier Peter Lougheed, calling him the greatest premier the province had.

The amending formula is complicated. It requires a unanimous vote by all provinces, the Commons and the Senate for certain changes, including major ones to the Senate itself. It requires the support of seven out of 10 provinces representing more than 50 per cent of the population for other changes — and Smith made a point on Friday to a conservative conference that she believes that the latter requirement is a threshold that can be met now that there are conservative-leaning governments in eight provinces.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, a leader of separatist voices in Alberta, said Saturday in an interview with the Star that a lot of the “gestures” by Carney are “temporary and relationship-based” and “not constitutionally based; they’re not structural, they’re not statutory based.”
“And that means Albertans continue to be vulnerable. We could have another national energy program. We could have an export tax imposed which would be devastating to our economy.”
Wilson said the federal government can only truly address those demands with “actual structural reforms, not just nice photo-ops.”
On the eve of its referendum, Alberta now stares down a fundamental question: is Monday’s vote the finish line, or the starting point to a years-long struggle over separation?
Independence leaders are vowing to keep up the fight regardless of the outcome and in the face of expectations from pollsters and federalist Albertans that their opinion is the minority.

The margin of victory will determine the force with which that movement can assert itself in Alberta’s political culture, or how reassured federalists can be of the province’s chances of staying in Confederation.
That raises the pressure of the high-stakes referendum even higher.

Thomas Lukaszuk, the former Progressive Conservative deputy premier who traversed the province in his maple leaf-speckled RV, first collecting signatures for a petition rejecting independence and then later campaigning ahead of Monday’s vote, says a win must be big enough to “send a very strong message.”

“It has to be decisive, and that means we as Canadians have to accept it as being decisive. I am not the one to define what decisive means, but at the end of this painful and divisive process we as Albertans and we as Canadians have to be satisfied that Albertans have sent a clear signal to the rest of Canada and to the rest of the world that this country is united,” he said.
“Certainly, (a) 50 per cent plus one vote would not do it, but in the realm of 70 per cent and higher would definitely send a very clear signal.”

Lukaszuk spoke after sharing a stage at back-to-back evening rallies with the prime minister, who travelled to Alberta Thursday and Friday to urge voters to turn out to ensure a “decisive” win that he said is needed to be commanding.
Throughout rallies and whistle stops in Calgary, Edmonton and Red Deer, Carney hammered home a message that suggested people should not take polls for granted.

The stakes are also high for Smith, who said the separatists in her own party should accept the results of a decisive vote to defeat the movement, but she declined to say how she would deal with those in her ranks who refuse to abide by the outcome.

Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a national unity rally in Red Deer, Alta. on Friday alongside, from left, former Medicine Hat MP Monte Solberg, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and former premier Ed Stelmach.
All the leaders who have been making their final pitches against Alberta separatism are looking for the same answer to Question 10 in the Alberta referendum — a big No.

Where that unity gets shattered, though, is what they want on the day after the referendum. The closing arguments by Mark Carney , Danielle Smith and Pierre Poilievre show sharply different ideas about what happens after Monday’s voting is over.

Carney’s “lead, not leave” pitch to Alberta says he’ll view a No vote as a mandate to put separatism aside and get on with bigger things. Poilievre’s “restoration, not separation” is a bid for Alberta to put its faith in him to get relations with Ottawa back on track.
Smith, for her part, is hoping that the referendum gives her a No to separation but a big Yes to go after more power for Alberta on everything from immigration to judicial appointments.
Those are very different day-after scenarios.
Even as they stood side by side in a Red Deer brewery on Friday afternoon, Carney and Smith had to confront the fact that they’re coming at this referendum from diverging angles.

“As you know, we don’t always agree on everything. We often disagree quite publicly on several things, but today we can all agree that on Question 10 that we are voting for option one to remain in Canada,” Smith told the crowd.
Just the day before, the premier spelled out just how wrong she believes Carney is about the other nine questions on the referendum.

“He has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were,” Smith wrote, slamming Justin Trudeau’s government, as she often does, for creating the conditions that have led to Alberta wanting more control over immigration.
“That’s why I’m encouraging Albertans to vote ‘yes to the rest.’ ”
In the midst of all this is Poilievre, who is trying to tell Albertans to keep their grievances, but put away their aspirations to break away from Canada.
Speaking in Calgary on Friday, to a room that May well have had some separatist-leaning folks in the crowd, the Conservative leader pointed his remarks in their direction.

“Canada is more than a government. It is a people, a flag, a land, a history, and a promise ... What you really want to restore is the Canada that you knew and still love,” he told the Canada Strong and Free gathering. “So, our real goal should not be separation. It should be restoration.”

What all these leaders know is that Alberta’s frustrations or grievances — whether they agree with them all or not — won’t go away when the votes are counted on Monday. Some new polling released on Friday by Abacus Data backs that up.

Abacus found that while 68 per cent of Albertans trust that the votes will be tallied fairly, only 40 per cent, including the remain and separatist voters alike, trust that both sides will respect the outcome.
Moreover, 61 per cent of respondents said they expect another referendum on separation further down the road.

“I think that tells us something important about the political environment in Alberta,” Abacus CEO David Coletto wrote. “A referendum can settle a question on the ballot without resolving the grievances that put it there.”

(The survey was conducted with 1,021 eligible Alberta voters from Oct. 7 to 13, 2026. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is approximately plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.)

This tells us that Carney, Smith and Poilievre are not finished making the unity case to Alberta, and that the flurry of closing arguments was really just the prelude to what happens in the days afterward.

And here again is where their paths diverge. Carney believes the unity case is argued through pipelines and big projects. Smith believes the unity case is made with structural and constitutional change. Poilievre believes unity comes with a Conservative government in Ottawa.

Three leaders, all who grew up in Alberta, are seeing the future of the separation debate through different lenses. Little wonder that Albertans May wake up confused on Tuesday morning, no matter how clearly the province speaks, as expected, against separation.

At their Red Deer press conference on Friday, Smith and Carney maintained that it is possible for them to keep disagreeing and still get things done for Alberta. Smith said it comes from looking for the win-win, and more than just a compromise. The prime minister called it “tough collaboration.”
What we learned through all their final pitches, then, was there’s more tough collaborating ahead.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at a news conference about her province’s upcoming independence vote, in Calgary, ON May 22, 2026.
Alberta is staring down the snout of “a big lie,” argues Patrick Lennox.

A colossal deception has led to Monday’s pre-referendum vote, which offers Albertans two choices: “Remain a province of Canada” or “hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

The right choice is obvious: Albertans should vote to remain. But Lennox, an author and international relations scholar, writes in his new book “On Treason,” that even being forced into this position amounts to “psychological warfare.” The domestic political actors who’ve triggered this vote have entered into an “alliance with the Trump administration’s continual and escalating efforts to have us question our right to exist as a sovereign nation.”
And Lennox has a word for that: “Treason.”

To assault the public with lies both big and small, transmitting them in great quantities and at high velocity, has been the modus operandi of the separatists. And it draws from a well-studied playbook.

When Nigel Farage first started campaigning to yank the United Kingdom out of the European Union, he did so by pushing bizarre, hallucinatory conceptions of how Brussels meddles in Brits’ day-to-day lives. He yammered them at rallies and painted them on buses.

When Donald Trump told the voting public his 2020 election victory was stolen, he did so by weaving together laughable tales of bamboo paper ballots (imported from China) and sentient voting machines. Other populists the world over point to migrants and refugees and insist they are weapons of nefarious political actors lurking in the shadows.

The U.K. is poorer and more miserable for Brexit, democracy is collapsing in the United States and Europe is still electing extremists who have plenty of grievances but no real idea how to remedy them.

It is impossible, Lennox argues, to divorce what is happening in Alberta from the broader trend of the liberal world slamming the car door on its hand. A former RCMP intelligence officer based in Edmonton, Lennox uses his book to chronicle the rise and follies of Alberta’s independence-seekers — the lawyer being sued by former clients, the disgraced surgeon, the political Loki fined $120,000 by Elections Alberta for financial violations.

He tours among the conspiracy theorists who, buoyed by the so-called Freedom Convoy, are responsible for advancing this crackpot scheme to split Alberta from Canada. And he captures how these weirdos, whose past efforts have attracted no more than a few thousand supporters, colluded — or at least claimed to collude — with Trump’s effort to seize Canada.
These losers would still be on the political margins were they not being validated by one person: Premier Danielle Smith.
Before returning to politics, and even since becoming premier, Smith has openly allied with independence activists. Because Smith, despite what she says, is a willing consumer of this big lie.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Smith came to believe in a version of Canada that she experienced online — in which Canadian democracy was in twilight, evil forces had seized the levers of power to silence patriots and the health establishment was profiting from the deaths of thousands (if not millions).

Believing in this big lie required Smith to see her fellow citizens in Victoria, Toronto, Ottawa and Quebec as the traitorous ones. Even as she ran for office promising to work within the federation, Smith was secretly plotting to run through the emergency exit.

There is a genuine disgruntlement in Alberta, I know. As journalist Tyler Dawson writes in “The Republic of Alberta,” his recent book about the vote, “while Alberta May not have a great nationalist novel (like Quebec), there are any number of open letters, reports from government and think tanks, and manifestos to back the views of discontented Albertans, separatists or not.” This all turned the idea of an independent Alberta from an absurd fantasy into something more tangible. There are plenty of “normal” Albertans, Dawson writes, “who believe something is deeply wrong with their province’s place in Canada.”
That’s all quite reasonable.

And to be against the Canadian Confederation isn’t treasonous. A significant portion of Quebec has, famously, never been happy with our arrangement as a country — the majority of seats in the National Assembly are now held by sovereigntists. My native Nova Scotia bitterly fought Confederation, worried that annexation to Canada would allow its fishery to be plundered and doom the province’s most lucrative industry. (They were right.) Certainly, some will vote for independence without really wanting it, perhaps believing it will buy Alberta leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.

But this isn’t about self-determination nor figuring out which configuration of self-governance would most benefit Albertans. This vote is predicated on lies. The instigators lie about a plot to destroy Alberta, they lie about the state of our conflict with Washington, they lie about the bountiful abundance that awaits their province as an independent republic — it’s lies all the way down. When my colleague Richard Warnica spent time with Mitch Sylvestre , the man whose name sits atop the referendum petition, he heard beliefs “dangerously disconnected from reality.”
You cannot separate the instigators of this cause from its outcome.

As we’ve seen time and time again — from Brexit to Maga — paranoid populism only dresses up in the concerns of regular people. But at the earliest opportunity, proponents of these big lies revert to form. Given power, they will continue to pursue their imagined enemies, line their own pockets and find new windmills to tilt at.

Whatever the separatists claim, they do not care about the rights of First Nations people nor the concerns of working Albertans. The instigators of this cockamamie vote are hungry for power, and they will happily give away the farm to the Americans to get it.

The only way to destroy the big lie is for Albertans to turn out overwhelmingly to reject it. This independence vote will almost certainly fail — but the bigger the failure, the better we’ll be able to exorcize ourselves of this for good.
On Monday, every voter in Alberta should head to the polls and make the point loudly. Bring a friend, a neighbour, even an enemy.
Because as Lennox writes, “when big lies are allowed to circulate uncontained for too long, horrendous things begin to happen.”

Alberta separatists at a rally outside the provincial legislature in Edmonton on Saturday. Alberta voters decide in a referendum on Monday if they want the province to begin the process of separating from Canada.
Edmonton — A key separatist leader rejected calls to end the campaign for Alberta’s secession if the province’s independence movement loses the vote in Monday’s referendum.
“That’s not happening,” Keith Wilson told a crowd of about 1,000 supporters Saturday at their last major rally before the vote.

Wilson addressed the crowd from the steps of the Alberta legislature, with just two days left before the referendum that will decide whether the province will chart a course toward a future vote on secession.
“Regardless of what happens on Monday, we’ve already won,” he said.

The constitutional lawyer who represented key organizers during the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” and who become a major organizer in the push for independence, said it was important for supporters and organizers to “celebrate our successes.”
Speaker after speaker called on the crowd of independence supporters to not lose heart with the 150-day campaign in its last 48 hours.

Half a call to action, half a walk down memory lane about what the independence movement became this year through a 300,000- signature petition drive that began in the depths of winter to the hundreds of town halls staged across the province, speakers encouraged supporters not to give up, regardless of Monday’s outcome.
“We are moving in the right direction,” said Cory Morgan, a longtime advocate for Alberta independence.

Having spent more than two decades pushing for independence, Morgan told rallygoers that he planned to keep up his fight regardless of whether they earned 10 or 90 per cent of support in the referendum.
He suggested the country’s political leaders failed to understand how those pushing for separation had no plans to go anywhere, and that independence was a “movement” and a “culture.”
“We’ve made an incredible stride.”

For months, successive public opinion polling has shown that support for separation is a minority opinion in the province. Federalist organizers have nevertheless urged those who reject separatism to turn out to Monday’s vote, suggesting those stumping for independence are highly motivated.

Morgan also called for civility as he noted how personal the referendum has become and cautioned those listening in the crowd and more online from losing friendships or family just because they are on different sides on the issue.
“Stay together as people,” he said.
Separatist supporters waved an array of flags at Saturday’s rally in Edmonton.
His calls came as a sense of division has set in across the province, with some supporters of separation saying people feel afraid of being labelled by neighbours.

Chris Scott, a cafe owner in Mirror, Alta., who first became known within the province and online for opposing COVID-19 restrictions, told the crowd those who want to remain in Canada had few arguments to offer them and instead label those demanding independence as “dirty seppies” and a “fringe minority.”

While bitterness remains over the long-dismantled National Energy Program of the 1980s under former prime minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the 2015 election of his son, Justin Trudeau, who ushered in an environmental regime that inflamed feelings of Western alienation, the backlash to pandemic-era mandates has played an unmistakable role in fuelling a new generation of independence advocacy

But as separatist organizers look to convince more Albertans frustrated by the long-standing grievances against Ottawa to consider voting for the independence option, even if they are not sold on separation, those in Saturday’s crowd did not need any convincing.

Brandishing rows of Alberta flags both big and small, with some that read “Republic of Alberta,” supporters wore hats that declared “Make Alberta Great Again,” and held signs that included messages like “No to the EU, Vote Option 2.”
Supporters of waved Alberta flags, some that read “Republic of Alberta,” and wore hats that declared “Make Alberta Great Again” at Saturday’s rally.
Another name with which independence supporters expressed displeasure, but more in private, was Alberta Premier Danielle Smith .

Sandy Martel and her husband Barry are decades-long independence supporters as well as members of Smith’s United Conservative Party. The couple who attended the rally say they used to support Smith, but that began to change when she inked a new pipeline and energy pact with Carney last fall.
“I truly feel she’s turning,” Martel said.
“I think Carney’s paying her ... I think she’s being bought.”
That deal stands as the centrepiece of the relationship reset both Smith and Carney sought to undertake after years of acrimony under the prime minister’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

Despite the deal laying the groundwork for what culminated into an announcement just weeks ago that construction of a new million-barrel a day pipeline would be fast tracked from Alberta to the West Coast, independence supporters like Chris Anderson oppose the continual charging of an industrial carbon price and the push to build a massive carbon capture and storage network to reduce its level of emissions output.
As a UCP member, Anderson wants Smith gone.
“Everybody was under the impression that Danielle Smith was in support of this,” he said of Alberta’s independence.
Despite being a UCP member, Darlene Knezevich says she’s open to leaving the party altogether.
“To tell you the truth, if an independence-minded party were to form, I would jump on that bandwagon immediately because I don’t believe that (Smith) is going to help.”

Robert Martens says Smith had managed to win back his support after losing it when she crossed the floor as leader of the Wildrose Party to join the Progressive Conservatives more than a decade ago, before the parties were merged under Jason Kenney.
But Smith’s decision to come out in support of remaining in Canada has meant she won’t be able to win him back again, he says.
“That was her second time with me, and that was it.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney takes a selfie with supporters in Calgary on Oct. 15, 2026.

Calgary — Prime Minister Mark Carney blitzed through Calgary on Thursday as part of a whirlwind trip through Alberta days before the province’s referendum on separation, telling a packed evening rally of federalist supporters that only a decisive result would settle the issue.
With advance voting underway, Carney capped a day of campaigning alongside federalist groups with a speech to thousands gathered at a “Forever Canadian” rally.
Mark Carney was in Calgary for a Forever Canadian Rally just days ahead of a vote in Alberta on whether there should be a referendum on separation.
On a stage before a swelling crowd, Carney outlined the stakes in Monday’s vote.

He laid out that residents face a choice of whether to “build a stronger Alberta and an even greater Canada” for future generations or, he warned, “we can burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty.”
“What we need is a decisive result on Monday to settle this question,” Carney said to thunderous applause. He later urged Albertans to “lead, not leave.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney was met with well-wishers Thursday as he toured through Calgary to rally the pro-Canada vote ahead of Monday’s referendum on separation. Carney urged Albertans to not only vote for Confederation, but to also reject the nine other questions on the ballot involving immigration and the Constitution.
He urged Albertans not only to vote, but to show their Canadian pride by wearing red and displaying the maple leaf, as many in the crowd did Thursday evening.
“Don’t let anyone tell you that this is already decided,” Carney said. “Turnout will determine the outcome.”

He also pushed back against the argument advanced by independence leaders that Albertans need not support separation to vote for “Option 2,” the label attached to the proposal on the ballot, and could instead use it to express frustration with Ottawa.
“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and for Canada,” Carney said.

He nevertheless acknowledged that Ottawa had to repair its relationship with Alberta. Carney drew on his own experience growing up in Edmonton, where he recalled residents being made to feel like its resources “weren’t our own.”
Carney said the frustrations felt by Albertans were “real,” arguing they had shaped decades of provincial politics and contributed to the divisions on display today.

The prime minister’s appearance at the rally led to a crowd exceeding what his team had been expecting. Thomas Lukaszuk, the former deputy premier in the province who launched the “Forever Canadian” federalist group, told the crowd on stage that more than 7,000 people showed up.
Throughout multiple public appearances Thursday, Carney emphasized that with four days remaining before the vote, federalists could not let up.
He told one gathering of federalist volunteers earlier in the day that “polls don’t vote, people vote.”

At the same stop, he for the first time endorsed efforts urging voters to say “no to the nine” referendum questions accompanying the independence question, which deal with immigration and constitutional reform.
Speaking to volunteers with Public Interest Alberta’s campaign for Alberta to remain in Canada, Carney said, “We need to get people out to vote,” before urging them to also vote “no to the nine.”

He went further in an interview with a South Asian broadcaster when asked how Albertans should vote on proposals to abolish the Senate and change access to certain provincial services for residents without citizenship or permanent residency, including by allowing the province to charge a premium.
“We don’t need a referendum to make progress on taking control on immigration,” Carney told Red FM Calgary.
“We’ve taken control on immigration.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith responded on X, saying that while the pair have found “common ground on many things over the last 18 months,” he was failing “to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”

Carney has defended his government’s reductions to immigration levels, a shift first set in motion by former prime minister Justin Trudeau during his final months in office after years of increases following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Smith’s comments come as she urges Albertans to vote to remain in Canada while also saying “yes to the rest” of the questions on immigration and constitutional change, arguing they would give her a mandate to push for greater provincial sovereignty.
While polling suggests support for separation remains a minority view in Alberta, federalists say a strong turnout is key to putting the issue to rest.
The outlook for the immigration-related questions, however, appears less clear.

Grace Guan is an immigrant who has lived in Calgary for 16 years. She said she decided to get involved with the Public Interest Alberta’s campaign because she believes the questions blame immigrants for the province’s problems.
“I feel I should stand up,” Guan said.
Cesar Cala, a prominent advocate in Calgary’s Filipino community, said many temporary residents in Alberta are fearful of the proposed changes.

“I work with a lot of people who work here but have temporary permits,” he said. “They’ve been invited to help build Alberta, especially during COVID, and they put themselves in the line of danger, right? Front-line workers, workers in “the food industry and so on — they have temporary permits but their impact is permanent.”
Smith has argued Alberta needs greater control over immigration, saying population growth has strained the province’s ability to deliver services.
Throughout his stops on Thursday, Carney repeated his often-used line about Alberta’s referendum being staged as the country finds itself in a “more dangerous and divided world.”
His decision to visit the province did not go unnoticed by separatist leaders.
“I think they must be worried,” said Mitch Sylvestre, who leads the Alberta Prosperity Project.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith listens to a question during a press conference at the Canadian Forces Base in Edmonton on Wednesday.

Regardless of how the Alberta referendum turns out, it now looks like the Oct. 19 vote could decide a lot more than the question of separation. It May well determine Danielle Smith’s future as premier.

In a surprise twist, Alberta’s separatist leadership is now mobilizing to oust her as United Conservative leader, all part of a melodrama that calls to mind the warning: Play with the bull, get the horn.

Smith’s David Cameron-impersonation is not likely to end well for her. Just as Cameron lost a Brexit vote he never supported, then had to resign as UK leader, the same thing looks poised to happen in Alberta. Smith has lately let it be known, far and wide, she in fact is not a separatist.

CBC’s “The Fifth Estate” program reported on the weekend that, back in 2022, Alberta’s separatist leaders conspired to oust then-premier Jason Kenny for his refusal to even consider a referendum on sovereignty. The separatists then turned around and helped Smith become top dog.
At the time she had empathized with their project. Or at least seemed to, stating in a leadership debate: “I take your movement very, very seriously.”

Indeed, as leader, she adjusted Alberta referendum rules to tip the scales in favour of letting the separatists hold their vote, with fewer supportive signatures to be required and more time accorded to gather them. This delighted the separation crowd.

But now it’s 2026 and at a time when Smith finally has convinced Ottawa to co-operate with her in getting a pipeline built to the coast , Smith is being asked at every turn to elaborate on her personal inclinations about independence. She regularly states, she backs a strong Alberta within a united Canada .

Further, if the separatists lose the referendum next week, she pledges there will never be a second referendum on her watch. This, despite the separatist declaration that in the event of a loss, they fully intend to fight on, and seek yet another vote.

It now appears Smith’s strategy regarding the separatist referendum was aimed at keeping its proponents onside — in the interests of continuing as the party’s leader. Her decision to abandon them at the finish line definitely is not going down well.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the self-declared separatist leaders in the UPC, has recently gone so far as to call for a coup to topple the premier. Smith acknowledges she is being referred to by her opponents as “public enemy No. 1,” and is no longer even in contact with the separatist leaders.
The idea has been floated by the separatists that they’d like their political party to become a dedicated separatist party, like Quebec’s Parti Québécois .

While polls suggest nearly three quarters of Albertans are expected to nix the sovereignty adventure, half or more of United Conservatives Party members are said to favour the idea of ditching the Canada connection. And that is what makes the separatists’ threats to see Smith ousted so potent.

Trouble first surfaced for Smith last November at the party’s annual convention where she was vigorously booed as she tried to sell the support she’d won from Ottawa’s for her proposed pipeline to the coast. At that gathering, she reiterated her preference for a strong Alberta within Canada. None of it went down well.

It is not just separatists who have a beef with Smith. By last month, reported the Angus Reid Institute, the bloom was well and truly off the rose, with 56 per cent of Alberta residents disapproving of the premier’s performance. Just two in five approved of the job she was doing — the lowest level of support since she became premier.
Life certainly would not have been easy for Smith had she exhibited greater candour when she was campaigning for the leader’s job, fessing up about her pro-Canada perspective to the party members.
But had she done that, at least the separatist faction would not have wound up feeling so jilted and thirsting for revenge.
Their mistake, of course, was in assuming Smith was supportive of their cause when in fact she was simply a garden-variety political opportunist.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has “some perspectives” on the Alberta independence question in a video released a week out from the referendum.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is “worth fighting for,” exactly a week out from the referendum where Albertans will choose whether to set the province down a potential path of secession.
On Thanksgiving Monday, the Prime Minister’s Office released a short video of Carney delivering some remarks, saying that this year’s holiday “is a bit different.”

It comes as those campaigning for both the independence and federalist sides enter their final push, with numerous rallies and events planned across Alberta ahead of the Oct. 19 vote . Advance voting starts Tuesday.
“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future,” he says in the video.
“Whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Carney says he has some “perspectives” on the matter, pointing to the fact that he was raised in Edmonton and educated “right here” at St. Francis Xavier high school in the city, indicating the classroom he sits in.
Carney says lately, he has returned “home” often to the province, given the projects and announcements his federal Liberal government has made.
He specifically mentions “a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity for hundreds of thousands of people in this province and across the country.”
He goes on to say that “Canada is working,” but cautions that such progress can be undone should the country find itself split.

“The truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. You can’t build big things on fault lines,” Carney says. “And we should recognize that the world has changed. Canada is facing real threats to our economy, our security and our way of life.”
“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours. It’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for.”
Monday’s video represents the latest comments Carney has made about the referendum.

He has previously characterized the vote as a “dangerous bluff,” and referred to his experience serving as Bank of England governor during Brexit, an event that Carney warned led to years of economic and political uncertainty.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has defended her decision to add an independence question to a set of existing referendum questions on constitutional and immigration reforms by saying thousands of Albertans signed their names to petitions on the issue over the past year.
Specifically, she added in the independence question after a court ruling quashed a petition that had been organized by separatist leaders in the province.
Albertans are now being asked to pick between two options: Either to remain a province of Canada, or to begin the legal process necessary to hold a future binding referendum on leaving.

Successive public opinion polls suggest support for separation is a minority opinion in the province. But independence leaders have been urging those frustrated by the province’s treatment from Ottawa as a way to cast a vote against the status quo.

Federalists have been urging those wanting to remain a part of Canada to turn out to the polls. Political heavyweights including former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper and former Alberta premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley have warned that a vote for independence will send a bad signal to investors.

Advance voting will run from Tuesday though Saturday. As of last week, Elections Alberta said it had verified more than 221,000 mail-in ballots, a record number reported by the provincial agency since Smith’s United Conservative Party government relaxed the rules around accessing them.

Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith at his office in Ottawa in May. Carney has warned that Alberta’s referendum question about a binding vote on whether to separate is not simply about sending a “message” to Ottawa.

Ottawa — High or low, no matter what number Alberta voters cast for the cause of a united Canada on Oct. 19, the stakes are high for the country and the challenges ahead will remain for Prime Minister Mark Carney .
Born just on the other side of the Alberta border in Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, and raised in Edmonton, Carney has crafted a political persona as a Western Canadian.

Not the cattle herder or wheat farmer kind. Not a cowboy. Not an oilpatch driller. More the high-flyer business investor kind. Comfortable in C-suites anywhere. A fervent Oilers fan, sure. But less “Redmonton” than Calgary cool, able to assess risk and, above all, to manage it.

After winning the Liberal leadership when Justin Trudeau exited the federal scene, Carney resisted queries about whether he’d run in an Alberta seat because he was from there, saying “people get classified in a way that limits the breadth of experience.” He ended up winning in an Ottawa suburb.

Carney wielded his own breadth of experience — Harvard and Oxford-trained, leader of two G7 central banks — as his main weapon in the Canada-U.S. trade fight and as he branded the Liberals as oil-and-gas friendly, and himself as a cool-eyed study in calm in the face of all storms.

When Premier Danielle Smith upended expectations last spring and tacked on a 10th question about Alberta’s future in a referendum that could launch a binding legal vote on whether to separate from Canada, Carney warned no one should be lulled into thinking this is simply about sending a “message” to Ottawa.
At the end of June, he warned again, “This is a real referendum,” a consequential vote and not a prelude to a more important one sometime down the road.
Carney reminded everyone of the years of uncertainty he’d witnessed — and steered the Bank of England through — after the Brexit vote that saw the U.K. eventually quit the European Union.
The Conservatives slammed the prime minister for “fear-mongering,” saying what was needed was hope.

Shuvaloy Majumdar, Conservative MP for Calgary Heritage, a friend of the premier’s, is adamant Smith did the right thing to respect Alberta’s law on citizen-led referenda initiatives and provide a “pressure valve” vote on future separation.
Carney is now called upon to demonstrate he has the vision, ambition and guts to address Alberta’s “fundamental grievances” with Ottawa, said Majumdar.

“On the shoulders of the prime minister in Canada, historically, there are two responsibilities: relationship with the United States and the national unity of the country. That’s our federation, that’s our geography. That is an enduring test for every prime minister, since Sir John A. Macdonald,” said Majumdar.
“And how you manage both will define not just your own future as prime minister but also the state of the country and its success in the world. Today, both relationships are on fire,” he added.

He said it’s not just about building more pipelines — “we should be building pipelines in every direction.” He said, “The fundamental issues of democratic and economic equality have not been reconciled for the West. Not even today.”
He frames the challenge posed by the Alberta vote as a bigger question, not just one of Carney’s political skills or future.
“What the stakes are for the country is the restoration of our federalism,” he said in an interview on Parliament Hill.

For Carney, the stakes in the vote are political and personal. It May reveal whether he is the champion of the West that Alberta has been waiting for, capable of extinguishing the flames Smith has fanned, or whether the vote will entrench Western alienation as a force and set the country on the path toward another existential vote .
Carney’s arguments in favour of unity have largely been factual and rational, macroeconomic, and less pulsing with passion.
No big emotional flag-waving rallies, so far. A planned unity speech for Canada Day was thwarted when thunderstorms grounded the prime minister’s plane.

Anne McLellan is a former Alberta MP and deputy prime minister who devotes much of her post-political career to bridging partisan divides with Conservative Lisa Raitt through the Coalition for a Better Future. She is campaigning for the federalist cause in Alberta and hints she expects Carney might turn up at one of a couple of federalist rallies expected next week in Alberta ahead of the vote.

Carney, she said, is a “passionate Canadian and any threat to this country, I think he feels viscerally, whether that threat comes from the United States, or whether it comes from a separatist in Quebec, or a separatist in Alberta.”
But she makes “a sharp distinction between what has happened in Quebec over the past 50-some years and what is happening right now in Alberta.”

“Those who wanted independence in Quebec formed a political party. They campaigned across the province. Yes, that was their central platform, but they also talked about building a socially progressive — up until (newly elected Premier Paul St-Pierre) Plamondon — but a socially-progressive Quebec.”

Quebec separatists “played by the rules that were there for every party. So, everyone knew who their donors were, knew where the money was coming from, knew who their spokespeople were. Their leadership was regularly talking to the press. You have none of that in Alberta,” she noted.

McLellan said disturbing revelations about how far a leading Alberta separatist group went last year to pitch an independent Alberta to the U.S. State Department (meeting with unidentified officials to reportedly pitch greater access to Alberta’s oil and water resources in exchange for financial support for their aspirational breakaway nation) “shocked” many Albertans and May alarm enough separatist sympathizers to abandon the cause.

But how it all plays out for Carney and the country “depends to some extent on the actual vote and then what the premier does too, right? But the premier and the prime minister are working very constructively together on behalf of Albertans,” she insisted.
There’s no question Carney is mindful of the power of the moment, where his government faces unity challenges in the east and west.
After Quebecers on Monday voted in an avowedly separatist but minority Parti Québécois government, the prime minister said, “This is a crucial time for our country.”
“Canada is working,” he had said a week earlier, after announcing his Liberal government is prepared to fast-track approvals for a new public-private oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast .

Certainly, Carney’s small Alberta caucus of three MPs — including one Conservative who defected to join Carney’s ranks — is conscious of the geopolitical moment for the country and the prime minister, and they argue that the pipeline is proof Carney can deliver.

Calgary Confederation riding MP Corey Hogan, the Liberal parliamentary secretary for energy, said Smith is the one who bears responsibility for imposing a referendum when she never campaigned for election on it, never let voters decide whether it was necessary. Smith caved to the pressure of divisions within the United Conservative Party, and now the fallout must be reckoned with, said Hogan.

“Federally, obviously this has been uncomfortable for all of us,” he said in an interview. “It’s been more uncomfortable for the Conservatives because it divides their voters in ways it doesn’t divide Liberal voters,” he added.

Either way, Hogan said, the reckoning will continue long after the Oct. 19 vote if voters give Smith and the UCP government “exactly what they want” on a range of questions that go beyond independence, including Alberta’s power to set immigration levels and services, withdraw from federal programs without penalty, appoint judges and elect senators.
Polls encouragingly show the federalist side likely to vote down a future binding vote on Alberta’s independence, but Hogan said the other questions matter.

“If Albertans just sort of shrug and say, ‘Oh OK, like I guess we just had an existential referendum about the future of our country because a faction of the premier’s party wanted it,’ well then I think this is not a conversation that goes away and it’s a bad harbinger for stuff to come,” he said.

Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne are convinced they’ve got a good offer to Alberta, to Quebec and to global investors as they seek to diversify the economy, and persuade the big money to come to Canada, despite any uncertainty.
In fact, Champagne rejects the suggestion that investors are worried.

“To be honest, I don’t hear that from investors much these days,” he said in an interview. “I think they see the opportunity that Canada is offering because we have the talent, strong industry, critical minerals, energy, access to market, and … if you look at the world today — you know the uncertainty index is peaking now — Canada is seen as a safe haven, and I think Canadians understand that. That’s why you know we’re much stronger together.”
Separatists gathered in late August at the Alberta Legislature in Edmonton for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project, which is related to the Alberta Prosperity Society.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday his government is closely tracking allegations of foreign interference in the Alberta referendum campaign, adding it is critical that votes are “free and fair.”
His first public comments came the day after a federal watchdog office revealed it notified a leading Alberta separatist group, among 60 others, about legal obligations to report foreign influence.

Asked about allegations of foreign interference in Alberta, where an Oct. 19 referendum will test the public demand for a vote on independence, Carney told the Star, “We follow these things closely, and it’s exceptionally important that all elections that are held in Canada and all votes are held are free and fair.”

Carney’s comments also came on a day when Elon Musk posted on X — the social media platform formerly known as Twitter that he owns — that Quebec , Alberta and Saskatchewan “should separate.” Musk, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, wrote, “they would be better off.”
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe responded on X in a terse reply: “No.”

Late Wednesday, Steven MacKinnon, the federal minister of democratic reform, issued a further statement on the Alberta referendum, saying the government is committed to “protecting the integrity of our democratic processes and institutions, and “the risk of foreign interference is real.”
He said Ottawa is working alongside Alberta provincial authorities including its elections office and local police “to ensure the integrity of the referendum.”
Albertans “can trust that their rights will be protected and that action will be taken against any attempts to undermine our democracy.”

The question of foreign influence (which refers to overt attempts to sway public opinion) and interference (which refers to covert activity to affect debates) in Canada’s elections and other fundamental votes has taken on greater urgency with the rise of technology and powerful online tools.

Canada’s foreign influence commissioner, Anton Boegman, said Tuesday his office reached out last month to Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the most vocal advocates of Alberta separatism, whose organizers travelled last year to Washington to meet with unnamed U.S. State Department officials.

The group, which is not registered as a third-party advertiser in the provincial referendum but advocates for Alberta independence and closer ties with the U.S., is among 60 organizations or individuals Boegman said his office contacted using a list compiled with assistance from Elections Alberta regarding activities related to the Oct. 19 vote.

Alberta Prosperity Project organizers met with Republican party political strategists from Michigan who developed a voter mobilization app that was credited with helping Trump win that state in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, according to reports published by the Globe and Mail and Press Progress.

Earlier this year, the Alberta group’s leaders acknowledged they travelled to Washington in 2025 to meet with officials at the U.S. State Department. The Globe, citing one organizer, reported Saturday that the Alberta separatists discussed greater American access to Alberta’s oil and fresh water resources in exchange for American financial support for Alberta’s independence.
Alberta separatists gather at the Alberta Legislature in Edmonton on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026, for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project.

One of the group’s leaders who acts as counsel for the group, Jeffrey Rath, has disputed the Globe’s characterization of the talks in Washington, and told the Star the group does not have any obligation to submit its contacts to the foreign influence transparency registry.

“We do not meet any of the criteria under the (Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act). The very first criteria is that you have an arrangement with a foreign principal ... we have no arrangement with anybody. Our contacts with the United States were purely informal,” he told the Star’s Stephanie Taylor.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, left, waits to deliver a speech on Alberta Day in Calgary, Alta., Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026.THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh
It’s not known who else Boegman has contacted, or what specific kind of foreign influence his office is worried about.

At first, the watchdog office refused to even publicly disclose the number of groups it contacted, with the commissioner only revealing that to a handful of reporters who pressed him following an appearance Tuesday at a parliamentary committee.
The number of those notified by Boegman’s office exceeds the number of groups that Elections Alberta has registered as third-party advertisers in the campaign, with 28 listed on its website.

Premier Danielle Smith’s government has asked Albertans to cast votes — on 10 separate ballots, one for each question — on whether the province should demand more power on immigration levels and services offered to newcomers, more say in judicial appointments, and the ability to opt-out of federal programs, as well as the final, potentially most explosive question: whether to trigger a second binding vote on taking Alberta out of Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to journalists as he makes his way to a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Oct. 7, 2026.

Carney has articulated a pro-unity argument in the past week — after announcing a major pipeline construction project would be fast-tracked, and after Quebec voters elected a minority separatist Parti Québécois government on Monday — that centres on the notion that “Canada is working.”

On Tuesday, he touted his government’s trade diversification agenda and Ottawa’s drive to build major capital-intensive resource and infrastructure projects. “You know, this is a crucial time for our country. It’s a crucial time for Quebec,” Carney said. “This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness.”
From left, Scott Burrows, CEO of the Pembina Pipeline Corp, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney shake hands after speaking in Fort McMurray on Oct. 1, 2026.

Ottawa— While Prime Minister Mark Carney has been clear about where he stands on Alberta independence, his government’s position on nine other Alberta referendum questions aimed at reshaping immigration and expanding provincial powers is far less so.
Now, some federalist groups campaigning for Albertans to remain in Canada on Oct. 19 are calling on leaders, including Carney, to speak up against the proposals.

Those nine questions formed the initial referendum package advanced by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party before it added a controversial 10th question on independence, following a court decision quashing a separatist-backed petition seeking a vote on secession.

Four of the nine questions revolve around Alberta seeking a mandate to work with other provinces to reopen the Constitution in hopes of gaining the power to appoint its own federal court judges and opt out of federal government programs without losing funding.
The five others ask about the province exerting more control over immigration.

Critics say the constitutional proposals sow division and advance an agenda that seeks to pull Alberta further away from the federation, while the immigration measures risk creating tiered access to health care, education and social services for newcomers, heightening calls for Carney and other federal leaders to weigh in.

“The 10th question, should we stay or should we go, is actually about Alberta and what Albertans think. The other nine questions are a stick in the eye to the government of Canada,” said Stephen Carter, one of the founders of Alberta’s Voice, a registered third-party advertiser on the stay side.
“The government of Canada needs to stand up and say, ‘These are not good ideas. This is a mistake.’”

On immigration, one referendum questions asks: “Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?”

Another asks whether residents support Alberta “introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta­ approved immigration status” be eligible to receive “provincially funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services.”

The other three ask whether residents support requiring those with “non-permanent legal immigration status” to live in Alberta for at least 12 months before becoming eligible for “provincially funded social support programs,” charging “a reasonable fee or premium” for health and education services, and requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections.

Smith’s government has launched an estimated $4-million advertising campaign urging residents to vote “yes” on the nine questions, as the premier argues greater provincial sovereignty is an antidote to Alberta’s grievances and an alternative to separation.
It argues that Alberta is bearing the brunt of federal immigration policies that have led to the inflow of thousands of temporary residents, putting a strain on services.

For Avnish Nanda, an Edmonton-based lawyer and spokesman for Our Alberta Advantage, an initiative of the Alberta Advantage Immigrant Support Society, putting immigration on the ballot has sparked “shock, fear and confusion” among newcomer and immigrant groups.
“It’s going to legitimatize and condone discriminatory treatment,” Nanda told the Star.
He suggests federalist groups and the provincial NDP could find themselves with a “hollow victory” if the separatist question is defeated but the immigration questions pass.
He says Carney and members of his cabinet ought to “make the case” about the economic need for immigration to support the labour force.

Public Interest Alberta, another third-party group campaigning against the nine other questions, has called on more leaders to speak out against them, arguing that with many residents still undecided, the time to do so is now.

The Angus Reid Institute recently released a report suggesting support for the nine reforms ranges between 48 and 62 per cent depending on the question, with many respondents reporting some confusion over the wording.

Despite independence being on the ballot, the Ottawa-Alberta relationship has warmed significantly since Carney and Smith hit a reset after a tumultuous decade under prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose energy policies led to a backlash that inflamed the province’s long-standing sense of Western alienation. The centrepiece of that new relationship is a pact to construct a new oil pipeline to the West Coast, aided by major regulatory reforms and taxpayer funding from Ottawa.
“Canada is working,” Carney said this week as he announced that pipeline would be the first project to be fast-tracked under new federal government powers.
Smith also touted the deal as an example of “co-operative federalism,” while acknowledging there remains outstanding issues in the relationship to work out.

Sofia Ouslis, a spokeswoman for the Prime Minister’s Office, said in a statement that Carney “has been very clear that Canada and Alberta are stronger together and that the risks from this referendum are real.”

“Albertans are leading the fight for a united Canada through the many campaigns and tens of thousands of volunteers mobilizing across the province. The federal government is a genuine partner in this work to show that Canada works for every part of this country,” said Ouslis.
“Our government has taken action since being elected to restore sustainability to Canada’s immigration system.”

The statement added that long-standing mechanisms exist should any one province or territory want to reopen the Constitution, with amendments requiring the support of at least seven provinces representing half of the country’s population, the House of Commons and Senate.
“Our priorities are those of Albertans and Canadians — building a stronger, more independent, economy and Albertans are seeing results,” Ouslis wrote.

Corey Hogan, the Liberal MP for Calgary Confederation and parliamentary secretary for energy and natural resources, told the Star that when it comes to the nine questions, “there’s no official position of the government of Canada” and that they are ones which Albertans must wrestle with.
He pointed to Alberta’s history of holding referendums, including during the tenure of Jason Kenney, who advanced questions on equalization and daylight saving time.
Within the province, Hogan said, there is a “hyper-fixation” on the independence question. He also suggested it would be wise for people to focus on what has clearly become the “main thing.”

“The federal government obviously has an interest in the future of the federal government,” he said. “I’m not sure that it would be appropriate, even, for the federal government just to wade in on every single one of those nine questions.”
Nevertheless, Hogan, who recently voted by mail, said he voted “no to the nine.”
“I do not think we want to send a signal that you can get what you want as provincial government by playing with the future of this country.”

For Marci Surkes, a former Liberal staffer who joined Trudeau’s office after the Liberals were shut out of Saskatchewan and Alberta in the 2019 federal election, Carney has a “delicate dance” to perform.
Much of what’s on the Alberta referendum ballot reflects reforms Quebec has undertaken, she said.

“Each one of those ballot questions, ON its own, needs to be carefully considered in terms of what more can the federal government conceivably allow Albertans to determine for themselves or to allow their government to determine without risking any additional tears to the fabric of the federation.”

Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, the lone cabinet minister representing an Alberta riding, told the Star in a statement that she voted against the nine questions and urged other Albertans to think carefully about their ballots.

“My message to Albertans is to take the time to understand what each referendum question could mean for our province, our country, our future, and reflect on what our priorities are and what problems we are actually trying to solve,” the Edmonton MP said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks in a televised address on May 21, 2026.
Calgary—The province of Alberta is now within spitting distance of a vote on independence.

This fall’s referendum-on-a-referendum, as some critics are calling it, will be of “monumental importance,” Premier Danielle Smith says. Asking residents if they want to go forward with a binding referendum, it edges a province closer to an independence vote — and marks the first time the province in question isn’t Quebec.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith spoke to media the day after announcing the province would vote on whether it should stay in Canada or take steps to hold a binding referendum to leave Canada. Smith would not answer whether she was concerned about her job security as separatists express ire over her framing of a referendum question about secession. (May 22, 2026)

As long as Alberta has been a province, there has been a deep vein of frustration with the faraway government in Ottawa that has long been seen by many as eager to take Western resources but less keen on Western voices.
“It’s not driven by anger. It’s almost like a feeling of unrequited love. That’s the best way to put it,” Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta, told the Star last year .
But the number of Albertans who want to leave Canada has always been small — and largely ignored, despite their best efforts.

Over the last 50 years, would-be separatists have fielded more than a dozen parties in federal and provincial elections and still failed to get traction, former premier Jason Kenney argued on a Calgary stage last week. (The height of their success was Gordon Kelser, who, as anger at the National Energy Program was at its peak in 1982, won a federal byelection in a rural riding that he held for just over two months before being defeated.)

“They couldn’t get elected dogcatcher,” Kenney said. (In the wake of Smith’s announcement, Kenney has revealed himself to be one of the backers of a new campaign to urge Alberta to remain in the country, Vote to Stay .)
So how did the separatist movement go from fringe idea to province-wide vote? Here’s a rough timeline.
2017: Jason Kenney creates the United Conservative Party

The Ndp’s 2015 provincial election victory shocked the country, ending 44 consecutive years of governing by the Progressive Conservatives. It also handed former federal minister Jason Kenney a mission: to unite the province’s two right wing parties and win back government.

His new United Conservative Party stitched together the weakened Progressive Conservatives and the smaller, more right-wing Wildrose Party. The UCP went on to win a resounding victory over the New Democrats in 2019 and remains in government today. Kenney has stressed that he wrote loyalty to Canada into the Ucp’s founding documents, but the party struggles to balance its moderate and libertarian factions.
2022: Kenney is replaced by Danielle Smith

The COVID pandemic proved an unsurmountable political challenge for Kenney, as the UCP fractured over his implementation of public health measures. He stepped down after receiving just 51 per cent support in a leadership review.

Kenney was replaced by one of his fiercest critics , a radio host named Danielle Smith who would famously refer to the unvaccinated as “the most discriminated-against group” in her lifetime. She drew support from party members who were angry about public health mandates and what they saw as government overreach. Smith said she hoped to be a “force of unity.”
December 2024: Donald Trump’s ‘51st state’

U.S. president-elect Donald Trump refers to Canada as his country’s 51st state for the first time, provoking anger across the country. But Trump’s musings also begin to inflame separatist tensions in Alberta among those who see America as more ideologically aligned and pro-oil.

“It’s one thing to decide to leave a marriage and have to find a new place to live and set up a household and manage on your own,” Lisa Young, a political scientist at the University of Calgary, told the Star last spring . “It’s another thing to leave a marriage and move in with someone else, who’s already got a place to live and who welcomes you.”
March 2025: Smith warns Mark Carney of a ‘national unity crisis’
Days after Mark Carney succeeds Justin Trudeau as prime minister, he and Smith meet for what she calls a “frank discussion.”

Much of Smith’s time in office had been spent criticizing Trudeau’s handling of Western issues, and Smith says she has given Carney a list of demands — from “unfettered” market access for oil to lifting the West coast tanker ban — that need to be met in six months in order to avert an “unprecedented national unity crisis.”
April 2025: Smith lowers referendum bar

In a move widely seen as appeasing the separatists, Smith lowers the bar for residents to propose policy changes or referendum questions. Whereas the law had previously required signatures from 10 per cent of the population, the new threshold is 10 per cent of those who voted in the last election. She also extends the time they have to do it.
Smith continues to stress she is pro-Canada, but separatist leaders, many of whom were also against COVID measures, increasingly see her as enabling their cause.
May 2025: Smith says referendum prospect vents frustration
Asked about rising separatist tensions, Smith implies that a potential referendum is keeping her party together: “If there isn’t an outlet, it creates a new party.”
August 2025: A pro-Canada petition launches

Fearing that separatists are preparing to launch their own petition, former PC deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk launches a pro-Canada version in an attempt to beat them at their own game. He hopes his petition, which asks signatories to confirm loyalty to Canada, will be accepted as policy by the government, instead of going to a vote.
The Forever Canada petition launches even before the new relaxed rules have kicked in. It blows through its goal , gathering more than 400,000 signatures by October.
January 2026: Separatist petition kicks off

The first attempt at a separatist petition is blocked by a judge who says it violates Charter and treaty rights. The government changes the rules to allow petitions to go ahead even if they violate the Constitution. The separatists, under a group called Stay Free Alberta, begin gathering signatures.
March 2026: Separatism emerges in Smith’s party

In one of the first major expressions of support from an elected official, UCP MLA Jason Stephan writes an op-ed inviting Albertans to sign the separatist petition. Polls suggest separatist sentiment is in the minority, but is associated with conservatism and support for Smith’s party. Smith says MLAs are welcome to their own opinions, but the government’s stance is pro-Canada.
May 2026: Separatist petition blocked, frustrations mount

Separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre says he has 300,000 signatures to submit to Elections Alberta but a judge quashes the petition, saying it violates treaty rights. The separatists vow to appeal, and Smith calls the decision “incorrect” and “anti-democratic.”
Frustrated with Smith’s leadership, prominent separatist Jeff Rath tells his supporters to buy UCP memberships to push for pro-independence policies.
May 21, 2026: Smith announces a referendum question

In a speech that blasts the earlier court decision as a “legal mistake” Smith pitches her own referendum question for the first time, and says Albertans will vote Oct. 19 on whether they want to pursue a binding referendum.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks during a news conference in Calgary, Alta. on May 22, 2026.
Canadians need to stare down the stark reality of what happened in Alberta this week. Premier Danielle Smith has moved her province closer to separation than it has ever been.

This brewing national-unity crisis has not come about from the tyranny of the majority — it has been created by a minority wielding too much power for its size, and by politicians like Smith who believe its complaints with the federation can be appeased.

With her plan to have a referendum on a referendum, as it’s being called, Smith has created not just a steam vent for separatist grievance, as it was no doubt intended, but a path to turn that into independence.
Basically, the ballot question asks Albertans to decide whether they’re happy with their current state in the federation or if they would like a referendum on independence.

Separatists are annoyed it’s a two-step path, not the one, clear question they wanted on Oct. 19. But it’s more than they had before Smith’s Thursday-evening announcement and Canada has to live with all the uncertainty this is going to create in the months leading up to the referendum.

Though she says she will be campaigning on the remain-in-Canada side, her Thursday and Friday remarks were littered with separatist-style grievance about Liberal governance, much like Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also did on Friday.
“We will continue to work on undoing the last 10 years of damaging Trudeau-NDP policies and fight for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada,” Smith told reporters on Friday.
Poilievre struck a similar tone: “We’re now facing a referendum in the second year of Mr. Carney’s mandate. We have to ask ourselves: what is he really doing to unite the country?”

If that’s how they intend to frame their referendum pitch for the next six months, they run the danger of whipping it up to a point where even on-the-fence Albertans decide why not keep the pressure on the rest of Canada to placate those grievances?

The premier said she was doing this because she didn’t want to kick the can further down the road, but that’s exactly the result of a ballot question that presents people with the choice to make up their mind sometime in the future.

That’s the gift Smith gave to the separatist advocates with this new referendum question — more time — time to convert the curious into believers; time to keep turning up the pressure for more appeasement from Ottawa.
Still, some of the most ardent separatists didn’t seem all that grateful in the immediate aftermath, calling for Smith to be deposed and for Alberta to stop working with Mark Carney.

One post on X by declared independence advocate, Jeff Berube, was a lengthy denunciation of Smith’s referendum question but also of Carney’s approach to the United States. Berube appears to be worried that Canada’s trade status with the U.S. is in threat, and only Alberta independence can meet the moment.
His post was reposted by Jeff Rath, a prominent pro-independence lawyer who boasted earlier this year about the Donald Trump administration’s interest in Alberta separation.
That’s a whole other dimension of this referendum — the Trump interest — that has been made all the more real by an actual ballot question on independence now looming over Alberta and Canada.

Smith was asked on Friday whether she was worried about becoming the David Cameron of Canada — a reference to the British prime minister who called a referendum on getting the U.K. out of the European Union promising to campaign on the remain side. Brexit won that referendum.

I went leafing through Cameron’s memoir of those times and saw the parallels and why people are increasingly using Brexit as a warning for the path on which Smith has embarked. The Brexit choice also landed at a time when Brits were growing more insular, more worried about immigration and Cameron’s party was riven on the issue. All that runs through Alberta’s referendum, almost eerily.
Cameron says in that memoir that the Remain side was too focused on the technical arguments, while Brexit advocates campaigned more on emotion.

That should be a strong warning to Smith, and to Carney too, who was in the U.K. for Brexit as bank governor. Carney’s statement on Friday, depicting Canada as a country in the midst of renovation, was maybe worryingly technocratic. Note to all: maybe talking about a memo of understanding isn’t going to cut through the emotions at play here.

The lurking peril in Smith’s ballot question is that she’s essentially offering Albertans a choice between the status quo and time to consider bigger change. If Albertans are in a change mood, that’s trouble for the remain side.
Smith is presenting herself as prepared for what she’s unleashed on her province on the country this week. But is the rest of Canada prepared?

content_blocks.text: While Western alienation is nothing new for the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polling suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minster Mark Carney, his win viewed as another hit against the deep-blue Conservative province.
content_blocks.html: While western alienation is nothing new for the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polling suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minster Mark Carney, his win viewed as another hit against the deep-blue Conservative province.

content_blocks.text: Anger had been brewing for years after the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose environmental policies were viewed by many in the province as stymying the development of its resources. Even before that, his “Trudeau” last name triggered Albertans’ distrust, remembering the legacy left behind by the long-dismantled National Energy Program by his father, former prime minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

stories.title: Investors buying unsold Toronto condos at 40% discount to original selling price, report finds
stories.summary: Six bulk buyers in the Toronto region bought 339 units in the most recent quarter, or 45% of new condo purchases, Urbanation report says
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
Large investors bought unsold newly built condos in the Toronto region at a 40-per-cent discount to the original selling price and accounted for nearly half the preconstruction sales in recent months.

These investors paid an average of $763 per square foot for a completed and unsold unit in the third quarter, according to a report from condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

They often buy a minimum of a few dozen units from a developer as a bulk purchase. In the most recent quarter ended in September, there were six bulk buyers in the Toronto region that bought 339 units. The bulk buys accounted for 45 per cent of the 760 new condo purchases in the quarter.

Real estate companies or investment funds have gotten a cheaper price than individual buyers trying to find a deal among the glut of unsold units in the Toronto and Hamilton area.

Individuals paid an average of $1,033 per square foot for a newly built condo in the third quarter, according to Urbanation.

“Two straight quarters of higher sales show that buyers will step in at the right price,” Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand said in a news release. “Bulk investors are acquiring completed units at heavily discounted prices.”

The bulk purchases included a transaction by High Art Capital, an Ontario government-backed fund that is turning a portion of its units into affordable rentals. High Art paid $22.3-million for 43 units in a condo complex called Line 5 in midtown Toronto, The Globe and Mail first reported in September.

That works out to about $518,000 per unit and is close to the typical selling price of a condo on the resale market in the Toronto region. That is unusual because newly built condos normally sell at a significant premium to those on the resale market

This is the second quarter since the federal and Ontario governments’ HST rebate on new homes has been in place. It is also the second period where new condo sales have been markedly higher than last year.

Buyers can get a maximum of $130,000 rebate on the HST for new homes priced up to $1.5-million until the end of March, 2027. The temporary tax break went into effect in April and is designed to help developers get rid of unsold inventory, which it has managed to do to some extent.

At the end of September, there were 5,127 newly built units that were unsold. That was down 7 per cent from the end of June. (The unsold inventory does not include the units that developers have had to take back because buyers have defaulted on their purchases.)

Those who bought preconstruction units at the height of the market have seen the value of their units plunge over the past four years, according to realtors and property appraisers.

Many preconstruction buyers have not been able to close if their lender does not provide them with a mortgage at the original purchase price.

For the many individual investors who have been able to close, they are losing money on their investment because they either cannot find renters or the rent is not enough to cover the cost of their mortgage payments, condo fees and other property expenses.

That has led to a drop in preconstruction condo sales, which is a precursor to a condo tower being built. In the third quarter, there were only 60 condo units in the preconstruction phase that were sold in the Toronto and Hamilton region.

Mr. Hildebrand called the preconstruction market dormant and said this will lead to a major decline in new condos being built.
