stories.title: Alberta votes on leaving Canada: 1.4 million ballots cast in advance; record turnout expected today
stories.summary: More than 800,000 advanced ballots were already cast before voting day, with results expected to roll in late Monday night.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
Polls opened for Alberta’s historic referendum on Monday, with voters lining up to cast a ballot over whether the province should consider separating from Canada.

Voting day follows months of debate over the separation question, which has divided many in the province and prompted both sides to ramp up efforts to sway public opinion in recent weeks.

The referendum, which includes one question on proposed separation and another nine on various other constitutional matters, is expected to draw record numbers to the ballot box. Elections Alberta estimates record turnout as high as 85 per cent, compared with an average of just over 50 per cent in recent general elections. According to the agency, 1.4 million voters, or 43.1 per cent of eligible voters, have already cast advanced ballots or special ballots before Monday. That compares with 809,988 advanced and special ballots cast in the 2023 election, or 27.5 per cent of eligible voters.

Monday’s referendum vote is not explicitly a vote to leave Canada, but gives voters the option of either remaining in Canada or holding a second vote on whether to secede.

Polls opened at 9 a.m. MT and will remain open until 8 p.m. local time. However, some polling stations reportedly opened late on Monday and will remain open past 8 p.m. Elections Alberta will start counting advanced and special ballots starting at 5 p.m. MT. Early results will start rolling in after the final vote has been cast.

The separation question will be counted first and results are expected late Monday night. Check back here for the latest results after polls close. Results for the other nine questions will be announced within 48 hours.

The other nine questions ask Albertans whether Alberta should be given more control over immigration rates, work with other provinces to abolish the federal Senate, or give the province the right to opt out of certain federal programs, among others. Five of the 10 questions relate to immigration policy, including asking whether the province should halt some public services like health care to non-permanent residents.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she prefers that the province remain in Canada, despite the fact that it was her government that changed the law to enable the referendum on separation to be held. The premier has called for an “independent Alberta within a united Canada” and has been working closely with Prime Minister Mark Carney to repair the province’s fractured relationship with Ottawa.

Together, the pair have announced a flurry of joint projects in an effort to shore up support for the federalist side, including Carney’s promise to back the province’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline and pump $8 billion in new military spending in the province.

Carney was in Alberta last week for a final campaign aimed at pushing Albertans to vote to remain, saying the country is stronger united, particularly in the face of what he calls a dangerous and divided world.

Meanwhile, Alberta’s pro-separatist advocates have also been calling on voters to get out the vote, with some arguing a vote for separation can give the province useful leverage in its negotiations with Ottawa.

While results of the referendum are unlikely to be known until late Monday night, polling has consistently shown that roughly three quarters of voters support remaining in Canada, while the other 25 per cent are sympathetic to the separatist cause.

1. Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

2. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

3. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

4. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

5. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

6. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

7. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

8. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

9. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

10. Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

stories.title: Members of Quebec's official Opposition Liberals sworn in at the legislature
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Millard urged his caucus to serve with clarity and humility today as they were sworn in at the provincial legislature.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Millard urged his caucus to serve with clarity and humility today as they were sworn in at the provincial legislature.

Millard said his party’s work isn’t done after a strong Oct. 5 election result.

The party more than doubled its seat count, going from 18 to 40 and will serve as the official Opposition to the minority Parti Québécois government.

Former premier Jean Charest was on hand to watch as his son Antoine was sworn in as the new representative for the Verdun riding.

All of the Liberals opted to swear the oath to the Quebec people and not to the King, after the oath to the monarch was made optional in 2022.

One member, Affine Lwalalika, was not sworn in since a judicial recount is underway in her riding.

Milliard told his elected members to be proud, but also urged them to approach the role with “a healthy dose of clarity and humility.”

“If our work of rebuilding were complete, we would be the ones forming the government today,” he said, adding, “There are still many regions to win back.”

“The result on Oct. 5 is certainly an important milestone, but it is by no means the culmination of all our efforts.”

He said it’s unclear how long the minority PQ government led by Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will last, and called for both discipline and teamwork.

“When it comes to resolving crises, the government will find in us a reliable and open partner, but when it comes to creating crises … it will find in us a tough and unyielding opponent,” he said.

Milliard also stated that the Quebec Fleur-de-lis is “just as striking alongside the Maple Leaf,” in a plea for federalism that drew thunderous applause.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. designer Bob Masse created groovy poster art for leading rock bands
stories.summary: With an art style featuring ornate Art Nouveau lines and distorted, hand-drawn lettering, he did work for Sixties groups including the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane; and he had a career revival later in life that saw him designing posters for U2, Neil Young and the Tragically Hip
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
Bob Masse tuned in to the 1960s California scene, turned on to copious mind-altering substances, and dropped some of the grooviest psychedelic posters of the era.

The British Columbia graphic artist befriended band members of the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane, partied with Janis Joplin and hung out with musicians living in Laurel Canyon in the Hollywood Hills, including a fellow Canadian by the name of Joni Mitchell, whom he described as a “skinny little girl with buckteeth.”

Mr. Masse, who has died at 81, created far-out concert posters for such bands as the Dead, the Doors, Jefferson Airplane, the Steve Miller Band, and Country Joe and the Fish.

Mr. Masse was a rare poster artist from the 1960s to continue working well into the next century.

Years after his initial success, he was rediscovered and his career revived, a flashback of sorts, as he enjoyed a long, fruitful span crafting glorious posters for such performers as Tori Amos, Pearl Jam, Alanis Morissette, Smashing Pumpkins and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

Youthful looking throughout his life, he was often asked to reminisce about the events and characters of the Sixties, though it must be said the chaotic nature of those times and his own indulgences left his memories somewhat foggy.

As he once said, “I got my mind blown in San Francisco.”

It was while he was in California hanging out with hippie bands that he came across a 50-year-old graphic design manual that changed his life.

Robert Joseph Masse was born in Vancouver on April 5, 1945, the first of four children for the former Lillian Mae Sharp and Joseph Frank Masse. Joe was serving with an artillery unit of the Canadian Army during the Second World War when he went on a blind date with Lill, a packer for a wholesale grocery firm. They married in 1944. After leaving the armed services, the elder Mr. Masse worked as a furniture polisher and refinisher with Woodward’s department store.

Young Bob liked to draw in the basement of the family’s home in Burnaby, a community adjacent to Vancouver. He got a formal education in design at the Vancouver School of Art (now the Emily Carr University of Art + Design).

A practicum sent him across the street to the Queen Elizabeth Theatre, where he offered to create for free a concert poster for a folk singer from Minnesota via Greenwich Village who was about to make his debut in the city. The poster featured six candid black-and-white photographs of the tousled, unkempt, smoking, guitar-strumming poet-singer in two vertical rows, with the date and place in all lower case, sans-serif letters. Dozens of the posters were placed around town before anyone realized Mr. Masse had rendered Bob Dylan’s surname as “Dylon.”

Mr. Masse created posters for coffeehouses featuring folk music such as the Inquisition and the Bunkhouse before doing the same for teenaged promotor Jerry Kruz, whose Afterthought promotions included light shows and the new sounds coming from California bands, as well as local talent. He was paid $10 per poster.

A trip to San Francisco introduced Mr. Masse to concert posters – by the likes of Wes Wilson, Stanley Mouse and others – featuring ornate Art Nouveau lines and distorted, hand-drawn, barely legible lettering.

“I went through a structured system [at art school], and all of a sudden people were coming out with totally bizarre designs,” he said. “It was a total breakdown in the rules.”

At the same time, he came across a copy of Strong’s Book of Designs , a 1917 manual by Charles Jay Strong featuring a phantasmagoria of ribbons, borders, show cards, airbrush designs and illustrations of such objects as butterflies, as well as fanciful typography, much of it reproduced in glorious colour.

He crashed for free in an old Victorian house at 710 Ashbury St., the communal home and headquarters of the Grateful Dead. When the band came to British Columbia, Mr. Masse agreed to meet them at the border.

“They were driving this psychedelic-painted bus, like a Ken Kesey bus, and the border officials almost fainted when they saw these guys,” he told Neal Hall of the Vancouver Sun in 2007.

Mr. Masse produced several memorable posters for the band’s shows in Vancouver, as well as for the Trips Festival, an 11-hour concert held at a hockey rink in suburban Richmond in 1967 featuring such acts as the Jefferson Airplane, Magic Fern, the Collectors and Painted Ship (the latter two both from Vancouver), as well as the Cougar and Darks Pandemonium Light Show Company (the latter being a whimsical name for the lighting crew). He also made posters for shows at Dante’s Inferno and the Retinal Circus, nightclubs at the same address on Davie Street in downtown Vancouver.

Mr. Masse returned to California where he designed posters and newspaper advertisements for the Whiskey A Go Go while living in an apartment above the Los Angeles nightclub. He later lived in a garage in Laurel Canyon, an area that was home to many of the city’s rock musicians.

He hung out backstage with the Doors and Ms. Joplin, who once complained to him about a lack of male groupies. “Nobody chases me,” she told him. “I’m not getting any action here.” Mr. Masse later confessed regret at not having taken the hint.

On his return to British Columbia in the 1970s, Mr. Masse adopted a softer, more pastoral style with more pastel colours, influenced by the imagery of Alphonse Mucha, the Mitteleuropean artist who became known for his theatrical posters for Sarah Bernhardt in the 1890s.

Mr. Masse abandoned poster making for years, as clients demanded edgier designs than he cared to create, supporting himself through commercial and advertising work.

One day, he called friend Rob Frith, a poster collector and record store owner, about a cache of old posters his parents had kept in their basement. When Mr. Frith visited the artist’s apartment, he discovered to his horror that Mr. Masse was using his old work to light fires in his fireplace. He bought the entire stack.

In 1992, Mr. Frith offered to pay for the printing if Mr. Masse made a poster for a forthcoming show by the Scottish musician Donovan on his Mellow Yellow Tour. With the deadline looming, the artist recycled an old image he had used years earlier for Honey’s Creative Sandwiches, a lunch spot next to his studio in Vancouver’s Gastown. In the original, a bare-chested nymph in a flowing, diaphanous robe with flowers in her hair is depicted holding a sandwich. For the concert poster, the food was replaced by a crystal ball.

He once again became an in-demand poster designer with his signature style called on by such artists as U2, Neil Young and the Tragically Hip. He also designed covers for the front page of the Georgia Straight newspaper on its 30 th and 50 th anniversaries, homages to the publication’s underground roots.

As well, his earlier work was rediscovered. One of his posters was included in The Art of Rock , a 1987 coffee-table book considered a vital reference for collectors of such rock ’n’ roll ephemera as posters, tickets, handbills and backstage passes.

When Mr. Frith sought to get approval for a reissue of a Grateful Dead poster, he called the band for permission. They well knew the poster; an original was hanging in their office. For Mr. Masse, this was the beginning of a profitable period of selling reproductions.

Among his many other notable works were album covers, including for the Collectors, which became the band Chilliwack. He also did the cover art for two albums issued by Mr. Frith featuring the sounds of Vancouver, including one released in August.

For all his psychedelic and pastoral works, his most ubiquitous design was likely an orange cartoon fox with heavy-lidded eyes drawn for Cfox, a Vancouver rock radio station.

“He’s everywhere, that little bugger,” he once lamented.

Mr. Masse, a resident of Salt Spring Island, where he maintained a studio, died in hospital there on Sept. 21 from Parkinson-plus syndrome, a group of neurodegenerative diseases. He had earlier suffered a minor stroke and was recuperating from the lingering effects of a motorcycle accident. He leaves Claire Norris, his partner of 33 years. He also leaves a sister, Bonnie, and brothers Ray and Len, the latter who drew a DoodleArt poster titled Ecology that sold more than a million copies. An earlier marriage for Mr. Masse ended in divorce. He had no children.

The artist’s career spanned a time when the government went from prosecuting possession of weed to selling it. As well, the posters for which he was once paid a pittance have become valuable collectibles. One of Mr. Masse’s original Grateful Dead posters, for which he believed he had been paid $100 in 1967, sold at auction in the United States five years ago for more than $15,000. As the Grateful Dead sing on Truckin’ , “What a long, strange trip it’s been.”

stories.title: Measles outbreak over after two years, Phac says
stories.summary: More than 6,400 people were infected across 10 provinces, Public Health Agency of Canada says
stories.author: Hannah Alberga
stories.content:
A measles outbreak that spanned two years and infected thousands of people in Canada is over.

The Public Health Agency of Canada made the declaration in a press release Monday, stating that more than 6,400 people were infected across 10 provinces.

Two infants in Ontario and Alberta who were infected with measles while in the womb died after they were born.

The outbreak began in New Brunswick in October 2024 and about a year later led to the loss of Canada’s measles elimination status due to ongoing transmission of the highly contagious disease for more than 12 months.

Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Joss Reimer says that although it’s encouraging to see the outbreak declared over, it doesn’t mean that measles is gone.

Infectious disease experts have attributed the return of measles to declining vaccination rates, misinformation-fuelled vaccine hesitancy and distrust of authority, as well as disruptions to routine immunizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Measles continues to circulate globally, and we can expect to see further travel-related cases here at home,” Reimer said in a statement.

Ontario, which was one of the most affected provinces, declared its outbreak over last fall, while Alberta’s ended in July. Public health officials in Manitoba said the province’s last laboratory-confirmed case was in August.

stories.title: High personal income taxes drag down Canada's tax competitiveness, new study finds
stories.summary: It puts further pressure on Ottawa to take significant steps in the federal budget that is expected in less than a month.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government’s recent efforts to make Canadian taxes more competitive have not yet put any significant dents internationally, a new study released Monday has found, putting further pressure on Ottawa to take significant steps in the federal budget that is expected in less than a month.

The annual study, by The Tax Foundation’s Center for Global Tax Policy, gave Canada an overall rank of 15th among 38 industrialized countries — the same as last year but slightly ahead of the United States.

Canada’s score, and its economy, were dragged down largely by high personal income taxes, which ranked 28th overall among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd) countries. Canada ranked 22nd in direct taxation on wages and salaries and 34th on income from capital gains and dividends.

But the national grade was much better on consumption taxes, with Canada placing 8th, despite the national disdain for the GST and its provincial counterparts. The report, titled the 2026 International Tax Competitiveness Index Rankings, also noted that Canada, unlike many countries, does not apply wealth, estate or inheritance taxes.

Not surprisingly, after more than a year of a trade war with the United States, Canada was given a poor grade (28th) in its cross-border tax regime.

The study noted that Canada has taken some steps to make its tax regime more competitive, but that other countries are doing the same. Many countries, the report noted, are trying to rely more on sales and payroll taxes, which are less harmful economically, while cutting corporate and personal income taxes.

“A well-structured tax code is easy for taxpayers to comply with and can promote economic development,” the report says. “In contrast, poorly structured tax systems can be costly, distort economic decision-making, and harm domestic economies.

After a decade of waning competitiveness under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, the Carney government has made it a priority to try to turn Canada’s economic performance around and part of the strategy has been to lower taxes. Ottawa has eliminated the consumer portion of the carbon tax, cut the GST on first-time homebuyers, eliminated the digital services tax cancelled the planned increase in the capital gains inclusion rate and made a tepid cut to personal income taxes.

Ottawa also took a big swing at improved competitiveness last month when it introduced the Building Canada Strong Act, designed to speed up infrastructure projects, improve trade and transportation links and amend labour rules in federally regulated sectors to try to avoid strikes and other work stoppages.

Those changes have not yet been passed into law, so were not included in The Tax Foundation’s study. Its cutoff for policy changes was July.

The U.S., Canada’s predominant trading partner and competitor, ranked 17th in the competitiveness rankings, two spots behind Canada. The U.S. placed eighth overall in corporate competitiveness, and 17th overall on personal taxes: 20th on taxation of wages and 26th on taxes of capital gains and dividends.

The U.S. score was hampered by a very poor rating (37th) on cross-border tax rules, far behind Canada’s 28th place and ahead of only one country.

The Canadian Taxpayers Federation said the new report should be a “wake-up call” for Ottawa to cut both income and business taxes, made even more important by the trade war with the U.S.

“Canadian workers and businesses are fighting to survive tariffs and our governments are making it harder by imposing less competitive business and income taxes than the Americans,” said Franco Terrazzano, the federation’s federal director, in a release.

But Canadian business leaders, according to a Kpmg survey released late last week, believe that the Carney government is getting the message, with 71 per cent of respondents saying they’re confident the upcoming budget will help Canadian business

The survey also found that they would like the budget to rank the Canada-U.S. trade conflict (62 per cent) as the most pressing issue, following by attracting foreign investment (44 per cent), accelerating major projects (34 per cent), cost pressures on both businesses and households (34 per cent) and taxes / red tape (26 per cent).

The keys to an effective corporate tax system, The Tax Foundation’s report says, are neutrality and competitiveness.

As tax regimes become more complicated, as most have over time, they become less neutral in that they encourage biases towards, for example, labour over capital investment. And if a country’s corporate taxes are too high, it will drive investment elsewhere, reducing economic growth.

Estonia earned the top spot in the Oecd for its tax code for the 13th year in a row. It has a 22 percent tax rate on corporate income that is only applied to distributed profits and a flat 22 percent tax on individual income that does not apply to dividends. Estonia is followed at the top of the rankings by Latvia and New Zealand in the rankings.

France came dead last in the rankings, trailing only Colombia and Italy.

The Tax Foundation’s study compares national tax regimes, not those at the provincial or state levels.

stories.title: Proposed remedy for workers affected by Bill 148 could cost N.S. $470 million
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government says it has agreed to pay public sector employees an estimated $470 million in compensation over legislation introduced in 2015 to restrict their wages.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says it has agreed to pay public sector employees an estimated $470 million in compensation over legislation introduced in 2015 to restrict their wages.

Nova Scotia’s Minister of Finance, John Lohr said the government has reflected the cost of this settlement in its 2025-26 budget.

The government was ordered to compensate public sector employees after provincial Supreme Court Justice Ann Smith ruled in February that Bill 148 substantially interfered with the rights of several unions in the province.

Justice Smith must sign-off on the proposed remedy before it can go into effect .

The former Liberal government introduced Bill 148 in December 2015.

The legislation was enacted in 2017 and imposed wage restrictions for almost all public servants over a four-year period and eliminated awards for long-term service.

A lawyer for the Nova Scotia Justice Department says the remedy will see an estimated 81,000 public servants receive payouts to compensate for an infringement of their Charter rights that occurred as a result of Bill 148.

stories.title: ‘Just not acceptable’: Backlash grows over Nova Scotia AI data centre project
stories.summary: Criticism of Nova Scotia's move to build a large-scale AI data centre is growing, as both opposition parties are calling for an emergency sitting of the Legislature to debate it.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
Criticism of Nova Scotia’s move to build a large-scale AI data centre in Cape Breton is growing, as both opposition parties are calling for an emergency sitting of the legislature to debate the project because they say it lacks consultation and regulatory safeguards.

On Friday, energy and infrastructure company, EverWind , announced plans for $10 billion in private investment in a data centre campus at its existing Point Tupper site near Port Hawkesbury, N.S.

AI development company Anthropic , the creator of Claude AI, confirmed it had signed a long-term lease to use the centre.

In a Monday morning social media post, Official Opposition Leader Claudia Chender shared her letter to Premier Tim Houston, in which she said “tough questions about this project must be asked.”

“What is most alarming is that you seem to believe that non-binding federal guidelines endorsed by the AI industry itself and expectations you laid out in a social media post constitute a valid approach to ensure that data centres remain accountable to the people of Nova Scotia,” she wrote in part.

“Non-binding guidelines are not laws. This project needs to be regulated in the legislature, not on Facebook.”

Liberal MLA Becky Druhan voiced her support for Chender’s request for an emergency sitting. In her own letter to Houston, Druhan said Nova Scotians deserve to know what kinds of discussions took place and what commitments were made.

“The need for answers and protections is now even more urgent. In June, you told Nova Scotians that data centres were ‘not a today thing, not even a tomorrow thing.’ Yet last week, you participated in the announcement of a $10 billion project,” she wrote.

When asked during Friday’s announcement if the province would be legislating rules or requirements for data centres, the premier said there are a “number of checks and balances” currently in place.

In June, Canada announced a new AI strategy that includes proposals for the building of “large-scale” data centres .

“There’s an industrial approval process … that process will be ongoing. The environmental approvals, industrial approvals. There’s a very stringent process for industrial entities that set up in the province that doesn’t change,” he said.

“On top of that, the federal government has laid out their guidelines. The province has laid (out) their guidelines. So there’s a number of checks and balances along the way and we will continue to work through that process with the proponents.”

Community advocate, Julissa Stewart, said she and fellow residents in Richmond County feel they weren’t properly consulted and want a pause on the project until regulatory safeguards are in place.

“We need to engage the public in this because it’s impacting the residents. The residents are concerned and they want their voices to be heard, and doing it after the fact is just not acceptable,” she said.

“What happens if the project that gets built is not the project that was advertised? So what happens if they say it won’t use much power and then it uses far more than what was proposed?”

But there are environmental and health concerns about large-scale data centres across Canada, with heated debates and moratoriums imposed in some municipalities .

A rally was held in downtown Halifax the day after the EverWind announcement, with protesters saying the data centre seemed to have been “randomly announced” without any consultation.

“These companies don’t have a lot of information that they’re able to give us. We don’t know what this is going to look like. We already have wells that are drying up in the summertime. I don’t think we can afford to do this,” said protest organizer, Megan Boudreau, ON Saturday.

EverWind said its campus will begin with an initial 95-megawatt phase in late 2027. This will be followed by a 325-megawatt expansion targeted for 2028 subject to regulatory conditions.

At full development, EverWind expects the campus to reach a capacity of 420 megawatts to “meet growing demand for artificial intelligence and digital services.”

Part of the $10 billion investment is $2 billion to advance the company’s onshore wind energy projects.

Experts point out that the data centre will quickly become Nova Scotia Power’s largest industrial customer.

“If we’re going to build a project of this size in a province that’s pretty small, with some of the highest electricity rates in the country, some of the highest rates of energy poverty, with limited groundwater resources … then certainly I think there’s a lot that will still need to be clarified,” said Thomas McNeil, senior energy coordinator at the Ecology Action Centre.

EverWind said its plan is to fund the electricity infrastructure costs attributed to the project so costs aren’t passed on to ratepayers. The company noted the data centre will have “several hundred megawatt hours” of battery storage to support the facility.

But McNeil said independent analysis is needed to determine the impact a project of this size will have on the grid and power bills.

“What we can say for sure is that we’re already struggling with the reliability of our grid, so our ability to keep the lights on in regular conditions,” he said.

“We are, of course, starting to see more extreme weather events, more storms. And so there are questions about the long-term resiliency of the power grid in Nova Scotia as well. So, are we in a position in which we’re going to easily be able to increase demand on the grid at that scale without sacrificing reliability and our ability to keep the power on during a storm?”

Global News reached out to the Premier’s Office for comment.

Meanwhile, the warden of Richmond County, Lois Landry, said town halls are being organized to discuss the data centre.

Landry, who spoke at Friday’s announcement, said she herself only discovered the multi-billion investment involved an AI company and data centre that morning at a technical briefing for reporters.

“So there was really no confirmation about AI because there was no disclosure of the client until the client announced later that day,” she said.

Landry added that there is still no building permit application submitted for the project.

“They can’t apply for a permit without the final design, so I think they’re still working through that. And, the pre-construction work that they’re doing is essentially cutting trees on their own property which they are within their right to do,” she said.

stories.title: Harness racer dies in multi-horse collision at South Okanagan race course
stories.summary: The Desert Park Raceway in Osoyoos said a horse lost its step during a race and fell on the track, colliding with multiple trailing horses and drivers.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A harness racer died on the weekend after a multi-horse collision at a South Okanagan race course.

The Desert Park Raceway in Osoyoos said a horse lost its step during a race and fell on the track, colliding with multiple trailing horses and drivers.

“A tragic accident during the fifth race at Desert Park Raceway (Sunday) resulted in the fatality of driver Scott Knight,” the raceway said in a statement online.

“The #1 horse, Dillon James, driven by Don Ross, broke stride, lost his step and went down on the track. The trailing drivers and horses were unable to avoid the downed horse, leading to a multi-horse collision.”

Knight, 52, was driving the #4 horse, Wits Beach, while Carson Abbott, who was driving the #7 horse, Firm Ringo, was transported to Penticton Hospital for medical treatment.

Another driver was treated on site.

The raceway said that all three horses in the collision survived.

The remainder of Sunday’s live racing program was cancelled, along with Monday’s events.

The schedule will not resume until Monday, Oct. 26, the raceway said in the statement.

“It is an incredibly sad incident, and we are at a loss for words,” Kelly MacMillan, president of the Western Canada Horse Racing Association and operator of Desert Park Raceway, said in a statement.

“Scott was part of our family and I can’t begin to describe how we are feeling. We are all reeling in grief. Our thoughts and prayers go out to Scott’s family and everyone involved.”

stories.title: Strangers send hundreds of birthday cards to 100-year-old senior
stories.summary: Helen Nott can’t help but smile as she marks her 100 birthday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Helen Nott can’t help but smile as she marks her 100 birthday.

“I can’t tell myself that I am a hundred years old. I still think I’m about 60,” said the Huron County centenarian.

To mark her special day, her daughters put out an online call for as many birthday cards as they could hoping to hit 100 by their mom’s birthday on Oct. 13.

They far exceeded that with nearly 300 birthday cards now covering every centimetre of their mother’s room at Huronview Long Term Care Home in Clinton.

“Oh my gosh. It means the world to us that so many people would go out of their way to send the card to somebody that they don’t know, and have never ever met. So yeah, it’s wonderful. People are kind,” said Nott’s daughter, Dianne Bennett.

Cards came from children at a local school, and local friends and family, but the vast majority are from complete strangers from across North America. Some from as far away as Newfoundland and California.

“Many, many thanks people. I don’t know you, but I appreciate your card,” said Nott.

Nott believes the secret to reaching 100 lies in keeping busy. Something she’s been doing her entire life. Even today, working on her most recent craft project.

“I just couldn’t keep my hands quiet. They always had to be doing something. If I wasn’t doing something, there was something wrong with me. The fingers got to keep working,” said Nott.

Now those fingers are kept busy reading the hundreds of birthday cards, adorning her room sent from strangers from around the world.

A tradition that she hopes to repeat, for many more birthdays to come.

“I said, I’m going to go to 106. But I doubt it. We’ll get through 100 first, and then we’ll look after that afterwards,” she said.

“Oh my gosh. It means the world to us that so many people would go out of their way to send the card to somebody that they don’t know, and have never ever met. So yeah, it’s wonderful. People are kind,” said Nott’s daughter, Dianne Bennett.

Cards came from children at a local school, and local friends and family, but the vast majority are from complete strangers from across North America. Some from as far away as Newfoundland and California.
“Many, many thanks people. I don’t know you, but I appreciate your card,” said Nott.
Nott believes the secret to reaching 100 lies in keeping busy. Something she’s been doing her entire life. Even today, working on her most recent craft project.
“I just couldn’t keep my hands quiet. They always had to be doing something. If I wasn’t doing something, there was something wrong with me. The fingers got to keep working,” said Nott.
Now those fingers are kept busy reading the hundreds of birthday cards, adorning her room sent from strangers from around the world.
A tradition that she hopes to repeat, for many more birthdays to come.
“I said, I’m going to go to 106. But I doubt it. We’ll get through 100 first, and then we’ll look after that afterwards,” she said.

stories.title: Digital issues will stay sticking point in U.S. trade talks: former negotiator
stories.summary: Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
While digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the U.S., Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests, Canada’s former chief trade negotiator said Monday.

Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.

“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

Verheul said the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement can only go so far because it allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues,” he said.

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.

He said Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues.

Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.

“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms. The Crtc is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

stories.title: London police investigate south-end shooting, one person in hospital
stories.summary: London police are investigating a shooting in the city’s south end that sent a man to hospital early Sunday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London police are investigating a shooting in the city’s south end that sent a man to hospital early Sunday.

Police responded to a report of gunshots near Fennell Crescent and Ernest Avenue at about 1:30 a.m. on Oct. 18.

While officers were en route, police received a second call about a vehicle collision near Bradley Avenue and Ernest Avenue.

Officers found evidence of a shooting on Fennell Crescent. Shortly after the initial call, an adult male arrived at hospital with injuries sustained in the shooting.

During the investigation, it was determined the vehicle involved in the collision was also connected to the shooting.

Two men and one woman were seen fleeing the vehicle before officers arrived and have not been located, London police said.

Investigators believe the victim was targeted. He remains in hospital in fair condition.

The London Police Service’s Major Crime Section is asking anyone who was in the areas of Fennell Crescent and Ernest Avenue or Ernest Avenue and Bradley Avenue between 1:20 a.m. and 1:40 a.m. and has dashcam footage, surveillance video or information that could help the investigation to contact police.

stories.author: Lia Lévesque The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - Quebec Superior Court has rejected a motion by Amazon filed in connection with the company’s challenge to unionization efforts at its now-shuttered Laval warehouse.

By Lia Lévesque The Canadian Press

A union affiliated with the CSN was certified in May 2024, before the e-commerce giant shuttered all seven of its warehouses in the province.

Amazon had challenged the unionization, arguing the process violated workers’ freedom of association because a secret vote was not held.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Amazon argued that this violated the right of workers to freedom of association, but Quebec’s administrative labour tribunal ruled in October 2024 that the company didn’t have standing to invoke that right on behalf of others.

Amazon challenged the decision on procedural fairness grounds, asserting that it had not been given the opportunity to fully present its position.

Quebec Superior Court, however, has upheld the labour tribunal’s decision and dismissed the challenge.

In Quebec and British Columbia, workers can be automatically certified without a vote if a certain proportion of the workforce signs union cards, a law known as card-check certification. The Laval warehouse was certified through this process.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Feds spent $4.8M on Microsoft licenses that government employees didn't even use: CTF
stories.summary: Records seen by Canadian Taxpayers Federation show 33,213 unused licenses costing $4.8 million and 20,000 more with no dollar figure given.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Government records reviewed by the Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF) show that the federal government spent at least $4.8 million last year on more than 53,000 Microsoft subscriptions and licences that went unused by government employees.

The information came from a question submitted on March 11 in the House of Commons by Adam Chambers, Conservative Member of Parliament for Simcoe North in Ontario. He asked for the total number of Microsoft licenses paid for by the government; their cost; how many users are able to access Microsoft products through them; and how many were unused. The response was tabled in the House on April 27. National Post has reached out to Chambers for more information.

In total, last year the government of Canada spent $4.8 million purchasing 33,213 Microsoft licenses that nobody used. However, it purchased another 19,860 unused licences without disclosing how much it spent on them.

“It’s more than $4.8 million,” Franco Terrazzano, CTF Federal Director, told National Post. “The 4.8 million is just for the 33,000 licenses and subscriptions that nobody uses. But there’s another almost 20,000 subscriptions that nobody uses, that the government just refuses to say how much is spent on those. So not only are they wasting money on subscriptions nobody’s using, they’re also refusing to tell taxpayers how much of our money they’re wasting.”

Assuming a price of $144.52 per licence based on the first group, the additional licenses would have cost another $2.87 million, for a total of $7.67 million.

Terrazzano said it took the CTF some time to pore through the data, which arrived separately from numerous government agencies and departments , but the takeaway is simple.

“It just seems like the most basic step,” he said. “If you’re an individual or a family and you need to find some savings in your own budget, I’m sure many Canadians have done this. Like, where can we cancel some unused subscriptions? So just finding that there are more than 50,000 Microsoft licenses and subscriptions that the government isn’t using, that seems like the first place that they should be cutting back.”

He added: “The government says it’s looking for savings, so cancelling subscriptions that nobody’s using seems like the most basic step to take to find those savings for taxpayers.”

Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada reported the highest number of unused licenses. It purchased 7,443 that nobody used, costing taxpayers $138,500.

Employment and Social Development Canada spent $68,940 on 150 Microsoft Teams Rooms Pro subscriptions last year but did not use any of these subscriptions, and did not respond to the Ctf’s request for an explanation.

The Canada Revenue Agency bought 4,588 unused subscriptions. It did not disclose how much those subscriptions cost, nor did it respond to the Ctf’s request for explanation.

National Defence didn’t disclose what type of subscriptions it purchased. Transport Canada didn’t say how many of its licenses were unused. Neither department responded to Ctf’s request for an explanation.

Statistics Canada spent the most on unused subscriptions, shelling out almost $1.2 million on 2,608 subscriptions that nobody used. It also spent $1,746 on 25 Teams Phone Standard subscriptions for a pilot project but didn’t use any of them.

The CTF said that when it asked the agency why, a Statistics Canada spokesperson told them: “Technical challenges were encountered.”

“Well, ‘technical challenges’ isn’t an excuse to waste taxpayers’ money,” said Terrazzano. “A couple of other agencies, we reached out to and they just refused to to respond back or disclose certain information. So along with the the hefty price tag for all these unused subscriptions, there’s also a lack-of-transparency issue here.”

This is not the first time the CTF has called out governments for overspending on unused software licences. In December 2024, it noted that the city of Toronto had spent $11 million on unused licences over the previous five years, including almost $8 million on Microsoft licenses. Among the findings was news that the city bought 10,000 licenses for Microsoft 365 in 2021 even though its network was only able to handle 6,000 users.

“If bureaucrats blew millions on unused Microsoft 365 licenses, there’s no telling what kind of other wasteful spending taxpayers are on the hook for,” CTF Ontario Director Jay Goldberg said at the time.

The response was tabled in the House on April 27. National Post has reached out to Chambers for more information.
content_blocks.html: The information came from a question submitted on March 11 in the House of Commons by Adam Chambers, Conservative Member of Parliament for Simcoe North in Ontario. He asked for the total number of Microsoft licenses paid for by the government; their cost; how many users are able to access Microsoft products through them; and how many were unused. The response was tabled in the House on April 27. National Post has reached out to Chambers for more information.

content_blocks.text: In total, last year the government of Canada spent $4.8 million purchasing 33,213 Microsoft licenses that nobody used. However, it purchased another 19,860 unused licences without disclosing how much it spent on them.

“It’s more than $4.8 million,” Franco Terrazzano, CTF Federal Director, told National Post. “The 4.8 million is just for the 33,000 licenses and subscriptions that nobody uses. But there’s another almost 20,000 subscriptions that nobody uses, that the government just refuses to say how much is spent on those. So not only are they wasting money on subscriptions nobody’s using, they’re also refusing to tell taxpayers how much of our money they’re wasting.”
Assuming a price of $144.52 per licence based on the first group, the additional licenses would have cost another $2.87 million, for a total of $7.67 million.
Terrazzano said it took the CTF some time to pore through the data, which arrived separately from numerous government agencies and departments , but the takeaway is simple.

“It just seems like the most basic step,” he said. “If you’re an individual or a family and you need to find some savings in your own budget, I’m sure many Canadians have done this. Like, where can we cancel some unused subscriptions? So just finding that there are more than 50,000 Microsoft licenses and subscriptions that the government isn’t using, that seems like the first place that they should be cutting back.”
He added: “The government says it’s looking for savings, so cancelling subscriptions that nobody’s using seems like the most basic step to take to find those savings for taxpayers.”

content_blocks.text: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada reported the highest number of unused licenses. It purchased 7,443 that nobody used, costing taxpayers $138,500.

Employment and Social Development Canada spent $68,940 on 150 Microsoft Teams Rooms Pro subscriptions last year but did not use any of these subscriptions, and did not respond to the Ctf’s request for an explanation.
The Canada Revenue Agency bought 4,588 unused subscriptions. It did not disclose how much those subscriptions cost, nor did it respond to the Ctf’s request for explanation.

National Defence didn’t disclose what type of subscriptions it purchased. Transport Canada didn’t say how many of its licenses were unused. Neither department responded to Ctf’s request for an explanation.

Statistics Canada spent the most on unused subscriptions, shelling out almost $1.2 million on 2,608 subscriptions that nobody used. It also spent $1,746 on 25 Teams Phone Standard subscriptions for a pilot project but didn’t use any of them.
The CTF said that when it asked the agency why, a Statistics Canada spokesperson told them: “Technical challenges were encountered.”

“Well, ‘technical challenges’ isn’t an excuse to waste taxpayers’ money,” said Terrazzano. “A couple of other agencies, we reached out to and they just refused to to respond back or disclose certain information. So along with the the hefty price tag for all these unused subscriptions, there’s also a lack-of-transparency issue here.”

This is not the first time the CTF has called out governments for overspending on unused software licences. In December 2024, it noted that the city of Toronto had spent $11 million on unused licences over the previous five years, including almost $8 million on Microsoft licenses. Among the findings was news that the city bought 10,000 licenses for Microsoft 365 in 2021 even though its network was only able to handle 6,000 users.

stories.title: How are you decorating your lawn this Halloween? Let us know

stories.content:
It’s that time of year again, when ten-foot-tall skeletons come out of storage and take over our neighbourhoods. When Halloween comes along, Canadians everywhere flex their landscaping skills and create the spookiest displays for trick-or-treaters.

Last year, we asked you to share your best Halloween decorations with us , and you didn’t disappoint. From a homemade zombie coral reef to haunted corn fields to skeletons playing pickleball, we highlighted the best of the best that Canadians showed off in 2025.

For a future story, we want to see what you have in store for this Halloween. Have you been preparing your decorations all summer? Do you have a signature lawn design you bring out every year? Are you trying something new?

stories.title: Indigenous Toronto man with a criminal record of 101 break-ins gets time served
stories.summary: Court heard that the man's 16 most recent break-ins cost victims $26,000.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Toronto man with Indigenous heritage who has 101 break-ins on his criminal record won’t serve any more time in jail after his recent sentencing, even though he was arrested with nearly an ounce of fentanyl.

Kieron Tierney — who had already done time for 85 previous break-ins — was sentenced to time served and probation for 16 more break-ins in an Ontario Court of Justice Gladue Court. The same judge handed him a suspended sentence on the drug charge after Tierney pleaded guilty to possession of fentanyl for the purpose of trafficking.

Gladue Courts stem from a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling that said judges should consider the often-tumultuous personal backgrounds of Aboriginal accused and seek alternatives to prison time if possible.

“Kieron Tierney has now accumulated 549 days of pre-trial custody on the present charges,” Justice André Chamberlain wrote in an Oct. 8 decision.

Even if he applied only the standard credit of multiplying days spent in pre-trial custody by 1.5, Tierney would have already served more than two years in custody, said the judge.

“The Crown nevertheless seeks a total sentence of four years’ imprisonment, noting that, unlike his previous matters, the present offences include the more serious charge of possessing nearly one ounce of fentanyl for the purpose of trafficking.”

Chamberlain started his decision with a quote from the Supreme Court of Canada in the 2016 case of Cheyenne Sharma, an Indigenous woman who pleaded guilty to importing two kilograms of cocaine in exchange for $20,000 from her boyfriend — a task she said she carried out to avoid seeing her and her daughter evicted.

“Sentencing law cannot erase this country’s colonial past. Nor can it remove the causes behind an offender’s crime. But it is uniquely positioned to ameliorate — or aggravate — the racial inequalities in our criminal justice system,” the country’s top court said in the Sharma decision.

The Gladue Court heard Tierney’s 16 most recent break-ins cost victims $26,000.

“This represents a substantial financial impact and is a significant aggravating factor,” Chamberlain said, noting Tierney’s lengthy record is “undeniably extensive.”

Tierney began using opioids at 15 and is now addicted to fentanyl, the judge said, noting his “ongoing struggles with depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.”

For 188 days of full or partial lockdown during remand at the Toronto South Detention Centre, Tierney spent “much of his time triple-bunked in a two-person cell, often leaving him to sleep on the floor near the toilet,” his lawyer said, noting his client had a “ serious toothache” that went untreated behind bars for 10 months.

“We keep building jails to lock people up and expand our capacity,” said the judge. “Politicians bemoan the criminal justice system’s catch-and-release policies, yet they can hardly staff the jails we have now. Kieron Tierney pays the price for that failure through substandard care and a total disregard for his medical and cultural needs.”

Tierney, who traces his Indigenous ancestry through his paternal grandmother, was denied “Indigenous cultural and spiritual supports” at Toronto South, Chamberlain said.

“It May be seen that although imprisonment is intended to serve the traditional sentencing goals of separation, deterrence, denunciation and rehabilitation, there is widespread consensus that imprisonment has not been successful in achieving some of these goals,” he said.

“Over-incarceration is a long-standing problem that has been many times publicly acknowledged but never addressed in a systematic manner by Parliament. In recent years, compared to other countries, sentences of imprisonment in Canada have increased at an alarming rate.”

Tierney “has been separated from the community in particularly harsh conditions for over 18 months,” said the judge.

“Given the clear message from the Supreme Court of Canada, ON many fronts, to work to address over-incarceration and give real meaning to the life circumstances of individuals coming before the court, I am not satisfied that a further period of incarceration will serve any benefit to either the community, the victims or Kieron Tierney himself.”

Tierney has completed his GED, withdrawn from opiates, and “regained the support of his family,” Chamberlain said. “He deserves a chance to prove himself and to move forward with his life in a healthier fashion.”

The judge recognized “the risk and harm to the community posed by fentanyl. The risk of overdose and death is significant.”

But Tierney is a fentanyl addict who needs treatment “and support to stay off the streets and stay safe,” Chamberlain said. “He will not find that in the provincial system. He is just as unlikely to access it through the federal system.”

stories.content:
Alberta voters head to the polls Monday to cast ballots in a historic referendum asking them to answer 10 questions, including whether to hold a formal vote on separating from Canada. Question 10 — about separation — will be counted first.

Early results will likely be released sometime after 8 p.m. MT Monday when all polling stations are closed — with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday. Global News will have live coverage over the course of the day and night, and you can read the latest updates here.

stories.title: CFB Wainwright: What we know about the Canadian Armed Forces members killed in the fire
stories.summary: All four were based in Edmonton and serving in the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (3 Ppcli) at the time.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Four members of the Canadian Armed Forces were killed in a grass fire at an army base in Wainwright, Alberta over the weekend.

They were identified as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark. They died during a “fire-related training incident” at 4 p.m. MT (6 p.m. ET) on Oct. 17, according to CAF . Nearly 40 others were injured.

Here’s what we know about them.

All four were based in Edmonton and serving in the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (3 Ppcli) at the time.

Kane Lewis, a friend of Lykkemark, started a GoFundMe for him with permission from the Lykkemark family. It exceeded $15,000 on Monday.

“We went to high school together and played rugby. We both joined the army at the same time and were fortunate enough to be in the same platoon for basic training. That’s where he became more than just a friend; he became a brother,” Lewis wrote in the description of the fundraiser.

“He was always looking out for everyone and always kept himself in check. The staff and all the other soldiers liked him. After basic training, Hayden went on to infantry school, and that’s where we parted ways. However, we still kept in touch.”

The funds will be used to “ease some of the stress caused by this tragedy.”

Lewis’ father shared a Facebook post about Lykkemark and his son, saying they were best friends. The post showed a photo of both of them wearing military gear.

“They walked into the military recruiting office together, went through basic training together in Quebec, and began their journeys in the Canadian Armed Forces side by side,” he wrote.

“Watching my son go through the pain of losing his best friend has been incredibly difficult. These young men had so much ahead of them.”

Wong, 26, originally from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, was described as an “incredible person” in a statement from his family, CityNews reported .

“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces,” the statement said. According to his family, he attended the University of Alberta and received a bachelor of commerce degree. He also had a real estate certificate and a civil-military leadership certificate.

The Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said on Facebook it was “deeply saddened” by his loss.

“Uncommonly strong winds cause the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area,” he said.

The entire battalion is made up of roughly 350 soldiers. The battalion breaks down into different companies, and it was the Charlie Company — made up of 84 soldiers — that was affected by the fire.

“I will be travelling to Alberta and unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the mayoral campaign,” she wrote. “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. stories.title: CFB Wainwright fire highlights long, painful process of burn recovery, specialists say
stories.summary: Toronto - Burn specialists in Toronto and Hamilton say their hospitals are ready to support their Alberta colleagues as they care for dozens of patients injured in Saturday's devastating fire at CFB Wainwright.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland and Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The coming days and weeks will be critical for patients with severe burns from Saturday’s devastating fire at a military base in central Alberta as they face life-threatening risks of infection and a long, painful road to recovery, burn specialists say.

Dr. Vincent Gabriel, medical director at Calgary Firefighters Burn Treatment Centre at Foothills Medical Centre, said Monday that there are several variables in how a patient recovers, including age, the percentage of the body that’s burned and any complications that May arise.

But for serious cases in general, “we would count recovery from burn injury not in days or weeks … but in months and in years, with the hope that a burn survivor returns to their pre-injury role,” Gabriel said, stressing that he was not giving details about any of the specific patients involved in the fire at CFB Wainwright.

“Unfortunately, there are times where there’s permanent impairment, so it’s a long process,” he said.

Four people died in the fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, and 39 were hospitalized, officials said. Nineteen patients were in critical condition as of Sunday.

Gabriel said Alberta is fortunate to have two hospital-based burn centres — one in Calgary and one in Edmonton — and that each had eight beds.

He noted that the burn team can also provide care to patients in other areas of the hospital if the burn unit is full.

Other hospitals, including in Red Deer, Alta., are treating some of the injured.

Burn facilities elsewhere in Canada, including the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto and the burn program at Hamilton Health Sciences Centre, said they are ready to support their Alberta colleagues in any way needed — including receiving patients.

Dr. Alan Rogers, a burn surgeon and intensive care specialist at Sunnybrook, said the hospital could also send temporary skin frozen in its tissue bank.

The skin in the bank comes from the cadavers of people who donated their skin when they died and is used to cover areas where a patient’s skin has burned off, he said.

It’s an interim measure until the patient is stable enough to receive grafts of skin from non-affected parts of their body.

“It acts a bit like your own skin for a while. That’s usually about two weeks, Rogers said. “The reason we can’t use it permanently (is) it gets rejected.”

But because losing their natural skin barrier compromises the patient’s immune system, their body doesn’t reject the donated skin right away.

It also means that burn patients are highly susceptible to infections.

“For those patients who survive long enough to get to the burn centre, infection would be the leading cause of death,” Rogers said.

“The sooner we can restore good quality skin coverage, the risk reduces. But that can take many, many weeks. So, in the interim, they are at risk for infection until their skin is healed.”

Seriously burned patients need to be in isolation rooms to protect them. Those rooms also require temperature control because patients’ ability to regulate their own body heat is compromised.

Another danger to patients is an “overwhelming” inflammatory and hypermetabolic response that extensive burns trigger, which strains the patient’s organs, he said.

Dr. Marc Jeschke, director of the burn program at Hamilton Health Sciences Centre, said burn patients “are the sickest patients in the hospital.”

“It is (a) severe injury that causes significant burden to the patients, to the families, to the loved ones, to everybody,” Jeschke said.

“It is not over like a fracture when you walk out a couple of days later. This is something that will affect their lives forever.”

Rogers said severely burned patients must endure multiple surgeries over weeks or even months — first to remove the burned tissue and cover the areas with the cadaver skin or skin substitutes — then later to get their own skin grafted on.

Those skin graft procedures are among the most painful parts of the process, he said, creating additional wounds that need to heal.

For the most severe patients, burn centres can take a piece of their skin and send it to a lab to grow it, but the process takes about six weeks and is expensive.

The burn team prioritizes areas of the body to be covered, including the face and hands, he said.

They can use techniques such as expanding the skin grafts to cover more exposed areas on other parts of the body. But that’s not something they do on the face or hands because they require more elasticity in the skin.

The length of time a patient will need to stay in hospital is roughly one to two days for every one per cent of the body that is burned, Rogers said.

That means someone with 20 per cent of their body burned would need to be in hospital for three or four weeks, he said.

It’s possible for younger healthy adults to survive burns to 80 per cent of their body, although other injuries, including smoke inhalation, are also factors in survival, he said.

Anesthesiologists, nurses, dietitians, occupational therapist, and mental health professionals all play a critical role in patient recovery, the burn specialists all say.

Burn centres bring in psychologists, psychiatrists and social workers from the time the patient is admitted to help them, along with their loved ones, deal with the enormous toll of treatment, and an often life-changing injury.

Daily wound care, keeping patients moving their limbs, controlling their pain, and making sure they get enough vitamins and nutrition to sustain the long healing process are also essential parts of the process.

“It is almost like running a marathon and even more, not just for two hours,” Jeschke said.

“It is running a marathon for days and weeks and months.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

article_images.alt: Doerkson says B.C. Conservative growth projection of 3.2% 'absolutely doable'

stories.title: Doerkson says B.C. Conservative growth projection of 3.2% 'absolutely doable'
stories.summary: British Columbia's interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson says his party's projection of 3.2 per cent economic growth by 2029 represents about one per cent "more optimism" than the New Democrats had previously budgeted.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives’ projection of 3.2 per cent economic growth by 2029 represents about one per cent “more optimism” than the New Democrats previously budgeted for, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson said.

The Conservatives’ figure is more than 50 per cent higher than a 2.1 per cent average growth forecast in B.C.‘s last budget and considerably higher than recent projections by the Bank of Canada and International Monetary Fund at the national level.

The elevated growth forecast underpins some of the Conservatives’ costed platform, which said it would yield $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years.

Ross Hickey, associate professor of economics at the University of B.C.‘s Okanagan campus, said the Conservatives’ costed platform was “a little bit thin on the details and a little bit thick in terms of wishful thinking.”

But Doerkson told a campaign stop in Maple Ridge, B.C., in the final days before the Oct. 24 provincial election that 3.2 per cent growth was “absolutely doable.”

“I’ve talked to so many industries that are just waiting for a change in government to invest in this province,” he said on Monday.

Doerkson said “fear” under the previous NDP government had deterred investment across industries including natural gas, forestry, mining and agriculture.

The Conservative platform unveiled on Sunday promises to shrink the $14 billion forecast deficit to $10.8 billion, based on gross domestic product growing by 2.5 per cent next year, 2.8 per cent the following year and 3.2 per cent in 2029.

NDP Leader David Eby said the Conservatives were “torquing the numbers” and their platform had “major omissions” in how the party would pay for its plans.

“They failed to cost basic platform commitments like their cut to the (Provincial Sales Tax) on alcohol, which costs almost $300 million,” Eby told a campaign stop in Vancouver on Monday.

“It is all with the aim of minimizing the reality of the cuts they’re going to have to make.”

Hickey said the Conservatives’ calculations assume B.C.‘s economy would grow at a certain pace, but the Conservatives’ proposals are untested, and many factors influencing growth are outside the provincial government’s control.

“Ultimately, what will happen with growth … depends more on what’s happening with the global economy than who our premier is,” he said in an interview.

“Just saying ‘we’re pro-growth’ so then we’re going to grow more? (It) doesn’t add up to me.”

Hickey said the NDP probably had projections and ideas that were “equally silly” and likened campaign promises across the political spectrum to works of fiction.

“What’s missing in a lot of these is the plan of how the actions lead to the outcome.”

The NDP platform projects about $1.8 billion in new revenue by the 2029 fiscal year, thanks to “targeted economic growth” resulting from final investment decisions on major projects, such as the second phase of LNG Canada’s facility in Kitimat.

B.C.‘s election campaign on Monday also turned to Alberta’s referendum on whether the province should remain in Canada or look to separate from the rest of the country.

Eby pointed to three Conservative candidates who had apparently joined a Facebook group linked to the separatist movement in Alberta, while Doerkson said the NDP leader’s attempts to impugn his patriotism were “disgusting.”

Doerkson said the B.C. Conservatives stand for a strong and united Canada, though he didn’t directly answer a question about potential separatist views in his party.

The Conservative platform promises to save $7 billion over four years by cutting annual contingency funding from $5 billion to $3 billion each year. They would do so by shifting contingency expenses to ministerial budgets, but they have not provided details on whether and how the ministries would balance their books as a result.

NDP candidate Adrian Dix, who has led B.C.‘s health and energy ministries, said contingencies funding has mostly been used to pay for “health-care caseload pressures and unavoidable expenses” such as the cost of fighting wildfires.

“Doerkson’s plan starts with a $1 billion cut for the remainder of this year,” he said during a campaign news conference on Monday. “That means cuts this year to surgeries, to primary care clinics, and reduced services in hospitals.”

Doerkson, meanwhile, said there had been “misrepresentations” about his party’s plans, and the Conservatives would “fully fund health care.”

“We are looking at attrition though, and I think that shows in our plan with respect to the public service sector for sure,” he said.

— With files from Chuck Chiang and Nono Shen

stories.title: Three people confirmed dead after Highway 401 crash near London
stories.summary: Elgin County OPP officers confirm three people have died after a crash on Highway 401 near London.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Elgin County OPP officers confirm three people have died after a crash on Highway 401 near London .

The fatal crash happened on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 4:03 p.m. in the Township of Southwold.

OPP, Medavie EMS Elgin and local fire services responded to the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Mill Road for a report of a multi-vehicle collision.

Police say initial information indicated traffic had slowed due to an earlier collision in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Colonel Talbot Road in Middlesex County.

Investigators have determined that there were three individuals inside a sedan that was struck from behind by the commercial vehicle, after traffic had slowed due to an earlier collision.

The identities of the three victims have not been confirmed.

The investigation is continuing, and updates will be provided as they become available.

Police encourage anyone with information or dashcam footage that captured the vehicles involved in this collision to contact the OPP at 1-888-310-1122.
