stories.title: Everything confirmed so far about CFB Wainwright fire and how it unfolded
stories.summary: At least four members of the Canadian Armed Forces have died and dozens are injured after a scheduled training exercise on Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
At least four members of the Canadian Armed Forces have died and dozens are injured after a scheduled training exercise on Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta.

Officials say a grass fire quickly overwhelmed soldiers in the area as a sudden change in wind direction and strength expanded the fire over a large area. Investigators say it could be weeks before details of how the fire started can be determined.

On Monday in the House of Commons, the victims were remembered during a moment of silence before party leaders expressed their condolences for those who died and were injured.

Prime Minister Mark Carney began the remarks, saying the House was meeting “united in grief.”

“This loss touches every corner of our nation,” he said.

This is what has been confirmed so far about what happened at CFB Wainwright over the weekend, with all times Alberta local (Mountain) time.

A unit of military personnel at CFB Wainwright, which is about 200 kilometres from Edmonton, were conducting a planned training exercise near a grassy area on the afternoon of Oct. 17 when the fire ignited and spread rapidly, according to officials.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, gave details of what transpired at a press conference on Oct. 18, and said 84 members of 3rd Battalion of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were training with live munitions in the area.

Rutland said most of the soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were doing simulations of an attack on enemies, which was in preparation for potential deployment overseas, including in Latvia and other regions.

A fire ignited within the training area of CFB Wainwright at approximately 4:00 p.m. (local time) on Oct. 17, 2026, Rutland said.

Training leaders were aware of a nearby grass fire that had ignited about a kilometre from where soldiers were positioned, but the fire was not immediately determined to be a threat.

A preliminary investigation suggests a munition from the live training exercise May have sparked a fast-moving grass fire, which caused an explosion, according to multiple separate military sources verified by Global News on Oct. 17.

Rutland said the fire did not start within the training area, and the cause of the fire was still being investigated. He added that despite reports of explosions in the area, officials do not believe the fire was the result of any oil and gas infrastructure “nor any outside interference.”

As of publication, no further details on how the fire started have been revealed.

Rutland said the fire was about a kilometre away from personnel before the wind suddenly shifted.

Earlier on Saturday, Environment Canada had issued a high-wind warning for Alberta. Gusts of up to 100 km/h in some parts of the province tipped over semi-trailer trucks and toppled trees.

“Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area,” said Rutland.

“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds,” he later added.

Rutland said his commander on the ground confirmed in the span of 30 seconds to a minute “they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them.”

Dozens of emergency crews, including those from the Canadian Armed Forces and the town of Wainwright, were immediately called to help bring the fire under control.

Health officials and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith would later confirm at a press conference on Oct. 18 that 30 emergency units, including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft, were deployed directly into Wainwright on Oct. 17. Saskatchewan also provided air ambulance support, Smith added.

Acute Care Alberta issued a statement as responders arrived on the scene at CFB Wainwright.

“Emergency Health Services – Alberta (EHS – Alberta) is on scene, and supporting care and transport related to an incident at CFB Wainwright. We appreciate the dedication and expertise of all first responders. All further questions can be redirected to the Government of Canada, at this time.”

Shortly after emergency crews were called to the scene, health agencies and local medical teams across Alberta were notified to prepare resources, personnel and capacity for an influx of patients.

By 6:00 p.m. on Oct. 17, health agencies were on a coordinating call and stood up a command centre, according to Dr. Sayeh Zielke, CEO of Acute Care Alberta, speaking at a press conference on Oct. 18.

Hospitals declared a Code Orange, which is in the event of a mass casualty incident, Zielke said, and helps prepare for a rapid influx of patients by clearing the decks, finding staff and freeing up beds as necessary. It also puts on hold some elective surgeries and other procedures to free up specialists like anesthesiologists, she added.

Acute Care Alberta issued an updated statement once the Code Orange was declared, and advised Albertans to “use emergency care resources wisely.”

“Significant care resources are required to support this response, both from EHS-Alberta and in Edmonton-area emergency departments. To meet these immediate care needs, while addressing routine demand for emergency care, Code Orange has been activated at several acute care facilities across Alberta,” the statement said.

At around 7:30 p.m. Mountain time on Saturday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced from Ottawa that there were multiple fatalities and many more were injured.

“I want to begin by addressing the very tragic events that have occurred today at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” said McGuinty.

“The Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence, partners across the federal Government, including public safety, are working with the government of Alberta and municipal governments to mobilize all necessary support and working through the details of what actually occurred.”

McGuinty stressed at the time that because it was an active situation, few other details could be shared.

“Our public safety officials are coordinating. At this time the first responders and local authorities are doing their important work so we will keep Canadians informed as details are made available.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post on Sunday at 9:45 a.m. that Canadian flags will be flown at half-mast at federal buildings across the country.

He said Canada stands with the service members at CFB Wainwright and their families.

He added that the next of kin of those who lost their lives have been notified.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost,” Carney said.

“Our hearts go with and we are praying for the wounded, and we stand in solidarity and compassion for the families, the friends, and the colleagues of all those affected by this tragedy.”

Later on Sunday, at about 1:35 p.m., Acute Care Alberta said in a statement that hospitals had lifted the Code Orange declared on Saturday night.

Acute Care Alberta said that patients were transferred from healthcare centre in Wainwright to the University of Alberta and Royal Alexandra hospitals in Edmonton, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

“It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta,” the statement said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, speaking to reporters in Wainwright, said he was hearing about incredible acts of bravery as a devastating fire ripped through the nearby military base.

He said some soldiers ran toward the danger to help and are now paying the price, fighting for their lives in hospital.

He asked everyone to pray for Wainwright.

Poilievre represents the area as part of the Battle River—Crowfoot riding.

Late Sunday, at about 5:00 p.m. local time, the Department of National Defence gave a press conference, where Rutland, Smith and McGuinty provided further details on what transpired.

Smith said that 39 patients were being cared for in hospital, including 19 in critical condition. She added that all patients have been accounted for, and no other patients were awaiting transport.

“We know that the road ahead, especially for those who are suffering from severe burn injuries, will be long requiring weeks and months of intensive and specialized care,” said Smith.

The victims of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta were remembered during a moment of silence in the House of Commons before party leaders expressed their condolences for those who died and were injured.

Carney began the remarks, saying the House was meeting “united in grief.”

The four victims were Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Poilievre said he remembered meeting Goulding when celebrating Canada Day at the base.

“I remembered meeting him. Strong, handsome, polite, a real gentleman,” Poilievre said. “His mother described him as: ‘an exceptional athlete, a natural leader, and a passionate young man who always accomplished his goals. He was the light of my life.’“

He went on to pay tribute to Farrell, Wong and Lykkemark, quoting words made by their family members in social media posts.

Poilievre also commended those who responded, including other soldiers and firefighters.

– with files from Global News’ Sean Prevail, Karen Bartko, Jeff Semple and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Murder parole rules ‘unconstitutional’, B.C. judge rules
stories.summary: Prescribing 25 years of parole ineligibility infringes upon Charter guarantees against cruel and unusual punishment, judge says
stories.author: Darryl Greer
stories.content:
A British Columbia Supreme Court judge says a section of the Criminal Code restricting multiple murderers from applying for early parole under the so-called “faint-hope” clause is unconstitutional.

Justice Brenda Brown ruled on Monday that the section of the code prescribing 25 years of parole ineligibility infringes upon the Charter of Rights and Freedoms’ guarantees against cruel and unusual punishment.

Her decision has delayed sentencing again for Abhijeet Singh, Gurkaran Singh, and Khushveer Toor, who were found guilty of first-degree murder in May for the home-invasion killings of Arnold and Joanne De Jong.

The judge did not give reasons for the decision on Monday, but lawyers will be back in court for another argument that will involve whether the infringement can be justified under Section 1 of the Charter.

The De Jong family said outside court that they were frustrated and disappointed over the sentencing delay, believing the killers would hear their ultimate sentence on Monday, more than four years after the slayings.

The trial heard that Arnold De Jong, 77, died by asphyxiation, with his entire head and face wrapped in duct tape, while 76-year-old Joanne De Jong was bludgeoned and had her throat slashed.

The De Jong’s daughters, Heather Hoogland, Sandra Barthel and Kimberley Coleman were at the hearing on Monday with their spouses, along with dozens of other supporters of the family.

“I think we’re just shocked. (It) just took the wind out of our sails. I don’t think it makes sense to us,” Barthel said outside court after the hearing. “How can people murder two people and then apply for reduced sentence? It’s mind boggling, it’s infuriating, and it just reiterates that we’re the only ones with a life sentence here.”

Hoogland said the delay in the sentencing was “like a gut punch.”

Coleman said it had been frustrating dealing with years of delays in the trial of the three men.

“It would certainly be nice to have the sentencing and move on from the court proceedings,” she said.

“We remain fighters and we will still fight for our parents’ name and justice that is due for this crime.”

Helen Leusink, Joanne De Jong’s sister, said after the hearing that the family and its supporters were expecting the men to be sentenced, and the decision “just prolongs the fact that we wait and we wait, and we think that this should come to a conclusion, and it doesn’t seem to happen.”

“It doesn’t change the fact that this has gone on for many, many years and it’s time we come to the conclusion and it just makes me more and more disappointed in our justice system and how it operates,” Leusink said outside the courthouse.

The three men had done work around the De Jong’s home in the months before the killings, and their lawyers argued it was a “botched robbery” that led to the murders.

Singh, Singh and Toor, the court heard, stole cheques, credit cards, and a power washer from the home, paying off cellphone bills and cashing cheques into their own bank accounts shortly after murdering the couple.

The judge found the men knew they’d be recognized by the De Jongs, and planned to kill them to ensure the success of the home invasion.

“Because of this, they could not leave the De Jongs alive at the conclusion of the home invasion,” Brown wrote in her conviction judgment.

“Even if the invaders were masked, police would likely be able to learn of their identity in short order after asking the De Jongs about recent activity at their house. Again, they would be arrested. If the De Jongs were left alive, the time to use any stolen property May be limited and police investigation May start sooner.”

A first-degree murder conviction carries a life sentence without chance of parole for 25 years, but lawyers for the trio wanted their clients to be able to ask for the right for early parole, through the faint-hope clause in the Criminal Code.

The section of the code ruled unconstitutional by Brown seeks to exclude multiple murderers from the faint-hope clause allowing some killers to seek judicial review of their parole ineligibility period once they have served more than 15 years.

paragraphs: A British Columbia Supreme Court judge says a section of the Criminal Code restricting multiple murderers from applying for early parole under the so-called “faint-hope” clause is unconstitutional.

Justice Brenda Brown ruled on Monday that the section of the code prescribing 25 years of parole ineligibility infringes upon the Charter of Rights and Freedoms’ guarantees against cruel and unusual punishment.

Her decision has delayed sentencing again for Abhijeet Singh, Gurkaran Singh, and Khushveer Toor, who were found guilty of first-degree murder in May for the home-invasion killings of Arnold and Joanne De Jong.

The judge did not give reasons for the decision on Monday, but lawyers will be back in court for another argument that will involve whether the infringement can be justified under Section 1 of the Charter.

The De Jong family said outside court that they were frustrated and disappointed over the sentencing delay, believing the killers would hear their ultimate sentence on Monday, more than four years after the slayings.
The trial heard that Arnold De Jong, 77, died by asphyxiation, with his entire head and face wrapped in duct tape, while 76-year-old Joanne De Jong was bludgeoned and had her throat slashed.
The De Jong’s daughters, Heather Hoogland, Sandra Barthel and Kimberley Coleman were at the hearing on Monday with their spouses, along with dozens of other supporters of the family.

“I think we’re just shocked. (It) just took the wind out of our sails. I don’t think it makes sense to us,” Barthel said outside court after the hearing. “How can people murder two people and then apply for reduced sentence? It’s mind boggling, it’s infuriating, and it just reiterates that we’re the only ones with a life sentence here.”
Hoogland said the delay in the sentencing was “like a gut punch.”
Coleman said it had been frustrating dealing with years of delays in the trial of the three men.
“It would certainly be nice to have the sentencing and move on from the court proceedings,” she said.
“We remain fighters and we will still fight for our parents’ name and justice that is due for this crime.”

Helen Leusink, Joanne De Jong’s sister, said after the hearing that the family and its supporters were expecting the men to be sentenced, and the decision “just prolongs the fact that we wait and we wait, and we think that this should come to a conclusion, and it doesn’t seem to happen.”

“It doesn’t change the fact that this has gone on for many, many years and it’s time we come to the conclusion and it just makes me more and more disappointed in our justice system and how it operates,” Leusink said outside the courthouse.
The three men had done work around the De Jong’s home in the months before the killings, and their lawyers argued it was a “botched robbery” that led to the murders.

Singh, Singh and Toor, the court heard, stole cheques, credit cards, and a power washer from the home, paying off cellphone bills and cashing cheques into their own bank accounts shortly after murdering the couple.
The judge found the men knew they’d be recognized by the De Jongs, and planned to kill them to ensure the success of the home invasion.
“Because of this, they could not leave the De Jongs alive at the conclusion of the home invasion,” Brown wrote in her conviction judgment.

“Even if the invaders were masked, police would likely be able to learn of their identity in short order after asking the De Jongs about recent activity at their house. Again, they would be arrested. stories.title: Union calls out Carney government over cuts to translation bureau
stories.summary: A federal union is speaking out against cuts to the federal translation bureau and is accusing the Carney government of hypocrisy as Ottawa defends French language standards in trade talks with the U.S.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A federal union is speaking out against cuts to the federal translation bureau and is accusing the Carney government of hypocrisy as Ottawa defends French language standards in trade talks with the U.S.

The translation bureau is a federal government service under Public Services and Procurement Canada that provides translation and interpretation services to departments and private clients.

A government document containing highlights of the translation bureau’s business plan for 2025 to 2030 says the bureau plans to drop 339 employees through natural attrition over five years to ensure its financial viability.

Attrition is the gradual reduction of positions through retirements and resignations.

The document says the plan reflects “an overall drop” in demand for traditional translation services.

It also says departments are turning to online translation services “via free internet tools” or are “investing on their own to deploy translation tools powered by artificial intelligence.”

Mario Morneau, spokesperson for Public Services and Procurement Canada, said in an email the plan is to accomplish the reduction through attrition and because it’s based on client demand, the final number could vary.

“This attrition is expected to occur across a range of occupational groups, including translation, administrative and management positions,” he said.

The Canadian Association of Professional Employees is condemning the plan and says the decision puts Canada’s official languages at risk.

The union said more than 90 per cent of translations in the federal government are from English to French and that when the quality of translation declines, it is francophones who feel the impact.

“The result is a two-tier system by degrading the language services francophones depend on to access public services and Canada’s democratic institutions in their own language,” said the union.

In a media conference, Carney accused U.S. negotiators of trying to limit Canada’s ability to negotiate other trade deals, restrict its protections for language and culture and reduce tariffs for cars but not trucks.

Carney cited both the visibility of Canadian content on streaming services and French-language product labelling when he described the collapse of the trade talks. Four days later, a government official, who refused to be quoted on the record, told The Canadian Press that French labels were never part of the conversation.

LeBlanc then told Radio-Canada that while the U.S. had identified French-language labels as a trade irritant in the past, the issue on the table just before the trade talks ended was online discoverability.

Those rules, which are currently under development at the Crtc, would ensure Canadian and French-language content is available and visible on online streaming platforms.

U.S. representatives have maintained they don’t have an issue with French language protections.

Bloc Québécois MP Yves Perron said in the House of Commons last month that “we cannot use French as a shield against Donald Trump and then turn around and regard it as an unnecessary expense that needs to be cut.”

“While being a useful tool, artificial intelligence can never replace human judgment and a nuanced understanding of human language,” he said. “We will not attract the next generation of talent by allowing people’s working conditions to deteriorate. A strong internal capacity within the public service is essential to preserving French.”

Kelly Burke, Canada’s official languages commissioner, said in a statement that the government must ensure the substantive equality of Canada’s two official languages in federal services and communications.

“This means, among other things, that translation and interpretation services must meet the highest standards of quality in order to respect the language rights of all Canadians,” said Burke.

The Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages’ 2025-2026 annual report said federal institutions must ensure that their language obligations and their employees’ language rights are respected and taken into account during any budget reduction exercises.

“I will continue to monitor this situation closely,” said Burke.

Burke added that while artificial intelligence can be useful for translation and interpretation when deployed properly, a qualified professional needs to be involved to avoid errors.

Morneau said the translation bureau will adjust its plans if demand for translation services increases.

“The Bureau remains fully committed to providing quality linguistic services in both official languages, tailored to the needs of our clients, budgetary realities and the expectations of Canadians,” he said. “It will maintain the in-house capacity required to fulfil the demand for high-quality translations while continuing to draw on the expertise of Canada’s language industry when needed.”

-With files from Anja Karadeglija

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Air Canada to charge $30 if you call them to book your flight
stories.summary: Passengers looking to avoid the new charge, which is not refundable, can avoid the phone and book online or through the airline's app.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Air Canada has just added a new fee, this one to tickets booked through the airline’s telephone call centre. Beginning Oct. 15, all new bookings made by calling the airline carry a $30 non-refundable fee. The charge is per passenger, so booking flight for a family of four would cost $120.

The fee does not apply if the booking is made through another method.

“Air Canada’s website and mobile app make it easy to book and manage your travel,” the airline said in announcing the change . “Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support.”

It also noted that the new fee “aligns with the approach currently in place for Aeroplan flight reward bookings,” meaning Aeroplan reward customers were already paying it. National Post has reached out to Air Canada to find how long this has been the case, and for more information.

“If you’d still prefer to book by phone, our Contact Centre agents remain available to provide expert guidance and personalized support when you need assistance, including in situations that May require additional care or cannot be completed through our self-service options,” the airline said.

It’s also worth noting that the fee does not apply if a previously booked flight (whether booked by phone, online or through the app) is affected by a delay, cancellation or another disruption, and you phone for assistance or to rebook.

“Contact Centre agents can continue to help with existing reservations, travel disruptions and other questions about your journey,” the airline said, adding: “You can also manage many disruption-related needs through Air Canada’s digital self-service options, where you can accept a new flight, change your itinerary or request a refund without needing to call.”

A response to a call to the airline’s customer service centre at 1-888-247-2262 on Monday morning included a mention of the $30 fee and a warning that wait times May exceed an hour, although there is also an option to have an agent call you back.

The airline also notes that customers who require specialized care and support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt from the new fee.

Last April, Air Canada amended its baggage fees on international routes to $90 for the first checked bag in the lowest economy fare, and $120 for the second. This was an increase from $70 for the first bag and between $100 to $115 for the second. Its economy standard and flex rates include one free checked bag. The change came amid soaring fuel prices after the U.S.-led attacks on Iran.

Similar changes the following month applied to domestic, U.S. and Caribbean flights, but with a cost of $45 for the first checked bag and $60 for the second, up from $35 and $50.

content_blocks.text: Air Canada has just added a new fee, this one to tickets booked through the airline’s telephone call centre. Beginning Oct. 15, all new bookings made by calling the airline carry a $30 non-refundable fee. The charge is per passenger, so booking flight for a family of four would cost $120.
The fee does not apply if the booking is made through another method.

“Air Canada’s website and mobile app make it easy to book and manage your travel,” the airline said in announcing the change . “Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support.”
content_blocks.html: “Air Canada’s website and mobile app make it easy to book and manage your travel,” the airline said in announcing the change. “Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support.”

content_blocks.text: It also noted that the new fee “aligns with the approach currently in place for Aeroplan flight reward bookings,” meaning Aeroplan reward customers were already paying it. National Post has reached out to Air Canada to find how long this has been the case, and for more information.

“If you’d still prefer to book by phone, our Contact Centre agents remain available to provide expert guidance and personalized support when you need assistance, including in situations that May require additional care or cannot be completed through our self-service options,” the airline said.

It’s also worth noting that the fee does not apply if a previously booked flight (whether booked by phone, online or through the app) is affected by a delay, cancellation or another disruption, and you phone for assistance or to rebook.

“Contact Centre agents can continue to help with existing reservations, travel disruptions and other questions about your journey,” the airline said, adding: “You can also manage many disruption-related needs through Air Canada’s digital self-service options, where you can accept a new flight, change your itinerary or request a refund without needing to call.”

A response to a call to the airline’s customer service centre at 1-888-247-2262 on Monday morning included a mention of the $30 fee and a warning that wait times May exceed an hour, although there is also an option to have an agent call you back.
The airline also notes that customers who require specialized care and support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt from the new fee.

Last April, Air Canada amended its baggage fees on international routes to $90 for the first checked bag in the lowest economy fare, and $120 for the second. This was an increase from $70 for the first bag and between $100 to $115 for the second. Its economy standard and flex rates include one free checked bag. The change came amid soaring fuel prices after the U.S.-led attacks on Iran.

stories.title: Expert explainer: What is the U.S. Congress and what will be decided in the midterms?
stories.summary: Political science professor Matthew Lebo explains the U.S. midterm elections and what's at stake for the House and Senate.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
On Nov. 3, American voters will decide who controls the House of Representatives and the Senate in a swath of midterm elections.

Political science professor Matthew Lebo, an expert in American politics, spoke to Western News to explain what’s being decided in the midterm elections and why they are so important.

Matthew Lebo (ML): In the history of polling in the United States there has never been a midterm election with a president as unpopular as Donald Trump is now. This could mean a huge swing toward the Democrats and a very different second half to Trump’s second term in office.

The closest comparator would be the 2006 midterm elections during George W. Bush’s second term. The Iraq War was going badly, the economy was not great, the federal government was heavily criticized for its response to Hurricane Katrina. So, you saw a big swing toward the Democrats – they took over the House, they took over the Senate and that was all a prelude to a decisive Democratic win in the 2008 presidential election.

The experience in 2006 tells us what can happen with an unpopular president, and Trump is even less popular now than Bush was then. Polls suggest Republican senators will lose in Ohio, Iowa, Texas, Alaska, maybe even Kansas and Nebraska – these are very Republican states. We can be a little skeptical about polls, I’m not buying them 100 per cent, but the numbers now are staggeringly bad for Republicans.

ML: Congress is the legislative branch of the federal government. It has two chambers – the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Senate, as a body, is as powerful as the House of Representatives, unlike in Canada where the Senate is not as powerful as the House of Commons.

The U.S. Congress is the branch that makes legislation and sits parallel to the executive branch (the president, vice president and cabinet). The branches are supposed to check each other’s powers. The House and the Senate have some different areas of responsibility, but both must agree for a bill to pass.

ML: The party that holds the majority in either body sets the agenda. Bills can only be considered when the majority party allows it. All the committees are chaired by a member of the majority party. Appointments to the Cabinet and Supreme Court must be confirmed by a majority of members in the Senate. When the president is of a different party than either or both majorities in Congress, then government becomes more confrontational.

Especially with Donald Trump, if there are Democratic majorities in the House and in the Senate, then it will likely become more than confrontational. Government would come to a standstill in many respects. There wouldn’t be any legislation that’s passed – for a bill to become law it must be passed by the House and the Senate and then signed by the president. If the president doesn’t sign it, it only becomes law if two-thirds of the House and Senate pass it.

There probably wouldn’t be confirmations of executive appointments like to the Cabinet or the courts and there would likely be open investigations of Donald Trump and his people conducted by Congress.

ML: In Canada, we have a British-style system, also called a Westminster or parliamentary system. The prime minister is a member of the majority party in the House of Commons and so, when the majority in the House of Commons puts a bill forward, it only does so knowing the majority party, including the prime minister, supports it. You can’t have divided government in Canada. You can have a minority government, but it is not possible for the largest party in the House of Commons to be different than the prime minister’s party. In the U.S. however, the majority party in the House and Senate can be different than the president’s own party.

ML: When the Constitution was written, four years was considered an appropriate length of time for a president to be elected, but the Framers of the Constitution wanted members of the House to be more responsive to the people, with faster turnover of representatives. So, those 435 seats in the House of Representatives are elected every two years.

Senators were not originally elected, they were appointed by state legislatures. It was only about 110 years ago that senators became elected. One-third are replaced every two years, so those elections are staggered. The Senate has 100 members (two per state) and this year, there are 35 elections to the Senate.

ML: Most importantly, they’ll decide who holds the majority in the House and the Senate.

For the last two years, there’s been a Republican House majority and a Republican Senate majority and so when President Donald Trump has made unconstitutionaldecisions, he has not had Congress pushing back on him.

If Democrats win majorities in both the House and the Senate, there will be much more oversight of the president. There will likely be hearings and subpoenas. Attempts to remove President Trump through the impeachment process seem likely as well.

Tariff policy is up to Congress, not the president. The Supreme Court has told Trump his Liberation Day tariffs were unconstitutional, but Trump implemented them anyway, because he knows Congress isn’t going to push back and it will take the Supreme Court a year to get around to the case. Democrats in the House and Senate could assert their authority to try ending tariffs much more quickly – they May even be able to get some Republicans on board as well.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: B.C. judge says parole rules for murderers unconstitutional
stories.summary: Abbotsford British Columbia - A British Columbia Supreme Court judge says a section of the Criminal Code on parole eligibility for multiple murderers is unconstitutional, delaying sentencing of three men convicted of killing an Abbotsford, B.C., couple in 2022.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Abbotsford British Columbia - A British Columbia Supreme Court judge says a portion of the Criminal Code restricting multiple murderers from applying for early parole under the so-called “faint-hope” clause is in breach of a section of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Justice Brenda Brown ruled on Monday that the section of the code prescribing 25 years of parole ineligibility infringes upon Charter guarantees against cruel and unusual punishment.

Her decision has delayed sentencing again for Abhijeet Singh, Gurkaran Singh, and Khushveer Toor, who were found guilty of first-degree murder in May for the home-invasion killings of Arnold and Joanne De Jong.

The judge did not give reasons for the decision on Monday, but lawyers will be back in court for another argument that will involve whether the infringement can be justified under Section 1 of the Charter.

The De Jong family said outside court that they were frustrated and disappointed over the sentencing delay, believing the killers would hear their ultimate sentence on Monday, more than four years after the slayings.

The trial heard that Arnold De Jong, 77, died by asphyxiation, with his entire head and face wrapped in duct tape, while 76-year-old Joanne De Jong was bludgeoned and had her throat slashed.

The De Jong’s daughters, Heather Hoogland, Sandra Barthel and Kimberley Coleman were at the hearing on Monday with their spouses, along with dozens of other supporters of the family.

“I think we’re just shocked. (It) just took the wind out of our sails. I don’t think it makes sense to us,” Barthel said outside court after the hearing. “How can people murder two people and then apply for reduced sentence? It’s mind boggling, it’s infuriating, and it just reiterates that we’re the only ones with a life sentence here.”

Hoogland said the delay in the sentencing was “like a gut punch.”

Coleman said it had been frustrating dealing with years of delays in the trial of the three men.

“It would certainly be nice to have the sentencing and move on from the court proceedings,” she said.

“We remain fighters and we will still fight for our parents’ name and justice that is due for this crime.”

Helen Leusink, Joanne De Jong’s sister, said after the hearing that the family and its supporters were expecting the men to be sentenced, and the decision “just prolongs the fact that we wait and we wait, and we think that this should come to a conclusion, and it doesn’t seem to happen.”

“It doesn’t change the fact that this has gone on for many, many years and it’s time we come to the conclusion and it just makes me more and more disappointed in our justice system and how it operates,” Leusink said outside the courthouse.

The three men had done work around the De Jong’s home in the months before the killings, and their lawyers argued it was a “botched robbery” that led to the murders.

Singh, Singh and Toor, the court heard, stole cheques, credit cards, and a power washer from the home, paying off cellphone bills and cashing cheques into their own bank accounts shortly after murdering the couple.

The judge found the men knew they’d be recognized by the De Jongs, and planned to kill them to ensure the success of the home invasion.

“Because of this, they could not leave the De Jongs alive at the conclusion of the home invasion,” Brown wrote in her conviction judgment.

“Even if the invaders were masked, police would likely be able to learn of their identity in short order after asking the De Jongs about recent activity at their house. Again, they would be arrested. If the De Jongs were left alive, the time to use any stolen property May be limited and police investigation May start sooner.”

A first-degree murder conviction carries a life sentence without chance of parole for 25 years, but lawyers for the trio wanted their clients to be able to ask for the right for early parole, through the faint-hope clause in the Criminal Code.

The part of the code ruled in breach of section 12 of the Charter by Brown seeks to exclude multiple murderers from the faint-hope clause allowing some killers to seek judicial review of their parole ineligibility period once they have served more than 15 years.

Further arguments in the case have now been scheduled for November, and the sentencing of the men now set for February 2027.

The federal government under former prime minister Stephen Harper abolished the faint hope rule for multiple murderers sentenced after December 2011.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa has a case for suing Cleveland-Cliffs. But what does it hope to achieve?
stories.summary: Stelco owner’s CEO has taken credit for convincing Trump to increase tariffs on imports of U.S. steel
stories.author: Nicolas Lamp
stories.content:
Nicolas Lamp is an associate professor at the faculty of law at Queen’s University.

At first glance, Cleveland-Cliffs’s layoffs at Stelco are clearly in violation of an undertaking made to Ottawa when it bought the Hamilton steelmaker in 2024. However, the company points out that the interpretative guidelines relating to the Investment Canada Act stipulate that “where inability to fulfill a commitment is clearly the result of factors beyond the control of the investor, the investor will not be held accountable.”

Cleveland-Cliffs argues that it cannot comply with its undertaking because of the tariffs on Canadian steel imports imposed by the Trump administration, which necessitated the layoffs. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has countered that Cleveland-Cliffs has backed the tariffs, and therefore “they cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure.” It appears increasingly likely that the government will take the company to court.

The CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs does not deny that he has supported the tariffs and continues to do so. On Monday, Lourenco Goncalves doubled down on this stance.

A key question that a court would have to decide is whether Cleveland-Cliffs’s support for the tariffs means that the tariffs are no longer a “factor beyond the control of the investor” for the purposes of the Investment Canada Act. It appears that is likely.

This relevant provision has never been interpreted by a court, but we can reason by analogy from the law of contract (in previous litigation between the Government of Canada and U.S. Steel, then the owner of Stelco, the Federal Court noted that both parties saw undertakings under the Investment Canada Act as “akin” to a contract). In contract law, a party can only claim that a contract was “frustrated” by a supervening event if that event occurred “without the fault of either party.” The question thus becomes: Does Cleveland-Cliffs’s support for the tariffs mean that the tariffs are its “fault”?

If Cleveland-Cliffs had merely expressed support for tariffs that would have been imposed anyway, the government’s case would be weak. However, Mr. Goncalves went much further: He has taken credit for convincing President Donald Trump to increase the U.S. tariffs on steel from 25 per cent to 50 per cent, stating: “I’m very happy with 50 per cent. … I have my fingerprints on that 50 per cent. In other words, I influenced that.”

That statement is as much of a smoking gun as the Canadian government could hope to find in order to convince a court that the tariffs were, at least in part, the “fault” of Cleveland-Cliffs and hence not “beyond the control of the investor.”

But even though the Government of Canada has a strong substantive case, the question remains: What can it hope to achieve?

Ms. Joly has consistently drawn attention to three types of remedies that the Investment Canada Act provides: monetary penalties, a court order directing compliance and a court order for divestiture.

The simplest remedy would be monetary penalties, which can reach up to $10,000 a day. However, what would be the purpose of seeking such penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs? The only conceivable purposes – apart perhaps from deterring other companies from breaching their commitments – would be to obtain leverage against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially force it to agree to a sale of Stelco. It appears extremely unlikely that penalties would convince the company to hire back the workers, especially since the penalties would further weaken its financial position.

The government could also try to get a “court order directing compliance” – essentially, a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to hire back the workers. However, it is extremely unlikely that a court would grant such an order. Again, we can look to contract law for guidance. Courts will not order the “specific performance” of a contract where doing so would require continuing supervision by the court, which would be the case if a court ordered Stelco to rehire the workers. It is inconceivable that a court would order Cleveland-Cliffs to reinstate hundreds of workers.

Finally, the government could seek a court order for divestiture: a forced sale of the company. Such an order could open the door to government ownership of the company, should no private buyer step up, which is something the government May well want to consider.

However, if the government’s ultimate goal is to nationalize the company, there would be much quicker ways to achieve it than court proceedings: Namely, the government could negotiate for the sale of the company or follow the British example and expropriate it via legislation (with compensation).

Both would be quicker than lengthy court proceedings and would allow the new management that the government would put in place to rehire the workers before the company’s customers move on.

stories.title: Trump says U.S. is losing money 'unwisely' spent on Canadian health-care
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump suggested at a campaign rally that Canada pays for its healthcare by short changing the U.S. on trade.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
President Donald Trump took a swipe at former prime minister Justin Trudeau and Canada’s health care system in a rant on Saturday against the country and its “emboldened” leaders.

“You know, we had Trudeau, who’s not a good — not a good guy — loser, I mean, you know, I don’t — a loser,” Trump said during a rally in the city of Highland Heights, in Kentucky, where he was campaigning for Republicans ahead of crucial elections on Nov. 3 in which the House, Senate and 36 state gubernatorial seats are up for grabs.

Likely referring to Prime Minister Mark Carney, he then noted that Canada’s “current guy’s good … but he’s not nice when it comes to trade.”

“For years we’ve lost billions and billions of dollars, and they just felt so emboldened,” Trump said.

Kentucky is one of several red states targeted by the Carney government’s dollar-for-dollar tariffs. Several Canadian provinces have also banned U.S. alcohol, which includes the state’s sizeable bourbon industry. According to U.S. government figures, 17 per cent of Kentucky’s total goods exports in 2025 went to Canada, its largest market.

Trump also raised a long-standing gripe that the U.S. is “losing” US$90 billion to Canada. That money, he added, was for the “privilege of allowing Canada to have a health-care system and other things that they shouldn’t be having.”

“They spend money — they spend our money very unwisely,” he added.

Trump, who previously noted that the U.S. does not need “anything” from Canada, also said that a trade deal with the country would land “at some point.”

“We’re making a deal that’s gonna be amazing,” he said.

stories.title: Stiles unavailable to canvas for Chow as Toronto election enters final week
stories.summary: Marit Stiles's unavailability to support Chow on the ground comes at a moment when the incumbent Toronto mayor is locked in a tight race with opponent Brad Bradford.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles says that despite her support for Olivia Chow’s re-election campaign, she’s unavailable for last-minute campaign activities that could boost Chow’s profile in the pivotal final week before election day.

During an unrelated news conference at Queen’s Park on Monday, Stiles said while other NDP MPPs are supporting other municipal races around the province, her schedule doesn’t have room for her to do the same in her own political backyard.

“I’m actually on the road, I think, quite a bit between now and then. Me personally, I’m going to be, I think, ON the road between now and then quite a lot,” Stiles said.

Stiles’s unavailability to support Chow on the ground comes at a moment when the incumbent Toronto mayor is locked in a tight race with opponent Brad Bradford. While Chow has consistently led polling, her lead has been squeezed by some gains in momentum by Bradford.

The latest Liaison Strategies polling from Oct. 13 puts Chow at 51 per cent support and Bradford at 46 per cent. The polling reflects the views of a random sample of 1,000 Toronto residents the firm contacted between Oct.8 to Oct. 9.

“The polls don’t always tell the whole story,” Stiles said, before adding that she’s spoken with Toronto residents who are excited about the possibility of Chow staying on as mayor.

“They are proud of her accomplishments. I expect she’ll be the victor,” she said.

NDP sources insisted Stiles is planning to officially endorse Chow in the final days of the campaign and her team has yet to determine the final election day schedule.

Meanwhile, Chow’s campaign staff, they said, is also filled with former provincial NDP members. The NDP caucus is also available for voter engagement, they added.

Sources also pointed out that others who endorsed Chow – former Premier’s Kathleen Wynne and Bob Rae – are also unlikely to join the campaign trail.

Stiles emphasized that residents need to get out there and vote, as she said “there’s a lot of powerful forces out there” that do not want to see representatives elected, including those who support tenants.

She said “absolutely 100 per cent supports Mayor Olivia Chow in her re-election.”

Toronto will head to the polls on Monday, Oct. 26.

stories.title: Southern Ontario set for week of sunshine, seasonal temperatures
stories.summary: Southern Ontario is expected to enjoy a prolonged stretch of sunny, seasonable weather this week, with daytime highs remaining in the mid to upper teens and little chance of significant precipitation.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southern Ontario is expected to enjoy a prolonged stretch of sunny, seasonable weather this week, with daytime highs remaining in the mid to upper teens and little chance of significant precipitation.

CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison said Monday’s forecast featured clear skies and comfortable temperatures across the region.

“It’s a beautiful start to the week,” Atchison said. “Sunshine and gorgeous conditions are expected across southern Ontario, with temperatures climbing into the mid to upper teens this afternoon.”

London reached 18 C on Monday under mainly sunny skies, while much of southern Ontario experienced clear conditions and light winds.

Overnight temperatures are expected to cool to between 2 C and 7 C, which Atchison said is typical for this time of year. Areas along the shorelines of Lake Huron and Lake Erie will remain slightly milder overnight.

“Clear conditions hold overnight, and temperatures are right around where we should be for this time of year,” she said.

The sunny pattern is expected to continue through the work week, with only a few fair-weather clouds in the forecast.

Atchison said highs are expected to range between 16 C and 18 C on Tuesday, with temperatures remaining steady through the rest of the week. Forecast highs in London are expected to reach about 17 C on Wednesday, before climbing back to between 17 C and 18 C Thursday and Friday.

The pleasant conditions are also expected to extend into the weekend, with a mix of sun and cloud forecast for both Saturday and Sunday.

“We are in for a fantastic stretch of gorgeous weather in southern Ontario,” Atchison said.

No significant rain is currently forecast over the next seven days.

stories.title: Canadians step up to give blood after fire at Alberta military base kills four
stories.summary: Wainwright - Canadian Blood Services says it has been "deeply moved" by a surge in public support following a deadly fire at a military base in Wainwright, Alta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Canadian Blood Services says it has been “deeply moved” by a surge in public support following a deadly fire at a military base in Wainwright, Alta.

The non-profit reported Monday that it saw a fourfold increase in the number of appointment bookings for blood donations on Sunday.

Close to a dozen people were at the Edmonton Canadian Blood Services branch at opening Monday morning. Some had appointments booked before the fire, while others rushed to claim spots that were quickly being filled.

Michael Harper said he arrived Monday morning hoping they would take his donation as a walk-in appointment. Harper said he was an army reservist and his unit served in the same armoury as Sgt. Morgan Wong — one of soldiers who died in Saturday’s fire.

“I left the forces in 2022, and at this stage I feel that the best thing I can do right now is come to donate some blood and just show my support,” Harper said.

Harper said he’d done field exercises and training courses at CFB Wainwright in the past.

While he didn’t know Wong well, Harper said the sting of the news is still there.

“The Forces being as close-knit as it is, it does hurt when you hear that some people that you knew or even just people that serve are affected or hurt. I just want to do what I can here.”

Rachel Glendenning, an RCMP officer, said she booked her appointment Sunday night and loves that people are coming out to show their support this way. She said she used to be a regular donor, but hadn’t for a few years and this is a good reminder to get back in the habit.

The need for blood hit home for Nicole Strong, who said her brother needed blood transfusions “many years ago” after he lost a limb in a workplace accident.

“That’s why I’m here. My heart just goes out to everyone that’s affected by this,” she said.

“When I went on yesterday to make the appointment (9 a.m.) this was the only available appointment left.”

Canadian Blood Services said Monday Alberta and Saskatchewan saw the strongest surge in public interest in blood donations. Donation events in those provinces are almost fully booked over the next few days, the non-profit said.

It said the public’s response to the crisis demonstrates Canadians’ “generosity” and “the importance of maintaining a strong, prepared blood system.”

“One of the most meaningful ways people can help is by booking and keeping donation appointments in the days and weeks ahead,” it said in an email, adding that “maintaining a healthy blood supply is an ongoing effort and donations made in the coming weeks will be just as important as those made today.”

Canadian Blood Services said it’s continuing to monitor the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met.

Defence officials have said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area of CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, when a fire struck on Saturday.

Strong winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing across the Prairie landscape, killing four and sending 39 to hospital, 19 in critical condition.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday many of the injured have serious burns.

The fire claimed the lives of Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Canadian Blood Services said in a statement Sunday that those who want to help by donating blood are encouraged to do so in the coming days and weeks.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said people have been lining up to donate blood, bring meals to first responders and open their homes to those grieving.

In an August blog post on treatment of burn victims after wildfires, U.S.-based The Blood Connection said plasma in donated blood can help prevent clotting, regulate blood pressure and balance a patient’s fluids.

It says over the first 24 hours after a patient is burned, fluid leaks rapidly from damaged or burned blood vessels into surrounding tissues, causing blood pressure to drop.

“In the following days, as the body attempts to repair itself, plasma may also be introduced to stabilize blood vessel walls and return the body’s blood pressure to normal,” The Blood Connection said. “For patients who experience hemorrhaging, plasma is vital to ensure that bloods clot, and internal bleeding doesn’t become life-threatening.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— With files from Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa

stories.title: News publishers launch copyright suit against AI company Anthropic in Ontario
stories.summary: A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada’s largest newspapers is suing the artificial intelligence company Anthropic in an Ontario court.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada’s largest newspapers is suing the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court.

Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model Claude.

“Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, building an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital — all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the News Media Companies,” says the statement of claim.

“In doing so, Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched to the detriment of the News Media Companies.”

The lawsuit, filed on Oct. 6, was first reported by the news site Cartt.CA. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.

The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites’ terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures they put in place to restrict copying of their content.

The claim says the news outlets “are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada’s journalistic content — from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage,” and collectively have millions of readers.

“To obtain content for ingestion into its models and services, Anthropic deliberately ‘scrapes’ (i.e. accesses and copies) enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the Plaintiffs’ Websites,” the claim says.

stories.title: Beluga rescued from Marineland dies in California
stories.summary: An ultrasound determined Cyprus’s intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.

SeaWorld San Diego says in a Facebook post that Cyprus, a nine-year-old male beluga that arrived at the park on Aug. 22 stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound later determined the animal’s intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

It says Cyprus had been doing well since his arrival, eating consistently and interacting with his trainers and animal care team, along with two other rescued belugas.

But it notes belugas can mask discomfort or underlying concerns that are not immediately visible, and it says a full necropsy will be conducted.

Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada, and 30 of its belugas and four dolphins were transferred to other facilities in a mass relocation effort.

SeaWorld San Diego says the other rescued belugas in its care are in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings.

“As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues,” the facility said in its social media post on Sunday.

It said that after the necropsy is completed, the cause of Cyprus’s death will be shared with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Less than two weeks ago, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago said Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga that was relocated from Marineland, died despite efforts to save her.

Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels, Shedd said.

Shedd said it performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.

A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo also died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

stories.title: Fatal CFB Wainwright fire the latest tragedy at the Alberta CAF base
stories.summary: Since 2005, at least seven other soldiers have been killed while stationed at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
While the vast majority of Canadian Armed Forces members’ deaths have occurred during wartime, the CAF has known no shortage of non-wartime tragedies at domestic and international bases over its storied and valiant history.

Before the fire that swept through the training area at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday, killing four soldiers and injuring 39 more — 19 critically — “10 Canadians have died in accidents while serving in the military” since 2020, according to The Canadian Virtual War Memorial .

One of those was Cpl. James Choi, a 29-year-old member of the Royal Westminster Regiment based in New Westminster, B.C., who was shot during a nighttime live-fire training exercise at CFB Wainwright in October 2020.

Choi, who had joined just four years prior and was training with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (Ppcli) at the time, was treated on the scene before being flown to Edmonton, where he died in hospital, National Post reported at the time.

Cpl. Lars Callsen of the Ppcli’s 3rd Battalion was charged in May 2021 with one count of negligence in Choi’s death, but prosecutors with the Department of National Defence opted not to pursue the charges, CBC reported in 2023.

Defence officials didn’t explain why at the time and said Callsen returned to serve with his unit.

The busy base in Wainwright, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is home to the Caf’s Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre (Cmtc) and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre (3 Cdtc), and has experienced several fatal incidents in the last 20 or so years.

In April 2017, Royal Canadian Dragoons Sgt. Robbery (Bobby) J. Dynerowicz, a 31-year-old veteran of 12 years who’d served two tours in Afghanistan, died in a single-vehicle crash when the light armoured vehicle (LAV) he was commanding crashed on a heavily travelled gravel road on the base.

Three other soldiers aboard were injured, per the Edmonton Journal.

That particular vehicle, the LAV-III, had been involved in 14 rollover incidents resulting in at least eight deaths since it was introduced for use in 1999, the Ottawa Citizen reported in 2014.

The Citizen’s report was prompted by a rollover that May that caused the death of Lt.-Col. Dan Bobbitt, commanding officer of the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery’s 2nd Regiment, based in Garrison Petawawa, Ont.

The 43-year-old married father of three had served two tours in Bosnia and one in Afghanistan before his death.

The accident happened during Exercise Maple Resolve, the largest Canadian military exercise of the year at CFB Wainwright with about 5000 personnel, the Citizen reported .

In November 2014, 20-year-old Pte. Pete Allen, a rookie soldier with barely a year of service under his belt, died from injuries suffered when the three-metre-high lookout-type tower he was standing on collapsed.

As reported by National Post , Allen was recruited in October 2013, completed basic training in January and had been posted to Wainwright’s 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre to become a regular force infantry soldier.

Cpl. Christopher Deliva, a 27-year-old from Montreal, died in hospital after suffering serious injuries in May 2007 when the 10-tonne truck he was driving rolled over while rounding a curve at Wainwright, the Montreal Gazette reported.

The supply technician had joined the military in September 2000 and was set to deploy in Afghanistan in 2009.

Another Quebec-born service member, Pte. Patrick Dessureault, a 24-year-old from Alma, is believed to have “died instantly” in September 2005 when the LAV-III he and three other visiting soldiers from CFB Valcartier were in rolled over into Battle River during a night exercise.

His commanding officer told the Gazette that Dessureault was in the vehicle’s hatch and suffered a fatal neck injury.

He’d enlisted two years prior and was training for an overseas deployment in 2006.

Soldiers from other allied countries often visit CFB Wainwright for joint training exercises, one of whom was killed in an airfield accident in 2008.

That May, 25-year-old U.S. Army Specialist Josef Cerfus was killed while practicing “swing load” operations with a Chinook helicopter when the netted load fell on him. He was pronounced dead at the hospital in Wainwright.

Tens of thousands of soldiers from Canada and elsewhere have schooled in the art of war at CFB Wainwright since it was first established as a military training area in 1941 after the namesake town’s mayor asked Ottawa to take over adjacent vacant land that was once Buffalo National Park — one of several national parks created in Canada after the turn of the 20th century to help protect Prairie plains bison populations.

For roughly 17 months after Wwii, it housed over 1,000 German prisoners of war, after which it reverted to a training ground for the Korean War, according to an archived government website . The 609-square-kilometre facility earned CFB designation in 1968 and has been the Canadian Army’s main training area in Western Canada ever since.

Forces stationed there include the Ppcli and the Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group.

The Royal Canadian Air Force also routinely uses the area and its airfields, as have international forces, including the British Army, which ended a twenty-year residency in 2005.

Its regular personnel are roughly 700 military members and 300 civilians.

His commanding officer told the Gazette that Dessureault was in the vehicle’s hatch and suffered a fatal neck injury.
He’d enlisted two years prior and was training for an overseas deployment in 2006.

content_blocks.alt: Pte. Patrick Dessureault
content_blocks.caption: Pte. Patrick Dessureault was a member of the second battalion, the Royal 22nd Regiment based in CFB Valcartier in Quebec. Photo by Department of National Defence

content_blocks.text: Soldiers from other allied countries often visit CFB Wainwright for joint training exercises, one of whom was killed in an airfield accident in 2008.

That May, 25-year-old U.S. Army Specialist Josef Cerfus was killed while practicing “swing load” operations with a Chinook helicopter when the netted load fell on him. He was pronounced dead at the hospital in Wainwright.

Tens of thousands of soldiers from Canada and elsewhere have schooled in the art of war at CFB Wainwright since it was first established as a military training area in 1941 after the namesake town’s mayor asked Ottawa to take over adjacent vacant land that was once Buffalo National Park — one of several national parks created in Canada after the turn of the 20th century to help protect Prairie plains bison populations.

For roughly 17 months after Wwii, it housed over 1,000 German prisoners of war, after which it reverted to a training ground for the Korean War, according to an archived government website . The 609-square-kilometre facility earned CFB designation in 1968 and has been the Canadian Army’s main training area in Western Canada ever since.

content_blocks.text: Forces stationed there include the Ppcli and the Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group.
The Royal Canadian Air Force also routinely uses the area and its airfields, as have international forces, including the British Army, which ended a twenty-year residency in 2005.
Its regular personnel are roughly 700 military members and 300 civilians.

stories.title: Quebec's strategic maple syrup reserve running dry amid high demand
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - The head of Quebec's maple syrup producer's association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.
stories.author: Stéphane Rolland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - The head of Quebec’s maple syrup producers’ association says the province’s strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers President Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn’t miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions.

As a result, the producers’ association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product. (Oct. 19, 2026)

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

“Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero,” Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry’s economic benefits. That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

“We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available,” Goulet said. “Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established.”

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year. “It’s always hard to beat an exceptional year,” Turenne said.

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have. However, he believes the industry can still grow. “There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves,” he said.

Investments from Quebec City “are too low for our liking,” says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly-elected Parti Québécois government.

“When we’re told that we have an industry that’s thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level,” he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States “We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent,” Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec. More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group’s report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

“Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry,” Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers’ group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry’s importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, “if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages,” Goulet said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Trial for man accused in Pearson gold heist hears more from key figure in case
stories.summary: A man who received a prison sentence for his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist says on the day of the theft, he communicated with the man currently on trial.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man who received a prison sentence for his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has told a Brampton, Ont., court that on the day of the theft, he communicated with the man currently on trial in the case.

Arsalan Chaudhary returned to the witness stand today in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and he was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

His testimony in Sidhu’s trial was paused last week after he said that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan had left him traumatized.

Chaudhary testified today that he told Sidhu the truck and driver were ready on the day of the gold heist and that Sidhu replied, “OK.”

Chaudhary told court last week that he planned the heist with another man who is still wanted by authorities, and he ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars.

He said he melted some of the gold before travelling to Pakistan, where he was kidnapped and abused until he gave up the loot.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

stories.title: Pamela Wallin resigns Senate seat 2 years before mandatory retirement
stories.summary: Pamela Wallin, a former broadcaster, was embroiled in the expense scandal that rocked the Senate in 2013, but was never criminally charged.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier

Pamela Wallin, a former broadcaster who was at the centre of an expense scandal that rocked the Senate , has resigned her seat in the Upper House.

A notice from the Clerk of the Senate Monday indicated that Wallin, 73, had resigned her seat as of Oct. 18. There’s so far no explanation for why the senator, who represented Saskatchewan since her appointment in 2009, resigned before the mandatory retirement age of 75.

Wallin was appointed on the advice of then-prime minister Stephen Harper in 2009. The former CBC and CTV broadcaster was one of the most recognizable faces for years in the Red Chamber.

She remained a recognizable face during the Senate expense scandal, which rocked the Upper House and destabilized Harper’s government in 2013. She, along with former senators Mike Duffy and Patrick Brazeau, became the focus of media reporting and later police investigations into dodgy spending and expense claims.

An audit of Wallin’s spending ended in her repaying roughly $150,000, including interest, for expense claims the Senate retroactively deemed inappropriate.

While court documents revealed that the RCMP believed Wallin had broken the law and were trying to gather proof of criminal wrongdoing, the police force announced in 2016 that Wallin would not be charged.

“I’m very relieved after three long years … I’m glad this nightmare is over,” Wallin told reporters at the time.

Wallin was suspended without pay from the Senate during the scandal and left the Conservative caucus, most recently sitting with the Canadian Senators Group. The former broadcaster has kept a low profile in recent years.

Wallin’s office did not immediately return Global News’ request for an interview Monday morning.
