stories.title: Carney expected to speak in House of Commons on CFB Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: Four members of the military were killed when a nearby grass fire surged into a training area and overwhelmed soldiers at CFB Wainwright.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to give condolences for the victims of the deadly CFB Wainwright fire as MPs return to the House of Commons.

Carney previously spoke Sunday, telling Canadians that the next of kin of four service members who died in Saturday’s fire had been notified.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost,” Carney said at the time.

He will speak at 11 a.m. Eastern, according to his official itinerary.

The four soldiers killed have been identified as: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aida Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

Wong was from Edmonton and a member of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment. The other three were all members of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry (3PPCLI). Though they were based at the Edmonton Garrison, Farrell called Prince Albert, Sask. home while Goulding hailed from North Vancouver and Lykkemark from Langley in B.C.’s Lower Mainland.

Their deaths came after a routine training exercise for Edmonton-based soldiers descended into chaos at CFB Wainwright when a violent, sudden surge of wind caused a nearby grass fire towards the soldiers at lightning speed.

“This was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it,” Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, Commander of 1st Canadian Division, said during an update Sunday afternoon.

About 350 troops with the 3PPCLI were participating in exercises at the base, located 200 km southeast of Edmonton.

Rutland said the grass fire was known well beforehand but not considered a threat . It was located about a kilometre away and considered sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to take place nearby on Saturday afternoon.

But the surge of wind changed conditions, with the flames then jumping the base fence and threatening nearby rural areas and the town of Wainwright.

A total of 39 other troops were sent to hospital, with 19 in critical condition as of Sunday afternoon.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said when she announced the casualty count and confirmed many have serious burns.

The wounded are being cared for in four hospitals: the University of Alberta and Royal Alexandra in Edmonton, Foothills in Calgary and the regional hospital in Red Deer.

King Charles III and politicians across Canada are among those to have paid condolences for those killed and injured in the fire.

— with files from Global News’ Karen Bartko, Jeff Semple and Ashleigh Stewart

stories.title: What we know about the 4 soldiers who died in fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: A fire that quickly ripped through a Canadian Armed Forces training ground in Alberta on Saturday killed four soldiers and injured 39 more.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted October 19, 2026 9:48 am.

A fire that quickly ripped through a Canadian Armed Forces training ground in Alberta on Saturday killed four soldiers and injured 39 more.

Here are the four soldiers who died:

Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

In a social media post, his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”

“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.

She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province would be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.

“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

“To Shaun’s family, to the families of the other fallen service members, and to everyone carrying the weight of this loss today, please know that Saskatchewan stands with you, and that you are in our prayers in the difficult days ahead.”

The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic. He later quit to join the army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto Csis,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted new army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and served with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.

“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.

“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”

They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.

He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of Sergeant Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and all those who lost their lives yesterday at Wainwright,” the 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said in a social media post.

“Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones and everyone affected by this tragedy.

“We will remember them.”

stories.title: Beluga rescued from closed Ontario park dies in California
stories.summary: A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed facility.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.

SeaWorld San Diego says in a Facebook post that Cyprus, a nine-year-old male beluga that arrived at the park on Aug. 22 stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound later determined the animal’s intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

It says Cyprus had been doing well since his arrival, eating consistently and interacting with his trainers and animal care team, along with two other rescued belugas.

But it notes belugas can mask discomfort or underlying concerns that are not immediately visible, and it says a full necropsy will be conducted.

Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada, and 30 of its belugas and four dolphins were transferred to other facilities in a mass relocation effort.

SeaWorld San Diego says the other rescued belugas in its care are in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings.

“As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues,” the facility said in its social media post on Sunday.

It said that after the necropsy is completed, the cause of Cyprus’s death will be shared with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Less than two weeks ago, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago said Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga that was relocated from Marineland, died despite efforts to save her.

Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels, Shedd said.

Shedd said it performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.

A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo also died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

stories.title: Gas prices drove inflation up to 3.1% in September, says StatCan
stories.summary: The annual pace of inflation rose to 3.1 per cent in September as war in the Middle East continued to drive up gas prices, Statistics Canada said Monday.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The annual pace of inflation rose to 3.1 per cent in September as war in the Middle East continued to drive up gas prices , Statistics Canada said Monday.

The agency released the latest consumer price index report on Monday, which said the acceleration was led by a 27.8 per cent spike in gasoline prices last month compared with a year earlier, despite the switch to the less expensive winter gas blend.

Excluding gasoline, consumer prices increased 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September.

The agency said fuel oil and other fuels surged 57.8 per cent in September, hitting consumers hard in Atlantic Canada where many homes are heated with oil.

Meanwhile, grocery prices increased 1.7 per cent last month, the smallest yearly increase since May 2024, according to Statistics Canada.

Driving the slowdown was a 2.9 per cent drop in prices for fresh vegetables, while sugar and confectionary items fell 2.7 per cent.

Beef prices, meanwhile, rose at a slower pace in September, up 8.7 per cent compared with an 11 per cent increase in August.

Despite the year-over-year slowdown, the agency said prices for groceries have increased 33 per cent since September 2020.

Statistics Canada said shelter prices rose 1.8 per cent in September, up from 1.5 per cent in August.

In addition to the spike in fuel oil, the agency said a 4.9 per cent increase in mortgage insurance and 1.2 per cent increase in home maintenance and repair costs lead the acceleration.

stories.title: Timeline: How the deadly fire spread at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: A fire that quickly ripped through a Canadian Armed Forces training ground in Alberta on Saturday killed four soldiers and injured 39 more.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A fire that quickly ripped through a Canadian Armed Forces training ground in Alberta on Saturday killed four soldiers and injured 39 more.

Here is what is known about how it unfolded:

— Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said 84 members of 3rd Battalion of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were training with live munitions in an area of CFB Wainwright.

— He said most were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were doing a simulated attack on an enemy in preparation for deployments overseas.

— Rutland said leaders were aware of a grass fire that ignited roughly a kilometre away from the ongoing training, but it was not considered a threat.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland with the Canadian Armed Forces says a grass fire that killed four service members was considered under control before severe winds hit the area, causing it to spread rapidly in seconds. Rutland says 39 others are injured, including 19 in critical condition. (Oct. 18, 2026)

— Strong and sudden winds sent flames from the fire across the Prairie landscape in seconds, quickly bypassing fire guards and stopping soldiers in their tracks.

— Rutland said he was told by a commander on the ground that within 30 seconds to a minute, the fire was “right on top of them.”

— Emergency crews, including those from the Canadian Armed Forces and the town of Wainwright, were called to bring the fire under control.

— Dr. Sayeh Zielke, CEO of Acute Care Alberta, said by 6 p.m. on Saturday, health agencies were on a co-ordinating call and stood up a command centre.

— Hospitals declared a Code Orange to deal with the mass casualty incident and a rapid influx of patients.

— Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 30 emergency units, including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft, were deployed directly into Wainwright.

— Several Stars air ambulances flew to Wainwright throughout the night.

— At around 7:30 p.m. MT on Saturday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced from a TV studio in Ottawa that there were multiple fatalities and many more were injured.

— At 10:30 a.m. MT on Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed in a brief televised address from Ottawa that four soldiers died in the “violent, fast-moving fire,” calling it “one of the worst tragedies for the (Armed Forces) on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

— The Code Orange was lifted on Sunday.

— As of 3 p.m. MT Sunday afternoon, 39 patients were being cared for in hospital and at least 19 remained in critical condition, Smith said.

— Rutland said the Army currently does not believe the fire was the result of any explosion stemming from natural gas infrastructure on the base, nor any kind of outside interference.

— The military still must conduct a full investigation into field conditions and other factors that could have played into what transpired.

— Training at the Wainwright site was shut down on Sunday, but the battalion remains scheduled for a troop surge in Latvia in spring, so it will resume at a later date, Rutland said.

— Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday the federal government “will keep Canadians informed as we learn more.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— He said most were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were doing a simulated attack on an enemy in preparation for deployments overseas.
— Rutland said leaders were aware of a grass fire that ignited roughly a kilometre away from the ongoing training, but it was not considered a threat.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland with the Canadian Armed Forces says a grass fire that killed four service members was considered under control before severe winds hit the area, causing it to spread rapidly in seconds. Rutland says 39 others are injured, including 19 in critical condition. (Oct. 18, 2026)
— Strong and sudden winds sent flames from the fire across the Prairie landscape in seconds, quickly bypassing fire guards and stopping soldiers in their tracks.
— Rutland said he was told by a commander on the ground that within 30 seconds to a minute, the fire was “right on top of them.”
— Emergency crews, including those from the Canadian Armed Forces and the town of Wainwright, were called to bring the fire under control.
— Dr. Sayeh Zielke, CEO of Acute Care Alberta, said by 6 p.m. on Saturday, health agencies were on a co-ordinating call and stood up a command centre.
— Hospitals declared a Code Orange to deal with the mass casualty incident and a rapid influx of patients.
— Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 30 emergency units, including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft, were deployed directly into Wainwright.
— Several Stars air ambulances flew to Wainwright throughout the night.
— At around 7:30 p.m. MT on Saturday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced from a TV studio in Ottawa that there were multiple fatalities and many more were injured.

— At 10:30 a.m. MT on Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed in a brief televised address from Ottawa that four soldiers died in the “violent, fast-moving fire,” calling it “one of the worst tragedies for the (Armed Forces) on Canadian soil in peacetime.”
— The Code Orange was lifted on Sunday.
— As of 3 p.m. MT Sunday afternoon, 39 patients were being cared for in hospital and at least 19 remained in critical condition, Smith said.
— Rutland said the Army currently does not believe the fire was the result of any explosion stemming from natural gas infrastructure on the base, nor any kind of outside interference.
— The military still must conduct a full investigation into field conditions and other factors that could have played into what transpired.
— Training at the Wainwright site was shut down on Sunday, but the battalion remains scheduled for a troop surge in Latvia in spring, so it will resume at a later date, Rutland said.
— Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday the federal government “will keep Canadians informed as we learn more.”

stories.title: CFB Wainwright training ‘as real as it can be,’ says retired major-general
stories.summary: Training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta is “as real as it can be” to prepare soldiers for combat operations, says a retired Canadian Armed Forces major-general.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
Training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta is “as real as it can be” to prepare soldiers for combat operations, says a retired Canadian Armed Forces major-general.

Four military members were killed, and dozens were injured after a fire broke out at the massive military base’s training area on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said at a press conference in Ottawa Sunday.

Retired Maj.-Gen. David Fraser, who spent much of his over 30-year military career training at CFB Wainwright, said that training can involve up to thousands of people depending on the exercise.

Some exercises are individual he said, providing an example of a member shooting a rifle at a gun range. Others are known as collective exercises, which involve two or more members, he said.

“They’re progressive,” Fraser said in an interview Sunday. “You start off with one person and you end up at some stage in the game probably with 5,000 or 6,000 people,” he said.

Fraser said training at the base 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton teaches regular and reserve forces to use every weapon in the military’s arsenal, including aircraft. The exercises can involve firing both unloaded and loaded weapons, he said.

Fraser described the exercises as organized and methodical and said something went wrong at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

“It’s very procedural, it’s complex, it’s detailed to make it as safe as possible,” he said.

Later Sunday, officials provided more information about how the trouble began.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland told a news conference in Edmonton that a grass fire was a kilometre away from the training exercises on Saturday afternoon and was considered sufficiently under control that the exercises were allowed to continue.

But Rutland said conditions — including a violent, sudden windstorm — sent flames racing over the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, landing right on top of the soldiers.

In addition to the four soldiers who died, 39 others were injured, 19 of whom are in critical condition.

CFB Wainwright is adjacent to the town of Wainwright, home to close to 7,000 people and located about 50 kilometres west of the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary.

The fast-moving fire quickly spread beyond the boundaries of the training area on Saturday, and both military and civilian responders worked to control the fire.

Fraser described the base as one of the Canadian military’s premier training areas, which was used to train forces that served on-the-ground in Afghanistan following the 911 terrorist attacks in the United States.

“The training area is essentially prairie with a lot of aspen trees and a lot of rolling terrain, and it’s really good for vehicles to go through,” he said. “It’s an outstanding training area.”

Forces participate in safety briefings before an exercise begins and are given specific instructions on what they are permitted to shoot and what orders they will be given to stop the exercise in the event something goes wrong, he said.

Fraser said the base is fenced off and there are signs advising the public that it is a Department of National Defence property. Additionally, he said personnel put up barriers and red flags to alert people when there are live firing exercises taking place.

He added that forces who undergo this training are well-versed in safety procedures and safety staff oversee the exercises.

“Any training starts off with dry training to refresh your skills, to make sure you’re ready to go and use anything that’s live,” he said.

Fraser said the priority for the armed forces is to notify the affected families and ensure that there is no further damage to the training base.

As well, he anticipated both the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP will conduct investigations to determine how the fire started.

The prime minister said Sunday family members of those who died have been notified and that those involved came from military bases across the country.

The four deceased have been identified as: Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

stories.title: Alberta Referendum: Live results and how to vote
stories.summary: The Alberta referendum polls are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., after which Global News will have in-depth results coverage and analysis online and on air.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Do we stay or go? At the crux of it, that’s the question Albertans have been grappling with for much of 2026 and soon, they will learn how their friends and neighbours feel.

The historic Alberta referendum asks the province’s voters 10 questions that could change the course of not just the Prairie province, but also Canada.

The vote, announced Feb. 19, initially contained nine questions to do with immigration and possible changes to Canada’s Constitution. Then on May 21, Smith announced a 10th question on separation was being added .

Global News will have in-depth, up-to-the-minute team coverage from across Alberta on both broadcast and streaming online.

Anchors Dallas Flexhaug and Carole Anne Devaney will be joined by veteran political reporter and Ottawa bureau chief David Akin for results analysis, along with insights from a political panel hosted by anchor Blake Lough. Reporters on the ground in several Alberta communities will also be providing updates and interviews.

From 8 p.m. MT to midnight, our Decision Alberta Referendum 2026 coverage will air online at the top of this post, as well as on YouTube and our Global TV app that is available on streaming services Prime Video, Apple TV, Roku, and select smart TVs.

Starting at 9 p.m., simultaneous coverage will also begin airing live on all Global News stations in Alberta.

Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

However, those still in line at 8 p.m. are asked to remain there, as you will be allowed to vote.

While voters could cast their ballot at any advance voting location in their electoral division, ON election day, you must vote at your assigned voting location in your electoral division. Electors cannot vote outside their electoral division.

Voters can search on Elections Alberta’s website to find out where their polling station is. Election Day voting locations are most commonly in schools, churches, community halls, and other public buildings.

Elections Alberta encourages voters to read and familiarize themselves with all 10 questions ( which can be reviewed here ) before reaching the ballot box.

There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none of them — your choice.

The ballots will go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them, and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.

Elections Alberta is expecting a record turnout, between 80 and 85 per cent of the province’s nearly three million electors.

You have as much time as you want to fill in the ballots, but officials estimate it’ll take most people about two minutes.

The Election Act requires employers to provide employees with paid time off (three consecutive, non-work hours) to vote during either one of the advance voting days or on Oct. 19.

Employers are not allowed to penalize staff for taking time to vote.

Elections Alberta notes that the employer retains the right to determine when to give the employee time off — whether it was on one of the days of advance voting or on Election Day.

You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.

There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.

Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.

The provincial agency said your “Where to Vote” card is not required to vote and cannot be used as identification, but it will speed up the voting process.

By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.

Question 10 — about separation — will be counted first.

Officials say early results are to be released sometime after 8 p.m. Monday — but only once the final ballot is cast and all polling stations are closed — with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.

GlobalNews.CA staff will be working overnight to bring you the latest results as they are released.

The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday. Those ballots will be counted in order from question one to nine.

The count timelines will depend on voting location closing times and voter turnout.

For more information, visit Elections Alberta’s website .

With files from The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Do we stay or go? At the crux of it, that’s the question Albertans have been grappling with for much of 2026 and soon, they will learn how their friends and neighbours feel.
The historic Alberta referendum asks the province’s voters 10 questions that could change the course of not just the Prairie province, but also Canada.
content_blocks.html: The historic Alberta referendum asks the province’s voters 10 questions that could change the course of not just the Prairie province, but also Canada.

content_blocks.text: The vote, announced Feb. 19, initially contained nine questions to do with immigration and possible changes to Canada’s Constitution. Then on May 21, Smith announced a 10th question on separation was being added .
content_blocks.html: The vote, announced Feb. 19, initially contained nine questions to do with immigration and possible changes to Canada’s Constitution. Then on May 21, Smith announced a 10th question on separation was being added.

content_blocks.text: How do I watch the results?
Global News will have in-depth, up-to-the-minute team coverage from across Alberta on both broadcast and streaming online.

Anchors Dallas Flexhaug and Carole Anne Devaney will be joined by veteran political reporter and Ottawa bureau chief David Akin for results analysis, along with insights from a political panel hosted by anchor Blake Lough. Reporters on the ground in several Alberta communities will also be providing updates and interviews.

From 8 p.m. MT to midnight, our Decision Alberta Referendum 2026 coverage will air online at the top of this post, as well as on YouTube and our Global TV app that is available on streaming services Prime Video, Apple TV, Roku, and select smart TVs.
content_blocks.html: From 8 p.m. MT to midnight, our Decision Alberta Referendum 2026 coverage will air online at the top of this post, as well as on YouTube and our Global TV app that is available on streaming services Prime Video, Apple TV, Roku, and select smart TVs.

content_blocks.text: Starting at 9 p.m., simultaneous coverage will also begin airing live on all Global News stations in Alberta.
How do I vote?
Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.
However, those still in line at 8 p.m. are asked to remain there, as you will be allowed to vote.

While voters could cast their ballot at any advance voting location in their electoral division, ON election day, you must vote at your assigned voting location in your electoral division. Electors cannot vote outside their electoral division.

Voters can search on Elections Alberta’s website to find out where their polling station is. Election Day voting locations are most commonly in schools, churches, community halls, and other public buildings.
content_blocks.html: Voters can search on Elections Alberta’s website to find out where their polling station is. Election Day voting locations are most commonly in schools, churches, community halls, and other public buildings.

content_blocks.text: Elections Alberta encourages voters to read and familiarize themselves with all 10 questions ( which can be reviewed here ) before reaching the ballot box.
content_blocks.html: Elections Alberta encourages voters to read and familiarize themselves with all 10 questions (which can be reviewed here) before reaching the ballot box.

content_blocks.text: There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none of them — your choice.
The ballots will go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them, and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.
Elections Alberta is expecting a record turnout, between 80 and 85 per cent of the province’s nearly three million electors.
You have as much time as you want to fill in the ballots, but officials estimate it’ll take most people about two minutes.
Can I vote during work hours?
content_blocks.html: Can I vote during work hours?

content_blocks.text: The Election Act requires employers to provide employees with paid time off (three consecutive, non-work hours) to vote during either one of the advance voting days or on Oct. 19.
Employers are not allowed to penalize staff for taking time to vote.
Elections Alberta notes that the employer retains the right to determine when to give the employee time off — whether it was on one of the days of advance voting or on Election Day.
What identification is needed?
content_blocks.html: What identification is needed?

content_blocks.text: You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.
There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.
content_blocks.html: There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

content_blocks.text: Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.
Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.
The provincial agency said your “Where to Vote” card is not required to vote and cannot be used as identification, but it will speed up the voting process.
How long before I know the results?
content_blocks.html: How long before I know the results?

content_blocks.text: By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.
Question 10 — about separation — will be counted first.

Officials say early results are to be released sometime after 8 p.m. Monday — but only once the final ballot is cast and all polling stations are closed — with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.
GlobalNews.CA staff will be working overnight to bring you the latest results as they are released.
The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday. Those ballots will be counted in order from question one to nine.
The count timelines will depend on voting location closing times and voter turnout.
For more information, visit Elections Alberta’s website .

stories.title: Canadians step up to give blood after fatal fire at Alberta military base
stories.summary: Some are rolling up their sleeves to give blood as the military town of Wainwright, Alta., mourns the four soldiers killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Some Canadians are rolling up their sleeves to give blood as the military town of Wainwright, Alta., mourns the four soldiers killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong.

Defence officials have said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area of CFB Wainwright , southeast of Edmonton, when disaster struck Saturday.

Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically.

Among the dead are Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says people have been lining up to donate blood, bring meals to first responders, and open their homes to those grieving.

Canadian Blood Services says in a statement that people who want to help by donating blood are encouraged to do so in the coming days and weeks.

“We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” the non-profit says in the post on its website.

CFB Wainwright is 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. It is one of Canada’s busiest bases and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

Canada’s military has said that the grass fire was known well beforehand but, at roughly a kilometre away, was not considered a threat.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, told reporters Sunday that the 84 members of 3rd Battalion were doing two exercises at the time.

Most were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were doing a simulated attack on an enemy.

What happened next is an anomaly, he said.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground. He said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” he told a news conference.

Medical personnel from neighbouring areas, including Saskatchewan, were called in. Some were seen parachuting into the base. Alberta health officials invoked a critical Code Orange — a call for hospitals to find staff and free up beds to handle a mass casualty incident — that has since been called off.

Rutland said there would be a full investigation, adding that there’s a lot to consider: Did the fire move that quickly because of the wind? Did it move unseen through foliage to surprise the soldiers? Was it both?

Premier Danielle Smith confirmed at the news conference that many of the injured have serious burns. Hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer are treating the wounded.

Flags on provincial and federal buildings have been lowered to half-mast to pay tribute to the deceased.

The tragedy comes as Albertans head to the polls Monday for a referendum that, among other things, asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding vote on leaving.

McGuinty said those affected were soldiers and reservists from across the country.

“This loss reaches communities in every province,” he said.

Earlier Sunday in Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the “worst tragedies for the (Armed Forces) on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Asked what she makes of the reaction by those across the country, Smith said Alberta has a long and proud history of supporting the Canadian Armed Forces.

Shortly after Alberta was brought under Confederation in 1905, thousands of residents enlisted in the military to fight in the First World War, Smith said.

“We were very honoured to have been able to assist at a terrible time for the Armed Forces. And we’re very honoured as well now to be giving all of those soldiers who are injured the very best care,” she said.

“And I think we’re all very, very hopeful for a full recovery of everyone.”

stories.title: Low price on Pickering home gets low bids; higher price gets a deal
stories.summary: This 38-year-old house has an attached, double garage, and formal living and dining areas
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
1642 Pepperwood Gate, Pickering, Ont.

Asking price: $929,900 (July 15)

Previous asking price: $748,800 (July 6)

Selling price: $890,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $173,300 (October, 1995)

Taxes: $5,990 (2025)

Days on the market: 30

Property days on market: 38

Listing agent: Trevor C. Nicolle, Royal LePage Signature Realty

Agent Trevor C. Nicolle told his clients that they had a better chance of selling their three-bedroom house for close to $900,000 by generating multiple offers. To that end, they stuck a low $748,800 asking price on the home about 40 kilometres east of downtown Toronto. Six buyers made their bids, but none were acceptable to the seller.

“Anything below $1-million has a lot of eyes on it based on affordability,” said Mr. Nicolle. “We ended up with six offers, all of which were very conservative, some even below our asking price. It’s not an unusual circumstance, but we didn’t get where we needed to be.”

Mr. Nicolle moved to Plan B: raising the home’s price to $929,900. They got over 130 visitors, but it was a previous bidder who came back to negotiate a deal.

“We had over 100-plus showings and still faced an uphill battle to get it sold,” Mr. Nicolle said. “But we succeeded.”

“One of the original buyers who came in with an offer took 30 days to negotiate to where we ended up, at $890,000.”

This 38-year-old house has an attached, double garage, formal living and dining areas, a family room with a fireplace, and a sunroom with access to a deck.

There are four bathrooms and two kitchens, including one in the basement. The lower level also has a recreation area, one bedroom and two entrances, including sliding doors to a patio on the 28-by 121-foot lot.

“It has a lower level with income potential, which was an advantage, and it was a beautiful house,” Mr. Nicolle said.

“It’s in a culturally diverse neighbourhood, and it was on a street with a public school as well.”

stories.title: Nvidia challenger Tenstorrent raises $1.5-billion, valuing Toronto-founded company at $6.2-billion
stories.summary: AI semiconductor maker reportedly rebuffed buyout attempts by Intel and Qualcomm earlier this year
stories.author: Sean Silcoff, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence semi-conductor maker Tenstorrent Holdings Inc. has raised US$1.5-billion in fresh capital as it steps up efforts to challenge industry behemoth Nvidia Corp Nvda-Q .

The financing, which values Tenstorrent at US$6.2-billion, including the money raised, follows reports earlier this year that U.S. chip stalwarts Intel Corp. Intc-Q and Qualcomm Inc. Qcom-Q had both tried to buy Tenstorrent for upward of US$5-billion.

The Austin, Tex.-based company was founded in Toronto 10 years ago but relocated to the United States in 2023 after its first investor, Jim Keller – one of Silicon Valley’s top chip architects – became chief executive officer. The company’s Toronto office is still one of its largest hubs, where 200 of its 1,000 employees work. Tenstorrent also has operations in Silicon Valley; Tokyo; Belgrade, Serbia; and Bangalore, India.

The deal was led by two American private capital firms, Los Angeles-based Trace Capital, founded by National Football League linebacker-turned-private capital investor Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X LLC of New York. Other backers in the deal include Agostinelli Group, Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest, Cadence Venture Capital, Maverick Silicon, Eclipse Venture Equity, Protagonist Management LLC, Fidelity Management & Research Co., Morgan Stanley, Sandisk Corp. and T. Rowe Price.

Other notable past investors include South Korea’s AFW Partners, Samsung Securities and Hyundai Motor Group and LG Electronics, plus Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Export Development Canada and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan. Montreal-based Real Ventures was an early investor and generated a windfall return when it sold out last year, making back the entirety of its $88-million third fund.

Tenstorrent is building specialized hardware and software for processing a range of AI workloads, promising to deliver faster speeds than the graphics processing units (GPUs) sold by Nvidia. The upstart says its Galaxy-branded technology is equipped to run large language models that power chatbots and agents and for generating AI video.

Nvidia has become the world’s most valuable public company, surpassing US$5-trillion in market capitalization, by maintaining a tight grip on the market for AI computer chips owing to its in-demand GPUs, which have become the industry standard.

But Nvidia faces several challengers. A handful of AI compute startups are targeting the inference market, which refers to hardware for running AI models, as opposed to hardware for training models. Nvidia’s GPUs can do both but competitors are tailoring their hardware to deliver faster inference speeds. The market for inference, according to experts, is also expected to be much larger. AI company Cerebras Systems Inc., for example, went public earlier this year and has partnered with OpenAI.

Some of the biggest buyers of GPUs, namely OpenAI and Meta Platforms Inc., are also building their own chips designed to work with their AI models, both in partnership with Broadcom Inc. That could weaken Nvidia’s lock on the market and pricing power.

Nvidia, however, has ample resources. Last December it struck a deal to license technology from U.S. inference chip startup Groq Inc. and hired its executives.

Tenstorrent is looking to scale up manufacturing of its Galaxy servers for the fast-growing market for open-weight large language models that compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Open-weight models are free for developers to modify, unlike proprietary models. Anyone can download the parameters – numerical values that dictate the model’s behaviour – of an open-weight model and tweak them to have more control over how the model functions.

Tenstorrent is also licensing its intellectual property to others.

“We built one architecture and sell it at every size,” Mr. Keller said in a statement. “The future of compute is open, scalable and owned by the people building it.”

George Bousis, managing partner with Miami-based venture capital firm Protagonist, said in a statement “few companies design the chip and the software that runs on it. Tenstorrent does both, and its video generation results beat industry benchmarks ahead of our expectations. We are excited to double down” on the company.

This is Tenstorrent’s third nine-figure financing; it raised US$693-million in a late 2024 deal that valued the company at US$2-billion, and US$200-million-plus in spring 2021.

Tenstorrent was founded in Toronto by Ljubisa Bajic, a former colleague of Mr. Keller’s when they worked for chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (Mr. Keller has previously designed chips for AMD, Apple and Tesla). After Mr. Keller succeeded Mr. Bajic as Tenstorrent’s CEO in 2023, Mr. Bajic left to co-found another Toronto-based AI compute startup called Taalas; it was acquired by AMD in August for an undisclosed sum.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence semi-conductor maker Tenstorrent Holdings Inc. has raised US$1.5-billion in fresh capital as it steps up efforts to challenge industry behemoth Nvidia Corp Nvda-Q .

The financing, which values Tenstorrent at US$6.2-billion, including the money raised, follows reports earlier this year that U.S. chip stalwarts Intel Corp. Intc-Q and Qualcomm Inc. Qcom-Q had both tried to buy Tenstorrent for upward of US$5-billion.

The Austin, Tex.-based company was founded in Toronto 10 years ago but relocated to the United States in 2023 after its first investor, Jim Keller – one of Silicon Valley’s top chip architects – became chief executive officer. The company’s Toronto office is still one of its largest hubs, where 200 of its 1,000 employees work. Tenstorrent also has operations in Silicon Valley; Tokyo; Belgrade, Serbia; and Bangalore, India.

The deal was led by two American private capital firms, Los Angeles-based Trace Capital, founded by National Football League linebacker-turned-private capital investor Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X LLC of New York. Other backers in the deal include Agostinelli Group, Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest, Cadence Venture Capital, Maverick Silicon, Eclipse Venture Equity, Protagonist Management LLC, Fidelity Management & Research Co., Morgan Stanley, Sandisk Corp. and T. Rowe Price.

Other notable past investors include South Korea’s AFW Partners, Samsung Securities and Hyundai Motor Group and LG Electronics, plus Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Export Development Canada and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan. Montreal-based Real Ventures was an early investor and generated a windfall return when it sold out last year, making back the entirety of its $88-million third fund.

Tenstorrent is building specialized hardware and software for processing a range of AI workloads, promising to deliver faster speeds than the graphics processing units (GPUs) sold by Nvidia. The upstart says its Galaxy-branded technology is equipped to run large language models that power chatbots and agents and for generating AI video.

Nvidia has become the world’s most valuable public company, surpassing US$5-trillion in market capitalization, by maintaining a tight grip on the market for AI computer chips owing to its in-demand GPUs, which have become the industry standard.

But Nvidia faces several challengers. A handful of AI compute startups are targeting the inference market, which refers to hardware for running AI models, as opposed to hardware for training models. Nvidia’s GPUs can do both but competitors are tailoring their hardware to deliver faster inference speeds. The market for inference, according to experts, is also expected to be much larger. AI company Cerebras Systems Inc., for example, went public earlier this year and has partnered with OpenAI.

Some of the biggest buyers of GPUs, namely OpenAI and Meta Platforms Inc., are also building their own chips designed to work with their AI models, both in partnership with Broadcom Inc. That could weaken Nvidia’s lock on the market and pricing power.
Nvidia, however, has ample resources. Last December it struck a deal to license technology from U.S. inference chip startup Groq Inc. and hired its executives.

Tenstorrent is looking to scale up manufacturing of its Galaxy servers for the fast-growing market for open-weight large language models that compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Open-weight models are free for developers to modify, unlike proprietary models. Anyone can download the parameters – numerical values that dictate the model’s behaviour – of an open-weight model and tweak them to have more control over how the model functions.
Tenstorrent is also licensing its intellectual property to others.
“We built one architecture and sell it at every size,” Mr. Keller said in a statement. “The future of compute is open, scalable and owned by the people building it.”

George Bousis, managing partner with Miami-based venture capital firm Protagonist, said in a statement “few companies design the chip and the software that runs on it. Tenstorrent does both, and its video generation results beat industry benchmarks ahead of our expectations. We are excited to double down” on the company.
This is Tenstorrent’s third nine-figure financing; it raised US$693-million in a late 2024 deal that valued the company at US$2-billion, and US$200-million-plus in spring 2021.

Tenstorrent was founded in Toronto by Ljubisa Bajic, a former colleague of Mr. Keller’s when they worked for chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (Mr. Keller has previously designed chips for AMD, Apple and Tesla). After Mr. Keller succeeded Mr. Bajic as Tenstorrent’s CEO in 2023, Mr. Bajic left to co-found another Toronto-based AI compute startup called Taalas; it was acquired by AMD in August for an undisclosed sum.

stories.title: How community organizations are trying to fight voter apathy in this Toronto election
stories.summary: Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan
stories.content:
Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.

What looked like an outdoor festival at Lawrence Heights Community Centre was a fair held to raise civic engagement and encourage the city’s residents to vote in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The non-partisan event, organized by North York Harvest Food Bank, was attended by several groups including Voice the Vote, a joint initiative by Toronto Metropolitan University’s Democratic Engagement Exchange and United Way Greater Toronto.

Jonathan Dong stood behind a table, a mock ballot box and papers laid out in front him, talking to people and handing them Voice the Vote election handbooks.

“I think that participating in our democratic process, especially considering … how many people around the world aren’t able to cast a vote, is incredibly important,” Dong said in an interview.

“Showing up is how people know that you’re important, and if you don’t show up, you don’t get a say in what happens in the country, in your city, in your own backyard.”

In previous municipal elections, the city has seen what observers described as a worrying downward trend in voter participation.

In the 2023 mayoral byelection won by Olivia Chow, 37 per cent of eligible voters participated. Turnout was less than 30 per cent in the 2022 municipal election and about 41 per cent in 2018.

Across the province, overall voter turnout was nearly 33 per cent in the 2022 municipal elections and roughly 38 per cent in 2018, according to Association of Municipalities of Ontario data.

The turnout at Toronto’s advance polls in the upcoming election was robust, however, with more than 222,000 people casting their ballots early – the highest number in more than a decade.

Dong said he wants to do his part to battle voter apathy.

As a Chinese Canadian who lives in Richmond Hill north of Toronto, he said many voters in his community are particularly disconnected from the electoral process and as a result they don’t have enough representation in government.

“I think it’s very important to have the conversations within these communities to increase that representation and increase our voter turnout,” he said.

At the voter information event, two white posters glued on a wall were decorated with colourful sticky notes on which members of the community wrote why voting matters to them.

“Support for unhoused neighbours,” “a clean city,” and “mental health safety” were among the dozens of notes.

Meanwhile, two taxis were seen ferrying voters to advance polling sites and then bringing them back to the community centre.

Warren Epstein was among those who voted early. He stood by Rania Ahmed, the project lead at Democratic Engagement Exchange, and asked her to write a few messages for him on a poster that focused on affordability and more support for seniors like himself.

“You need people who are going to do things for the people and the senior citizens, and you want to make sure that the right people are voted in for the right activities,” Epstein said.

“And it is time for change.”

Ahmed said Voice the Vote’s 15-member team is trying to help people “feel more hopeful about their future” by leveraging their own communities.

“A lot of people actually don’t know … that the issue they care about is actually tied to their municipal government and not the provincial (or) federal,” she said.

Ahmed said the initiative also provides micro-grants for organizations and individuals who come up with project or event ideas for elections and civic engagement in Toronto, York and Peel regions.

The funding for the initiative comes from United Way. The charity’s senior public affairs officer, Abby Tait, said while the organization has taken part in similar efforts in previous elections, Voice the Vote is a more thought out project aimed at increasing turnout across the city, including among immigrant communities and younger people.

Tait said the idea was born in the summer of 2025, after back-to-back provincial and federal elections.

“So we kind of seized this long runway and said, ‘let’s build something really ambitious,’” she said.

“We developed this kind of community-led project that would really be focused on grounding the municipal election in the local issues that matter to people.”

She said Voice the Vote is using the United Way’s vast network of around 300 agencies to reach communities.

“You can’t have a healthy community if people feel like they have no agency in their community, that they’re not connected to it,” she said.

Roughly 200 people attended the event in Lawrence Heights earlier this month, and around 20 of them were taken to an advance polling site to cast their ballots, said Sarah Watson, the director of community engagement at North York Harvest Food Bank.

Watson said while the food bank can provide emergency support for people in need, it can’t change systemic issues such as lack of affordable housing, food insecurity or unsafe communities.

“We’re really trying to connect them with the electoral process so they can have some influence over who is in government and who is making changes on these issues,” she said.

“A lot of our community members feel like their voices aren’t heard … and when that happens again and again, it can be frustrating and it can cause people to disengage,” Watson added. “We really want to encourage people that it is worth participating, that their voices should be heard.”

Event participant Esther Johnson agreed, saying she will head to the polls on election day because she believes every vote counts.

For people who choose not to vote in this election, “it’s their loss,” she said. “If they’re not interested in… having the input, don’t complain.”

More than 50 candidates are vying to become the mayor of Canada’s largest city, but polls suggest incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford are locked in a fierce competition one week before election day.

Lydia Miljan, a political-science professor at the University of Windsor, said there are reasons to believe more people will participate in Toronto’s electoral process this time around, given the tight race between the two leading mayoral candidates.

“It just depends on how closely people are following Toronto politics right now, and I think it’s getting in my feeds even down here,” she said. “So, it is heating up quite significantly.”

Miljan said voter turnout is generally lower in municipal elections because it can be overwhelming to take part in a process that elects the mayor, councillors and school board trustees all at once.

She said the lack of political parties giving people a “shortcut” on where local election candidates stand, and the movement of voters between wards in large cities can further suppress turnout.

But in order to have a healthy democracy, residents need to show up, she said.

“It is incumbent upon citizens, regardless of how long they’ve lived in that city, to really make an effort to cast their ballot.”

Event participant Esther Johnson agreed, saying she will head to the polls on election day because she believes every vote counts.
For people who choose not to vote in this election, “it’s their loss,” she said. “If they’re not interested in… having the input, don’t complain.”

More than 50 candidates are vying to become the mayor of Canada’s largest city, but polls suggest incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford are locked in a fierce competition one week before election day.

Lydia Miljan, a political-science professor at the University of Windsor, said there are reasons to believe more people will participate in Toronto’s electoral process this time around, given the tight race between the two leading mayoral candidates.
“It just depends on how closely people are following Toronto politics right now, and I think it’s getting in my feeds even down here,” she said. “So, it is heating up quite significantly.”
Miljan said voter turnout is generally lower in municipal elections because it can be overwhelming to take part in a process that elects the mayor, councillors and school board trustees all at once.
She said the lack of political parties giving people a “shortcut” on where local election candidates stand, and the movement of voters between wards in large cities can further suppress turnout.
But in order to have a healthy democracy, residents need to show up, she said.
“It is incumbent upon citizens, regardless of how long they’ve lived in that city, to really make an effort to cast their ballot.”

stories.title: New Brunswick data centre debate highlights cross-country tension over AI facilities
stories.summary: Chris Watson says he was very concerned when he reviewed a New Brunswick business development agency's recent correspondence about data centres.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Chris Watson says he was very concerned when he reviewed a New Brunswick business development agency’s recent correspondence about data centres.

Over the past year, he has been at the forefront of citizen-led opposition to a major data centre project in his neighbourhood in Saint John, N.B.

But when he reviewed the correspondence, released through right-to-information legislation by Opportunities New Brunswick, he discovered the existence of another proposal from a company trying to bring one of the energy-hungry projects to his area.

“It’s not surprising, but it’s just deeply disappointing,” he said in a recent interview with The Canadian Press.

Watson said the correspondence shows how New Brunswick is entertaining data centre proposals without sharing important information with the people who will be most affected.

He also said it shows how the provincial government is scrambling to review projects without adequate rules or guidelines to ensure it can protect both citizens and the environment.

NB Power, the province’s Crown-owned electric utility, confirmed there are 10 applications from data centre projects that would need up to 900 megawatts of power.

But the utility is declining to identify all of the projects on this list, saying that the applications are confidential. A spokesperson would not confirm if the publicly known projects are on the list.

The Liberal provincial government sees the plants as a potential opportunity to generate economic growth through tax revenue, private sector buy-in and job creation.

The debate playing out in New Brunswick highlights the challenges facing provincial and municipal governments as they face a surge in applications for data centres.

The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.

The New Brunswick government is currently working on a policy framework for data centre development that it recently sought public feedback on.

“Data centre development could be an opportunity for New Brunswick to generate economic growth through tax revenue, private sector investment, construction and permanent job creation, and potential offshoot economic and community benefits,” the provincial government said on its feedback page.

Watson, who is part of a grassroots community group called Save Lorneville, says the government should impose a moratorium on new data centre projects until it has stronger policies in place to protect residents, businesses and the environment.

Among the publicly known proposed data centres in New Brunswick, none have acquired final approval.

A 400-megawatt data centre is at the heart of a $2 billion artificial intelligence hub proposed through a joint venture by Beacon Data Centers of Alberta and U.S. firm VoltaGrid.

The Beacon Data Centers project will get about half its power from the grid and the rest from an on-site power plant. It’s currently under regulatory review.

Billed as Atlantic Canada’s first hyperscale artificial intelligence facility, the project sparked intense backlash from some residents who lived near the industrial park where it’s set to be built, including Watson and his group.

Just this month, Fredericton-based Faster Than Light introduced its plan for a $2.7 billion, 375-megawatt data centre publicly for the first time.

And then there is the proposal from U.S. firm Cross River Infrastructure Partners that was discovered by Watson and his neighbourhood advocacy group. The proposal is located in the same Spruce Lake Industrial Park as the Beacon Data Centers project.

Cross River Infrastructure wrote to the Opportunities NB minister in a letter dated April 28 asking for 50 megawatts of power for a “large-scale data centre campus” that could include future expansion.

Meanwhile, the NB Power spokesperson said the 10 applications it has received will not necessarily be approved to connect to the grid. The spokesperson also said large projects like data centres would require contractual flexibility to protect the grid and avoid pressure on customer rates.

Thomas Bateman, a political science professor at St. Thomas University in Fredericton, said people are opposed to data centres, in part, because of anxiety about artificial intelligence.

“They don’t know if it’s good or bad — or if it’s going to mean the end of civilization as we know it, or if its going to cure cancer,” he said. Bateman added the other big point of contention is the amount of energy required to run the facillities.

A majority of Canadians aren’t sold on data centres, according to new polling from the non-profit Angus Reid Institute.

The poll found 64 per cent of Canadians say their own respective provincial governments should limit the development of large data centres. Less than one in five people would encourage more, while the rest were not sure or couldn’t say.

The online survey was conducted from Sept. 8-16 among a representative randomized sample of Canadian adults who are members of the Angus Reid Forum. Online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

Canadian opposition to big data centres appears to be at odds with the federal Liberal government’s goals. Ottawa is promoting a major AI data-centre buildout as part of its sovereign-compute and digital-sovereignty agenda.

And despite the political pressure, some provincial governments haven’t shied away from capitalizing on the potential the big facilities have as a revenue stream.

Bell Canada is building what’s expected to be the country’s largest Canadian-owned data centre outside Regina, Sask.

The $1.7-billion plant, which will use 300 megawatts of power from the provincial grid, was approved before Saskatchewan’s new framework was in place.

In Alberta, Meta earlier this year announced a $13-billion-plus, one-gigawatt AI data centre in Sturgeon County, north of Edmonton. Hundreds of people protested against the project and the Alberta’s technology minister was booed at a round of town halls.

Approaches have varied in Eastern Canada.

In September, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said his Progressive Conservative government would consider proposals from the sector due to changing conditions like geopolitics and Ottawa’s stance.

Meanwhile, Newfoundland and Labrador’s energy minister said the province could sell excess power to one.

In Quebec, the power utility is proposing to double the rates that data centres currently pay as large-power customers in the province.

A consultant hired by Hydro-Quebec also told a public hearing that energy consumption from data centres in North America could increase by 133 per cent between 2024 and 2030.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY (October 19, 2026) –Middlesex County is proud to be celebrating Local Government Week and the important role municipal government plays in building strong communities.

This week, Middlesex County will highlight the people, partnerships, and services key to its success. Through essential services like infrastructure, housing, paramedic services, long-term care, and community supports, Middlesex County staff are focused on making our communities great places to call home.

"Local Government Week is an opportunity to recognize the essential role we have in supporting residents," said Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke. "Local governments are working tirelessly to build strong, vibrant, and welcoming communities now and into the future.”

Middlesex County serves a large and diverse geographic area, supporting communities across the region by collaboration with local municipalities, community organizations, and the provincial and federal governments.

Residents are encouraged to take this opportunity to learn more about local government and the services provided by Middlesex County. Join us on our social media channels each day this week to learn more our services and initiatives.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

MEDIA CONTACT:

Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division mediarelations@middlesex.ca

Middlesex County is a great place to call home. Our modern telecommunications infrastructure, excellent health and social services, retail shopping, recreation facilities, beautiful landscapes and great people, make Middlesex the place to be!

MIDDLESEX COUNTY (October 19, 2026) –Middlesex County is proud to be celebrating Local Government Week and the important role municipal government plays in building strong communities.

This week, Middlesex County will highlight the people, partnerships, and services key to its success. Through essential services like infrastructure, housing, paramedic services, long-term care, and community supports, Middlesex County staff are focused on making our communities great places to call home.

"Local Government Week is an opportunity to recognize the essential role we have in supporting residents," said Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke. "Local governments are working tirelessly to build strong, vibrant, and welcoming communities now and into the future.”

Middlesex County serves a large and diverse geographic area, supporting communities across the region by collaboration with local municipalities, community organizations, and the provincial and federal governments.

Residents are encouraged to take this opportunity to learn more about local government and the services provided by Middlesex County. Join us on our social media channels each day this week to learn more our services and initiatives.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

stories.title: Are our drug laws making things worse?
stories.summary: A look at the politicization of harm reduction efforts and how initiatives like Dulf could be the solution to B.C.'s drug crisis.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
A B.C. Supreme Court judge found that a section of Canada’s Controlled Drug and Substances Act was unconstitutional, and gave Ottawa six months to fix it.

The ruling came after a pair of drug activists, Eris Nyx and Jeremy Kalicum, were convicted on drug trafficking charges after their downtown Vancouver compassion club, DULF, was raided by police in 2023. Their charges have since been stayed.

Host Maria Kestane speaks to Michelle Gamage, a health reporter from The Tyee , and Dr. Dan Small, a medical anthropologist with the University of British Columbia, to discuss the politicization of harm reduction efforts, and how initiatives like DULF could be the solution to B.C.’s drug crisis.

stories.title: Manitoba grieves with CFB Wainwright after deadly fire
stories.summary: Several Manitoba politicians are offering their condolences to those who were killed and seriously injured at Canadian Forces Base in Wainwright on Saturday.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Manitoba politicians are offering their condolences to those who were killed and seriously injured at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday.

Four people were killed and dozens of others injured after a grass fire ignited during a live-fire training exercise and rapidly spread in high winds. Flags at CFB Winnipeg and federal buildings across the province were lowered to half-mast Sunday.

Premier Wab Kinew called the fire is a terrible tragedy and said his heart goes out to everyone affected.

“Manitoba stands ready to help in any way we can,” Kinew said in a social media post.

Jeff Fawcett, mayor of Brandon, said the loss is felt across the nation. He described Brandon as a “military city” because of its proximity to CFB Shilo.

Fawcett said some people from CFB Shilo could be deployed to Wainwright or have connections to the base, as cross-training is common.

Watch the video above for the full story.
