stories.title: B.C. Conservatives platform promises $2.6 B in growth, $10.8B deficit
stories.summary: The British Columbia Conservatives say their platform will create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives say their election platform amounts to restraint, not austerity, and will create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030.

The document released Sunday, with related costs, says that if Gross Domestic Product grows by 2.5 per cent in 2027, 2.8 per cent in 2028, and 3.2 per cent in 2029, the province will collect an additional $2.62 billion, compared with the Ndp’s own forecast.

But the figures assume that provincial growth would exceed national growth rates. The July forecast from the Bank of Canada projects GDP growth in 2027 to reach 1.4 per cent and 1.8 per cent by 2028.

The latest report from the International Monetary Fund also says that advanced economies would grow by 1.9 per cent next year, while overall growth rates for 2027 would be three per cent. That overall figure includes growth rates for economies like China’s and India’s.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson didn’t make himself available after the platform was released on Sunday, but said at an earlier event that he reviewed the document before it was made public.

“I just had a final look at it in the car on the way over here, and it will be open for criticism, I suppose, this afternoon. But it looks really great to me. I’m really excited about the opportunity to certainly attack the deficit and grow the economy in this province.”

The platform says that traditional industries like mining, energy and agriculture are all fundamental to British Columbia’s prosperity.

Conservatives, it says, will quickly restore confidence in these industries, cut red tape, speed up permits for projects, and support more production and processing in B.C. .

It says the net new “revenue from unleashing growth” includes a 15 per cent increase in gas production over the previous forecasts by 2029-2030.

Conservatives say their plan to “supercharge” the economy will bring in new revenue without cutting front-line services or raising taxes, while giving struggling taxpayers and businesses needed relief.

Promised tax cuts, which were announced earlier in the campaign, include raising the provincial basic personal exemption amount from $13,126 to $32,000, and no provincial sales tax on major projects until they start operating, so taxes arrive with revenue.

Starting in 2026, those tax cuts would add up to $11.3 billion by 2030, the platform says.

The Conservatives say they would fully fund health care, and their plan would add new operational spending estimated at $1.42 billion per year, with growth revenue exceeding spending every year.

Doerkson had promised the platform would be out before people had an opportunity to vote.

It was released late Sunday afternoon ahead of the Oct. 24 general vote, although advanced voting began Oct. 16.

The platform says a Conservative government, if elected, would chop spending by freezing outside hiring, cutting consultants, and will review spending on numerous government ministries.

The 71-page platform says the core review would trim about $1.8 billion over four years, while the hiring freeze and attrition of staff outside the front lines would save about $2 billion over the same period.

Doerkson said in a letter introducing his party’s platform that his job would be about making the lives of B.C. residents easier and better.

“I’ll work to get the economy moving, bring your costs down, and create good jobs. I’ll fully fund and protect our health care, and fix the mess David Eby and the NDP have made so that British Columbians aren’t dying on wait-lists or going to closed ERs when they need help.”

The New Democrats say the platform is “packed full of shell games, wildly unrealistic growth projections, and deep health care cuts hidden in plain sight.”

The NDP said in a statement released Sunday that the Conservatives claim they would save $2 billion a year from cuts to the contingencies envelope, but that funds health care caseload pressures and other unavoidable expenses like fighting wildfires.

“Cutting contingencies is a backdoor health-care cut,” it said.

The NDP said in an earlier statement Sunday that Doerkson has a budget gap of $6 billion after announcing items such as a new women and children’s hospital and changing the Massey tunnel replacement from the current plan of a tunnel to a bridge.

It added that the party’s growth claims are unrealistic.

“Doerkson seems to plan to pretend he can, quote, ‘flip a switch’ and make billions of dollars appear out of thin air. It doesn’t work like that,” the NDP says in its statement.

stories.title: Fire risk was low before sudden wind shift sparked deadly base fire: CAF memo
stories.summary: An internal Canadian Armed Forces memo says the fire index was low for a scheduled live-ammunition training exercise Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta, when an “unexpected and sudden wind change” sparked a runaway grass fire that killed four soldiers and seriously injured dozens more. “During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds...
stories.author: Charles Rusnell
stories.content:
An internal Canadian Armed Forces memo says the fire index was low for a scheduled live-ammunition training exercise Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta, when an “unexpected and sudden wind change” sparked a runaway grass fire that killed four soldiers and seriously injured dozens more.

“During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” the memo states.

Earlier on Saturday, Environment Canada had issued a high-wind warning for Alberta. Gusts of up to 100 km/h in some parts of the province tipped over semi-trailer trucks and toppled trees.

Issued Sunday by the Strategic Joint Staff (SJS) and obtained by Global News, the memo also said the fire jumped a fire guard and spread outside the base, forcing the evacuation of one family home. The fire has been contained but is still burning.

The SJS directly reports to the chief of defence staff, Canada’s highest-ranking military officer.

The staff memo specifies that the dead and injured are from C or Charlie Company, Third Battalion of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, which is based at Edmonton Garrison.

Four soldiers were killed, another 31 suffered “very serious or serious” injuries, and six to eight others had minor injuries, it said.

Fifteen soldiers were intubated and sent to the University of Alberta and Royal Alexandra hospitals in Edmonton.

The memo cautioned that the situation was “fluid” and “these casualty reporting numbers are considered accurate but May change over time with ongoing assessments of casualty status.”

At a news conference Sunday afternoon, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland identified the four deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, and Privates Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Their families have been notified.

Rutland said the training was to prepare the soldiers for a global response task force “ready to move within hours to any hotspot around the world,” and for deployment to Latvia in April and May to bolster the brigade there.

“This was high-intensity combat training with live munitions.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference it was one of the worst tragedies on Canadian soil in peacetime.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost,” Carney said, adding that, to honour them, flags on all federal buildings will be flown at half-mast.

The Royal Canadian Air Force dispatched seven Griffon helicopters from Edmonton, and one Hercules aircraft from Winnipeg.

Ten search-and-rescue technicians parachuted from the Hercules onto a field in Wainwright, a town of about 6,500 people, about 200 km east of Edmonton, near the Saskatchewan border.

The non-profit charity, Stars, or Shock Trauma Air Rescue Service, dispatched air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, and nearby towns sent ground ambulances to assist in the transfer of the injured.

Investigators with the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service are en route to Wainwright, and the RCMP have offered investigative support, the memo states, adding that the process of casualty confirmation and next-of-kin notification has begun.

stories.title: Four Canadian soldiers killed by 'uncommon, rapid' grass fire at CFB Wainwright: officials
stories.summary: A fire broke out at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Here's all the details we know about the casualties and how it happened.
stories.author: Cindy Tran
stories.content:
Federal and provincial officials on the ground in Edmonton on Sunday afternoon provided an update on the fire that broke out at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright which led to four people dying and 39 more injured.

Maj.-Gen. L.W. Rutland, Commander of the 1st Canadian Division battalion, told reporters soldiers were undergoing a preparatory training activity at the CFB Wainwright when a grass fire broke out at 4 p.m. on Saturday. Rutland said the fire began a kilometre away when the wind shifted.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” Rutland said.

“This was uncommon, rapid and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it.”

Rutland said despite the forecast for wind conditions, the weather for the majority of Saturday was within standard protocol — well below 50 kilometres.

Within 20 to 30 minutes of the incident being reported, the first evacuation occurred and within less than an hour and a half there were multiple partners on the ground. Rutland described the response as “extremely rapid action” which is by design.

Rutland said parachuters that were flown in were search and rescue technicians part of air force efforts and government efforts to get more capacity on the ground as soon as possible.

The training activity was for the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry for two roles — the Global Response Task Force and to go to Latvia in the spring. Rutland said it was the Charlie Company or “C Company” that was impacted.

There are about 84 soldiers in the C Company in the 350-plus range for the entire battalion, Rutland said.

Rutland said the activity was “high-intensity combat training” with live munitions. He said soldiers were split between throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a “section attack” where 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.

The fire moved quickly and struck what is called the administration area of the section attack range — the grenade range was not affected.

The size of the fire has not been determined, but Rutland said range control was aware there was a fire for several hours and were monitoring it.

Rutland said soldiers train for all types of conditions and if protocols needs to change following the ongoing investigation they will. He would not comment on whether not the incident was preventable.

A fire marshal is currently on the ground investigating the cause of the fire. Rutland said the cause is not believed to be related to oil and gas facilities and teams have gone in to ensure the infrastructure is not damage with a preliminary assessment has determined it is not.

During the training exercise on Saturday grenade launchers, grenades and smaller arms ammunition were moving through the training area. Rutland said the cause of the fire could have been any of the listed or none at all.

The cause could be a multitude of things, Rutland said.

Rutland said with the number of casualties — four dead, 39 hospitalized and 19 of whom are in critical condition, along with the complexity it will take nearly a month for the board of inquiry to make a report to the public.

The families of the injured and deceased have all be notified.

Premier Danielle Smith said on Saturday 30 emergency units including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft were deployed directly Wainwright with dedicated medical teams across the Edmonton corridor and beyond.

“To handle the sudden surge, code orange protocols were activated at the facilities managing the rapid influx of injured patients,” Smith said.

“An active emergency response was sustained across the system for more than 10 hours, with patients transported and receiving care at facilities across the province.”

There were no armoured vehicles on site as it is a light infantry battalion, but there were trucks, ambulances and light vehicles on site. There is no information on the impact the fire had on vehicles.

The C Company has been moved out of the training area and the rest will move back home for a certain period of time. The remainder of the battalion took a “maintenance day” on Sunday and did not train to allow leadership to determine what will happen in the coming days.

“The rest of the battalion is still slated to go to Latvia, so they will pick up this training and and do it. Whether it’ll be tomorrow at a later date, I can’t say at this minute,” Rutland said.

paragraphs: Federal and provincial officials on the ground in Edmonton on Sunday afternoon provided an update on the fire that broke out at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright which led to four people dying and 39 more injured.

Maj.-Gen. L.W. Rutland, Commander of the 1st Canadian Division battalion, told reporters soldiers were undergoing a preparatory training activity at the CFB Wainwright when a grass fire broke out at 4 p.m. on Saturday. Rutland said the fire began a kilometre away when the wind shifted.
“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” Rutland said.
“This was uncommon, rapid and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it.”
Rutland said despite the forecast for wind conditions, the weather for the majority of Saturday was within standard protocol — well below 50 kilometres.

Within 20 to 30 minutes of the incident being reported, the first evacuation occurred and within less than an hour and a half there were multiple partners on the ground. Rutland described the response as “extremely rapid action” which is by design.
Rutland said parachuters that were flown in were search and rescue technicians part of air force efforts and government efforts to get more capacity on the ground as soon as possible.

The training activity was for the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry for two roles — the Global Response Task Force and to go to Latvia in the spring. Rutland said it was the Charlie Company or “C Company” that was impacted.
There are about 84 soldiers in the C Company in the 350-plus range for the entire battalion, Rutland said.

Rutland said the activity was “high-intensity combat training” with live munitions. He said soldiers were split between throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a “section attack” where 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.
The fire moved quickly and struck what is called the administration area of the section attack range — the grenade range was not affected.
The size of the fire has not been determined, but Rutland said range control was aware there was a fire for several hours and were monitoring it.

Rutland said soldiers train for all types of conditions and if protocols needs to change following the ongoing investigation they will. He would not comment on whether not the incident was preventable.

A fire marshal is currently on the ground investigating the cause of the fire. Rutland said the cause is not believed to be related to oil and gas facilities and teams have gone in to ensure the infrastructure is not damage with a preliminary assessment has determined it is not.

During the training exercise on Saturday grenade launchers, grenades and smaller arms ammunition were moving through the training area. Rutland said the cause of the fire could have been any of the listed or none at all.
The cause could be a multitude of things, Rutland said.

Rutland said with the number of casualties — four dead, 39 hospitalized and 19 of whom are in critical condition, along with the complexity it will take nearly a month for the board of inquiry to make a report to the public.
The families of the injured and deceased have all be notified.

Premier Danielle Smith said on Saturday 30 emergency units including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft were deployed directly Wainwright with dedicated medical teams across the Edmonton corridor and beyond.
“To handle the sudden surge, code orange protocols were activated at the facilities managing the rapid influx of injured patients,” Smith said.
“An active emergency response was sustained across the system for more than 10 hours, with patients transported and receiving care at facilities across the province.”

There were no armoured vehicles on site as it is a light infantry battalion, but there were trucks, ambulances and light vehicles on site. There is no information on the impact the fire had on vehicles.

The C Company has been moved out of the training area and the rest will move back home for a certain period of time. The remainder of the battalion took a “maintenance day” on Sunday and did not train to allow leadership to determine what will happen in the coming days.
“The rest of the battalion is still slated to go to Latvia, so they will pick up this training and and do it. Whether it’ll be tomorrow at a later date, I can’t say at this minute,” Rutland said.

stories.title: 4 killed in CFB Wainwright fire identified as dozens remain in hospital
stories.summary: Four members died in the incident at CFB Wainwright, with Alberta's premier saying more than three dozen have been injured and are in hospital.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four service members killed in the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland told reporters on Sunday afternoon that Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.c., had died. Their families have been notified.

“Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those we lost and with the injured members still receiving care,” Rutland said during a news conference. “We stand with the teammates, friends, and units affected by this terrible tragedy. The well-being of our people is our highest priority.”

Dozens more were injured in the incident.

In a post on Facebook, Prince Albert, Sask., resident Patricia Farrell confirmed her son Shaun was among those killed in Saturday’s incident.

“It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our heavenly father,” she wrote on Facebook. “We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time.”

Farrell asked for privacy as the family grieves.

All four members were serving at CFB Edmonton with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Light Infantry, and participating in a training exercise at Wainwright.

“(It was) to prepare for two roles, to become what’s called our global response task force, ready to move within hours to any hotspot around the world,” Rutland said, adding it was also to prepare to go to Latvia in April and May to bolster the brigade there. “So this was high intensity combat training with live munitions.”

Rutland said during the training, a grass fire ignited in the training area. An investigation into the cause of the fire is underway, but uncommonly strong winds caused it to spread rapidly and change direction towards the range administrative area.

Military and civilian emergency services responded to control the fire, which the Municipal District of Wainwright said was being held as of late night Saturday.

Environment Canada had issued a warning of high winds for Alberta earlier in the day, with a windstorm hitting large areas of the province. Gusts reached up to 100 km/h, toppling trees, sending signs flying, and rolling garbage cans down streets.

Asked about the weather conditions, Rutland said forces train in all types of conditions and never know what environment they’ll face. But while the majority of the day saw weather within standard procedures, when the incident occurred the weather “was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith also spoke at the news conference and provided more details on the dozens of people injured in the incident.

She said 39 patients were being cared for in hospital, and at least 19 were in critical condition.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Oro-Medonte, Ont., said in a social media post Sunday morning that her eldest son was among those injured.

“Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright,” Keane said.

She went on to say while she’s staying in the mayoral race, she was was travelling to Alberta to be with her son and family and would be unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the campaign.

“We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community,” Keane said.

Within the past 24 hours, patients were transferred from the Wainwright Health Centre to four facilities, the University of Alberta Hospital, the Royal Alexandra Hospital, the Foothills Medical Centre, and the Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

— with files from Global News’ Jeff Semple, Karen Bartko and Ashleigh Stewart

stories.title: What we know about deadly explosion and fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after an explosion and fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after an explosion and fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.

Thirty-nine people were hospitalized, 19 of them in are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday at the military base east of Edmonton. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as the fire spread rapidly, prompting a major medical response across the region.

The Canadian Armed Forces says it is still assessing the full extent of the impact.

Live Updates: Officials providing update after ‘fast-moving’ CFB Wainwright fire kills 4 soldiers

Here is what we know so far:

Four military members killed, dozens injured

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths and injuries Sunday.

Family members of those killed have been notified, Carney said. Those affected included personnel from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers serving with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

In his remarks on Sunday, Carney described the scale of the tragedy.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta. What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces in Canadian soil in peace time,” he said.

In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland told reporters that the fire broke out during a training exercise ahead of the soldiers’ deployment to Latvia.

The officials at CFB Wainwright were aware of the fire for several hours before it turned toward the training area, Rutland said. Despite the knowledge, the soldiers continued to carry out their exercises.

CAF officials believe there was no damage to oil and gas infrastructure as a result of the fire, Rutland said.

CFB Wainwright victims identified

The following members were killed during the fire at CFB Wainwright, according to Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland:

Sergeant Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Alta., from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry

Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Aidan Goulding from North Vancouver, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Nearly 40 patients receiving treatment at regional hospitals

The medical response has placed significant demands on hospitals and emergency services in the Edmonton region.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, the CEO of Acute Care Alberta told reporters 19 people are in critical condition, eight are stable, and 12 are ambulatory and are receiving care for injuries that can be assessed without admission.

Dr. Steve Fisher, an emergency physician at Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CTV News Edmonton on Sunday that patients had sustained burns of varying severity, with the most seriously affected being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital, which has a burn intensive care unit.

The scale of the response prompted Acute Care Alberta to ask residents to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible Saturday night, unless they required emergency care.

The agency said “significant resources” were needed from Emergency Health Services and Edmonton-area emergency departments into the night.

Stars Air Ambulance dispatched two air ambulances from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Helicopters and two aircraft also landed at a nearby medical evacuation site as emergency personnel worked to transport and treat the injured.

Soldiers were working with hand grenades: CAF

The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and reservists were taking part in high-intensity training ahead of deploymen, Rutland said.

The Charlie Company, or C Company soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a section attack, with 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy when the fire broke out, he added.

Code Orange lifted after emergency response

A Code Orange is activated when a mass-casualty event places pressure on the health-care system because of a surge in patients. The code remained in effect for more than 10 hours before being lifted shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday.

Investigation underway, terrorism not likely

The Canadian Armed Forces will undertake a board of inquiry to examine the events of Oct. 17, Rutland said.

A spokesperson for National Defence said Sunday there were no indications the incident was the result of terrorist activity.

“As emergency responders continue their work and the situation continues to evolve, the full extent of the impact remains under assessment. Our immediate priority is supporting those affected and notifying next of kin. We will not confirm casualty or injury details until that process is complete,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton.

“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity.”

Retired major-general David Fraser, a CTV military analyst and former commander of Nato forces in southern Afghanistan, described the incident as the worst training tragedy he had witnessed during his military career.

“We are now dealing with the worst tragedy that I’ve seen in my entire career,” Fraser told CTV News Channel.

Fraser, who was previously posted at Wainwright and trained there extensively, said he had seen no indications the incident was anything other than an accident.

He said Canadian military bases have established safety procedures for live-fire and other training exercises. He expects those procedures to remain in place until investigators determine whether changes are needed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was travelling to Edmonton on Sunday to receive a briefing on the latest developments. He said the Department of National Defence was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

I am on my way to Edmonton. I will get briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident that occurred at CFB Wainwright. The Department of National Defence continues to work closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Thank you to first… — David McGuinty (@DavidMcGuinty) October 18, 2026

High winds contributed to rapidly spreading fire

The Municipal District of Wainwright said high winds caused the fire to spread rapidly into the surrounding area Saturday.

Officials said the fire crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being managed south of Wainwright.

Crews faced volatile conditions as parts of Alberta experienced wind gusts of up to 100 km/h. Municipal information officers told CTV News Edmonton late Saturday that the spread was under control.

Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.

The fire is not believed to be a result of oil and gas infrastructure or outside interference, but the cause is still under investigation.

Video shows fire burning near CFB Wainwright

Video captured from private property about one kilometre from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday shows flames burning in the area as smoke billows across the sky.

The footage offers a glimpse of the fire that prompted a major emergency response at the Alberta military base.

Military families urged to seek support

The Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre opened Sunday to support military families affected by the incident.

Families were invited to connect in a safe and supportive space as they dealt with the aftermath.

People needing additional assistance can call the Family Information Line at 1-800-866-4546 for free, confidential support, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

Officials have said supporting those affected and notifying next of kin remain immediate priorities

Canadian Blood Services calls for donations

Canadian Blood Services is offering its condolences to those affected by the CFB Wainwright fire and encouraging Canadians to donate blood to help support injured patients.

“Our top priority is ensuring patients in Canada receive the blood and blood products they need. We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” a media spokesperson wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton on Sunday.

The organization said appointments remained available in Alberta and across Canada, adding that donations in the coming weeks would help maintain the national blood supply.

“We are grateful to the many people who have already reached out to ask how they can help. Donating blood is one meaningful way to support patients in Canada, both now and in the weeks ahead. Many appointments are still available throughout Alberta and across Canada, and donations in the coming weeks will help to keep our national inventory strong.”

Political and military leaders offer condolences

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the loss of life and injuries as heartbreaking and said her government was working with federal officials and local authorities.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.

Alberta is mourning alongside the Canadian Armed Forces and the families, friends and colleagues of those affected by the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright yesterday. The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I… pic.twitter.com/pKIG6vQuPS — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 18, 2026

Smith said she would travel to Edmonton to meet with provincial ministers and federal officials. The province activated its Emergency Management Cabinet Co-ordination Committee and raised the Provincial Emergency Coordination Centre to Level 3.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also offered assistance with recovery efforts, saying his province stood “ready to help.”

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said .

Maritime premiers also expressed condolences , noting the close ties between military personnel, their families and communities across Canada.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said the tragedy would be deeply felt in the region surrounding the base.

“If you live in east central Alberta in the Wainwright area, this base is part of your life, “ Kenney told CTV News Channel on Sunday. “You get to know the soldiers and the base staff (is) a very large part of the whole broader community out in that sparsely populated area.”

Kenney said Albertans have a “deep regard for the sacrifices taken by our men and women in uniform.”

Nato’s Military Committee also offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a full recovery.

On behalf of the Nato Military Committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured. Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many… pic.twitter.com/3zdIR9k9g5 — Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone - Nato CMC (@CMC_NATO) October 18, 2026

Community and military personnel await further answers

The tragedy has affected military families and communities well beyond Wainwright, as personnel from bases across Canada were among those involved.

A Barrie-area mayoral candidate, Cathy Keane, said her eldest son was critically injured in the incident. In a social media post Sunday, she said she would travel to Alberta to be with him and her family.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she said.

Election day locations in Wainwright to open as planned

Elections Alberta says voting locations in Wainwright will be opened as planned on Oct. 19, officials told reporters.

Eligible voters in the area will be able to cast their 10 ballots at the Wainwright Communiplex and the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29 Wainwright.

Pro-Canada rally goes ahead in Edmonton

A pro-Canada rally was held in Edmonton on Sunday and while attendees were focused on the referendum on Monday, the incident in Wainwright was still top of mind. Organizer Gil McGowan said the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.

McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, thanked first responders from around Canada and said it’s a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.

Albertans are set to vote on Monday whether the province should remain in Canada or if a referendum should be held on separation.

Smith told reporters the upcoming referendum on Monday will go ahead.

Thirty-nine people were hospitalized, 19 of them in are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday at the military base east of Edmonton. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as the fire spread rapidly, prompting a major medical response across the region.
The Canadian Armed Forces says it is still assessing the full extent of the impact.

Here is what we know so far:
Four military members killed, dozens injured
Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths and injuries Sunday.

Family members of those killed have been notified, Carney said. Those affected included personnel from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers serving with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
In his remarks on Sunday, Carney described the scale of the tragedy.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta. What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces in Canadian soil in peace time,” he said.
In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland told reporters that the fire broke out during a training exercise ahead of the soldiers’ deployment to Latvia.

The officials at CFB Wainwright were aware of the fire for several hours before it turned toward the training area, Rutland said. Despite the knowledge, the soldiers continued to carry out their exercises.
CAF officials believe there was no damage to oil and gas infrastructure as a result of the fire, Rutland said.
CFB Wainwright victims identified
The following members were killed during the fire at CFB Wainwright, according to Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland:
Sergeant Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Alta., from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry
Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Private Aidan Goulding from North Vancouver, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Nearly 40 patients receiving treatment at regional hospitals
The medical response has placed significant demands on hospitals and emergency services in the Edmonton region.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, the CEO of Acute Care Alberta told reporters 19 people are in critical condition, eight are stable, and 12 are ambulatory and are receiving care for injuries that can be assessed without admission.

Dr. Steve Fisher, an emergency physician at Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CTV News Edmonton on Sunday that patients had sustained burns of varying severity, with the most seriously affected being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital, which has a burn intensive care unit.

The scale of the response prompted Acute Care Alberta to ask residents to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible Saturday night, unless they required emergency care.
The agency said “significant resources” were needed from Emergency Health Services and Edmonton-area emergency departments into the night.

Stars Air Ambulance dispatched two air ambulances from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Helicopters and two aircraft also landed at a nearby medical evacuation site as emergency personnel worked to transport and treat the injured.
Soldiers were working with hand grenades: CAF
The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and reservists were taking part in high-intensity training ahead of deploymen, Rutland said.

The Charlie Company, or C Company soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a section attack, with 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy when the fire broke out, he added.
Code Orange lifted after emergency response

A Code Orange is activated when a mass-casualty event places pressure on the health-care system because of a surge in patients. The code remained in effect for more than 10 hours before being lifted shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday.
Investigation underway, terrorism not likely
The Canadian Armed Forces will undertake a board of inquiry to examine the events of Oct. 17, Rutland said.
A spokesperson for National Defence said Sunday there were no indications the incident was the result of terrorist activity.

“As emergency responders continue their work and the situation continues to evolve, the full extent of the impact remains under assessment. Our immediate priority is supporting those affected and notifying next of kin. We will not confirm casualty or injury details until that process is complete,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton.
“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity.”

Retired major-general David Fraser, a CTV military analyst and former commander of Nato forces in southern Afghanistan, described the incident as the worst training tragedy he had witnessed during his military career.
“We are now dealing with the worst tragedy that I’ve seen in my entire career,” Fraser told CTV News Channel.
Fraser, who was previously posted at Wainwright and trained there extensively, said he had seen no indications the incident was anything other than an accident.

He said Canadian military bases have established safety procedures for live-fire and other training exercises. He expects those procedures to remain in place until investigators determine whether changes are needed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was travelling to Edmonton on Sunday to receive a briefing on the latest developments. He said the Department of National Defence was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

I am on my way to Edmonton. I will get briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident that occurred at CFB Wainwright. Officials said the fire crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being managed south of Wainwright.

Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.
The fire is not believed to be a result of oil and gas infrastructure or outside interference, but the cause is still under investigation.

By Denio Lourenco

Posted October 18, 2026 6:49 pm.

Private Aidan Goulding of the Third Battalion from North Vancouver, B.C.

Pvt Shaun Farrell of the Third Battalion from Prince Albert, Sask.

Pvt Hayden Lykkemark of the Third Battalion from Langley, B.C.

Sgt Morgan Wong of the Royal Edmonton Regiment from Edmonton, Atla.

Canadian Armed Forces and provincial leaders address the CFB Wainwright tragedy.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith confirms four people dead, 39 in hospital and at least 19 in critical condition.

Officials confirm at least seven fatalities in CFB Wainwright tragedy.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and provincial leaders across Canada begin reacting to the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.

Pray for Wainwright, everyone. There has been a serious incident that caused a fire at CFB Wainwright. Thank you to the brave firefighters and emergency responders working to save lives. stories.title: New Hitachi Energy plant is coming to London bringing more jobs
stories.summary: Hitachi Energy is investing a $479 million facility that is expected to bring more than 100 new jobs to London...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Hitachi Energy is investing a $479 million facility that is expected to bring more than 100 new jobs to London, the provincial government announced Friday.

The announcement came just one day after Pharmaline invested in a London factory expected to bring around 70 jobs.

“In the face of global economic uncertainty, our government continues to foster the competitive conditions needed for global companies to confidently expand their presence in Ontario and invest in long-term projects,” said Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli,

“We are proud to stand as a partner to Hitachi Energy’s latest investment, which will create new, high-value jobs for local workers and further position Ontario as a central hub for advanced manufacturing projects powering the economy and future.” Said Fedeli.

The new Transformer Insulation Factory is expected to be completed by 2028. In a press release by Hitachi, the investment will create a critical manufacturing capability that doesn’t exist in Canada.

The planned 21 thousand square meter facility will feature Canada’s first pressboard line and Hitachi’s first in the Americans, it is expected to produce a critical transformer insulation material closer to the North American market.

“The new Transformer Insulation Factory will strengthen supply resilience, support our customers’ growth ambitions, and help address one of the most critical bottlenecks in transformer manufacturing.” said Helmut Bockshammer the Manager of Insulation and Components Business Unit Transformers at Hitachi Energy.

The Canadian and Ontario Governments both announced a $20 million investment through the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) and Invest Ontario Fund, while Natural Resources Canada added $10 million to Hitachi Energy Canada Inc.

stories.title: In town linked closely to base, shocked residents of Wainwright react to grim news
stories.summary: The town and military base have been intertwined for more than 85 years
stories.author: Jana G. Pruden
stories.content:
Residents of Wainwright, Alta., are accustomed to the thunder of artillery fire and detonations from training exercises on the military base next door. It’s so close, sometimes people can feel the walls of their house rattle after an explosion.

“You hear explosions but you get used to it,” said long-time Wainwright resident Bob Porter, who described being inured to the sounds of the base as similar to being “nose blind.”

“Like, if you hear the train all day long, by the afternoon or next day, you don’t hear it,” he said. “The same with them out there shooting away.”

His wife, Tanya Porter, said she saw a wall of smoke south of Wainwright in the direction of the base at roughly 3:30 p.m. on Saturday, right as gusts of wind exceeding 100 kilometres an hour blew into town.

“I was like, ‘Is that a fire or dust?’ But I didn’t hear any explosion. They were bombing all day,” she said while she and Mr. Porter ate brunch at the Wainwright Legion on Sunday morning.

A fire that spread quickly during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday afternoon killed four Canadian Armed Forces members and injured 39 more, including 19 who are in critical condition, officials said Sunday.

The town and base have existed side by side for more than 85 years, since the Department of National Defence took over what was Buffalo National Park to create a military training and ammunition storage facility.

The base, which spans more than 1,500 square kilometres and is properly known as the 3rd Canadian Division Support Base Detachment Wainwright, is one of the country’s biggest and most highly used military training facilities.

Wainwright is located just over two hours southeast of Edmonton. The main gate to the base is minutes from Main Street, ON the southwest side of the town.

While the town of about 7,000 has other industries – including petroleum and agriculture – and military people travelling to Wainwright tend to stay mostly on the base, the two communities are inextricably linked.

Walking his dogs beside a retired Canadian Sherman military tank set in Wallace Park on Sunday morning, Greg Desrosenroll said he didn’t know any details about what happened on the base, but was very concerned about everyone involved.

“I’ve been here for a long time. It’s not the first accident,” said Mr. Desrosenroll, an army veteran who has worked on the base for more than 20 years as a civilian. “I don’t know. Was it the wind that caused it?”

Across the street, a man lowered the flags outside a provincial building to half-mast.

A vast area of rolling grasslands on and around the military base was charred black from fire, with white-grey smoke still drifting out of stands of trees in the gusting wind on Sunday afternoon.

Wainwright fire chief Aime Smyl said about 30 firefighters were still working to put out hot spots in the area. He added that Wainwright fire crews were only responding to fire that had moved outside the base, where the blaze had started.

Pre-existing signs posted on the base’s fenceline warn locals away from the property. One reads, “There ARE Bombs Inside. They CAN Kill YOU.”

On Sunday morning, about two dozen people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene, where some military families occasionally worship, to pray for those killed, injured or otherwise affected by the events on the base.

“It is with heavy hearts and concerned minds, as we think about the tragedy unfolding in our community,” Rev. Ryan Wood told the congregation. “We think of the families of those who have lost their lives, we want to pray for them today in the midst of this terrible loss and grief.”

He also thanked first responders and people from the community and surrounding area “who have been on a horrific scene, who are impacted by the tragedy and the loss that they’ve witnessed.”

Standing at the back of the church, Devon Thiessen was overcome by emotion.

“The impact of yesterday, and hearing about the tragedy and the traumas other people are experiencing, it really made me grateful for what I have,” he said, as tears welled in his eyes.

Around Wainwright, word about what happened on the base was beginning to circulate.

Working her shift at the Petro-Canada gas station, 17-year-old Talyn Rinas said she was playing in a volleyball tournament at Wainwright High School when her friend’s boyfriend, a volunteer firefighter, got a call-out.

“We heard his phone go off, and normally when it goes off they all leave, but it’s never anything serious. It’s just something small,” she said. They didn’t think anything of it until they left the school and saw ambulances flooding in.

“The whole parking lot was ambulances, just scattered,” she said.

She added that people are shaken up, and waiting to hear more details about what happened, as speculation and rumours travel on social media and in group chats.

“Everyone I’ve talked to is just sad that it happened, and it’s terrible,” she said.

Local officials spoke to reporters outside Wainwright Town Hall late Sunday afternoon, alongside Pierre Poilievre, federal Opposition Leader and Member of Parliament for Battle River-Crowfoot.

“Based on stories I’ve already heard, there are acts of courage that are almost unimaginable – people who ran towards rather than away from the danger, and are now paying a cruel price, fighting for their lives in hospitals,” Mr. Poilievre said.

Mike Wildeboer, reeve and councillor for the Municipal District of Wainwright, described the military base as “deeply intertwined within this community,” and said the tragedy will affect the entire area.

“Its members, civilian staff and families are our neighbours, our friends and our valued partners,” he said. “We stand with CFB Wainwright and all those affected during this profoundly difficult time.”

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh specifically thanked the local volunteer fire department and the staff of our “little Wainwright hospital.”

“Those people who, similar to our first responders, are serving people they know, not accustomed to such traumatic injuries, but more than rose to the occasion,” he said. “You know, when we speak that there are angels among us, you’re witnessing it.”

Editor’s note: A previous version of this story misspelled the last name of Devon Thiessen.

stories.title: Alberta’s referendum sees 1.3M votes cast in advance polls: elections body
stories.summary: A recent Ipsos poll conducted exclusively for Global News found seven in 10 Albertans plan to vote for Alberta to stay a province of Canada.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
More than a million Albertans have already voted in a referendum that asks fundamental questions about the province’s future, preliminary numbers show.

Elections Alberta says a total of 1,356,873 votes were cast between Oct. 13 and Oct. 17 through advance and special ballots. That’s compared to 809,988 votes cast at the same point during the 2023 provincial election campaign.

Broken down further, the agency says a total of 837,791 votes were cast at advance voting locations, with 519,082 special ballots mailed in.

By comparison, 758,637 advance votes were cast in 2023 and 51,351 special ballots. The agency notes special ballot totals from 2023 are “not directly comparable” to the referendum, as they weren’t available to all eligible electors and weren’t required to be received by mail.

There were a total of 3,148,343 eligible electors for the referendum, with the agency saying 43 per cent cast their ballot during the advance voting period. Only 27.5 per cent did so during the same period in the 2023 election.

A recent poll conducted exclusively for Global News by Ipsos shows proceeding to a binding vote on separation still draws little support.

The poll suggested seven in 10 Albertans planned to vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada, holding steady from previous polling conducted last month.

The proportion of voters who said they would vote for Alberta to begin the legal process of holding a binding referendum on separation increased three percentage points from September to 23 per cent.

That support is highest among men (27 per cent), those aged 35 to 54 (27 per cent) and those living outside Calgary and Edmonton (29 per cent).

Premier Danielle Smith has said that if voting goes the way polling suggests, she expects everyone to accept it and move on . Leaders of the independence movement contest that.

While separation is one of the questions on the ballot, nine others are related to immigration and the constitution.

A previous poll conducted for Global News in September found a strong majority (76 per cent) of Albertans were aware there were several questions in the upcoming referendum. Eighty-one per cent of Albertans said they planned to vote in the referendum with, 62 per cent saying they will vote on all 10 questions.

Global News will have in-depth team coverage on both broadcast and streaming online.

Anchors Dallas Flexhaug and Carole Anne Devaney will be joined by veteran political reporter and Ottawa bureau chief David Akin for results analysis, along with insights from a political panel hosted by anchor Blake Lough, and reporters on the ground.

From 8 p.m. MT to midnight, our Decision Alberta Referendum 2026 coverage will air on Globalnews.CA, as well as on YouTube and our Global TV app that is available on streaming services Prime Video, Apple TV, Roku, and select smart TVs.

Starting at 9 p.m., the special will also begin airing live on all Global News stations in Alberta.

— with files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan, Jace Maki and Karen Bartko

The precision of Ipsos polls containing online data is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the overall poll of 801 Albertans is accurate to within +/- 4.2 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all adult Alberta residents been polled. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls May be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to coverage error, and measurement error.

stories.title: Alberta pro-unity rally held in wake of CFB Wainwright fire on final day before vote
stories.summary: Edmonton - The leader of Alberta's flagship federalist referendum campaign is urging Albertans to keep in mind the privileges the Canadian military affords them after tragedy struck yesterday in the province.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Labour leaders and the head of Alberta’s flagship federalist referendum campaign say Saturday’s tragedy at the Wainwright military base demonstrates the need for unity, just one day before Alberta’s historic vote on its place in Canada.

Four military members were killed and dozens more seriously injured following a violent fire at CFB Wainwright, a massive military training base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of the Forever Canadian group, told pro-unity demonstrators gathering at the Alberta legislature Sunday that it was a “difficult day” to hold a rally.

Labour leaders and the head of Alberta's flagship federalist referendum campaign say the devastating fire at a military base southeast of Edmonton demonstrates the need for unity ahead of Alberta's separation referendum on Monday. Four military members were killed and dozens more seriously injured after a violent fire at CFB Wainwright. (Oct. 18, 2026)

But, he said it’s because of soldiers training across the country that Albertans are able to gather in protest.

”(They) give us the privilege and give us right to do exactly what we’re doing today,” he said.

“So as you’re waving your flags and you’re protesting, keep in the back of your mind those four soldiers and all the other ones who are injured because it is thanks to them that we are (here) today.”

Attendees waved Canadian flags strapped to hockey sticks, wore red and white, and hoisted signs denouncing Premier Danielle Smith’s referendum, some encouraging Albertans to “fight back!”

Voters go to the polls Monday to decide if Alberta should stay in Canada or if it’s time for a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

The rally, spearheaded by the Alberta Federation of Labour, came one day after separatists assembled at the legislature with blue Alberta flags to cheer for independence.

On Sunday, Federation leader Gil McGowan led the crowd in a moment of silence for first responders and those killed or injured in Wainwright.

“Our fellow Canadians did not stop to worry about the referendum, about the separatist debate. They just knew that other Canadians were in need, and they responded to the call,” he said.

“That’s why we are stronger together in one Canadian federation,” McGowan said to cheers and applause.

He was joined by Indigenous leaders and the heads of labour unions representing workers across the province.

Sandra Azocar, President of the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees, said the impact of the tragedy extends far beyond Wainwright.

“It impacts our entire province and our country. We stand with all Canadians today,” she said.

Heather Smith, United Nurses of Alberta president, thanked health-care workers for their work and compassion.

“It shows us all why being united matters,” she said.

The premier has said she wants Alberta to remain in Canada, but the vote is necessary to finally put the question of independence to rest.

At a news conference Sunday addressing the fire at CFB Wainwright, Smith said the province has a long and proud history of supporting the Canadian Armed Forces and is honoured to be assisting, including providing care to injured soldiers.

“I think that’s why can you see the reaction, not only among Albertans, but across the entire country and across the world,” she said.

Polls across the province will be open Monday, from 9 a.m. until 8 p.m.

Results on the independence question are expected to start trickling out in the wee hours of Tuesday morning.

Preliminary numbers suggest the final count could set a record.

Elections Alberta said Sunday that more than 1.3 million residents have already cast an advance or mail-in ballot, out of approximately 3.1 million who are eligible.

Aside from the 10th question on separation, Smith has put nine other questions on the referendum ballot.

Those nine ask whether her government should take more control and impose new rules on immigration, and pursue constitutional changes that take power away from Ottawa. Smith has said she needs that mandate to gain leverage to negotiate a better deal with Ottawa.

Campaigns across the province ramped up earlier this week, making last-minute appeals to get residents to the polls.

Prime Minister Mark Carney met with residents for two days in Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary, posing for selfies, shaking hands and spreading the message to keep the country whole.

In Calgary, he urged Albertans to say “no to the nine.”

During speeches in Edmonton and Calgary, he also said a vote against Canada amounts to “a dangerous bluff,” and pointed to his government’s plan to fast-track an oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast as proof that co-operative federalism can still work.

Opposition Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has also spoken multiple times in recent days for a united Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: New videos show ‘fast-moving’ fire burning near CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: A new video obtained by CTV News shows flames burning approximately one kilometre away from CFB Wainwright on Saturday.
stories.author: Chris Fox
stories.content:
A new video obtained by CTV News shows flames burning approximately one kilometre away from CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

The footage was captured at a private property near the military base.

In the footage, flames are visible alongside a roadway and heavy smoke can be seen billowing through the air.

A separate video from the same property shows the aftermath of the fire.

In that footage, a wide swath of brush appears to have been burnt and smoke is still visible in the late afternoon sky.

At a news conference earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said four service members were killed and dozens of others were wounded after an explosion resulted in a “violent, fast-moving fire” at the military base.

stories.title: CFB Wainwright: Latest on deadly explosion, fire at Alberta military base
stories.summary: The latest updates on the deadly fire and explosion at CFB Wainwright, which left several soldiers dead and dozens more injured.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A preliminary investigation into the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright suggests a munition from a live training exercise sparked a fast-moving grass fire, causing Saturday’s explosion, according to multiple military sources.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that four service members perished and their next of kin have been notified, adding that dozens more were seriously injured.

Separate military sources told Global News that at least seven people died and dozens more were injured at the base, located around 200 kilometres from Edmonton.

The Department of Defence and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith are slated to hold a news conference at 3 p.m. MT.

Here are the latest developments (all times local to Alberta):

Alberta health officials say they have ended the Code Orange alert that was invoked Saturday night for some hospitals in Edmonton and elsewhere.

Code Orange is a call for hospitals to essentially clear the decks, find staff and free up beds as necessary to handle a mass casualty incident.

The province says its response to Saturday’s fire involved 22 ground ambulances, six planes and two helicopters, and included help from Saskatchewan.

The patients in Wainwright have now been moved to four hospitals: two hospitals in Edmonton, one in Red Deer and one in Calgary.

Gil McGowan, organizer of a pro-Canada rally currently underway at the legislature in Edmonton, says the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.

McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, says the way first responders from around Canada selflessly stepped up to offer aid is a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.

Albertans vote Monday on whether the province should stay in Canada or whether it’s time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

Polls of Albertans before Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum and since then have indicated strong support to stay in Canada.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh, in an interview, says he knew something was wrong Saturday afternoon when the regular window-rattling boom of artillery that inaugurates the start of military training exercises at CFB Wainwright suddenly fell silent.

Immediately after, he says, there were sirens and the sound of helicopters racing in.

He says that just before midnight military medical personnel literally dropped from the sky to help, their red parachutes illuminated by flare lights.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has issued a statement calling the fire at CFB Wainwright “heartbreaking.”

She paid tribute to the health workers that managed the tragedy.

She says the province has convened its emergency management cabinet committee to co-ordinate the response.

The prime minister says he has asked the military to give the public a detailed account of what is known about the fire so far.

Mark Carney says that will be later today in Alberta, with Defence Minister David McGuinty, Eleanor Olszewski, the minister of emergency preparedness, and Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division.

He says they will be joined by provincial ministers and senior officials.

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirms four military members were killed and dozens more were injured in the fire.

Carney called the fire “violent” and fast-moving.

The Nato Military Committee is sending its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims at CFB Wainwright.

It says in a statement that Wainwright is where so many Canadian soldiers and allies have trained for the hardest tasks of the profession.

It says those killed served “our common security” and that the committee will honour their memory.

The United States Ambassador to Canada says his “heart is heavy” for the Canadian Armed Forces community.

Pete Hoekstra says on social media that he’s praying for the families of those who died and for the full recovery of the service members injured.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says in a social media post that Canadian flags will be flown at half-mast at federal buildings across the country.

He says Canada stands with the service members at CFB Wainwright and their families.

Carney is expected to make a statement later today.

The Armed Forces say there’s no indication the fire that erupted at an Alberta military base, resulting in deaths and injuries, was the result of terrorist activity.

A spokesperson also says in an email that the incident at CFB Wainwright remains under investigation and that more information will be provided as it becomes available.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says in a social media post that he’s on his way to Edmonton.

He says he’s being briefed on the latest developments in the “terrible incident” at CFB Wainwright.

He says: “To the families and everyone in Wainwright: Canada stands with you.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to make a statement later today.

With files from Karen Bartko and Jeff Semple, Global News

stories.title: Lender says it won’t relax construction loan standards for condo developers hit by sales downturn
stories.summary: Developers need at least 70% of units sold before lenders will finance projects
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
A major Ontario condo construction lender says it won’t relax its loan criteria for developers despite a sharp drop in projects and industry calls for more support.

In the fourth year of the real estate downturn, developers have been shelving or postponing condo projects because mom-and-pop investors are no longer interested in buying preconstruction units.

Individual investors used to account for the vast majority of preconstruction condo purchases in the Toronto region. The lack of investors means that developers cannot sell the amount of units required to qualify for construction financing.

Lenders typically require 70 per cent of a project’s units be sold before they will provide the developer with financing to launch construction.

“The 70 per cent remains a good metric,” said Kevin VanKampen, head of business banking with Meridian Credit Union, the province’s largest credit union that has been providing condo developers with loans for at least two decades.

With condo prices falling, Mr. VanKampen said “that type of an environment would not be particularly inviting for lenders to take what some would perceive to be a bit of a speculative way of lending.”

Meridian and other lenders have maintained strict lending standards even as developers have called for relief. Several developers told The Globe and Mail in the spring that they have been urging lenders to make it easier to get construction financing because they are sitting on projects that cannot move forward.

On the resale market, the typical condo price in the Toronto region is down 7 per cent in September from a year ago, according to Canadian Real Estate Association data. The average price per square foot for preconstruction units is down 1 per cent year-over-year, according to condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

Mr. VanKampen said lowering the 70-per-cent threshold could create a scenario where financial institutions start accumulating a portfolio of unsold condo units if developers run into financial problems, which would represent more risk to the lender.

Currently, there are 5,127 newly-built condo units in the Toronto and Hamilton region that are unsold, according to Urbanation. That does not include the units that developers have had to take back because buyers have defaulted on their purchase.

The development industry has been looking for other ways to finance condo construction and says without a lower lending threshold, the market will remain stuck.

“If the threshold is not lowered, I expect new development to remain stalled,” said Shaun Hildebrand, president of Urbanation. “Projects will keep getting shelved because they cannot reach the presale level lenders require,” he said.

One of the most recent cancellations was a condo project called M6 in Mississauga, west of Toronto.

The tower was launched in 2023 and designed to be 58 storeys with nearly 900 units. It was the sixth phase of a larger condo development with more than 5,000 residential units. The Globe and Mail previously reported that developers were unable to reach the sales threshold required to begin construction.

The lack of preconstruction sales has slowed condo home building. There were 4,150 condo unit construction starts in the Toronto region in the first six months of the year, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. At that pace, there would be 8,300 condo starts this year. That would mark the lowest level since 1998, when condo buildings were only starting to be built.

That downward trend is expected to accelerate given the dearth of new project launches, which occurs well before a developer can break ground on their building.

So far this year, there have been four preconstruction condo project sale launches, according to data from new home research company Zonda Urban. That compares to 101 launches during the real estate boom in 2021.

With individual investors gone, developers have had to rely on buyers who plan to live in the units. Those types of buyers prefer to make purchases after construction has started or when the building is completed. Coming up with 20- to 25-per-cent deposit is also a challenge.

At today’s prices, the average deposit would be $164,000 for a 500-square-foot unit. And constructing a condo building can take years.

Zonda’s vice-president of advisory, Jasmine Young, said there needs to be a financing model that doesn’t require buyers to commit so far in advance.

“To put down the 25-per-cent deposit for a home seven years from now is difficult,” she said.

In the fourth year of the real estate downturn, developers have been shelving or postponing condo projects because mom-and-pop investors are no longer interested in buying preconstruction units.

Individual investors used to account for the vast majority of preconstruction condo purchases in the Toronto region. The lack of investors means that developers cannot sell the amount of units required to qualify for construction financing.
Lenders typically require 70 per cent of a project’s units be sold before they will provide the developer with financing to launch construction.

“The 70 per cent remains a good metric,” said Kevin VanKampen, head of business banking with Meridian Credit Union, the province’s largest credit union that has been providing condo developers with loans for at least two decades.

With condo prices falling, Mr. VanKampen said “that type of an environment would not be particularly inviting for lenders to take what some would perceive to be a bit of a speculative way of lending.”

Meridian and other lenders have maintained strict lending standards even as developers have called for relief. Several developers told The Globe and Mail in the spring that they have been urging lenders to make it easier to get construction financing because they are sitting on projects that cannot move forward.

On the resale market, the typical condo price in the Toronto region is down 7 per cent in September from a year ago, according to Canadian Real Estate Association data. The average price per square foot for preconstruction units is down 1 per cent year-over-year, according to condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

Mr. VanKampen said lowering the 70-per-cent threshold could create a scenario where financial institutions start accumulating a portfolio of unsold condo units if developers run into financial problems, which would represent more risk to the lender.

stories.title: Here's a look at past fatalities on Canadian military bases
stories.summary: Edmonton - Four military members were killed and dozens injured after a fire erupted Saturday at CFB Wainwright southeast of Edmonton.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Four military members were killed and dozens injured after a fire erupted Saturday at CFB Wainwright southeast of Edmonton.

There have been several fatalities at Canadian military facilities over the years. Here’s a list of some of them:

October 2020: A soldier died after being shot during live-fire training at CFB Wainwright. The soldier was airlifted to an Edmonton hospital and died the following morning.

April 2017: Sgt. Robert J. Dynerowicz of the Royal Canadian Dragoons was killed and three other soldiers were injured in a vehicle accident during Exercise Rugged Bear at CFB Wainwright.

November 2014: Pte. Steven Allen, 20, of Victoria, died when a lookout tower collapsed during infantry training at CFB Wainwright. Another soldier in the tower wasn’t seriously injured.

May 2014: Lt.-Col. Dan Bobbitt, commanding officer of the 2nd Regiment, Royal Canadian Horse Artillery, died when a light armoured vehicle rolled over during a training mission for Exercise Maple Resolve 2014 at CFB Wainwright. Four other soldiers were injured.

March 2014: Nine soldiers from the 2nd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taken to hospital after two military trucks collided during a training exercise near CFB Shilo in Manitoba.

January 2011: Cpl. Jean-Michel Deziel died after falling from a roof while installing a telecommunications antenna at CFB Valcartier in Quebec.

May 2008: U.S. army specialist Josef Cerfus, 25, died after being struck by a cargo load carried by a Chinook helicopter during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright. His unit was participating in Exercise Maple Guardian, which was preparing Canadian troops for deployment to Afghanistan.

May 2007: Cpl. Christopher Deliva, 27, of Quebec City, died when the 10-tonne military truck he was driving rolled at CFB Wainwright. He had been helping to return vehicles and equipment after a month-long training exercise for troops preparing for Afghanistan.

May 1999: Trooper Kevin Craig Zufelt, 30, was found dead inside a parked Coyote armoured vehicle while working alone during a training exercise at Camp Wainwright. He suffered a head injury, but officials were unsure what caused it. Nineteen paratroopers were also injured during a night jump earlier in the same exercise.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: CFB Wainwright fire fatalities identified as three from the Princess Pats, one from Loyal Edmonton Regiment
stories.summary: Three are from Ppcli, one from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, all based in Edmonton
stories.author: Edmonton Journal
stories.content:
The four Canadian Armed Forces members killed in the fire at CFB Wainwright have been identified.

Major-General L.W. Rutland, Commander 1st Canadian Division, Canadian Armed Forces, said Sunday afternoon that three of the men are from the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based out of CFB Edmonton and the fourth is from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment.

The Ppcli soldiers killed are Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Shaun Farrell and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, while the Loyal Edmonton member has been identified as Sgt. Morgan Wong from Edmonton.

The four were killed during an outdoor exercise on a section attack range when a fire swept into the area, Rutland said.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” Rutland said.

Wong, a University of Alberta grad, had been with the Canadian Armed Forces since 2017, according to his LinkedIn page.

The Loyal Edmonton Regiment is a reserve regiment. In his day job, Wong had worked over the past three years in a pair of provincial government departments: Treasury Board Secretariat and Hospital and Surgical Health Services.

Earlier Sunday, Farrell’s mother, Patricia, posted on Facebook about his death.

CFB Wainwright Live Updates: Four dead in base tragedy, Carney says; Code Orange at Alberta hospitals stood down

'I felt something was wrong': Wainwright Mayor says town reeling in wake of base tragedy

“It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father,” her post read.

“​We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time.”

In a separate post Saturday night, after the training accident, Farrell said Shaun is “in CFB Wainwright taking part in the training there,” asking people to pray for her son.

According to a post earlier this year, Farrell said Shaun had only recently joined the military, expressing pride in her son committing, “to something much larger” than himself.

In a Facebook post after the announcement of the soldiers’ names, Kim Goulding posted a tribute to Aidan.

“You were so bright, kind, and so excited, and so, so proud to serve in the CAF,” she wrote. “You had just graduated in August and had your whole life ahead of you — way too young.”

In addition to the deaths, 39 soldiers were injured, including 19 critically, Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday afternoon.

In a statement Sunday afternoon, Acute Care Alberta said 30 units, including ground ambulances, planes and helicopters, took patients to hospitals in Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary.
