stories.title: Supreme Court to take on B.C. Aboriginal title case after province appeals
stories.summary: Indigenous rights and territorial claims are at the fore of public debate as the province gears up for election
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada on Thursday agreed to hear an Aboriginal title case from British Columbia, where the provincial government is challenging the amount of land awarded to a small First Nation.

In 2024, the Nuchatlaht won Canada’s second-ever declaration of Aboriginal title on Nootka Island, ON the Western edge of Vancouver Island. But the lower court in B.C. at the time granted title to only a small portion of the Nuchatlaht’s claim.

In April this year , the B.C. Court of Appeal ruled the declaration of Aboriginal title applied to the Nuchatlaht’s entire claim: 201 square kilometres – more than a third of Nootka Island.

The Supreme Court’s decision to take the case comes amid a provincial election in British Columbia this month during which the array of Indigenous court cases involving Aboriginal title and other rights have vaulted such legal questions to the fore of public debate.

The new case also lands as judges on the top court are saying yes to twice as many appeal applications than they had this decade. There had been criticism in the legal profession that the Supreme Court was not hearing enough cases.

On Thursday, the Nuchatlaht appeal was one of five the court agreed to hear, increasing the total of new cases this year to 48, the most since 2017.

A hearing on the Nuchatlaht case has not yet been scheduled and likely wouldn’t happen before next spring or possibly next fall.

The Nuchatlaht case centres around questions of what amounts to sufficient Indigenous occupation of land in the mid-1800s to establish Aboriginal title, when the British asserted sovereignty in the region, and how to delineate the geographic breadth of a claim if occupation of the land was variable.

The case will feature arguments over how courts apply the Supreme Court’s landmark Aboriginal title judgment in 2014, the Tsilhqot’in Nation ruling that marked the country’s first declaration of Aboriginal title to land in northwestern B.C.

In the B.C. government’s application to the Supreme Court to have its appeal of the Nuchatlaht ruling heard, the province cited a “time of intensifying Aboriginal title litigation in British Columbia and beyond” that urgently requires the consideration of the country’s top court.

The provincial government argued that the B.C. Court of Appeal’s backing of the full Nuchatlaht claim to 201 square kilometres amounted to a “loosening of the test for Aboriginal title” and that the original declaration to about 11 square kilometres should be restored.

Jack Woodward, counsel for the Nuchatlaht, said in an interview on Thursday that B.C.’s decision to appeal could backfire if the Supreme Court reaffirms the appellate-court ruling.

Mr. Woodward, who was one of the Tsilhqot’in Nation’s lawyers in 2014, also called on the next provincial government to pull out of the Supreme Court case and allow the B.C. Court of Appeal declaration of Aboriginal title to stand. The incumbent NDP is contesting a tight election against the opposition B.C. Conservative Party. The final day to vote is Oct. 24.

“There’s no reason to continue with this,” Mr. Woodward said. “I would encourage a re-elected NDP government or the new government to think hard of whether they want to do this.”

The B.C. government declined to comment on Thursday, citing the election campaign and a government in caretaker mode with communication limited to critical health and safety information.

The Nuchatlaht is a small First Nation, with about 160 members. Its case for Aboriginal title did not include land claimed by other Indigenous groups or private land.

This is a contrast to last year’s Cowichan Tribes ruling at the trial court in B.C., which recognized Aboriginal title over about 800 acres of land in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond and sparked worries over implications for private-property ownership. There are multiple appeals planned in the Cowichan case for the B.C. Court of Appeal.

After the Nuchatlaht’s initial victory in 2024, winning Aboriginal title to a portion of their claim, the B.C. provincial government quietly gave up a portion of Nuchatlitz Park on the northwestern tip of Nootka Island as a result of that ruling.

In the B.C. Court of Appeal ruling this year, the judgment noted that the province’s Forest Act and Park Act no longer applied to the 201 square kilometres to which the Nuchatlaht won a declaration of Aboriginal title. That means public access to the park is no longer assured.

The new case also lands as judges on the top court are saying yes to twice as many appeal applications than they had this decade. There had been criticism in the legal profession that the Supreme Court was not hearing enough cases.
On Thursday, the Nuchatlaht appeal was one of five the court agreed to hear, increasing the total of new cases this year to 48, the most since 2017.
A hearing on the Nuchatlaht case has not yet been scheduled and likely wouldn’t happen before next spring or possibly next fall.

The Nuchatlaht case centres around questions of what amounts to sufficient Indigenous occupation of land in the mid-1800s to establish Aboriginal title, when the British asserted sovereignty in the region, and how to delineate the geographic breadth of a claim if occupation of the land was variable.

The case will feature arguments over how courts apply the Supreme Court’s landmark Aboriginal title judgment in 2014, the Tsilhqot’in Nation ruling that marked the country’s first declaration of Aboriginal title to land in northwestern B.C.

In the B.C. government’s application to the Supreme Court to have its appeal of the Nuchatlaht ruling heard, the province cited a “time of intensifying Aboriginal title litigation in British Columbia and beyond” that urgently requires the consideration of the country’s top court.

The provincial government argued that the B.C. Court of Appeal’s backing of the full Nuchatlaht claim to 201 square kilometres amounted to a “loosening of the test for Aboriginal title” and that the original declaration to about 11 square kilometres should be restored.
Jack Woodward, counsel for the Nuchatlaht, said in an interview on Thursday that B.C.’s decision to appeal could backfire if the Supreme Court reaffirms the appellate-court ruling.

Mr. Woodward, who was one of the Tsilhqot’in Nation’s lawyers in 2014, also called on the next provincial government to pull out of the Supreme Court case and allow the B.C. Court of Appeal declaration of Aboriginal title to stand. The incumbent NDP is contesting a tight election against the opposition B.C. Conservative Party. The final day to vote is Oct. 24.
“There’s no reason to continue with this,” Mr. Woodward said. “I would encourage a re-elected NDP government or the new government to think hard of whether they want to do this.”
The B.C. government declined to comment on Thursday, citing the election campaign and a government in caretaker mode with communication limited to critical health and safety information.
The Nuchatlaht is a small First Nation, with about 160 members. Its case for Aboriginal title did not include land claimed by other Indigenous groups or private land.

This is a contrast to last year’s Cowichan Tribes ruling at the trial court in B.C., which recognized Aboriginal title over about 800 acres of land in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond and sparked worries over implications for private-property ownership. There are multiple appeals planned in the Cowichan case for the B.C. Court of Appeal.

After the Nuchatlaht’s initial victory in 2024, winning Aboriginal title to a portion of their claim, the B.C. provincial government quietly gave up a portion of Nuchatlitz Park on the northwestern tip of Nootka Island as a result of that ruling.

In the B.C. Court of Appeal ruling this year, the judgment noted that the province’s Forest Act and Park Act no longer applied to the 201 square kilometres to which the Nuchatlaht won a declaration of Aboriginal title. That means public access to the park is no longer assured.

stories.title: Why Trump is reviving 51st state rhetoric with midterms in less than 3 weeks
stories.summary: During a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump revived his rhetoric on wanting Canada to be '51st state' of the United States.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail as Republican candidates across the country face tough races in the midterm elections , and he has fallen back on a familiar target – Canada.

During a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, Trump revived his rhetoric on wanting Canada to be “51 st state” of the United States.

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” Trump told the crowd at his rally.

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” Trump said, adding that Canada would be “doing something just like Greenland.”

This was an apparent reference to an Arctic security agreement Trump signed with Denmark and Greenland last month, paving the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and easing tensions over his repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States.

Trump’s comments came as U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

“Keep your nose out of American politics,” Hoekstra said during a podcast interview.

Hoekstra was referring to an anti-tariff ad paid for by the Ontario government and Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s comments that Canada’s counter-tariffs would target specific U.S. states.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Joly denied the claims that Canada was attempting to interfere in American politics.

“We’ll never do that and we’ll never accept that also being done to us in Canada,” she said.

Polling shows Republicans trailing in several key races, including in states bordering Canada where Trump’s trade war with Ottawa has become an election issue.

“Canada is being put on the table,” said University of Ottawa political science professor Emily Regan Wills.

Nowhere is that more evident than in Michigan, the heart of the American auto manufacturing sector, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers narrowly in most polls in their U.S. Senate race.

Rogers has attempted to put some distance between themselves and Trump’s trade policies, urging an end to the trade war with Canada.

He said in his debate with El-Sayed that he’d urged the White House privately to reach a trade deal with Canada and end the president’s tariffs. Canada is Michigan’s largest trading partner, as it is for many Great Lakes and Midwestern states.

Days before, Rogers unveiled a new ad in which he said, “We know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end the tariff war — now.”

That’s a noticeable departure from Rogers’ earlier, less specific statements praising Trump’s “America First” economic agenda while saying tariffs are not a “one-size-fits-all” solution.

“Americans in border states are used to being able to interact with Canada,” Wills said.

“Visiting, vacationing, shopping, that’s all being profoundly disrupted at this moment.”

In Maine, another state hit hard by Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, veteran Republican Susan Collins is trailing narrowly in most polls behind Democrat Troy Jackson.

During a debate, Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”

While prominent Republicans in tight races seek to distance themselves from his rhetoric, Trump is doubling down.

“I truly think this is psychological, this is not strategic. Donald Trump’s response to being told ‘no’ is to go harder,” Wills said.

For Republicans, Trump’s rhetoric might do more harm than good in border states.

“It would be great for other Republicans if he would stop talking about it. The issue is that nobody has yet discovered how to get Donald Trump to stop talking about something he wants to talk about,” she said.

“He doesn’t really have an ‘off’ button or ‘maybe that’s an inside thought’ button,” Wills added.

Trump’s own approval rating was at 37 per cent on Thursday, remaining steadily low for several months leading up to the midterms.

Trump’s renewed rhetoric around Canada’s sovereignty is likely intended to create a “rally around the flag” effect that is “supposed to make Americans feel embattled,” she said.

Whether that works is less clear.

The comments also come as U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive. The consumer price index rose 3.7 per cent in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4 per cent in August.

Some experts suggest Trump May be trying to shift the burden of high prices from himself to other targets, including Canada, but it May not connect with the voters as it has in the past.

“The American people are paying more and getting less because of the choices of Donald Trump,” said Todd Belt, professor of political management at George Washington University.

“You can’t out-message the economy. People get angry when you tell them that things are good and they know how much money they have at the end of the month,” he added.

–With files from Associated Press

stories.title: 7 times Trump reignited '51st state' rhetoric, suggesting 'that's the only way it works' for Canada
stories.summary: Donald Trump has reignited his "51st state" rhetoric, despite his administration warning Canada against getting involved in U.S. politics.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has reignited his rhetoric around Canada becoming the “51st state,” shortly after his administration warned Canadian politicians against getting involved in U.S. affairs.

In a podcast appearance on Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said America is “closely watching Canadian activities” for election interference, referencing comments from Canada’s Industry Minister, ⁠Mélanie Joly, about retaliatory tariffs. “Keep your nose out of American politics,” he said.

Joly has hit back against his claims, saying: “We never do that, and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada,” while speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday. “What I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments…and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Later that day, Trump reiterated his ongoing stance that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state at a campaign rally in Arizona. Here are seven key occasions the U.S. president has suggested annexing Canada.

On Wednesday, Trump listed a number of grievances he has with Canada in his speech at Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport, adding: “They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works.”

He said: “Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not anymore. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town.”

The U.S. president also suggested Canada will “be doing something just like Greenland,” adding that it “just adds to our beautiful plate,” referring to the U.S.

He made the comments the same day Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians against engaging in behaviour that could be inferred as election interference.

After almost a year of silence from Trump on the 51st state topic, the U.S. president renewed the rhetoric after Canada entered a technical recession in June this year.

In a post on Truth Social , Trump wrote “51st state!” with a link to a Bloomberg report about the technical recession. Hoekstra then shared the post on his X account just hours before the Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette were due to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington, D.C.

In September 2025, Trump referenced his desire for Canada to become the 51st state during his address to U.S. military officials in Virginia.

In the speech, he claimed work on the “Golden Dome Missile Defence Shield” was proceeding and that Canada had recently contacted him to say “they want to be a part of it.”

“To which I said, ‘Well, why don’t you just join our country? You become the 51st state and you get it for free,” he suggested.

On April 28, 2025, the day of Canada’s federal election, Trump told Canadians to “elect the man” who will let Canada become the 51st state in a Truth Social post.

“Elect the man who has the strength and wisdom to cut your taxes in half, increase your military power, for free, to the highest level in the World, have your Car, Steel, Aluminum, Lumber, Energy, and all other businesses, Quadruple in size, With Zero Tariffs OR Taxes, if Canada becomes the cherished 51st,” the post read.

He added: “America can no longer subsidize Canada with the Hundreds of Billions of Dollars a year that we have been spending in the past. It makes no sense unless Canada is a State!”

The post came just a few days after Trump sat down for an interview with Time magazine ’s senior political correspondent Eric Cortellessa and editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs.

“You’ve talked about acquiring Greenland, taking control of the Panama Canal, making Canada the 51st state,” Cortellessa said. “Maybe you’re trolling a little bit on that one. I don’t know.”

Trump’s answer was short: “Actually, no, I’m not.”

Trump’s comments in the Time interview doubled down on statements he made earlier that month in an interview that aired during the Super Bowl pre-show.

When asked whether his talk of annexing Canada is “a real thing,” Trump told Fox News Channel’s Bret Baier: “Yeah, it is.”

“I think Canada would be much better off being the 51st state because we lose $200 billion a year with Canada. And I’m not going to let that happen,” he said. “Why are we paying $200 billion a year, essentially a subsidy to Canada?”

Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. loses hundreds of billions of dollars a year to Canada during his second term as president. But according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative , the U.S. goods trade deficit with Canada was US$48.3 billion in 2025, a 21 percent decrease ($12.9 billion) over 2024 and far less than Trump has claimed.

In January 2025, before the inauguration for his second term, Trump threatened to use “economic force” to make Canada the 51st state and called the border between the two countries an “artificially drawn line.”

“You get rid of that artificially drawn line and you take a look at what that looks like, and it would also be much better for national security,” he said at a news conference at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. “And don’t forget, we basically protect Canada.”

Then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau responded with a post on X, in which he said: “There isn’t a snowball’s chance in hell that Canada would become part of the United States.”

Trump first floated the idea of Canada becoming the 51st state during a dinner with then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at Mar-a-Lago in November 2024.

A few days later, in December that year, Trump called Trudeau “governor.” In a Truth Social post on Dec. 10, 2024, the U.S. president said it was a pleasure to have dined “with Governor Justin Trudeau of the great state of Canada” and that he looked forward to seeing “the governor again soon” to continue their “in-depth talks on tariffs and trade.”

It was the start of a long-running commentary from Trump on the annexation of Canada, which has now lasted almost two years.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet hears and sees woman's final moments
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet has watched and listened to some of the 29-year-old woman's final moments before she fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press

Toronto - Regis Korchinski-Paquet expressed difficulty breathing and reported losing control in a fight with her family in a series of agitated 911 calls shortly before she fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony while police were inside her home, a coroner’s inquest heard Thursday.

Some of the 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman’s final moments were laid bare as jurors watched a compilation video that overlaid the recordings of five 911 calls and two police microphones with Cctv footage from the hallway outside her home and video from a police cruiser on May 27, 2020.

The calls made to 911 over roughly half an hour late that afternoon, including three by Korchinski-Paquet herself, brought six police officers and two paramedics to the west Toronto building in short succession.

Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, Claudette Beals, was the first to call at 5:13 p.m., telling the operator she needed police immediately because her son and daughter were fighting. Shouting could be heard in the background as Beals paced in the hallway.

Over the course of the 12-minute call, which overlapped with some of the others, Beals knocked on a neighbour’s door, shouted at her children that police were coming, and eventually told the operator that the siblings had an argument and “a fight broke out.”

“My daughter had a seizure this morning, and so this is how basically it all started,” she said.

“I just want the both of them out of my house. I don’t want no contact with neither one of them again.”

Meanwhile, Korchinski-Paquet made her first call to 911 at 5:15 p.m., breathing heavily as she told the operator she was being attacked and needed police immediately.

“I can’t breathe!” she shouted, prompting the operator to tell her to catch her breath and explain what happened.

“My brother just attacked me,” she said before the call was transferred to the paramedic service. The call ended shortly after the operator confirmed emergency crews were on the way.

In two more calls at 5:22 p.m. and 5:30 p.m., Korchinski-Paquet said her brother and mother attacked her after she told her brother to turn down the TV.

“My brother just jumped up and started punching me in my head and choked me, and my mom jumped in and started attacking me as well,” she said in the earlier of the two calls. When asked if they had weapons, she said the pair “pulled out knives” but couldn’t say where the knives were now.

“I broke two bottles because I got so angry that I threw them at them in the hallway. I could not control myself,” she said.

Korchinski-Paquet, who paced up and down the hallway in the security footage, also told the operator she had epilepsy, had experienced a seizure and wasn’t feeling well.

Her brother, Reece Korchinski, called 911 at 5:17 p.m. as he took refuge in the stairwell by the apartment.

Korchinski told the operator his sister started the fight but that he defended himself and managed to get the knives out of her hands before leaving the home and getting his fiancée and their children to do the same.

“My mom was trying to control me and my sister from arguing, but obviously once my sister pulled out the knife, there’s no controlling that,” he said.

He noted his sister’s epilepsy several times, adding she’d had two seizures that day and had “clearly” not calmed down afterward.

“My sister, she doesn’t know what she’s doing, because tonight she’ll apologize to me if I don’t end up going to jail for trying to protect myself and my family,” he said.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest earlier this week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia in their wake. She had two seizures the morning of the day she died, inquest counsel said.

A neurologist who examined Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death testified that in the years before her death, she showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis on several occasions. Both are mental states that can follow seizures.

Dr. Julien Hébert, who also watched the video as part of his review, said Korchinski-Paquet sounded distressed and repetitive in the recordings, as though she couldn’t remember her earlier calls.

Inquest counsel Roger Shallow warned jurors Thursday that the recordings would be difficult to see and hear, as he offered sympathies to Korchinski-Paquet’s grieving family.

“I take no shame in sharing with you that, in compiling this and watching it once it came together, I wept, and I’ll probably weep again tonight,” he said.

“To the family of Regis: This video is going to depict your daughter, your sister, your auntie, your loved one in the few final moments before this tragedy occurred, both in visual and in sound. My heart bleeds at the thought of the agony viewing this might cause you.”

Const. Adam Vandenbrink was the first to arrive at the building at 5:20 p.m. and was told to wait for backup, according to the narrative. Const. Shane Beaudoin was second, and the two went up together at 5:29 p.m. Const. Brian Villeneuve followed suit about a minute later.

Constables Glenn Weddell and Frances Mallinger arrived at 5:31 p.m. and both had wireless microphones that captured heavily muffled and distorted audio from the scene. Two paramedics, Jessica Smitheram and Ronald Warzek, got there around the same time. Const. Christopher Beninger was the last at the scene at 5:36 p.m.

On the Cctv video, the officers can be seen arriving in waves, with the first few appearing to talk to Korchinski-Paquet and her mother by the elevators sometime before Korchinski-Paquet’s third call to 911. There was no sound in that portion of the video.

Another conversation appeared to take place once Villeneuve arrived after her third call.

Korchinski-Paquet went into the apartment at 5:35 p.m., and several first responders went in and out between then and 5:41 p.m., as did her mother and brother.

At one point, a voice can be heard saying Korchinski-Paquet reported experiencing seizures. “She’s quite hard to reason with,” the voice said as shouting could be heard in the background. “She’s a little erratic.”

Korchinski-Paquet fell from the balcony around 5:39 p.m., the narrative said.

Around that time on the video, a radio called for an ambulance, “Asap.”

Soon after, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother yelled “No!” then repeatedly sobbed “oh my God” as she came out of the apartment and walked up and down the hallway, at one point appearing to pound on the neighbour’s door.

A voice can be heard urging her to sit down and catch her breath before saying, “I got you.”

Korchinski-Paquet’s death, which came days after the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, shook the city. Thousands of protesters took to Toronto’s streets to demand change to policing in the weeks that followed.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death, finding it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to the one next door.

The inquest will not look into the investigations conducted by various watchdog organizations, but its scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy.

A Toronto police employee is set to continue testifying Friday on the logistics of 911 call centres.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version had an incorrect first name for Const. Adam Vandenbrink, based on information provided at the inquest.

In two more calls at 5:22 p.m. and 5:30 p.m., Korchinski-Paquet said her brother and mother attacked her after she told her brother to turn down the TV.

“My brother just jumped up and started punching me in my head and choked me, and my mom jumped in and started attacking me as well,” she said in the earlier of the two calls. When asked if they had weapons, she said the pair “pulled out knives” but couldn’t say where the knives were now.
“I broke two bottles because I got so angry that I threw them at them in the hallway. I could not control myself,” she said.
Korchinski-Paquet, who paced up and down the hallway in the security footage, also told the operator she had epilepsy, had experienced a seizure and wasn’t feeling well.
Her brother, Reece Korchinski, called 911 at 5:17 p.m. as he took refuge in the stairwell by the apartment.

Korchinski told the operator his sister started the fight but that he defended himself and managed to get the knives out of her hands before leaving the home and getting his fiancée and their children to do the same.
“My mom was trying to control me and my sister from arguing, but obviously once my sister pulled out the knife, there’s no controlling that,” he said.
He noted his sister’s epilepsy several times, adding she’d had two seizures that day and had “clearly” not calmed down afterward.
“My sister, she doesn’t know what she’s doing, because tonight she’ll apologize to me if I don’t end up going to jail for trying to protect myself and my family,” he said.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest earlier this week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia in their wake. She had two seizures the morning of the day she died, inquest counsel said.

A neurologist who examined Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death testified that in the years before her death, she showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis on several occasions. Both are mental states that can follow seizures.
Dr. Julien Hébert, who also watched the video as part of his review, said Korchinski-Paquet sounded distressed and repetitive in the recordings, as though she couldn’t remember her earlier calls.
Inquest counsel Roger Shallow warned jurors Thursday that the recordings would be difficult to see and hear, as he offered sympathies to Korchinski-Paquet’s grieving family.
“I take no shame in sharing with you that, in compiling this and watching it once it came together, I wept, and I’ll probably weep again tonight,” he said.

“To the family of Regis: This video is going to depict your daughter, your sister, your auntie, your loved one in the few final moments before this tragedy occurred, both in visual and in sound. My heart bleeds at the thought of the agony viewing this might cause you.”

Const. Adam Vandenbrink was the first to arrive at the building at 5:20 p.m. and was told to wait for backup, according to the narrative. Const. Shane Beaudoin was second, and the two went up together at 5:29 p.m. Const. Brian Villeneuve followed suit about a minute later.

Constables Glenn Weddell and Frances Mallinger arrived at 5:31 p.m. and both had wireless microphones that captured heavily muffled and distorted audio from the scene. Two paramedics, Jessica Smitheram and Ronald Warzek, got there around the same time. Const. Christopher Beninger was the last at the scene at 5:36 p.m.

On the Cctv video, the officers can be seen arriving in waves, with the first few appearing to talk to Korchinski-Paquet and her mother by the elevators sometime before Korchinski-Paquet’s third call to 911. There was no sound in that portion of the video.
Another conversation appeared to take place once Villeneuve arrived after her third call.
Korchinski-Paquet went into the apartment at 5:35 p.m., and several first responders went in and out between then and 5:41 p.m., as did her mother and brother.

At one point, a voice can be heard saying Korchinski-Paquet reported experiencing seizures. “She’s quite hard to reason with,” the voice said as shouting could be heard in the background. “She’s a little erratic.”
Korchinski-Paquet fell from the balcony around 5:39 p.m., the narrative said.
Around that time on the video, a radio called for an ambulance, “Asap.”

Soon after, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother yelled “No!” then repeatedly sobbed “oh my God” as she came out of the apartment and walked up and down the hallway, at one point appearing to pound on the neighbour’s door.
A voice can be heard urging her to sit down and catch her breath before saying, “I got you.”

Korchinski-Paquet’s death, which came days after the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, shook the city. Thousands of protesters took to Toronto’s streets to demand change to policing in the weeks that followed.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death, finding it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to the one next door.
The inquest will not look into the investigations conducted by various watchdog organizations, but its scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy.
A Toronto police employee is set to continue testifying Friday on the logistics of 911 call centres.

stories.title: Carney stumps for unity as Alberta referendum approaches
stories.summary: Prime Minister urges supporters to vote to stay in Confederation and reject nine other questions put on ballot by Alberta Premier
stories.author: Bill Graveland and Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken his unity message to Alberta ahead of Monday’s referendum, urging people to vote for the province to remain in Canada and reject Premier Danielle Smith ’s other nine ballot proposals.

In prepared remarks ahead of a speech in Calgary on Thursday evening, Mr. Carney spoke of the country’s strength when united and warned Albertans of the consequences of voting against choosing to keep the province wedded to Confederation.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” Mr. Carney was set to tell a packed house at a downtown Calgary rally.

Monday’s referendum will ask voters to weigh in on 10 questions, one of them on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating. The other nine questions, authored by Ms. Smith’s government, deal with limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services, charging them fees for health care and education, and numerous constitutional changes such as abolishing the federal Senate.

The Prime Minister has been critical of Ms. Smith’s decision to call the referendum. In May, he described it as a “dangerous bluff,” likening it to Britain’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union. (Mr. Carney was governor of the Bank of England at the time.)

He used similar language for his speech on Thursday night: “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said in his prepared remarks.

“Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

Mr. Carney has spent much of the referendum campaign on the sidelines, choosing to make his pitch to Albertans indirectly, by demonstrating Ottawa’s willingness to co-operate with the province. This has included dramatic policy shifts, particularly around environmental safeguards, and standing with the Premier as they announced a proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast .

Alberta’s referendum – the first time the province has put a secession question to voters – is occurring at a time of tremendous stress on national unity. While many Albertans prepare to vote on Monday, a newly elected separatist Quebec government will pose challenges for Ottawa, and U.S. President Donald Trump has shown few signs that the continuing tariff war and musings about annexation will end.

On Thursday night, Mr. Carney was set to say that the referendum “comes at the worst possible time,” pointing to what he described as a more dangerous and divided world.

“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”

Mr. Carney’s push alongside Ms. Smith to build a new bitumen pipeline – most recently by designating it a project of national interest – has underscored a desire to blunt many Albertans’ deep frustration with Ottawa’s direction on energy and environmental policy under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“I won’t sugarcoat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Mr. Carney was expected to say at the Thursday event, held by Forever Canadian, one of the most prominent federalist groups in the province.

He added that recently, Albertans were made to feel their “energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

“What should have brought us together began to divide us. Contributing to a half century of politics that have too often pulled us apart,” he said in his prepared remarks.

It was the second time this week that the Prime Minister had made the case for unity directly to Albertans . On Monday, he released a short video shot in a classroom at St. Francis Xavier Catholic High School in Edmonton, which he attended as a teenager. In the video, he said that Albertans were being asked to decide on what he called “a long and uncertain process” of separation. “We are stronger together,” he said.

But Thursday was the first time he had encouraged Albertans to vote against the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes.

As he made several stops in Calgary earlier in the day, he told Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” putting him in direct opposition to Ms. Smith, whose government has spent $4-million in advertising to campaign in favour of the proposals.

The Premier says she needs approval on them to fortify her mandate, and that they would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

Ms. Smith clapped back at Mr. Carney’s comments later in the day, writing on social media that “it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”

The Prime Minister is continuing his pro-Canada campaign on Friday in Red Deer, Alta., where he’ll share a stage with Ms. Smith, and attend another Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton in the evening.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to give an address on Friday morning in Calgary at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference, a conservative gathering.

Advance voting opened earlier this week. Elections Alberta said in an e-mail on Thursday morning that roughly 815,000 Albertans had so far cast their ballots – about 27 per cent of all eligible voters.

Campaigners have been divided on how Mr. Carney should support the federalist effort and whether Ottawa should bankroll groups fighting to keep Alberta in Canada. (Alberta’s election-finance rules prohibit the federal government from funding referendum advertisers.)

Some have argued that the Prime Minister shouldn’t leave any cards on the table and use his immense popularity in Alberta to his advantage by giving the federalist side a boost. Others have said he should keep his hands out of it, and that circumventing election-finance rules would backfire.

Mr. Carney in September said his government wouldn’t help fund Alberta’s numerous pro-Canada campaigns , which struggled to raise money through the summer.

Federalist groups have since closed the distance on separatist campaigns that were flush with cash early on. Separatist groups have now scooped up about 59 per cent of all donations during the campaign, down from early September when roughly 75 per cent of all contributions were floating to them.

“I won’t sugarcoat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Mr. Carney was expected to say at the Thursday event, held by Forever Canadian, one of the most prominent federalist groups in the province.
He added that recently, Albertans were made to feel their “energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”
“What should have brought us together began to divide us. Contributing to a half century of politics that have too often pulled us apart,” he said in his prepared remarks.

It was the second time this week that the Prime Minister had made the case for unity directly to Albertans . On Monday, he released a short video shot in a classroom at St. Francis Xavier Catholic High School in Edmonton, which he attended as a teenager. In the video, he said that Albertans were being asked to decide on what he called “a long and uncertain process” of separation. “We are stronger together,” he said.
But Thursday was the first time he had encouraged Albertans to vote against the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes.

As he made several stops in Calgary earlier in the day, he told Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” putting him in direct opposition to Ms. Smith, whose government has spent $4-million in advertising to campaign in favour of the proposals.
The Premier says she needs approval on them to fortify her mandate, and that they would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

Ms. Smith clapped back at Mr. Carney’s comments later in the day, writing on social media that “it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”
The Prime Minister is continuing his pro-Canada campaign on Friday in Red Deer, Alta., where he’ll share a stage with Ms. Smith, and attend another Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton in the evening.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to give an address on Friday morning in Calgary at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference, a conservative gathering.

Advance voting opened earlier this week. Elections Alberta said in an e-mail on Thursday morning that roughly 815,000 Albertans had so far cast their ballots – about 27 per cent of all eligible voters.

Campaigners have been divided on how Mr. Carney should support the federalist effort and whether Ottawa should bankroll groups fighting to keep Alberta in Canada. (Alberta’s election-finance rules prohibit the federal government from funding referendum advertisers.)

Some have argued that the Prime Minister shouldn’t leave any cards on the table and use his immense popularity in Alberta to his advantage by giving the federalist side a boost. Others have said he should keep his hands out of it, and that circumventing election-finance rules would backfire.
Mr. Carney in September said his government wouldn’t help fund Alberta’s numerous pro-Canada campaigns , which struggled to raise money through the summer.

Federalist groups have since closed the distance on separatist campaigns that were flush with cash early on. Separatist groups have now scooped up about 59 per cent of all donations during the campaign, down from early September when roughly 75 per cent of all contributions were floating to them.

stories.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers temporarily stops accepting tips after data breach
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto Crime Stoppers has temporarily stopped accepting tips after it says more than 175,000 of them were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Toronto Crime Stoppers has temporarily stopped accepting tips after it says more than 175,000 of them were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names.

Oct. 22, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

ROY/SDV[](http://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/toronto-crime-stoppers-temporarily-stops-accepting-tips-after-data-breach/article_8a318452-e086-58d4-9997-c28a02b7f3a1.html)

By The Canadian Press

The organization, which allows people to submit confidential crime tips to law enforcement, says in a statement that the tip software it has used since 2018 was hit by a data breach in March.

It says the company that owns the software reported that 176,859 Toronto tips submitted between January 2022 and last November were included in the stolen data, as well as 14,973 names.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Toronto Crime Stoppers says the company, Navigate360, has not disclosed whether the names are of people who submitted tips, are named in them, or both, nor has it provided the text of the stolen tips, despite repeated requests.

The Toronto program pause comes after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach.

Toronto Crime Stoppers says it didn’t stop accepting tips sooner because Navigate360 initially said in April that Toronto data had not been taken, and when the company later said Toronto data was affected, it did not say what information was exposed.

It says it is working on a “safer way” to take tips and will share details in the coming days.

Toronto police say they are aware of new information regarding the breach, which they say “raises serious concerns regarding the protection of confidential information provided through the Crime Stoppers program.”

The force says it has suspended its use of the program while it reviews the new information and assesses the additional measures being put in place at the organization.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian convicted in U.S. terror plot gets 50 more years for stabbing prison staff
stories.summary: An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.

The U.S. Department of Justice says Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was an inmate at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania when he stabbed two correctional officers in December 2020.

It says the weapon, made from part of a steel desk in his cell, was used to stab one guard’s hand and the other guard’s head and face, causing the latter to lose his right eye.

Officials also say a note in El Bahnasawy’s sock made reference to a terrorist attack for the Islamic State, and a pledge of allegiance to the group was found in his cell.

He has been serving a sentence for plotting bombings and shootings on behalf of Isis in New York City.

The 28-year-old pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to Isis, a designated foreign terrorist organization. The additional sentence will be served consecutive to his previous 40-year conviction.

stories.title: Supreme Court to hear federal appeal over use of Emergencies Act
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government's legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the nation's capital in 2022.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government’s legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the national capital and at key border points four years ago.

For about three weeks in January and February 2022, downtown Ottawa was filled with protesters, including many in large trucks that blocked streets around Parliament Hill.

While many of the protesters were demonstrating against COVID-19 health restrictions, the protest attracted some with a variety of grievances against then-prime minister Justin Trudeau and his government.

On Feb. 14, 2022, the government invoked the Emergencies Act, which allowed for temporary measures, including regulation and prohibition of public assemblies, the designation of secure places, direction to banks to freeze assets and a ban on support for protest participants.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and others successfully argued in Federal Court that Ottawa lacked sound statutory grounds to usher in the emergency measures.

In January, a three-judge panel of the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously upheld the ruling, prompting the federal government to seek a hearing at the Supreme Court.

stories.title: Why has B.C.'s snap election caught both main parties unprepared?
stories.summary: When a snap election is called, at least one side would normally be prepared.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When a snap election is called, at least one side would normally be prepared.

But that hasn’t been the case in British Columbia, resulting in a provincial election campaign like no other, political watchers say.

The campaign has seen interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson going without media availabilities on several days, including on Tuesday and Wednesday in the home stretch, ahead of Saturday’s final voting day.

The NDP has meanwhile pivoted its messaging from focusing on U.S. President Donald Trump, to affordability, to the need for a stable majority.

And campaigning has also been notably muted with relatively few large-scale rallies, although both major parties have events scheduled this week.

Even the NDP campaign bus, which was adorned with Eby’s smiling face in 2024, is an anonymous-looking coach, devoid of slogans.

Hamish Telford, an associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said he had noticed the “lack of preparation.”

“This is especially surprising since the NDP called this election. You would think, if they were going to call a snap election, that they at least would be prepared, and that they would obviously catch the Conservatives off guard,” said Telford.

“This was an election of their making, and they are not entirely ready for it,” he added.

Telford said the NDP had initially been anticipating Eby running against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, a divisive and unpopular leader of the Conservatoves. But Findlay resigned and was replaced by Doerkson.

Eby called the snap election anyway.

Telford said he would have advised the NDP not to go through with it.

“They should have called the election off, but evidently things were too late, or they had built up too much momentum and couldn’t stop themselves.” said Telford.

Angelo Isidorou, who is chief strategist for the Conservatives, said snap elections can be messy compared with fixed-date polls.

“In this case, this is what makes this very unique … not only is it a snap election, but it was an election that took place at the same time as municipal elections, which never happens. So, it was all very chaotic,” said Isidorou of the Oct. 17 municipal polls across B.C.

He said the “biggest difference” between a snap election and a fixed-date election is the “predictability.”

“It’s difficult being in Opposition because you don’t know when the election is going to come, and when an election is called, you only have maybe over a week to recruit candidates and get them on the ballot because there’s a deadline. When there’s a fixed election, you can predict all of this,” said Isidorou.

“In this case, it wasn’t, and I think what surprised me the most is really how not prepared the NDP was,” said Isidorou, adding that otherwise, the NDP would have fielded a full slate of 93 candidates in every riding.

Elections BC said the NPD was one short of a full slate, after failing to nominate a representative in Peace River North.

But vetting may have suffered in the rush to field candidates.

While the Conservatives managed to fill their 93-riding slate, two candidates have since been disavowed by the party.

Jordan McIntosh, the 18-year-old former Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona, was dumped last Thursday over online posts that included saying Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

Another candidate, Joachim Agou, was ejected from the party earlier this month for online comments saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest group in Switzerland should have “reversed too.”

Political scientist Michael Prince said the election has “elements of some really unusual features.”

He said it was puzzling to see parties still fall into the trap of recruiting inappropriate candidates.

“They haven’t really thoroughly vetted their history of social media posts,” said Prince, the Lansdowne professor emeritus of social policy at the University of Victoria.

“We’ve seen, particularly on the Conservative side, candidates that have been removed by the leader or have stepped down very quickly,” he said. “So, that’s kind of the new unusual, but it’s been something that’s unfortunately pretty typical over the last several elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge mass shooting conspirator set to enter plea in U.S. court
stories.summary: Seattle - The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., is expected to enter a plea at an arraignment in a Seattle courthouse today.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
SEATTLE - The alleged co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and is set to go on trial in December, accused of aiding one of the worst school shootings in Canadian history.

James Bryant entered the plea in a brief arraignment appearance in Seattle on Thursday, after a grand jury last week indicted the 30-year-old Bellingham, Wash., resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

stories.title: Officials to provide update on fatal fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Edmonton - Officials are set to provide an update today about a devastating fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta that left four soldiers dead and dozens more injured.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Officials are set to provide an update today about a devastating fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta that left four soldiers dead and dozens more injured.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the 1st Canadian Division has said Saturday’s blaze began as a grass fire, but a violent windstorm sent flames racing toward soldiers training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

stories.summary: An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.

By Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press

The U.S. Department of Justice says Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was an inmate at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania when he stabbed two correctional officers in December 2020.

It says the weapon, made from part of a steel desk in his cell, was used to stab one guard’s hand and the other guard’s head and face, causing the latter to lose his right eye.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Officials also say a note in El Bahnasawy’s sock made reference to a terrorist attack for the Islamic State, and a pledge of allegiance to the group was found in his cell.

He has been serving a sentence for plotting bombings and shootings on behalf of ISIS in New York City.

The 28-year-old pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization. The additional sentence will be served consecutive to his previous 40-year conviction.

stories.title: Toddler in critical condition after group of children struck by vehicle in Oshawa
stories.summary: Police said the children were walking in the area of Ryerson Crescent and Sheridan Way with a daycare worker when they were all struck.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A two-year-old girl is in critical condition and four other children are also in hospital with minor injuries after they were struck by a vehicle in Oshawa, Ont.

Durham police said the incident happened at around 9:30 a.m. Wednesday.

Police announced at an afternoon news conference that the children were walking in the area of Ryerson Crescent and Sheridan Way with a daycare worker when they were all struck. The daycare worker, a woman, has also been taken to hospital with serious, but non-life threatening injuries.

The two-year-old was airlifted by Ornge ambulance to a Toronto-area trauma centre.

Investigators are at the scene looking into the cause of the incident, said Acting Sgt. Nicolas Gluckstein at the collision scene.

“We’ll look at any kind of distracted driving, whether it was cell phones or eating or anything of that nature. We’ll look at impairments, whether that’s a factor,” he said.

The driver has also been taken to hospital with minor injuries, and police suggested that it May be related to the emotional impact of the incident. Gluckstein said the driver remained on scene and is cooperating with investigators.

The intersection is shut down while police investigate.

stories.title: Carney and Ford set to announce support for workers amid trade war
stories.summary: Prime Minister Carney will begin the day with a meeting of the Liberal caucus and then with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, his office said in his itinerary on Wednesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney will be with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in Ottawa on Wednesday as the two are set to announce support for tariff-hit industries and workers.

Carney will begin the day with a meeting of the Liberal caucus and then with Ford, his office said in his itinerary.

Following his meeting with Ford, the two will “make an announcement to protect workers and strengthen Ontario industries.”

Later in the day, Carney will depart for Turkey.

The announcement comes as workers at an Ontario-based steel manufacturing plant are facing imminent layoffs.

Stelco announced last month that pressure from U.S. tariffs forced it to concentrate steel production at its Lake Erie Works plant in Haldimand, and halt production at its plant in Hamilton. Some employees would be offered transfers, but many would be out of work.

A resolution of the standoff between the federal government and Stelco is a “question of days,” Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Friday.

The federal government believes there have been “multiple breaches of the commitments” that Stelco made under the Investment Canada Act.

Stelco is facing financial penalties and “a potential forced divestiture,” which would force them to sell all their assets in Canada, Joly said.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said on Tuesday that the federal government would release its federal budget on Nov. 5, two days after the U.S. midterm elections.

Champagne announced the date during question period on Tuesday.

The budget will be second as Carney, who changed the schedule for how federal budgets are released by moving them from spring to fall.

Carney’s second budget date comes after the Parliamentary Budget Officer trimmed the 2026 and 2027 outlook for economic growth.

The PBO now projects gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent for 2027, down from 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent respectively.

–with files from Global’s Sean Previl

stories.title: Record $90M Lotto Max jackpot won in Alberta, OLG says
stories.summary: The record-setting $90 million Lotto Max jackpot was won in Alberta following Tuesday night’s draw, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The record-setting $90 million Lotto Max jackpot was won in Alberta following Tuesday night’s draw, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says.

The OLG didn’t say whether there was one winner or multiple in a news release Wednesday. The jackpot climbed to $90 million after several winner-less draws.

The OLG said multiple Ontario-based players won MaxMillion and MaxPlus prizes Tuesday night. Three $1 million prizes were sold in Brant County, Toronto and online.

Twelve MaxPlus tickets each worth $100,000, and five MaxPlus tickets worth $50,000 were sold elsewhere in the province.

LottoMax draws happen every Friday and Tuesday.

stories.title: Angine de Poitrine announce 2027 world tour
stories.summary: Angine de Poitrine is taking its alien invasion global.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Angine de Poitrine is taking its alien invasion global.

Quebec’s polka-dotted, self-proclaimed extraterrestrial duo has announced it will embark on a world tour in 2027.

It kicks off March 4 in Melbourne, Australia before touching down in South America, North America and Europe.

Among the eight Canadian dates are stops in Calgary, Ottawa and Winnipeg, as well as a performance at Toronto’s RBC Amphitheatre — marking their largest headlining show in the city so far.

The tour comes to a close in their hometown of Saguenay, Que.

In September, Angine de Poitrine won the $30,000 Polaris Music Prize for their second album, “Vol. II,” and the $10,000 SOCAN Polaris Song Prize for their track “Fabienk.”

They’re the first act to claim both prizes at the ceremony.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: First Nations say Elections Alberta unprepared for referendum turnout
stories.summary: Ottawa - First Nations in Alberta are celebrating the win for the pro-Canada side in Monday's referendum — but they're also raising concerns about a shortage of ballots in their communities.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - First Nations in Alberta are celebrating the win for the pro-Canada side in Monday’s referendum — but they’re also raising concerns about a shortage of ballots in their communities despite large, public efforts to increase voter turnout.

About three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation on Monday, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

Siksika Nation, located about an hour east of Calgary, said that while it’s pleased with the outcome, the polling station in their community was understaffed and didn’t receive enough ballots from Elections Alberta.

That led to long wait times and “unnecessary obstacles,” the First Nation said in a media statement.

“It is unacceptable that First Nations communities continue to encounter barriers to participating fully in Alberta’s democratic processes,” said the statement.

“Our people have fought too long for their democratic rights to be treated as an afterthought. The right to vote must be supported by meaningful and equitable access to the ballot box.”

Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi said chiefs worked in both English and their Indigenous languages to ensure voters had the information they needed to participate in the referendum.

“We went to these polling stations not out of fear, but for respect for our treaties,” Mercredi told The Canadian Press.

“When you defend the treaty, you end up defending the province, you end up defending Canada, you end up defending everybody that’s on treaty lands.”

While chiefs were prepared, Elections Alberta wasn’t, he said, referring to polling stations that opened late and those that ran out of ballots.

“If you listen to Elections Alberta, they would say that they did a fine job of making sure that people could vote, but they haven’t,” he said.

Mercredi said one community had to send its own employees to work at the polling station so that it was adequately staffed, while Fort Chipewyan had to have ballots delivered by helicopter because Elections Alberta didn’t realize the community was so remote.

“We have very serious concerns,” Mercredi said.

In an emailed statement, Elections Alberta said it delivered additional ballots to at least five First Nations communities and that in some cases, ballots had to be delivered three times throughout the day.

Elections Alberta said to prepare for higher turnout it delivered 1.5 times the number of ballots they believed communities would need, based on past voter registry data.

“This means we have seen higher turnout at these locations than we have in the past, showing higher voter engagement in these locations,” Elections Alberta said.

Elections Alberta said it’s aware of about 20 voters who were unable to vote in Samson Cree Nation because extra ballots did not arrive in time.

“This was unfortunate but could not be anticipated,” Elections Alberta said.

Tania Cameron, who helped boost First Nations turnout in the vote, said she was proud to learn several First Nations polling stations had to request more ballots.

She also said Elections Alberta should have been more prepared and the shortage of ballots is a slap in the face to community members who wanted their voices heard.

Cameron mobilized Indigenous voters in the 2015 federal election through the “Rock the Vote” campaign that some credit with helping to elect Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government.

A member of Niisaachewan Anishinaabe Nation in northwestern Ontario, Cameron helped inform Indigenous voters about what they needed to cast a ballot and how to secure necessary identification in that election.

For the referendum in Alberta, she put those same skills to work by training leadership on how to set up ID clinics and registration drives, and educating members on the ballot questions.

Indigenous people are less likely to vote in elections outside of their communities — a legacy of decades of distrust and tensions between their communities and federal and provincial governments.

Before 1960, First Nations people generally had to forfeit their Indian status in order to vote in an election.

Memories of those days still linger, making some Indigenous people wary of casting a ballot. Others see voting in outside elections as a breach of the unique treaties their communities have with the Crown.

“In elections, we choose our treaty partners — who is sitting across from us at the table as we work to uphold our treaty and work at making sure the province and federal government are upholding their end of the treaty,” Cameron said.

“In this case, I said we actually need to send a message that the province cannot erase treaty.”

A coalition of First Nations launched a court fight arguing the citizen-initiated petition to hold a separation vote was invalid because the province hadn’t followed through on its constitutional duty to consult First Nations.

In May, a judge agreed and quashed the petition. Soon after, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the government would appeal, putting the lawsuit in legal limbo.

Smith then announced the referendum anyway, citing the hundreds of thousands of Albertans who had signed petitions for one side or the other.

Elections Alberta said that while it’s difficult to estimate how many Indigenous voters cast a ballot in the referendum, the number of communities that requested polling sites increased by three.

Conservative MP Billy Morin, who represents the Edmonton Northwest riding and previously served as chief of Enoch Cree Nation, said he is happy Albertans rejected separatism.

“We’re all treaty people. It means more today than it did before this,” Morin told The Canadian Press outside the House of Commons on Tuesday.

“By our people showing up, I think it sends a strong message that we’re not just waiting around for Ottawa, provincial or federal governments to dictate to us like they have been for 150 years … We’re a small number but we made a difference.”

Morin said it’s now time to sit down and focus on the future, and for Albertans to speak to people they may disagree with, regardless how they voted.

“I’m happy to do that, and keep them in Canada,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson in Edmonton

stories.title: Carney, Ford to announce support for steel and auto sectors hit by tariffs
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are expected to unveil a new suite of supports for the steel and auto sectors hit by U.S. tariffs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The federal and Ontario governments are putting billions of dollars on the line to help bolster the province’s key sectors — steel, critical minerals and auto manufacturing — as they continue to manage the fallout of tariffs from the United States.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the $8.7-billion plan goes hand-in-hand with changes the Liberal government is making to speed up project reviews and push forward major projects, which will create massive demand for critical minerals and manufacturing capability.

“More jobs, more opportunity, more prosperity, more sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we choose,” he said.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, standing alongside Carney during the announcement in Ottawa on Wednesday, called the plan transformative.

Ford said it’s clear the Canada-U.S. relationship has changed permanently.

“No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were and we need to plan accordingly,” he said.

The plan includes a new steel action fund, with $3.5 billion in funding from Canada and $1.7 billion from Ontario over five years, to help steel companies expand the types of products they make.

Canada is spending billions more on defence procurement over the next several years. Protectionist policies brought in after the U.S. imposed tariffs on Canadian steel are also expected to bolster demand.

“At present, our steel companies rely heavily on the auto sector. In the future, pipes, rail, ports, defence will be increasingly important sources of demand,” Carney said.

He said the funding is expected to protect roughly 100,000 jobs in the sector and comes with a pledge to ramp up protections against foreign steel dumping through stronger border enforcement and other measures.

The move to protect jobs comes as the clock ticks down toward a deadline for the U.S.-based owners of Stelco to respond to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who wrote to them last week to demand they uphold job commitments made when they bought the Ontario company.

Stelco announced plans in September to lay off up to 500 workers in its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

Its owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, made legally binding commitments when it bought Stelco in 2024 to maintain at least the same number of unionized workers, and most of its non-unionized workers, for five years.

On Wednesday, Carney did not directly address questions about whether the federal or provincial governments would try to purchase Stelco to keep the plant open.

“When you make a commitment with the Government of Canada, you respect that commitment, and the government will hold companies to (that) responsibility,” he said.

The Canadian Steel Producers Association called the announcement an important show of support and applauded the measures to address steel dumping.

Another $1 billion in federal funding over three years will go toward building infrastructure — particularly roads — that will enable mining of critical minerals in the Ring of Fire region in northern Ontario. That matches an earlier spending pledge from Ontario.

Carney said the governments will create a working group with local Indigenous communities, some of which are opposed to development in the region. A government press release said that work will include “studying options for conservation and/or Indigenous protected areas” as development begins.

The province and federal governments also agreed to create a co-ordinated process for permits to streamline approvals.

“Canada will always be a country of high standards, but high standards do not mean decisions have to be slow,” Carney said.

The overall plan also includes $2.5 billion for the automotive sector, with the federal government chipping in $1.5 billion. Carney said that is aimed at helping automakers pivot to meet the growing demand for electric vehicles.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war has dragged on for more than a year and a half, causing a double-digit decline in auto exports on both sides of the border.

Carney said he spoke with Trump Wednesday morning “for quite some time” and Canada remains ready to sit down and negotiate with the White House when the administration is ready.

On Tuesday, Canada-U.S. Relations Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters that there are ongoing conversations with the Americans, though he did not say there were negotiations.

“We’re going to find a deal with the United States at some point that’s in the interests of the entire Canadian economy, and that’s the work we continue to do,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Record $90M Lotto Max jackpot won in Alberta, OLG says
stories.summary: The historic jackpot, first announced on Oct. 14, surpasses the previous Canadian lottery record of $85 million.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Canada’s record-setting $90 million Lotto Max jackpot has been won by a ticket sold in Alberta following Tuesday night’s draw, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) confirmed.

The historic jackpot, first announced on Oct. 14, surpasses the previous Canadian lottery record of $85 million .

The OLG says several major winning tickets were sold across the province as part of the Oct. 20 Lotto Max draw.

Among the biggest Ontario prizes were three Maxmillions tickets worth $1 million each, sold in Brant County, Ont., Toronto and through OLG.ca.

In addition, 12 MaxPlus tickets worth $100,000 each were sold in:

Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.

Hamilton, Ont.

Vaughan, Ont.

Ottawa, Ont.

United Counties of Prescott and Russell, Ont.

Oxford County, Ont.

Bowmanville, Ont.

Pickering, Ont.

Barrie, Ont.

Oakville, Ont.

OLG.ca

OLG.ca

Five additional MaxPlus prizes worth $50,000 each were sold in:

Welland, Ont.

London, Ont.

Simcoe County, Ont.

Unionville, Ont.

OLG.ca

OLG noted those prizes were shared with other winning tickets sold across Ontario and Canada.

Lottery officials are urging players to check their tickets using the OLG app or at a lottery retailer.

stories.title: Group assisting long-planned review of firearms — including SKS — has yet to meet
stories.summary: Ottawa — An advisory group that's supporting a federal review of firearms classification — including a look at the SKS rifle — is expected to hold its first meeting this fall, almost a year after Ottawa announced the review.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — An advisory group that’s supporting a federal review of firearms classification — including a look at the SKS rifle — is expected to hold its first meeting this fall, almost a year after Ottawa announced the review.

Public Safety Canada says members of the Firearms Classification Technical Advisory Group, appointed to provide expert advice to the department and the RCMP, “will be meeting later this fall.”

The Liberal government has faced fresh questions about the SKS after a document filed in a U.S. court said the killer in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting talked about having an SKS gun.

Eighteen-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people in the Feb. 10 Tumbler Ridge attack before taking her own life.

The RCMP has declined to release details about firearms used in the shootings, saying its investigation is ongoing.

The SKS has been used in police killings and other high-profile shootings.

It is also commonly used in Indigenous communities to hunt for food.

Prime Minister Mark Carney recently indicated the government would look at the advice of the classification advisory group before making any decision on the status of the SKS.

Since May 2020, Ottawa has outlawed approximately 2,500 types of guns on the basis they belong only on the battlefield. It has not banned the SKS.

Gun control advocacy group PolySeSouvient has long called on the government to impose an immediate ban on new sales of the SKS, to remove from circulation modern, assault-style versions of the rifle, and to implement a voluntary buyback of older models. It calls for an exemption for Indigenous hunters who use the SKS primarily for sustenance.

In early December last year, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the government would “shortly be launching a comprehensive review of the firearms classification regime” with an emphasis on simplicity and consistency.

“This review will be supported by an expanded advisory group, and will involve dedicated consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, including on the SKS, to ensure Indigenous perspectives and traditions are an active part of the process,” he said in a statement.

“The review will take a broad view of the legal framework for firearms, devices, magazines and ammunition to modernize the regime and ensure Canadians’ safety.”

In response to questions this month from The Canadian Press, the Public Safety Department said more information on the Technical Advisory Group and on engagement activities related to the classification review will be made available “in the near term.”

“Members will bring diverse technical knowledge, experience, and expert views from a wide range of perspectives,” the department said.

PolySeSouvient said this week that instead of implementing a comprehensive ban on assault-style firearms and high-capacity magazines, “the government keeps announcing new consultations and panels, and each one becomes another reason to postpone actual change.”

“Lives are at stake,” the group told The Canadian Press. “The government needs to stop consulting and start acting, before more people are killed in mass shootings.”

In a recent commentary on its website, the Canadian Shooting Sports Association said many questions remain about the Tumbler Ridge shootings, including which firearms were used, how they were obtained, and which — if any — had been seized by police previously.

“Reclassifying another firearm before answering those questions may satisfy the demand for immediate action,” the commentary said. “It does not prove that banning another firearm would have prevented this mass murder.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press
