stories.title: 'Hurting': Vigil in Wainwright, Alta., for soldiers caught in deadly fire
stories.summary: Wainwright - Almost every church in Wainwright, Alta., has a parishioner who's a soldier at the nearby military base.
stories.author: Bill Graveland and David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Four Canadian flags, one for each soldier killed during training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, fluttered in the wind late Wednesday as a prayer vigil at the town’s Church of the Nazarene got underway.

“I want to thank you for coming here this evening to honour those who lost their lives and who were injured,” Evangelical Free Church pastor Isaiah Mast told the crowd of 150.

“Thank you for coming here this evening to pray and support those who gave so heroically during this tragedy, and for the family and friends who have been impacted directly through it all. You being here matters a lot.”

Roughly 84 soldiers of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in a field exercise on Saturday when strong and sudden winds whipped a nearby grass fire straight into their path.

Four soldiers were killed, and 39 were wounded. As of Wednesday, Premier Danielle Smith said there were 27 in hospital, including 13 in critical condition.

At the vigil, prayers were said and the names of those who died — Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton — were read aloud, followed by a moment of silence.

“These courageous soldiers willingly placed themselves in harm’s way to secure our continued peace and freedom as Canadians,” said Pastor Dan Marchuk of the Wainwright Pentecostal Assembly.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the past few days have not been easy for anyone. He hopes those in hospital recover quickly and said things have started returning to normal at the base.

“I noticed the cannons are firing again because they never rest,” he said. “They never stop defending us and preserving our ability to gather in places like this.”

Earlier Wednesday, residents paid their respects to the soldiers who were at the training area that day but were not injured.

About 300 flag-waving supporters greeted two buses carrying soldiers from the base along an area highway.

Many in the crowd also held signs thanking troops for their service.

“Wainwright stands with you,” read one sign.

“Our condolences for your comrades and thank you for your service,” read another.

During the highway tribute, two military helicopters flew overhead as the two Forces buses slowly drove past the crowd.

The mayor said the town of roughly 7,000 people wanted to show support for the military.

“It’s a Highway of Heroes kind of thing in our own little community,” he said.

“After the incident, they continued on with their training and continued to do their jobs. And so I think the least we can do is show a sense of pride in them and appreciation for what they’re doing.”

Among those on the highway were several soldiers from the base, some holding regimental and Canadian flags.

Dolly Brooks and her husband were carrying flags. Her walker was also festooned with a flag and a yellow “Support Our Troops” ribbon.

Dan Brooks spent 33 years in the Forces, and the couple has lived in Wainwright for most of that time. The base is important to both of them.

“I’ve noticed from near and far and all over the world that we’re getting the support that we need and how we come together when we really need to,” said Dolly Brooks.

Her husband said it’s always painful when a soldier dies. “It’s not easy. It’s not the first time I’ve seen a soldier pass on, and it’s never nice.

“You always just hope that there’s a learning curve from what happened here, so we can prevent it in the future.”

Rhea Lovely grew up in a military family. Her father was driving one of the buses, she said.

The events of Saturday have hit the community hard, she said.

“Everyone’s been kind of sombre. The whole town’s been really quiet, but we’re just looking to support our troops because they are our town,” she said.

“It doesn’t matter where they were from in Canada. They are still family.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario drug funding decision leaves cancer patients disappointed, with few options
stories.summary: Toronto - Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.

A rare form of cancer in the 31-year-old’s knee had metastasized, spreading to her lungs. She has undergone radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgeries, though the synovial sarcoma couldn’t be fully removed.

Apitz-Grossman’s doctors are recommending a treatment approved in the United States but unavailable in Ontario. She needs it urgently but the Ontario Health Insurance Plan turned her down for out-of-country coverage. An appeal failed, as did an application under a Case-by-Case Review Program to get special permission for the treatment to be administered at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto.

She is still fighting.

“I so desperately would love to turn 32,” she said.

Apitz-Grossman and other Ontarians with Stage 4 cancer told by their doctors that they are good candidates for treatments unavailable in the province were buoyed last month when 37-year-old Alex Shved won a court challenge against his OHIP out-of-country denial for metastatic melanoma treatment.

Though Shved’s court decision was not necessarily directly applicable to all of their cases, they saw an opening, and their hopes were dashed when Health Minister Sylvia Jones responded to the court ruling by changing the rules.

Drug treatments will now only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed, a set of circumstances some patients see as impossibly narrow. The government said it clarified in regulation what was already long-standing policy.

“We’re protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas,” Jones wrote in a statement.

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2 billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year.”

Framing the move as a cost-saving measure is not sitting right with Apitz-Grossman.

“Are we saying that we could save like 5,000 or more people’s lives, and they’re proud of themselves for not doing that?” she said. “Is this supposed to be good news that we’re not going to save those people, so that we can instead buy a couple more private jets?”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford came under fire earlier this year for a government purchase of a $29-million private jet and quickly returned it.

The treatment Apitz-Grossman is seeking, Tecelra, is a personalized therapy made from a patient’s own T-cells, a type of white blood cell. Nearly half of patients in Apitz-Grossman’s situation respond to the treatment, and among those who respond, there is a 90 per cent chance of survival after a year and 70 per cent after two years, according to her oncologist.

But the treatment is costly, at US$727,000, Apitz-Grossman said. She feels terrible guilt for seeking such a pricey treatment, she said, but she wants to live.

“There has never been a moment where I have thought to myself, ‘Gosh, I wish that patient who was in the ICU for weeks and who it cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to save, hadn’t been saved,’” Apitz-Grossman said.

The origin of Jones’ $5.2-billion figure was unclear in her press release, and a government official later explained that it would be the additional cost if the province entirely stopped negotiating prices with drug manufacturers for public coverage in Ontario.

OHIP’s reason for denying Apitz-Grossman, Shved and others out-of-country drug treatment funding is that routinely paying for such requests while drugs are undergoing review for funding in Ontario would “undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada’s drug review processes.”

Kevin Nash, 59, has metastatic melanoma and is seeking the same tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy as Shved. Nash’s out-of-country application and subsequent appeal were also denied, and he does not believe the government’s reasoning.

“These companies make billions of dollars a year, not a billion, billions of dollars a year,” he said. “Do you think that they care one bit whether Kevin Nash goes to Buffalo for a treatment? That’s so preposterous.”

In Apitz-Grossman’s case, the manufacturer of Tecelra has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada. That means there is no review process in this case to undermine, she noted. Jones’ office said drugs that have not been approved by Health Canada are not funded in Ontario or any other province, and the recent clarification of the out-of-country rules did not change that.

Holly Wardlow, 61, is in a similar boat, with the government denying coverage through its Case-by-Case Review Program for a medication to treat her rare form of liver cancer because the drug was “expected to be reviewed for public funding in Ontario.”

That’s despite the manufacturer submitting two letters telling the province it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada.

“We just thought, ‘Well, this doesn’t make any sense,’” Wardlow said.

“We provided evidence that there is not going to be a population-based review. This drug is never going to be approved in Canada, let alone Ontario, because the manufacturer is not going to make an application, and they have evidence of that. And yet they provided the same reason for denying funding.”

Wardlow and her husband have been paying $78,000 a month for her to receive infusions in Ontario every two weeks, and her tumour has been shrinking with almost no side-effects, she said.

Their savings have been depleted and they have now started a GoFundMe.

“I’m getting out there and trying to stay fit, partly because I can, and partly because the weather is beautiful, and partly because I’m thinking ahead that surgery may be possible in the future,” Wardlow said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Young anglophones are still leaving Quebec, but at much lower rates, find researchers
stories.summary: Montreal - Having grown up in an English-speaking family in Montreal, Jeremy Schachter says the question of staying or leaving Quebec was a “very real” dinner-table conversation.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Having grown up in an English-speaking family in Montreal, Jeremy Schachter says the question of staying or leaving Quebec was a “very real” dinner-table conversation.

“So many of my friends have left. It’s just, people wonder about the future of the anglophone community,” he said.

Schachter himself moved to Toronto a year ago to join his girlfriend, who works as a social worker in the city. He is part of a long-standing movement of young English-speakers leaving Quebec to move elsewhere in Canada.

Data from the federal census shows that English-speakers are more likely to leave Quebec in favour of other provinces than French-speakers, but that the trend is slowing down.

This movement was especially strong in the 1970s and 1980s, said Simon-Pierre Lacasse, who recently wrote a paper exploring the migration of young anglophones out of Quebec.

“The ‘Anglo exodus’, as it’s often referred to, is something that’s really contingent to a specific period,” Lacasse told The Canadian Press.

In their research, Simon-Pierre Lacasse and student Meghan Rulli focused on young adults, who are more likely to move between provinces.

Their research paints a picture of how the rate of this migration has slowed down in recent decades.

Their research paper, published by the Quebec English-Speaking Communities Research Network, shows close to 20 per cent of English-speakers in Quebec left the province between the late 1960s and the early 1980s, with the net loss of around 121,000 anglophones in interprovincial migration between 1976 and 1981.

Between 2016 and 2021, the interprovincial anglophone migration was almost balanced, with a net loss of around 3900 anglophones in Quebec.

At the end of the most recent period, federal statistics reveal the overall English-speaking community in the province remained strong. Over 1.6 million Quebecers spoke English at home on a regular basis in 2021, according to the census.

This represents over 19 per cent of the Quebec population.

At the same time, the census numbers show that over 35 per cent of workers in the province said they regularly spoke English while on the job.

Lacasse said the numbers appear to suggest young English-speakers are better integrated in the province’s culture today than they were in the 1970s.

“To me, that was the big surprise. … If the goal is youth retention for the vitality of English-speaking communities, then maybe there is hope,” said Lacasse.

The researchers identified many “push” factors that might drive anglophones away from Quebec, including greater career opportunities elsewhere and economic concerns. Interwoven with many of these factors is the question of language.

“Language in Quebec, perhaps more than other provinces in Canada, is directly linked to identity and is politicized,” said Lacasse.

In 2022, the provincial government passed a bill that strengthened language legislation in the province. It imposed measures like French-only services for most Quebec residents and a cap on enrolment in some English-language colleges.

The bill also caused disruptions during the recent provincial election campaign after the election authority sent out French-only guides to all voters. A Superior Court judge temporarily suspended the bill’s provisions and ordered the agency to send out bilingual reminder cards to voters.

On Ki Lin, who was born in Hong Kong but moved to Montreal when they were eight years old, said they left Quebec to study at the University of Toronto mainly because they thought this was the best place to pursue their education.

Although Lin says financial concerns are keeping them in Toronto, the former Montrealer also noted having struggled to fully integrate into Quebec culture.

“There would be some people (who) would be very abrasive and very rude because my accent wasn’t the same as theirs. Or they would assume that if I had an accent, it meant that I wasn’t fluent enough to understand what they were saying,” said Lin.

The feeling that there is no space for English-speaking identities in Quebec lingers for many, said Lacasse.

“When I was living in Montreal, the overarching sentiment was that, you live here, but are you really welcome here? I don’t know. It was not so clear to me,” said Schachter.

This affects not only feelings of identity and belonging, but also professional development, with some anglophones feeling that they are not welcome in francophone workspaces, found the paper.

But English-speaking Quebecers’ relationship with the French language is also generational, said Lacasse, pointing out that those born after the Quiet Revolution in the 1960s, a period of nationalist political and social reform marked by a strengthening of the French-speaking Quebec identity, were more likely to understand the importance of French within the province.

The paper also highlights that young English-speakers in Quebec are increasingly bilingual.

Speaking with The Canadian Press, Schachter expressed attachment to the French language. He said he was recently offended when a man sitting close to him at a hockey game became upset to hear the national anthem sung in French.

“Even though I wouldn’t consider myself francophone … I think that’s really offensive,” he said.

Lacasse added English-speakers may find it easier to move to the rest of Canada, while French-speakers may face language barriers.

Lacasse said he is curious to see what trends will appear from the 2026 census data, which is set to be released in early 2027, especially after a period of high political tensions around language in Quebec.

From their new lives in Toronto, Lin and Schachter both reminisced about Montreal and Quebec.

“I would never consider myself Québécois, really, but there’s definitely something special about Quebec,” said Schachter.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Mother of First Nation woman who couldn't get medical transport and died seeks reform
stories.summary: If only. It's a phrase that plays over and over again in Eva Mamakwa's mind.
stories.author: Liam Casey and Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
If only. It’s a phrase that plays over and over again in Eva Mamakwa’s mind.

If only her daughter, Miranda Mamakwa, had made it to at least one followup appointment after open-heart surgery, she may be alive.

If only Indigenous Services Canada’s non-insured health benefits program had arranged travel for just one of her four missed appointments, Miranda may be alive.

The 31-year-old mother of three from Fort Severn First Nation died on Sept. 8, weeks after asking people on social media to seek action in case of her death.

“I don’t want this to happen to anyone else,” Eva Mamakwa said in an interview with The Canadian Press from her home before falling quiet, overcome with emotion. She is speaking out about her daughter’s death for the first time.

Since Miranda Mamakwa’s death, more than a dozen First Nations and tribal councils have filed a human rights complaint that alleges widespread neglect of their communities’ health needs, while chiefs have demanded reform from the federal agency in charge of arranging medical travel for remote First Nation people.

Indigenous Services Canada said it’s working to improve delivery of the service, while the minister in charge has said she requested a fact-finding mission on the circumstances that led to Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

Months ago, Mamakwa’s family was filled with hope as she underwent surgery at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute in April to replace a valve in her heart. She recovered over two weeks at the hospital in Ottawa, then two more weeks at the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre.

On May 24, she arrived home in Fort Severn First Nation, the most northerly community in Ontario that sits near the mouth of the Severn River on Hudson Bay.

Her doctors wanted to see her for several followups. She had blood clots and had been put on blood thinners, which required testing on an ongoing basis, Eva Mamakwa said. Doctors booked her daughter for an echocardiogram and an appointment with a vascular surgeon in Thunder Bay.

Miranda Mamakwa was thrilled to be back home; her children were excited and her mother was caring for her.

That excitement would soon abate.

Eva Mamakwa said she went to the First Nation’s nursing station to begin the administrative process to arrange travel back to Thunder Bay for her daughter’s first followup appointment. Nurses soon faxed Miranda’s documentation to the non-insured health benefits program — faxes are protocol — and the family waited to hear back on travel plans.

She said the agency never responded and her daughter missed her first appointment on May 28. Eva Mamakwa then called NIHB’s office in Sioux Lookout, Ont., and got someone on the line.

“I told her that it was extremely important that Miranda go to her followup appointments,” she said. “I talked to her and she listened to me and she said they would send her travel, but travel never came.”

She said the NIHB told her the request never arrived despite more than one tranche of faxes being sent.

The same thing occurred for followup appointments on June 11, July 2 and Aug. 6, Eva Mamakwa said, despite multiple faxes and phone calls.

“They didn’t care at all,” she said.

As the summer progressed, Miranda Mamakwa became more tired, slept more and started losing feeling in her fingers.

On Aug. 19, she wrote a Facebook post about the problems with NIHB and the missed appointments.

“If I die, pls go after (them),” she wrote.

On Sept. 6, she started to feel sick. Her stomach hurt and she began vomiting. “We just thought she might have caught the flu from her kids,” her mother said.

But Eva Mamakwa soon realized that “something was terribly wrong.”

Her daughter needed immediate help. Later that day, Skycare, which operates on behalf of provincial air and land ambulance Ornge, arrived, and airlifted her to the intensive care unit of the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre, some 850 kilometres away.

The next day, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, Miranda’s father, got a call from the ICU doctor.

“He told me that Miranda had a lot of bleeding in her brain, she was hemorrhaging,” she said. “Even if they send her down south (to Toronto), to try and help her, that she wouldn’t have survived it.”

The doctor told them to fly to Thunder Bay so they did, with Miranda’s children in tow. Eva Mamakwa’s oldest daughter was already at the hospital to support her sister.

They arrived to crushing news.

“There was no brain activity at all and we had to make a very difficult decision to take her off life support or not,” Eva Mamakwa said through tears.

“As much as I wanted to keep her, it wouldn’t have been a good idea because it was the machine that was helping her breathe,” she said.

“It was very, very heartbreaking seeing my daughter being disconnected. But up until the end, when her heart stopped, and everything shut down, her children were beside her. All of us were beside her. And then we watched her go.”

Eva Mamakwa’s words failed, briefly, as tears rolled down her cheeks while she relived the nightmare.

“Today my daughter would be here if her travel was made to attend her appointments, but sadly it didn’t happen,” she said. “I am holding NIHB accountable for my daughter’s passing.”

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said her department would review the circumstances of the case, and that Mamakwa’s community and family deserved answers.

The woman’s death became a clarion call to First Nation leadership across Canada. It came after hundreds of people staged a sit-in at the NIHB office in Sioux Lookout over missed medical appointments, calling for urgent reform.

Chief Archie Wabasse of Wunnumin Lake First Nation, a remote fly-in community some 500 kilometres north of Thunder Bay and 330 kilometres south of Fort Severn, broke into tears as he discussed the issue in a recent interview.

He said that in his community of 800 people, about 80 residents had a total of 147 missed medical appointments between March 2025 and March 2026 due to lack of transport.

There is no full-time doctor in the First Nation, but one rotates in for a week or two every month, for 12 to 14 visits a year. Demand for the doctor’s time far exceeds availability, and those visits lead to referrals to specialists in southern parts of the province.

“The problem is getting worse for my people,” an emotional Wabasse said.

He lists a number of community members who need help. One, with a pacemaker, who has already missed a few appointments. Another who needs dialysis in a few days, but has not heard back from NIHB about his travel. In one case, the band paid about $3,000 to send an elder to a specialist in Winnipeg after NIHB did not return calls, he said.

Wabasse said he met with the Indigenous Services minister to talk about the issue, months before Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

He said Gull-Masty told the chiefs in attendance about improvements being made to NIHB, but she declined their request to sit down with them and resolve on the spot what he sees as a relatively straightforward administrative issue.

“It is a solvable problem, but what we’re trying to do here is advocating, telling the minister, the decision makers, the prime minister, this could be solved in one day,” Wabasse said.

When asked about Wabasse’s description of that meeting with the minister, Indigenous Services Canada said regular dialogue with First Nations leaders about NIHB “has been an important part of our work to improve service levels.”

More than 12 First Nations and tribal councils filed a complaint on Oct. 1 with the Canadian Human Rights Commission against Indigenous Services Canada over what they say is effectively a denial of health care in their communities.

The joint complaint from Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council and Windigo First Nations Council alleges the federal department’s non-insured health benefits program is failing to meet the needs of community members for medical transportation.

The NIHB program for First Nations and Inuit people covers medical, dental and mental health care not available through private insurance or provincial health plans. First Nations leaders and physicians have long said the program is not working for communities, and that its employees are notorious for being slow in responding to queries, requests and filing reimbursements.

The complainants say NIHB fails to consistently arrange medical transportation, or it informs patients so late about the transport that they are forced to miss their appointments.

They say Eabametoong First Nation community members miss about 50 appointments per month, while North Caribou First Nation members missed almost 100 appointments in the past year.

The complaint said First Nations have attempted to raise the issue with Indigenous Services Canada from as early as 2014, to no avail.

“Due to ISC’s actions, First Nations are suffering and dying. This is known to ISC, and yet nothing has been done to change it,” the complaint said. “Years of NIHB failing to approve requests on a timely basis, considered in the context of costs associated with First Nation service-provision and remoteness, represents a choice to deny First Nations health care.”

The complainants are requesting a formal review and reform of the benefits program, along with $20,000 in compensation for each individual who missed an appointment due to NIHB’s failures, and an additional $20,000 for pain and suffering.

“The continued failure regarding medical transportation is the newest chapter in a long history of Canada’s colonial practices devaluing the health and safety of Indigenous people,” the complaint said.

Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Carolane Gratton said the department recognizes the serious impacts any gaps in service can have on people who rely on NIHB for medical transportation, and that it’s working to strengthen the delivery of the service.

The department implemented a simplified travel submission process in early October, meant to provide clients with more direct support from local medical transportation co-ordinators and create a “more consistent and streamlined experience,” Gratton wrote in an emailed statement. She said the department is looking into other actions that could improve call centre performance.

Indigenous Services Canada did not provide details when asked if there is a service standard for arranging medical transportation, nor how often that standard is met.

Gratton said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”

Julian Falconer, a longtime human rights lawyer who is representing the First Nations and tribal councils in the case, said their complaint is not about “simple negligence.”

“We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life,” he said. “It’s an outrage.”

The government’s response is a “perfect parallel” to what happened to Miranda Mamakwa after her surgery, he said.

paragraphs: If only. It’s a phrase that plays over and over again in Eva Mamakwa’s mind.
If only her daughter, Miranda Mamakwa, had made it to at least one followup appointment after open-heart surgery, she may be alive.
If only Indigenous Services Canada’s non-insured health benefits program had arranged travel for just one of her four missed appointments, Miranda may be alive.
The 31-year-old mother of three from Fort Severn First Nation died on Sept. 8, weeks after asking people on social media to seek action in case of her death.

“I don’t want this to happen to anyone else,” Eva Mamakwa said in an interview with The Canadian Press from her home before falling quiet, overcome with emotion. She is speaking out about her daughter’s death for the first time.

Since Miranda Mamakwa’s death, more than a dozen First Nations and tribal councils have filed a human rights complaint that alleges widespread neglect of their communities’ health needs, while chiefs have demanded reform from the federal agency in charge of arranging medical travel for remote First Nation people.

Indigenous Services Canada said it’s working to improve delivery of the service, while the minister in charge has said she requested a fact-finding mission on the circumstances that led to Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

Months ago, Mamakwa’s family was filled with hope as she underwent surgery at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute in April to replace a valve in her heart. She recovered over two weeks at the hospital in Ottawa, then two more weeks at the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre.
On May 24, she arrived home in Fort Severn First Nation, the most northerly community in Ontario that sits near the mouth of the Severn River on Hudson Bay.

Her doctors wanted to see her for several followups. She had blood clots and had been put on blood thinners, which required testing on an ongoing basis, Eva Mamakwa said. Doctors booked her daughter for an echocardiogram and an appointment with a vascular surgeon in Thunder Bay.
Miranda Mamakwa was thrilled to be back home; her children were excited and her mother was caring for her.
That excitement would soon abate.

Eva Mamakwa said she went to the First Nation’s nursing station to begin the administrative process to arrange travel back to Thunder Bay for her daughter’s first followup appointment. Nurses soon faxed Miranda’s documentation to the non-insured health benefits program — faxes are protocol — and the family waited to hear back on travel plans.
She said the agency never responded and her daughter missed her first appointment on May 28. Eva Mamakwa then called NIHB’s office in Sioux Lookout, Ont., and got someone on the line.

“I told her that it was extremely important that Miranda go to her followup appointments,” she said. “I talked to her and she listened to me and she said they would send her travel, but travel never came.”
She said the NIHB told her the request never arrived despite more than one tranche of faxes being sent.
The same thing occurred for followup appointments on June 11, July 2 and Aug. 6, Eva Mamakwa said, despite multiple faxes and phone calls.
“They didn’t care at all,” she said.
As the summer progressed, Miranda Mamakwa became more tired, slept more and started losing feeling in her fingers.
On Aug. 19, she wrote a Facebook post about the problems with NIHB and the missed appointments.
“If I die, pls go after (them),” she wrote.
On Sept. 6, she started to feel sick. Her stomach hurt and she began vomiting. “We just thought she might have caught the flu from her kids,” her mother said.
But Eva Mamakwa soon realized that “something was terribly wrong.”

Her daughter needed immediate help. Later that day, Skycare, which operates on behalf of provincial air and land ambulance Ornge, arrived, and airlifted her to the intensive care unit of the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre, some 850 kilometres away.
The next day, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, Miranda’s father, got a call from the ICU doctor.
“He told me that Miranda had a lot of bleeding in her brain, she was hemorrhaging,” she said. “Even if they send her down south (to Toronto), to try and help her, that she wouldn’t have survived it.”
The doctor told them to fly to Thunder Bay so they did, with Miranda’s children in tow. Eva Mamakwa’s oldest daughter was already at the hospital to support her sister.
They arrived to crushing news.
“There was no brain activity at all and we had to make a very difficult decision to take her off life support or not,” Eva Mamakwa said through tears.
“As much as I wanted to keep her, it wouldn’t have been a good idea because it was the machine that was helping her breathe,” she said.

“It was very, very heartbreaking seeing my daughter being disconnected. But up until the end, when her heart stopped, and everything shut down, her children were beside her. All of us were beside her. And then we watched her go.”
Eva Mamakwa’s words failed, briefly, as tears rolled down her cheeks while she relived the nightmare.
“Today my daughter would be here if her travel was made to attend her appointments, but sadly it didn’t happen,” she said. “I am holding NIHB accountable for my daughter’s passing.”
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said her department would review the circumstances of the case, and that Mamakwa’s community and family deserved answers.

The woman’s death became a clarion call to First Nation leadership across Canada. It came after hundreds of people staged a sit-in at the NIHB office in Sioux Lookout over missed medical appointments, calling for urgent reform.

Chief Archie Wabasse of Wunnumin Lake First Nation, a remote fly-in community some 500 kilometres north of Thunder Bay and 330 kilometres south of Fort Severn, broke into tears as he discussed the issue in a recent interview.
He said that in his community of 800 people, about 80 residents had a total of 147 missed medical appointments between March 2025 and March 2026 due to lack of transport.

There is no full-time doctor in the First Nation, but one rotates in for a week or two every month, for 12 to 14 visits a year. Demand for the doctor’s time far exceeds availability, and those visits lead to referrals to specialists in southern parts of the province.
“The problem is getting worse for my people,” an emotional Wabasse said.

He lists a number of community members who need help. One, with a pacemaker, who has already missed a few appointments. Another who needs dialysis in a few days, but has not heard back from NIHB about his travel. In one case, the band paid about $3,000 to send an elder to a specialist in Winnipeg after NIHB did not return calls, he said.
Wabasse said he met with the Indigenous Services minister to talk about the issue, months before Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

He said Gull-Masty told the chiefs in attendance about improvements being made to NIHB, but she declined their request to sit down with them and resolve on the spot what he sees as a relatively straightforward administrative issue.
“It is a solvable problem, but what we’re trying to do here is advocating, telling the minister, the decision makers, the prime minister, this could be solved in one day,” Wabasse said.

When asked about Wabasse’s description of that meeting with the minister, Indigenous Services Canada said regular dialogue with First Nations leaders about NIHB “has been an important part of our work to improve service levels.”

More than 12 First Nations and tribal councils filed a complaint on Oct. 1 with the Canadian Human Rights Commission against Indigenous Services Canada over what they say is effectively a denial of health care in their communities.

The joint complaint from Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council and Windigo First Nations Council alleges the federal department’s non-insured health benefits program is failing to meet the needs of community members for medical transportation.

The NIHB program for First Nations and Inuit people covers medical, dental and mental health care not available through private insurance or provincial health plans. First Nations leaders and physicians have long said the program is not working for communities, and that its employees are notorious for being slow in responding to queries, requests and filing reimbursements.
The complainants say NIHB fails to consistently arrange medical transportation, or it informs patients so late about the transport that they are forced to miss their appointments.
They say Eabametoong First Nation community members miss about 50 appointments per month, while North Caribou First Nation members missed almost 100 appointments in the past year.
The complaint said First Nations have attempted to raise the issue with Indigenous Services Canada from as early as 2014, to no avail.

“Due to ISC’s actions, First Nations are suffering and dying. This is known to ISC, and yet nothing has been done to change it,” the complaint said. “Years of NIHB failing to approve requests on a timely basis, considered in the context of costs associated with First Nation service-provision and remoteness, represents a choice to deny First Nations health care.”

The complainants are requesting a formal review and reform of the benefits program, along with $20,000 in compensation for each individual who missed an appointment due to NIHB’s failures, and an additional $20,000 for pain and suffering.

“The continued failure regarding medical transportation is the newest chapter in a long history of Canada’s colonial practices devaluing the health and safety of Indigenous people,” the complaint said.

Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Carolane Gratton said the department recognizes the serious impacts any gaps in service can have on people who rely on NIHB for medical transportation, and that it’s working to strengthen the delivery of the service.

The department implemented a simplified travel submission process in early October, meant to provide clients with more direct support from local medical transportation co-ordinators and create a “more consistent and streamlined experience,” Gratton wrote in an emailed statement. She said the department is looking into other actions that could improve call centre performance.
Indigenous Services Canada did not provide details when asked if there is a service standard for arranging medical transportation, nor how often that standard is met.
Gratton said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”
Julian Falconer, a longtime human rights lawyer who is representing the First Nations and tribal councils in the case, said their complaint is not about “simple negligence.”
“We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life,” he said. “It’s an outrage.”
The government’s response is a “perfect parallel” to what happened to Miranda Mamakwa after her surgery, he said.

stories.title: A look at past referendums in Canada as Albertans reject future separation vote
stories.summary: Famously, a razor-thin majority rejected the idea of Quebec leaving Confederation and becoming its own country in 1995.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Albertans voted in a referendum Monday against separation. In early results, about 76 per cent said they wanted the province to stay in Canada, while 24 per cent said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Albertans have voted in droves to stay in Canada. The result was satisfying for the pro-Canada movement, but separatists say it's just the beginning. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Here’s a look at some of the other referendums held across Canada:

2021 — Alberta on daylight time

The province asked residents whether it should adopt year-round daylight time — the time often used across Canada in the summer — to put an end to twice-yearly clock changes.

Out of more than 1 million votes, 50.2 per cent were against the idea, while 48.8 per cent were in favour of ditching clock changes.

Premier Danielle Smith announced this year that starting Nov. 1, the province is adopting year-round daylight time.

She said it’s to gauge opinion and that most people will agree. She said if she’s wrong, the government could put the matter to a vote in 2027.

2019 — Prince Edward Island electoral reform

Voters weighed in on electoral reform alongside the provincial election.

It followed similar votes in 2016 and 2005, which both failed to eliminate the voting practice known as “first past the post.”

The referendum asked: “Should Prince Edward Island change its voting system to a mixed member proportional voting system?”

The threshold for a win in either direction would have been 17, but neither side was able to secure that number — 13 districts voted against, while 14 voted in favour.

2018 — British Columbia electoral reform

After failed votes in 2009 and 2005, the province held a third referendum on electoral reform.

Out of all ballots received, 61.3 per cent voted to keep first past the post, while proportional representation got 38.7 per cent.

2007 — Ontario electoral reform

The referendum asked voters to chose between the existing first-past-the-post or the mixed-member proportional systems.

Voters overwhelmingly rejected mixed-member proportional representation, with Elections Ontario figures showing roughly 1.5 million people voted for change, while nearly 2.7 million voted against it.

2001 — New Brunswick video lottery terminals

Voters were asked whether the province should ban VLTs, following a 1999 campaign promise by former premier Bernard Lord.

“Should the province of New Brunswick continue to permit the legal and regulated operation of video gaming devices, commonly known as video lottery terminals?”

About 53 per cent were in favour of keeping VLTs, while 47 per cent were opposed.

New Brunswick was the first to allow VLTs after Ottawa, in 1985, allowed provinces and territories to operate the machines.

1997 — Newfoundland education

Newfoundlanders voted in on the churches’ role in the province’s education system.

The referendum asked: “Do you support a single school system where all children, regardless of their religious affiliation, attend the same schools where opportunities for religious education and observances are provided?”

More than 70 per cent of voters wanted to create a non-denominational public education system still allowing religious instruction and observance, ending the church-run school system.

In a similar vote two years earlier, voters narrowly approved the government’s plan to reform the church-run education system.

1995 — Quebec sovereignty

A razor-thin majority rejected the idea of the province leaving Confederation and becoming its own country.

In a dramatic campaign, the sovereigntist side came from behind to take a lead in the polls in the final weeks before the vote. In the end, 50.58 per cent voted no.

A previous vote in 1980 also rejected sovereignty.

1992 — Charlottetown accord

Ottawa asked Canadians to vote on constitutional changes that would have given Quebec greater powers to protect its culture. It would have also created a “Triple-E” senate — equal, elected and effective.

Canadians voted against the accord, with 54 per cent opposed and 45 per cent in favour.

The majority of voters in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland supported the accord. Those in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia opposed it.

1980 — Quebec sovereignty-association

Quebec’s government asked voters to give it a mandate to negotiate “sovereignty-association” with the rest of Canada. It would have given the province more powers but maintain an economic partnership with Canada.

Quebecers rejected the question, with 60 per cent of voters opposed and 40 per cent in favour.

1942 — Conscription

The federal government asked Canadians to vote on conscription during the Second World War.

Canadians voted to support the measure, with 64 per cent in favour.

Quebecers, however, were overwhelmingly opposed to conscription, with 73 per cent voting against it.

1898 — Alcohol Prohibition

In Canada’s first federal referendum, Ottawa had asked Canadians to vote on prohibiting alcohol.

The yes side narrowly won with 51 per cent in favour of the measure, and 49 per cent opposed it.

With such a close result, Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier decided there wasn’t enough support for legislating Prohibition.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. won’t drop digital issues in trade talks: former negotiator
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada’s former chief trade negotiator says that while digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the U.S., Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - While digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the United States, Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests, Canada’s former chief trade negotiator said Monday.

Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.

“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues.”

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.

Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues, he said.

Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.

“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Eric Miller, president of the consulting group Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, spoke on a separate panel at the conference and gave the example of Netflix, which gets more than half of its revenue outside the U.S.

“If you begin to have policies which are unfavourable to large U.S. tech companies, it doesn’t take too many markets like Canada and the European Union co-ordinating to see how this would have very detrimental effects to them,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

Canada will host an Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where the two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms, also known as discoverability. The CRTC is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

It’s not clear exactly which element of the Online Streaming Act is the source of the conflict. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in late August the United States had withdrawn its position on discoverability.

But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the United States is streaming companies having to make financial contributions toward Canadian content — a proposal the Liberal government has backed away from.

Meredith Lilly, a professor at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs, took part in the panel with Miller. She said Canada and the United States are likely to come to an agreement.

“I think that there is a landing zone that both sides will be able to agree on, and I anticipate that that will be keeping mandatory payments off … and Canada is going to be able to keep the discoverability piece of that,” she said.

The conference also heard that the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.

Lilly said that means the United States could retaliate on things like cars or canola. “And so there is some potential that is going to pit parts of Canada against the cultural sector,” she said.

She said while the United States might have tolerated the cultural exemption when Canada was using it to subsidize arts and culture, that might not be the case if it extends to demanding financial contributions from American companies for Canadian content.

“If we start trying to use it to extract capital from large American firms to subsidize the creation of Canadian content and they can’t even use those subsidized funds, they are going to play hardball with us and it could be the end of the cultural exemption,” Lilly said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Swph is Offering Vaccination Clinics
stories.summary: Respiratory illnesses are starting to pop up, and Southwestern Public Health is reminding residents to get vaccinated.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 19 October 2026 16:39

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Respiratory illnesses are starting to pop up, and Southwestern Public Health is reminding residents to get vaccinated.

OXFORD COUNTY - Flu season is here, and Southwestern Public Health is encouraging people to get vaccinated.

SWPH will offer influenza and COVID-19 vaccination clinics this fall at its St. Thomas and Woodstock offices, as well as select community locations throughout the region. Starting today, adults 65 years and older, pregnant individuals, residents and staff of congregate living settings, health-care workers, along with other high-risk and priority populations can begin booking appointments. The general public will be able to book appointments on October 26th.

Flu vaccines are also available through participating pharmacies and health-care providers, while COVID-19 vaccines are available through pharmacies. Residents can book an appointment online by clicking here or by calling 1-800-922-0096.

The Health Unit also has these tips to help prevent the spread of respiratory illness: getting vaccinated against influenza, COVID-19 and RSV, staying home when sick, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes, and considering wearing a mask in healthcare settings or if at higher risk of severe illness.

Southwestern Public Health has also relaunched its respiratory virus dashboard, which provides up-to-date information in the coverage areas. You can find the dashboard by visiting the Southwestern Public Health website .

OPP Investigating Collision Involving Tillsonburg Resident A two-vehicle collision is under investigation and involves a person from Tillsonburg.

A Fallen Firefighter Honoured in Woodstock A memorial service was held in Woodstock to honour a fallen firefighter who served with the Woodstock Fire Department.

PJHL Recap - Oct 16th to Oct 18th The Braves and the Trojans celebrated to victories, while the Merchants celebrated a win and suffered a loss.

Navy Vets Recap - Oct 16th Woodstock beat London 3-1 on Friday.

Input Needed for RRHS Strategic Plan Rural Roads Health Services includes the hospitals in Tillsonburg and Ingersoll.

Sanitary Sewer Work Begins in Tillsonburg Old Vienna Road between Van Street and Vienna Road will be closed until mid-December.

Two Charged with Drug Trafficking in Woodstock Two people were arrested in the James Street area on October 14th.

Local MP and Guests Visit Oxford Schools Bullying and safe communities were the topics of discussion as Oxford's MP and special guests toured schools in Oxford County.

Oxford OPP Investigating Serious Collision Early this morning, the Oxford OPP and other first responders were called to a serious collision on the 401.

PJHL Preview - Oct 16th to Oct 18th Tavistock, Norwich and Thamesford all have home games in Junior C hockey action tonight.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 16th The Woodstock Navy Vets will host the London Nationals at Southwood Arena tonight.

Norwich Curling Club Celebrates 70 Years with New Ice The club will be hosting an open house from 2:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. this Saturday.

Oxford Tourism Looking for Input Oxford Tourism has launched an online survey for residents, visitors, and tourism business operators.

Pedestrian Struck East of Shakespeare Police say the driver drove through a road closure barricade Thursday afternoon.

Unifor Local 636 Hosts Candidates Debate Residents in Woodstock had the opportunity to hear candidates answer questions as the municipal election draws closer.

Woodstock Police Briefs - Oct. 15th, 2026 A pair of theft investigations in the Friendly City results in charges.

Interview with the Warden - October 15th, 2026 He talked about snow removal, development charges, the Homelessness Support Centre, and more.

Student Stair Climb Back for Another Year The local high schools will go head to head to see who can raise the most money for United Way Oxford.

The Food Project Oxford Holds Open House It was a chance to learn and tour the facility that stores food items for many charities that serve the hungry in Oxford County.

2026 Operation Impact Results Released It was a busy Thanksgiving weekend for the 13 OPP Detachments across the West Region, including the officers in Oxford County.

stories.title: Canadians step up to give blood after fire at Alberta military base kills four
stories.summary: Some Canadians are rolling up their sleeves to give blood as the military town of Wainwright, Alta., mourns the four soldiers killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Residents of the town of Wainwright, Alta., are grieving after a deadly fire swept up by fierce winds overtook soldiers during a training exercise at the local military base Saturday, killing four and wounding dozens.

Sharon Pashko, 79, was among those who came out to the cenotaph on Monday to share her sorrow and offer words of support.

“It’s heartbreaking. My heart goes out to the families. There’s no words,” she said.

Pashko said she grew up in the military town and her uncle served at its commanding officer.

“The base has always been part of my home life and we always felt protected,” she said.

Pashko said she can see the local hospital from her home and it was “heartbreaking to see the ambulances going in.”

“Our community will go above and beyond,” she said. “I know we’ll do all that we can do to stand behind.”

A growing pile of brightly coloured flowers covers the base of the local cenotaph.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre laid a wreath there Monday. He said he has met with local groups “providing help to the wounded, families and everyone else out there that’s affected.”

Poilievre, whose federal riding of Battle River—Crowfoot includes the military base, said he was shocked by what happened.

“Fire is probably the most horrific way to die and when I learned that fire had struck one of our bases and potentially taken human life, I thought, ‘My God, it’s terrible.’ I said a prayer for them. I thought of their parents,” he said.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was also in town Monday to visit injured soldiers at the Wainwright hospital.

The minister’s office declined an interview request, saying it wanted to keep the focus on the injured military members and families who have lost loved ones.

McGuinty’s office issued a short statement on his behalf late Monday saying he visited leadership and Armed Forces members at CFB Wainwright on Monday. He was joined by Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski.

“In the face of profound loss, they have shown extraordinary strength, compassion and care for one another,” McGuinty said in his statement. “We will continue to stand with them and their families, and ensure they have the support they need.”

In Ottawa, the House of Commons held a moment of silence to honour the victims on Monday.

Poilievre told the House of Commons by video link that he personally met one of the deceased — Pte. Aidan Goulding, who was 23. The Conservative leader described him as “strong, handsome, polite” and a “real gentleman.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House all MPs stand “united in grief” over a tragedy that touches every corner of the country.

Carney also told the House that 50 investigators are on the ground at the Wainwright base trying to determine what caused the deadly fire.

The prime minister said the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy, with support from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He also told reporters he has absolute confidence in the military’s investigators.

“We will give them all the resources that they need,” Carney said. “There’s a few processes that we’ll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary.”

Defence officials said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area at Wainwright, 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, when the disaster struck on Saturday.

Strong winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing across the Prairie landscape, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 of them to hospital — 19 in critical condition.

National Defence identified the deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Their deaths left a trail of grief across the country.

In Langley, B.C., Trevor Plater, Lykkemark’s former rugby coach in his senior year at Langley Secondary School, said the whole team and his schoolmates thought of Lykkemark as their best friend.

“He’s always looking out for everybody. He wasn’t necessarily somebody who talked a lot but he had a big impact when he did and he was always listening and paying attention,” Plater said.

Lykkemark, who was 19 when he died, was “a wonderful kid” who led by example and made everybody feel connected to the team, Plater added.

He was particularly close to former teammate Kane Lewis, who set up an online fundraiser for his friend’s family. Lewis said in a statement on the donation page — which has raised more than $20,000 — that he and Lykkemark joined the army at the same time and were in the same platoon for basic training.

“That’s where he became more than just a friend; he became a brother. He was always looking out for everyone and always kept himself in check,” Lewis said.

In Farrell’s hometown of Prince Albert, Sask., the city government lowered its flags to half-mast and set out a book of condolences at city hall.

“Our community is grieving alongside those who knew and loved Shaun,” the City of Prince Albert posted on social media.

“We recognize the profound sorrow this tragedy has brought to his family, friends and all those affected.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell, Fakiha Baig and Aaron Sousa in Edmonton, from Nono Shen in Vancouver and Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet hears from police
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home is hearing from one of the officers called to the incident.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - There was no reason to fear for Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s safety until she suddenly walked out onto her 24th-floor apartment’s balcony, a Toronto police officer told an inquest into the 29-year-old woman’s death Monday.

Const. Shane Beaudoin said he had allowed Korchinski-Paquet to go into her home because she needed to use the bathroom, and asked her to talk to a paramedic when she emerged because he thought it could help de-escalate what remained a heated family dispute.

Instead, he said, Korchinski-Paquet went out onto the balcony, knocking down the air conditioning unit on the way, then used her bodyweight to block the door.

“At this point, it’s the first time to me that the balcony has come into play. She’s made no references to it. She’s not made any sort of remarks that she’s suicidal or that she wants to hurt herself,” Beaudoin testified.

“There’s been no reason to fear for her physical safety because at this point there’s officers on scene, everybody’s separated ... So anyway, now she’s on the balcony and now I am very concerned.”

Moments later, Korchinski-Paquet let go of the door and headed to the balcony rail, swinging her left leg toward the neighbouring balcony, he said.

As she disappeared from view, the officer said he believed she had crossed over to the other balcony, so he requested that the emergency task force be called in.

“At that moment, I didn’t know that she had fallen. I thought she had gone over to the neighbour’s unit and was maybe hunkered down on that balcony.”

It was only after he’d left the apartment to go knock on the neighbour’s door that Beaudoin heard from another officer that Korchinski-Paquet had fallen, he said, at 5:43 p.m.

“That information came to basically everybody in the hallway at the same time,” including Korchinski-Paquet’s mother and brother, he said.

Five calls were made to 911 the afternoon of May 27, 2020, three of them by Korchinski-Paquet, the inquest heard last week.

Jurors have previously watched a compilation video combining the recordings of the calls and two police microphones with CCTV footage from the hallway outside her home and video from a police cruiser.

In her calls, Korchinski-Paquet expressed difficulty breathing and said she had thrown two bottles at her family in the hallway because she lost control after being attacked by her mother and brother. When asked if anyone had mental health issues, Korchinski-Paquet said she had epilepsy.

Her mother and brother also mentioned Korchinski-Paquet’s epilepsy on their calls, noting that she was often agitated after her seizures. Her brother, Reece Korchinski, said she assaulted him with knives after a dispute over the TV volume.

Six police officers and two paramedics responded to the calls, the inquest heard.

Then-Const. Adam Vandenbrink testified Monday that he was the first officer to arrive at the scene and was told to wait for backup. He didn’t know Beaudoin, who arrived shortly afterward, because the officer worked in another division, he said.

They went up together and could hear an argument as the elevator approached the 24th floor, he said. Neither he nor Beaudoin could recall discussing a strategy to deal with the situation, but Vandenbrink said all officers had received the same training on de-escalation.

Vandenbrink said he ended up talking to Korchinski-Paquet while Beaudoin went down the hall to speak to her mother and brother. He could smell wine and saw smashed glass in the hallway, he said.

“She wasn’t listening to my questions, she was yelling over top of me,” said Vandenbrink, who left the force roughly three years ago. He described Korchinski-Paquet as “agitated” and “aggressive.”

When another officer arrived, Vandenbrink said he asked his colleague to speak to her while he went to debrief with Beaudoin. It was during that conversation that he heard about Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures that day, as well as a general idea of what prompted the 911 calls, he said.

He had just stepped into the door frame of the apartment to make room for paramedics when Korchinski-Paquet ran out to the balcony, he said. The fallen air conditioner partially blocked the balcony door, preventing it from opening fully, and Korchinski-Paquet had to squeeze through the opening, he added.

Within seconds, she had stepped over the railing, and Vandenbrink said he could see her hands gripping it like someone hanging from a bar at the gym as she appeared to shimmy toward the balcony next door.

He believed Korchinski-Paquet was making her way to the other balcony, and another officer told them to leave the apartment to avoid agitating her further, he said.

Eventually, as officers knocked on the neighbour’s door, Vandenbrink and Const. Glenn Weddell went back into the apartment to try to see Korchinski-Paquet, he said. Weddell slowly inched toward the balcony, eventually poking his head out the door, but still couldn’t spot her, he said.

“I remember him just taking like half a step out onto the balcony, just enough to look over the edge and he says, ‘She fell,’” Vandenbrink said.

“And then it didn’t even register to me at that time ... I probably went right into a state of shock, didn’t really realize what was happening.”

Rushing to get outside, he shared the news with those in the hall and heard Korchinski-Paquet’s mother “start to wail,” he said.

By the time he got outside, paramedics had covered Korchinski-Paquet’s body with a blanket, he said.

Vandenbrink and Beaudoin both testified that they never set foot on the balcony, nor did they know at the time about postictal delirium, an altered mental state that can follow seizures.

Answering questions from the presiding coroner, Vandenbrink said he did not perceive Korchinski-Paquet as a person in crisis at the time, but may have classified her as such if he’d known seizures could lead to delirium.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest last week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia afterward.

A neurologist who did not treat her but examined her records testified that Korchinski-Paquet on several occasions showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis.

Dr. Julien Hébert told the inquest that it would be “nearly impossible” to tell whether someone was acting aggressively due to delirium or psychosis after an epilepsy seizure or for some other reason without knowing their medical history.
