stories.title: How community organizations are trying to fight voter apathy in this Toronto election
stories.summary: Toronto - Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.

What looked like an outdoor festival at Lawrence Heights Community Centre was a fair held to raise civic engagement and encourage the city’s residents to vote in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The non-partisan event, organized by North York Harvest Food Bank, was attended by several groups including Voice the Vote, a joint initiative by Toronto Metropolitan University’s Democratic Engagement Exchange and United Way Greater Toronto.

Community members attended a fair held at Lawrence Heights Community Cetnre to raise awareness and boost turnout ahead of the upcoming municipal election. Organizers said around 20 event participants cast their ballots at a nearby advanced polling site on Oct. 9. (Oct 19, 2026)

Jonathan Dong stood behind a table, a mock ballot box and papers laid out in front him, talking to people and handing them Voice the Vote election handbooks.

“I think that participating in our democratic process, especially considering … how many people around the world aren’t able to cast a vote, is incredibly important,” Dong said in an interview.

“Showing up is how people know that you’re important, and if you don’t show up, you don’t get a say in what happens in the country, in your city, in your own backyard.”

In previous municipal elections, the city has seen what observers described as a worrying downward trend in voter participation.

In the 2023 mayoral byelection won by Olivia Chow, 37 per cent of eligible voters participated. Turnout was less than 30 per cent in the 2022 municipal election and about 41 per cent in 2018.

Across the province, overall voter turnout was nearly 33 per cent in the 2022 municipal elections and roughly 38 per cent in 2018, according to Association of Municipalities of Ontario data.

The turnout at Toronto’s advance polls in the upcoming election was robust, however, with more than 222,000 people casting their ballots early – the highest number in more than a decade.

Dong said he wants to do his part to battle voter apathy.

As a Chinese Canadian who lives in Richmond Hill north of Toronto, he said many voters in his community are particularly disconnected from the electoral process and as a result they don’t have enough representation in government.

“I think it’s very important to have the conversations within these communities to increase that representation and increase our voter turnout,” he said.

At the voter information event, two white posters glued on a wall were decorated with colourful sticky notes on which members of the community wrote why voting matters to them.

“Support for unhoused neighbours,” “a clean city,” and “mental health safety” were among the dozens of notes.

Meanwhile, two taxis were seen ferrying voters to advance polling sites and then bringing them back to the community centre.

Warren Epstein was among those who voted early. He stood by Rania Ahmed, the project lead at Democratic Engagement Exchange, and asked her to write a few messages for him on a poster that focused on affordability and more support for seniors like himself.

“You need people who are going to do things for the people and the senior citizens, and you want to make sure that the right people are voted in for the right activities,” Epstein said.

“And it is time for change.”

Ahmed said Voice the Vote’s 15-member team is trying to help people “feel more hopeful about their future” by leveraging their own communities.

“A lot of people actually don’t know … that the issue they care about is actually tied to their municipal government and not the provincial (or) federal,” she said.

Ahmed said the initiative also provides micro-grants for organizations and individuals who come up with project or event ideas for elections and civic engagement in Toronto, York and Peel regions.

The funding for the initiative comes from United Way. The charity’s senior public affairs officer, Abby Tait, said while the organization has taken part in similar efforts in previous elections, Voice the Vote is a more thought out project aimed at increasing turnout across the city, including among immigrant communities and younger people.

Tait said the idea was born in the summer of 2025, after back-to-back provincial and federal elections.

“So we kind of seized this long runway and said, ‘let’s build something really ambitious,’” she said.

“We developed this kind of community-led project that would really be focused on grounding the municipal election in the local issues that matter to people.”

She said Voice the Vote is using the United Way’s vast network of around 300 agencies to reach communities.

“You can’t have a healthy community if people feel like they have no agency in their community, that they’re not connected to it,” she said.

Roughly 200 people attended the event in Lawrence Heights earlier this month, and around 20 of them were taken to an advance polling site to cast their ballots, said Sarah Watson, the director of community engagement at North York Harvest Food Bank.

Watson said while the food bank can provide emergency support for people in need, it can’t change systemic issues such as lack of affordable housing, food insecurity or unsafe communities.

“We’re really trying to connect them with the electoral process so they can have some influence over who is in government and who is making changes on these issues,” she said.

“A lot of our community members feel like their voices aren’t heard … and when that happens again and again, it can be frustrating and it can cause people to disengage,” Watson added. “We really want to encourage people that it is worth participating, that their voices should be heard.”

Event participant Esther Johnson agreed, saying she will head to the polls on election day because she believes every vote counts.

For people who choose not to vote in this election, “it’s their loss,” she said. “If they’re not interested in… having the input, don’t complain.”

More than 50 candidates are vying to become the mayor of Canada’s largest city, but polls suggest incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford are locked in a fierce competition one week before election day.

Lydia Miljan, a political-science professor at the University of Windsor, said there are reasons to believe more people will participate in Toronto’s electoral process this time around, given the tight race between the two leading mayoral candidates.

“It just depends on how closely people are following Toronto politics right now, and I think it’s getting in my feeds even down here,” she said. “So, it is heating up quite significantly.”

Miljan said voter turnout is generally lower in municipal elections because it can be overwhelming to take part in a process that elects the mayor, councillors and school board trustees all at once.

She said the lack of political parties giving people a “shortcut” on where local election candidates stand, and the movement of voters between wards in large cities can further suppress turnout.

But in order to have a healthy democracy, residents need to show up, she said.

“It is incumbent upon citizens, regardless of how long they’ve lived in that city, to really make an effort to cast their ballot.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.
paragraphs: TORONTO - Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.
What looked like an outdoor festival at Lawrence Heights Community Centre was a fair held to raise civic engagement and encourage the city’s residents to vote in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The non-partisan event, organized by North York Harvest Food Bank, was attended by several groups including Voice the Vote, a joint initiative by Toronto Metropolitan University’s Democratic Engagement Exchange and United Way Greater Toronto.

Community members attended a fair held at Lawrence Heights Community Cetnre to raise awareness and boost turnout ahead of the upcoming municipal election. Organizers said around 20 event participants cast their ballots at a nearby advanced polling site on Oct. 9. (Oct 19, 2026)
Jonathan Dong stood behind a table, a mock ballot box and papers laid out in front him, talking to people and handing them Voice the Vote election handbooks.
“I think that participating in our democratic process, especially considering … how many people around the world aren’t able to cast a vote, is incredibly important,” Dong said in an interview.
“Showing up is how people know that you’re important, and if you don’t show up, you don’t get a say in what happens in the country, in your city, in your own backyard.”
In previous municipal elections, the city has seen what observers described as a worrying downward trend in voter participation.
In the 2023 mayoral byelection won by Olivia Chow, 37 per cent of eligible voters participated. Turnout was less than 30 per cent in the 2022 municipal election and about 41 per cent in 2018.
Across the province, overall voter turnout was nearly 33 per cent in the 2022 municipal elections and roughly 38 per cent in 2018, according to Association of Municipalities of Ontario data.
The turnout at Toronto’s advance polls in the upcoming election was robust, however, with more than 222,000 people casting their ballots early – the highest number in more than a decade.
Dong said he wants to do his part to battle voter apathy.

As a Chinese Canadian who lives in Richmond Hill north of Toronto, he said many voters in his community are particularly disconnected from the electoral process and as a result they don’t have enough representation in government.
“I think it’s very important to have the conversations within these communities to increase that representation and increase our voter turnout,” he said.
At the voter information event, two white posters glued on a wall were decorated with colourful sticky notes on which members of the community wrote why voting matters to them.
“Support for unhoused neighbours,” “a clean city,” and “mental health safety” were among the dozens of notes.
Meanwhile, two taxis were seen ferrying voters to advance polling sites and then bringing them back to the community centre.

Warren Epstein was among those who voted early. He stood by Rania Ahmed, the project lead at Democratic Engagement Exchange, and asked her to write a few messages for him on a poster that focused on affordability and more support for seniors like himself.
“You need people who are going to do things for the people and the senior citizens, and you want to make sure that the right people are voted in for the right activities,” Epstein said.
“And it is time for change.”
Ahmed said Voice the Vote’s 15-member team is trying to help people “feel more hopeful about their future” by leveraging their own communities.
“A lot of people actually don’t know … that the issue they care about is actually tied to their municipal government and not the provincial (or) federal,” she said.
Ahmed said the initiative also provides micro-grants for organizations and individuals who come up with project or event ideas for elections and civic engagement in Toronto, York and Peel regions.

The funding for the initiative comes from United Way. The charity’s senior public affairs officer, Abby Tait, said while the organization has taken part in similar efforts in previous elections, Voice the Vote is a more thought out project aimed at increasing turnout across the city, including among immigrant communities and younger people.
Tait said the idea was born in the summer of 2025, after back-to-back provincial and federal elections.
“So we kind of seized this long runway and said, ‘let’s build something really ambitious,’” she said.
“We developed this kind of community-led project that would really be focused on grounding the municipal election in the local issues that matter to people.”
She said Voice the Vote is using the United Way’s vast network of around 300 agencies to reach communities.
“You can’t have a healthy community if people feel like they have no agency in their community, that they’re not connected to it,” she said.

Roughly 200 people attended the event in Lawrence Heights earlier this month, and around 20 of them were taken to an advance polling site to cast their ballots, said Sarah Watson, the director of community engagement at North York Harvest Food Bank.
Watson said while the food bank can provide emergency support for people in need, it can’t change systemic issues such as lack of affordable housing, food insecurity or unsafe communities.
“We’re really trying to connect them with the electoral process so they can have some influence over who is in government and who is making changes on these issues,” she said.

“A lot of our community members feel like their voices aren’t heard … and when that happens again and again, it can be frustrating and it can cause people to disengage,” Watson added. “We really want to encourage people that it is worth participating, that their voices should be heard.”
Event participant Esther Johnson agreed, saying she will head to the polls on election day because she believes every vote counts.
For people who choose not to vote in this election, “it’s their loss,” she said. “If they’re not interested in… having the input, don’t complain.”

More than 50 candidates are vying to become the mayor of Canada’s largest city, but polls suggest incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford are locked in a fierce competition one week before election day.

Lydia Miljan, a political-science professor at the University of Windsor, said there are reasons to believe more people will participate in Toronto’s electoral process this time around, given the tight race between the two leading mayoral candidates.
“It just depends on how closely people are following Toronto politics right now, and I think it’s getting in my feeds even down here,” she said. “So, it is heating up quite significantly.”
Miljan said voter turnout is generally lower in municipal elections because it can be overwhelming to take part in a process that elects the mayor, councillors and school board trustees all at once.
She said the lack of political parties giving people a “shortcut” on where local election candidates stand, and the movement of voters between wards in large cities can further suppress turnout.
But in order to have a healthy democracy, residents need to show up, she said.
“It is incumbent upon citizens, regardless of how long they’ve lived in that city, to really make an effort to cast their ballot.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: What we know about the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after an explosion and fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after a fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.

Thirty-nine people were hospitalized, 19 of them in are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday at the military base east of Edmonton. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as the fire spread rapidly, prompting a major medical response across the region.

The Canadian Armed Forces says it is still assessing the full extent of the impact.

Live Updates: Officials providing update after ‘fast-moving’ CFB Wainwright fire kills 4 soldiers

Here is what we know so far:

Four military members killed, dozens injured

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths and injuries Sunday.

Family members of those killed have been notified, Carney said. Those affected included personnel from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers serving with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

In his remarks on Sunday, Carney described the scale of the tragedy.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta. What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces in Canadian soil in peace time,” he said.

In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland told reporters that the fire broke out during a training exercise ahead of the soldiers’ deployment to Latvia.

The officials at CFB Wainwright were aware of the fire for several hours before it turned toward the training area, Rutland said. Despite the knowledge, the soldiers continued to carry out their exercises.

CAF officials believe there was no damage to oil and gas infrastructure as a result of the fire, Rutland said.

CFB Wainwright victims identified

The following members were killed during the fire at CFB Wainwright, according to Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland:

Sergeant Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Alta., from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry

Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Aidan Goulding from North Vancouver, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Nearly 40 patients receiving treatment at regional hospitals

The medical response has placed significant demands on hospitals and emergency services in the Edmonton region.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, the CEO of Acute Care Alberta told reporters 19 people are in critical condition, eight are stable, and 12 are ambulatory and are receiving care for injuries that can be assessed without admission.

Dr. Steve Fisher, an emergency physician at Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CTV News Edmonton on Sunday that patients had sustained burns of varying severity, with the most seriously affected being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital, which has a burn intensive care unit.

The scale of the response prompted Acute Care Alberta to ask residents to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible Saturday night, unless they required emergency care.

The agency said “significant resources” were needed from Emergency Health Services and Edmonton-area emergency departments into the night.

Stars Air Ambulance dispatched two air ambulances from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Helicopters and two aircraft also landed at a nearby medical evacuation site as emergency personnel worked to transport and treat the injured.

Soldiers were working with hand grenades: CAF

The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and reservists were taking part in high-intensity training ahead of deploymen, Rutland said.

The Charlie Company, or C Company soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a section attack, with 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy when the fire broke out, he added.

Code Orange lifted after emergency response

A Code Orange is activated when a mass-casualty event places pressure on the health-care system because of a surge in patients. The code remained in effect for more than 10 hours before being lifted shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday.

Investigation underway, terrorism not likely

The Canadian Armed Forces will undertake a board of inquiry to examine the events of Oct. 17, Rutland said.

A spokesperson for National Defence said Sunday there were no indications the incident was the result of terrorist activity.

“As emergency responders continue their work and the situation continues to evolve, the full extent of the impact remains under assessment. Our immediate priority is supporting those affected and notifying next of kin. We will not confirm casualty or injury details until that process is complete,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton.

“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity.”

Retired major-general David Fraser, a CTV military analyst and former commander of Nato forces in southern Afghanistan, described the incident as the worst training tragedy he had witnessed during his military career.

“We are now dealing with the worst tragedy that I’ve seen in my entire career,” Fraser told CTV News Channel.

Fraser, who was previously posted at Wainwright and trained there extensively, said he had seen no indications the incident was anything other than an accident.

He said Canadian military bases have established safety procedures for live-fire and other training exercises. He expects those procedures to remain in place until investigators determine whether changes are needed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was travelling to Edmonton on Sunday to receive a briefing on the latest developments. He said the Department of National Defence was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

I am on my way to Edmonton. I will get briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident that occurred at CFB Wainwright. The Department of National Defence continues to work closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Thank you to first… — David McGuinty (@DavidMcGuinty) October 18, 2026

High winds contributed to rapidly spreading fire

The Municipal District of Wainwright said high winds caused the fire to spread rapidly into the surrounding area Saturday.

Officials said the fire crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being managed south of Wainwright.

Crews faced volatile conditions as parts of Alberta experienced wind gusts of up to 100 km/h. Municipal information officers told CTV News Edmonton late Saturday that the spread was under control.

Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.

The fire is not believed to be a result of oil and gas infrastructure or outside interference, but the cause is still under investigation.

Video shows fire burning near CFB Wainwright

Video captured from private property about one kilometre from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday shows flames burning in the area as smoke billows across the sky.

The footage offers a glimpse of the fire that prompted a major emergency response at the Alberta military base.

Military families urged to seek support

The Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre opened Sunday to support military families affected by the incident.

Families were invited to connect in a safe and supportive space as they dealt with the aftermath.

People needing additional assistance can call the Family Information Line at 1-800-866-4546 for free, confidential support, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

Officials have said supporting those affected and notifying next of kin remain immediate priorities

Canadian Blood Services calls for donations

Canadian Blood Services is offering its condolences to those affected by the CFB Wainwright fire and encouraging Canadians to donate blood to help support injured patients.

“Our top priority is ensuring patients in Canada receive the blood and blood products they need. We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” a media spokesperson wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton on Sunday.

The organization said appointments remained available in Alberta and across Canada, adding that donations in the coming weeks would help maintain the national blood supply.

“We are grateful to the many people who have already reached out to ask how they can help. Donating blood is one meaningful way to support patients in Canada, both now and in the weeks ahead. Many appointments are still available throughout Alberta and across Canada, and donations in the coming weeks will help to keep our national inventory strong.”

Political and military leaders offer condolences

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the loss of life and injuries as heartbreaking and said her government was working with federal officials and local authorities.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.

Alberta is mourning alongside the Canadian Armed Forces and the families, friends and colleagues of those affected by the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright yesterday. The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I… pic.twitter.com/pKIG6vQuPS — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 18, 2026

Smith said she would travel to Edmonton to meet with provincial ministers and federal officials. The province activated its Emergency Management Cabinet Co-ordination Committee and raised the Provincial Emergency Coordination Centre to Level 3.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also offered assistance with recovery efforts, saying his province stood “ready to help.”

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said .

Maritime premiers also expressed condolences , noting the close ties between military personnel, their families and communities across Canada.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said the tragedy would be deeply felt in the region surrounding the base.

“If you live in east central Alberta in the Wainwright area, this base is part of your life, “ Kenney told CTV News Channel on Sunday. “You get to know the soldiers and the base staff (is) a very large part of the whole broader community out in that sparsely populated area.”

Kenney said Albertans have a “deep regard for the sacrifices taken by our men and women in uniform.”

Nato’s Military Committee also offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a full recovery.

On behalf of the Nato Military Committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured. Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many… pic.twitter.com/3zdIR9k9g5 — Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone - Nato CMC (@CMC_NATO) October 18, 2026

Community and military personnel await further answers

The tragedy has affected military families and communities well beyond Wainwright, as personnel from bases across Canada were among those involved.

A Barrie-area mayoral candidate, Cathy Keane, said her eldest son was critically injured in the incident. In a social media post Sunday, she said she would travel to Alberta to be with him and her family.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she said.

Election day locations in Wainwright to open as planned

Elections Alberta says voting locations in Wainwright will be opened as planned on Oct. 19, officials told reporters.

Eligible voters in the area will be able to cast their 10 ballots at the Wainwright Communiplex and the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29 Wainwright.

Pro-Canada rally goes ahead in Edmonton

A pro-Canada rally was held in Edmonton on Sunday and while attendees were focused on the referendum on Monday, the incident in Wainwright was still top of mind. Organizer Gil McGowan said the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.

McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, thanked first responders from around Canada and said it’s a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.

Albertans are set to vote on Monday whether the province should remain in Canada or if a referendum should be held on separation.

Smith told reporters the upcoming referendum on Monday will go ahead.

With files from The Canadian Press

Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.

The footage offers a glimpse of the fire that prompted a major emergency response at the Alberta military base.

Families were invited to connect in a safe and supportive space as they dealt with the aftermath.
People needing additional assistance can call the Family Information Line at 1-800-866-4546 for free, confidential support, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

The organization said appointments remained available in Alberta and across Canada, adding that donations in the coming weeks would help maintain the national blood supply.

“We are grateful to the many people who have already reached out to ask how they can help. Donating blood is one meaningful way to support patients in Canada, both now and in the weeks ahead. Many appointments are still available throughout Alberta and across Canada, and donations in the coming weeks will help to keep our national inventory strong.”

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. stories.title: Emergency crews respond to major fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: No details have been released on injuries, fatalities or the cause of the blaze
stories.author: Jana G. Pruden
stories.content:
A massive fire killed and injured multiple people at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in eastern Alberta late Saturday afternoon, forcing the country’s military to scramble assets to support local authorities responding to the medical crisis.

Defence Minister David McGuinty confirmed at a press conference in Ottawa Saturday that a fire on the base was fanned by high winds and had spread beyond the military installation, but could not confirm how many had died.

“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he told reporters. “This is a very, very active and delicate situation.”

Around midnight, two bright red flares dropped from the sky before seven Canadian Forces members parachuted onto the football field of the local high school across the street from the Wainwright hospital. They were soon met by a helicopter that touched down to unload medical equipment, including what appeared to be a ventilator that the troops wheeled into the hospital.

Nearby, paramedics loaded two patients on stretchers into waiting ambulances, which then sped off.

Acute Care Alberta, the agency that coordinates medical services at acute health centres in the province, said a Code Orange had been declared at several ERs “to coordinate a response to an incident that results in multiple severe patients needing care at the same time.” The agency urged people in Edmonton, 200km northwest of CFB Wainwright, to avoid going to the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital so that patients coming from the military base could be prioritized.

STARS Air Ambulance spokesperson Natalie Hofstetter said aircraft had been dispatched from Edmonton and Saskatoon.

Early Sunday morning, few details were available about what had happened at the camp known for its large training exercises.

Satellite imagery from NASA’s wildfire surveillance system captured at least seven clusters of fire at the camp earlier Saturday night. A post on the Municipal District of Wainwright Facebook page said the wildfire had been held, but a watch would remain in place in case conditions changed.

Alberta MP Dane Lloyd, a former Canadian Forces reservist, said in a social media post on Saturday night that there was an explosion and fire in high winds.

“Hearing terrible news out of CFB Wainwright,” Mr. Lloyd wrote. “Please keep our soldiers, their families and the community of Wainwright in your prayers. God be with them all.”

Below his post, at least one person said they were awaiting news from their partner, who was a soldier on the base.

RCMP spokesperson Corp. Gina Slaney said she had been authorized to speak on behalf of the Canadian Forces to confirm that a fire was reported at the base around 4 p.m., and that it had extended beyond the boundaries of the training area.

June Winger, president of the Union of National Defence Employees, which represents more than 20,000 civilian military members, said her organization will continue to update and support its members.

“ Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the devastating fire at CFB Wainwright, especially the families, military personnel, civilian workers and community members impacted by this tragic incident,” she said. “I want to express my sincere gratitude to the firefighters, first responders and emergency personnel working tirelessly to protect lives and keep people safe.”

In a social media post, Premier Danielle Smith said there was “a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright that is affecting many of our brave military personnel.”

She said the province is in close contact with the federal government and Prime Minister Mark Carney as the situation evolves. Mr. Carney also posted on social media that “a serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.” He added: “Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province had deployed resources to Alberta and was ready to send more help if required.

B.C. Premier David Eby said he had reached out to Alberta to offer “all possible assistance.”

“Please hold Canadian Armed Forces members, their families and the emergency crews in your hearts tonight,” he posted on social media.

RCMP spokesperson Corp. Gina Slaney said she had been authorized to speak on behalf of the Canadian Forces to confirm that a fire was reported at the base around 4 p.m., and that it had extended beyond the boundaries of the training area.
June Winger, president of the Union of National Defence Employees, which represents more than 20,000 civilian military members, said her organization will continue to update and support its members.

“ Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the devastating fire at CFB Wainwright, especially the families, military personnel, civilian workers and community members impacted by this tragic incident,” she said. “I want to express my sincere gratitude to the firefighters, first responders and emergency personnel working tirelessly to protect lives and keep people safe.”
In a social media post, Premier Danielle Smith said there was “a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright that is affecting many of our brave military personnel.”

She said the province is in close contact with the federal government and Prime Minister Mark Carney as the situation evolves. Mr. Carney also posted on social media that “a serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.” He added: “Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected.”
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province had deployed resources to Alberta and was ready to send more help if required.
B.C. Premier David Eby said he had reached out to Alberta to offer “all possible assistance.”
“Please hold Canadian Armed Forces members, their families and the emergency crews in your hearts tonight,” he posted on social media.

stories.title: Quebec author abandons effort to document novel’s origins amid AI allegations
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has abandoned efforts to compile evidence supporting his denial that artificial intelligence was used to write his novel, his publisher has confirmed.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has abandoned efforts to compile evidence supporting his denial that artificial intelligence was used to write his novel, his publisher has confirmed.

The decision ends an effort previously disclosed by his publisher, Éditions du Boréal, to document how “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying,” was written, leaving questions about whether AI was used to write the novel unresolved even as the publisher continues to sell it.

In an email to The Canadian Press, Éditions du Boréal provided comments attributed to its co-director, Renaud Roussel, confirming that Orélien decided to end the effort.

“The publishing house supported him in this process, which he chose to end,” Roussel said.

“That decision is his to make, and we accept it, although we certainly would have preferred to be able to provide definitive answers to the allegations of AI use against him.”

Orélien did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Canadian Press about his decision to end the evidence-gathering process.

In September, Boréal publicly disclosed that it was collaborating with Orélien to compile a detailed record of his work on the manuscript before it was submitted to the publisher.

Orélien previously told French media outlet Libération that he was gathering evidence with his publishers in France and Quebec to support his account of how the novel was written.

Roussel clarified that the initiative came from Orélien, rather than the publisher, which supported him in the process. He maintained that Boréal’s position had not changed.

The Quebec publisher also confirmed that sales of the novel have slowed since the controversy began, although it declined to provide specific figures.

The book remains available in bookstores, but Boréal said it is currently out of stock at the publishing house, with a new printing expected next week.

Earlier this week, Floriane Claveau, a spokesperson for major Quebec bookstore chain Renaud-Bray, said the retailer had not observed any significant change in sales of the novel over the preceding weeks.

Meanwhile, Montreal-based Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec, the province’s library and archives institution, says interest in the novel has been exceptionally high, with 1,713 reservations for its digital edition through its online lending service as of Oct. 14.

Spokesperson Claire-Hélène Lengellé said demand has remained strong for several weeks.

In a statement released Wednesday, Boréal said it received Orélien’s manuscript on Sept. 12, 2025, and could not independently verify how the novel had been written before that date.

The publisher argued that its role was not to demand proof from authors, but to stand by them, leaving readers to decide whether to purchase the book.

Orélien, meanwhile, said in a statement released through Boréal on Tuesday that he had nothing to prove to those making accusations against him.

The author has denied using AI to write the novel, saying he began working on it in 2017 and completed a first draft of more than 300 pages in 2019.

The controversy has had other consequences. The novel was removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt earlier this month amid allegations of AI use and separate plagiarism allegations involving Orélien’s earlier writings.

Orélien acknowledged plagiarism in some of his previous work in his statement Tuesday, apologizing for what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth, while maintaining that no sentence in his novel was generated by a machine.

Boréal suspended promotional activities surrounding the novel in September, citing concerns for the author’s well-being, but confirmed on Wednesday that it would continue selling the book in the absence of definitive findings about the AI allegations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Separation, immigration, the Constitution: A look at Alberta's referendum questions
stories.summary: Edmonton - Here are the 10 questions Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is sending to a provincewide referendum on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Here are the 10 questions Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is sending to a provincewide referendum on Monday.

Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

What you need to know: Smith has said she wants to see Alberta have a similar accord as Quebec, which has an agreement with Ottawa that lets the province set its own eligibility requirements for economic migrants.

She said in February that a “normal” and “sustainable” level of immigration would represent less than one per cent of the population, or about 50,000 newcomers per year. But critics say Smith has failed to plan for the population growth it invited with a countrywide ad campaign in recent years.

Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

What you need to know: The premier has blamed overburdened public services on rapid population growth in the past five years.

The government’s website claims temporary residents cost the province more than $1 billion in health care, education and social services. Critics say those numbers don’t add up and that the government is ignoring the economic contributions and benefits they bring to Alberta.

The specific effect of a yes vote is unclear, since the government says it won’t define “Alberta-approved immigration status” until after the referendum.

Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?

What you need to know: The government says it won’t determine which programs would be affected until after the referendum, should Albertans vote yes.

Temporary workers are already ineligible for some provincial programs, such as Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped, and the Canadian Bar Association’s provincial chapter says this could run afoul of the Canada Health Act or the Charter’s equality provisions.

Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

What you need to know: A potential new charge wouldn’t be determined by the government until after the vote, though the premier told Calgary business leaders on Sept. 22 that a health premium could be as much as $1,900.

Education leaders in the province have come out against restricting access to schooling, saying it goes against internationally agreed children’s rights.

Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate, or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

What you need to know: Voting is already restricted to Canadian citizens, and both Elections Canada and Elections Alberta have reported very few cases of ineligible voting.

Smith has said it’s about strengthening the integrity of provincial elections. Critics say this policy would only make lineups at the polls more time-consuming and open the door to racial or ethnic bias at the voting booth.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

What you need to know: If approved by voters, this proposal would only commit Alberta’s government to working with other provinces and federal lawmakers to make changes to the Constitution.

Changes generally need approval from seven provincial legislatures covering 50 per cent of Canada’s population, as well as from the House of Commons and Senate in Ottawa.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

What you need to know: Abolishing the Senate would be even more difficult than other general constitutional amendments. It would need to be unanimously approved by all provinces and ratified by the Senate and the House of Commons.

PM says any overhaul must wait for broad national agreement, pushes back on scrapping the unelected Senate ahead of Monday’s vote.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

What you need to know: The federal “spending power” authority allows Ottawa to attach conditions to its funding for provinces, with health-care funding under the Canada Health Act as a key example.

A permanent provincial “opt-out” clause would require the Constitution to be amended.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

What you need to know: Under the Constitution, federal laws are given standing over provincial laws when jurisdictional issues arise.

This change to the Constitution would require approval from the Senate, the House of Commons and seven provinces representing at least half the country’s population.

Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

What you need to know: Advocates for separation say the province needs to get out from under federal taxation and regulation, freeing up wealth and sparking economic development. Federalists say the split would only hurt businesses and saddle landlocked Alberta with debt and the massive cost of delivering formerly federal services.

Smith has framed her other nine other questions on immigration and constitutional reform as a political compromise that could address Alberta’s grievances, gain leverage with Ottawa and avoid dismantling the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

The government’s website claims temporary residents cost the province more than $1 billion in health care, education and social services. Critics say those numbers don’t add up and that the government is ignoring the economic contributions and benefits they bring to Alberta.
The specific effect of a yes vote is unclear, since the government says it won’t define “Alberta-approved immigration status” until after the referendum.

Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?
What you need to know: The government says it won’t determine which programs would be affected until after the referendum, should Albertans vote yes.

Temporary workers are already ineligible for some provincial programs, such as Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped, and the Canadian Bar Association’s provincial chapter says this could run afoul of the Canada Health Act or the Charter’s equality provisions.

Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

What you need to know: A potential new charge wouldn’t be determined by the government until after the vote, though the premier told Calgary business leaders on Sept. 22 that a health premium could be as much as $1,900.
Education leaders in the province have come out against restricting access to schooling, saying it goes against internationally agreed children’s rights.

Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate, or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?
What you need to know: Voting is already restricted to Canadian citizens, and both Elections Canada and Elections Alberta have reported very few cases of ineligible voting.

Smith has said it’s about strengthening the integrity of provincial elections. Critics say this policy would only make lineups at the polls more time-consuming and open the door to racial or ethnic bias at the voting booth.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?
What you need to know: If approved by voters, this proposal would only commit Alberta’s government to working with other provinces and federal lawmakers to make changes to the Constitution.
Changes generally need approval from seven provincial legislatures covering 50 per cent of Canada’s population, as well as from the House of Commons and Senate in Ottawa.
Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

What you need to know: Abolishing the Senate would be even more difficult than other general constitutional amendments. It would need to be unanimously approved by all provinces and ratified by the Senate and the House of Commons.
PM says any overhaul must wait for broad national agreement, pushes back on scrapping the unelected Senate ahead of Monday’s vote.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?
What you need to know: The federal “spending power” authority allows Ottawa to attach conditions to its funding for provinces, with health-care funding under the Canada Health Act as a key example.
A permanent provincial “opt-out” clause would require the Constitution to be amended.

Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?
What you need to know: Under the Constitution, federal laws are given standing over provincial laws when jurisdictional issues arise.
This change to the Constitution would require approval from the Senate, the House of Commons and seven provinces representing at least half the country’s population.

Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

What you need to know: Advocates for separation say the province needs to get out from under federal taxation and regulation, freeing up wealth and sparking economic development. Federalists say the split would only hurt businesses and saddle landlocked Alberta with debt and the massive cost of delivering formerly federal services.

Smith has framed her other nine other questions on immigration and constitutional reform as a political compromise that could address Alberta’s grievances, gain leverage with Ottawa and avoid dismantling the country.

stories.title: What Albertans need to know about voting in the referendum
stories.summary: Get familiar with the ballot questions ahead of time, which are on the Elections Alberta website. Officials say it will help avoid confusion and delays.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Referendum day in Alberta is on Monday.

The provincial referendum has 10 questions about immigration policy, constitutional reform, and whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a binding, second referendum on quitting the country.

Advance voting locations opened Tuesday and close Saturday night.

Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Here’s what to expect when you go to vote:

How long will it take?

Get familiar with the ballot questions ahead of time, which are on the Elections Alberta website. Officials say it will help avoid confusion and delays.

They say they’re expecting a record turnout of between 80 and 85 per cent of Alberta’s nearly three million electors.

You have as much time as you want to fill in the 10 ballots, but officials estimate it will take most people about two minutes.

You should get a “where to vote” card in the mail ahead of time if you’re registered. Otherwise, visit Elections Alberta’s website to find out where to vote.

You must vote in your electoral division during advance voting or at your assigned location on Monday.

You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.

There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.

Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.

What if I’m not registered to vote?

A voting officer will ask you to sign a declaration that confirms your eligibility — including that you are a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old and that you normally reside in Alberta.

How many ballots are there?

There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none. Your choice.

The ballots go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.

What if I’m still in line when the polls close at 8 p.m.?

Stay in line. Don’t leave. You will be allowed to vote.

How long before I know the results?

By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.

Question 10 — about separation — is to be counted first. Officials say early results are to be released after 8 p.m. Monday, with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.

The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday.

stories.title: Toronto 18 ringleader no longer shows signs of extremism, granted full parole: board
stories.summary: One of the ringleaders of the thwarted Toronto 18 terror plot has been granted full parole after the Parole Board of Canada found he no longer showed "any signs of holding onto extremist beliefs or radical ideologies."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
One of the ringleaders of the thwarted Toronto 18 terror plot has been granted full parole after the Parole Board of Canada found he no longer showed “any signs of holding onto extremist beliefs or radical ideologies.”

Zakaria Amara, who helped recruit members for a group that aimed to storm Parliament Hill and bomb several locations around Toronto, has been on day parole with multiple conditions for four years, and the board upgraded his release after reviewing his case last week.

In a written decision issued Friday, the two-member panel says Amara, 41, undertook a process to deradicalize while incarcerated and has used his day parole “for its intended rehabilitative purpose,” demonstrating “positive change, both in attitude and in behaviour.”

It says he was closely supervised while on day parole and his internet use, friendships and relationships were monitored, with no reported safety concerns or breaches.

The decision, which includes several redactions, says Amara now plans to live in his own home and continue to structure his time around his full-time job, attending a mosque, seeing his family and “appropriate leisure activities.”

He is barred from communicating with anyone involved in criminal activity, including any of the others arrested in the June 2006 anti-terrorist raids, or come into contact with anyone with extremist ideologies, except in his work as a consultant with a specialized program.

He must also continue to participate in counselling and be subject to financial monitoring as well as restrictions on his phone and internet use.

The board’s decision comes two decades after the dismantling of the homegrown plot that shocked the country and shifted public discourse around terrorism.

Amara and an accomplice recruited people for a group based on jihadist ideologies, planning to carry out terrorist acts to demand the withdrawal of Canadian troops from Afghanistan.

The group eventually splintered in two, with Amara taking the helm of a plot focused on building truck bombs targeting the Canadian Security Intelligence Services headquarters, the Toronto Stock Exchange building, and a military base.

He was arrested on the day bomb-making materials were delivered to a warehouse.

Amara pleaded guilty to participating in a terror group with the intention of causing an explosion or explosions that were likely to cause serious bodily harm or death, and was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years. He challenged the sentence but it was upheld on appeal.

The parole board document said his “problematic and extremist ideologies and attitudes” remained during his first few years behind bars, which also included several incidents of misconduct.

His ideology “began to shift” in 2014 and he was eventually transferred to a medium-security institution in 2019, where correctional officers reported he was “respectful, polite and quiet,” the board said.

Amara was granted day parole for three months in 2022 and it was extended several times.

“During the latter part of your federal custody and for the past four years in the community, you have undertaken a process to distance yourself from extremist ideologies and others who share the same views,” the board wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

He is barred from communicating with anyone involved in criminal activity, including any of the others arrested in the June 2006 anti-terrorist raids, or come into contact with anyone with extremist ideologies, except in his work as a consultant with a specialized program.
He must also continue to participate in counselling and be subject to financial monitoring as well as restrictions on his phone and internet use.
The board’s decision comes two decades after the dismantling of the homegrown plot that shocked the country and shifted public discourse around terrorism.
Amara and an accomplice recruited people for a group based on jihadist ideologies, planning to carry out terrorist acts to demand the withdrawal of Canadian troops from Afghanistan.

The group eventually splintered in two, with Amara taking the helm of a plot focused on building truck bombs targeting the Canadian Security Intelligence Services headquarters, the Toronto Stock Exchange building, and a military base.
He was arrested on the day bomb-making materials were delivered to a warehouse.

Amara pleaded guilty to participating in a terror group with the intention of causing an explosion or explosions that were likely to cause serious bodily harm or death, and was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years. He challenged the sentence but it was upheld on appeal.
The parole board document said his “problematic and extremist ideologies and attitudes” remained during his first few years behind bars, which also included several incidents of misconduct.

His ideology “began to shift” in 2014 and he was eventually transferred to a medium-security institution in 2019, where correctional officers reported he was “respectful, polite and quiet,” the board said.
Amara was granted day parole for three months in 2022 and it was extended several times.

“During the latter part of your federal custody and for the past four years in the community, you have undertaken a process to distance yourself from extremist ideologies and others who share the same views,” the board wrote.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.
Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: What time is it? Confusion as Canada’s approach to daylight time shifts
stories.summary: There is more confusion and a reignited debate over the seasonal time change as millions of Canadians get set to turn the clocks back while some provinces scrap the move altogether.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
Ottawa - There is more confusion and a reignited debate over the seasonal time change as millions of Canadians get set to turn the clocks back while some provinces scrap the move altogether.

On Nov. 1, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories will no longer turn the clocks back one hour in favour of remaining on daylight time.

Most of Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada will, although parts of northwestern Ontario including Kenora, won’t so the region can align with neighbouring Manitoba.

“The Canadian time landscape is a real mess right now, I can’t even keep up with it,” said Patricia Lakin-Thomas, a biology professor at York University. “We desperately need some kind of organization to try to come up with something more systematic than this patchwork approach.”

As of Nov. 1, when it is noon in Toronto, it will be 10 a.m. in Vancouver. Alberta will now be only one hour behind most of Ontario.

Some experts argue the semi-annual change can be harmful to your health and that switching to permanent standard time is the way to go.

Lakin-Thomas said that is particularly true when considering the sunrise in Calgary on some mornings this winter won’t be until 9:30 a.m.

“You’re going to find it very hard and you’re going to feel and be essentially jet-lagged,” she said.

At Kaya’s Watch and Clock Shop in Ottawa, Mustafa Kaya uses the semi-annual time change as a reminder to replace the batteries in the dozens of clocks in his store.

“The time change is a good time for me to go over all the clocks and make sure they’re in sync again,” Kaya said. “Keeping it consistent would be huge, especially for a business like us.”

Ontario has said it would end the semi-annual switch, but only if Quebec and New York do so as well.

stories.title: Hitachi announces $479M plan to build transformer insulation factory in London, Ont.
stories.summary: Hitachi Energy, along with the federal and Ontario governments, have announced a $479-million plan to build a new transformer insulation factory as electricity demand is expected to skyrocket.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
London — Hitachi Energy, along with the federal and Ontario governments, have announced a $479-million plan to build a new transformer insulation factory as electricity demand is expected to skyrocket.

The 21,000-square-metre facility in London, Ont., is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

It would be the first in Canada to produce pressboard — a material made from paper pulp that’s key to keeping transformers cool — and the first one Hitachi would establish in the Americas.

The facility is expected to create 100 permanent skilled jobs.

Hitachi is shouldering the bulk of the investment, with the federal and Ontario governments collectively contributing $50 million.

Of that, $20 million is through the federal strategic response fund, $10 million is from Natural Resources Canada and up to $20 million is through the Invest Ontario Fund.

The transition to renewable electricity, industrial developments and a boom in artificial intelligence data centres are driving up demand for transformers and their components, said Bruno Melles, chief executive of Hitachi’s transformers business unit based in Zurich.

“Today we are in a situation where the industry for transformer manufacturing is going at a very high speed, but not all the industrial parts are going at the same speed,” Melles said in an interview ahead of the announcement.

“This is why we want to give a strong message to the market and say, ‘We want to be an integral part of the supply chain resilience and we are going to invest in order to ensure that the market is not going to have any shortage.’”

In May, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada’s new electricity strategy, which aims to double the country’s electricity grid by 2050.

Building new infrastructure has been a key focus for Carney’s government, and several power and transmission projects have been referred to the major projects office for a streamlined review.

“Electricity demand in Canada is growing at an unprecedented pace, something we’ve never seen before,” Carla Vincente, managing director of Hitachi Energy’s Canadian division, said in an interview.

“By ensuring that we have this factory operational by the end of 2028, we will be able to respond to the higher needs and demand for the transformers that are an essential part of anything that we want to do to be able to electrify.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: France to decide next month on extradition of ex-Manitoba law dean in fraud case
stories.summary: Winnipeg - A former law dean at the University of Manitoba wanted on a fraud charge is expected to learn next month if he will be extradited from France.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - A former Manitoba law dean — arrested in France amid allegations he mismanaged hundreds of thousands of dollars to fund a posh lifestyle in Canada — is expected to learn next month if he will be extradited.

A court release said Jonathan Black-Branch, the former dean at the University of Manitoba, is fighting being forced back to Canada to face justice.

stories.summary: Toronto - As Steven Galloway concluded his testimony in his defamation trial in Vancouver, in Toronto, author Margaret Atwood reiterated her stance as a defender of due process in his case.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - As Steven Galloway concluded his testimony in his defamation trial in Vancouver, in Toronto, author Margaret Atwood reiterated her stance as a defender of due process in his case.

Atwood, who was receiving an award at a Journalists for Human Rights event, spoke about her decision to sign an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the University of British Columbia handled the Galloway case.

stories.title: What Albertans need to know about voting in the referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Referendum day in Alberta is on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Referendum day in Alberta is on Monday.

The provincial referendum has 10 questions about immigration policy, constitutional reform, and whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a binding, second referendum on quitting the country.

Advance voting locations opened Tuesday and close Saturday night.

Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Here’s what to expect when you go to vote:

How long will it take?

Get familiar with the ballot questions ahead of time, which are on the Elections Alberta website. Officials say it will help avoid confusion and delays.

They say they’re expecting a record turnout of between 80 and 85 per cent of Alberta’s nearly three million electors.

You have as much time as you want to fill in the 10 ballots, but officials estimate it will take most people about two minutes.

What identification is needed?

You should get a “where to vote” card in the mail ahead of time if you’re registered. Otherwise, visit Elections Alberta’s website to find out where to vote.

You must vote in your electoral division during advance voting or at your assigned location on Monday.

You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.

There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.

Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.

What if I’m not registered to vote?

A voting officer will ask you to sign a declaration that confirms your eligibility — including that you are a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old and that you normally reside in Alberta.

How many ballots are there?

There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none. Your choice.

The ballots go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.

What if I’m still in line when the polls close at 8 p.m.?

Stay in line. Don’t leave. You will be allowed to vote.

How long before I know the results?

By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.

Question 10 — about separation — is to be counted first. Officials say early results are to be released after 8 p.m. Monday, with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.

The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec sovereigntists see fundamental rift with Alberta separatists
stories.summary: In their view, Quebec sovereigntists are motivated to preserve their cultural and linguistic identity, while Alberta separatists are motivated by the economy and political libertarianism
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
With just days before Alberta’s vote on an independence referendum, longtime Quebec sovereigntists are distancing themselves from the western province’s separatists.

Question 10 of 10 on Monday’s referendum ballot asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or if the government should start the legal process to hold a subsequent, binding referendum on separation.

Advance polls opened Tuesday and run until Saturday.

Quebecers may have a sense of déjà vu after voting on a similar question in 1980, when René Lévesque’s Parti Québécois asked whether the province should begin negotiations to leave Confederation. Nearly 60 per cent of Quebec voters were against Lévesque’s proposal.

A second referendum followed in 1995, narrowly won by the “No” side. But ardent sovereigntists see profound differences in the two movements.

Marie-Anne Alepin, president of the Société St-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal, a prominent Quebec nationalist group, believes Alberta is using the threat of separatism as leverage in negotiations with Ottawa. She sees the referendum as a means of pressure rather than a genuine desire to form a country.

“They want a bigger role within Canada and we want to leave,” she said. “They want more control over their oil and gas … we don’t want pipelines.”

But that hasn’t stopped some leaders in the Alberta separatist movement from claiming common cause.

Quebec elected the PQ – which has promised a third independence referendum – to a minority government on Oct. 5, leading figures in the Alberta separatist movement to rally behind premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and declare him a possible ally.

“Quebec rejected the status quo today,” wrote columnist Cory Morgan – a founding member of the Alberta Independence Party in 2001 – on social media after the PQ’s victory. “Alberta can do the same in two weeks by choosing to send a message with Option 2 on Question 10.”

Alberta separatist Jeffrey Rath also took to social media the day after the provincial election, saying that “for the first time in history, Alberta Independence will have the support of the elected government of Quebec.” He also congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and “the country of Quebec.”

The two, along with lawyer Keith Wilson, lamented that Quebec’s quest for independence is seen as legitimate while they say Alberta separatists are sneered at.

During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate. Rath said he met with the PQ leader during that visit.

But while they believe in the democratic process of a referendum, many Quebec sovereigntists do not identify with the Alberta separatists.

Former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée did not mince words when asked about Monday’s referendum.

“It’s mostly a waste because defeat is certain,” he said. “There’s really nothing much to gain from watching the Alberta independence movement, except maybe negative lessons.”

It’s a feeling shared by other sovereigntists.

Louise Harel, who was a PQ minister during Quebec’s 1995 sovereignty referendum and later served as interim leader of the party, agrees with Lisée. Both say the Quebec and Alberta sovereigntist movements are fundamentally different.

In their view, Quebec sovereigntists are motivated to preserve their cultural and linguistic identity, while Alberta separatists are motivated by the economy and political libertarianism. They also see a desire for Alberta to get closer to the United States, while Quebecers are wary of talk of assimilation.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she is against secession, while PQ leaders have openly called for sovereignty.

“In Quebec, the idea is to give a unique historical nation in North America, which … has valiantly resisted assimilation, the powers it needs to survive in a globalized world,” said Harel. “But there is no such issue of identity or culture in Alberta.”

While sovereigntist Quebecers also feel economically disadvantaged within Canada, Lisée said, the sentiment isn’t at the core of the movement. He also stressed that Quebec’s sovereigntist parties have historically been social-democrat, while the movement in Alberta seems tied to conservatism.

Daniel Turp, a Université de Montréal law professor who represented both the Bloc Québécois and the PQ, sees differences in the referendum process itself. Quebec’s two independence referendums included a single question on sovereignty.

As a result, there were mass mobilizations from both federalist and sovereigntist factions for weeks.

Public support for independence also varies widely between the two provinces.

On the eve of the 1995 referendum, public opinion was split evenly in the polls. Three days before Quebecers cast their ballots, Canadians from across the country made their way to Montreal to urge them to vote against independence.

Poll aggregator 338Canada shows less than 25 per cent support for Alberta to leave Canada as of Oct. 11.

“There hasn’t been a love-in in Alberta yet,” Turp said. “Maybe we’re not as worried because the polls show the option to remain will win.”

More than 90 per cent of registered voters cast a ballot in the 1995 referendum, which federalists won with 50.58 per cent of the vote.

“That’s the kind of voter turnout you see in countries where voting is mandatory,” said Harel. “I would be extremely surprised if voter turnout in the Alberta referendum were the same.”

But the sovereigntists do not reject the Alberta separatist movement entirely. All four said they sympathize with the desire for autonomy and self-determination.

“If Alberta were to vote yes, and then Ottawa would say, ‘well, you can’t leave,’ we will be on the side of Alberta,” said Lisée.

Harel added that while she does not see ideological similarities between separatists in Quebec and Alberta, the democratic process must be respected. She said that the Alberta referendum can give legitimacy to the one promised by the PQ.

Asked if they worry that a no vote on Monday could affect the PQ’s promised referendum, all four said no.

Alepin believes the two movements are too different for Albertans to influence Quebecers’ appetite for sovereignty.

Meanwhile, Lisée predicts that “the defeat of the yes side in Alberta will be a negative but very insignificant factor in [Quebec’s] referendum debate.”

If Alberta stays within Canada, Turp believes the province may be inspired by Quebec’s approach to negotiating more autonomy with Ottawa.

“And then they can organize a second referendum, like we did,” he added.
